title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Below is a performance-oriented, implementation-ready algorithm tailored to your exact data model and constraints, written so you can hand it directly to a Rust-focused coding agent. The emphasis is on minimal passes over memory, local refinement only, and strict geometric correctness.
I will assume:

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 0 — Parameters (critical for speed & robustness)
SEARCH_RADIUS_VOX = 6      // around each window
DILATION_STEPS    = 2      // interface thickness
MIN_RADIUS_EPS    = 1e-4

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
section: Step 1 — Iterate only over windows to refine

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 2 — Build local bounding box
Purpose: minimize memory touch
center = window.pos

bbox = cube(center, SEARCH_RADIUS_VOX)
clamp bbox to padded grid bounds

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 3 — Build region mask (binary)
Only voxels belonging to the two regions
mask[x] = (
    labels[x] == region_i ||
    labels[x] == region_j
)
Store as:

Vec<u8> or bitmask
Local indexing relative to bbox

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
section: Step 4 — Extract connected component containing window
text:
Step 4 — Extract connected component containing window
Fast flood-fill (stack-based DFS or BFS)
component = empty list
queue = [window.pos]

while queue not empty:
    v = pop
    if visited[v] continue
    mark visited
    add v to component

    for each 6-connected neighbor n:
        if mask[n] == true:
            push n
Key:

Connectivity constrained to the two regions
Automatically respects periodic padding

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 5 — Distance-field minimum search (throat candidates)
Scan only component voxels:
min_radius = +∞
candidates = []

for v in component:
    r = dgrid[v]
    if r < min_radius - eps:
        min_radius = r
        candidates = [v]
    else if abs(r - min_radius) < eps:
        candidates.push(v)

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 6 — Cluster minima (separate multiple throats)
Why: discretization often produces plateaus
clusters = connected_components(candidates)
6-connected is sufficient.

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
section: Step 7 — Validate each cluster as a true throat
text:
Step 7 — Validate each cluster as a true throat
For each cluster:

7.1 — Compute representative point

centroid or lowest-index voxel



7.2 — Region adjacency test
Ensure the inscribed sphere intersects both regions:
sample points on sphere surface:
    for direction in ±x, ±y, ±z:
        p = center + direction * radius
        label(p) must include region_i AND region_j (across directions)
Reject if not satisfied.

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 8 — Select best throat
Selection rule (recommended):

Smallest radius
Tie-breaker: closest to original window location

best_cluster = argmin(radius, distance_to_old_window)

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 9 — Sub-voxel refinement (optional but cheap)
Local quadratic fit:

Use 3×3×3 stencil
Fit paraboloid to d(x)
Solve for minimum

If skipped, voxel center is acceptable.

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 10 — Update window
window.pos    = refined_position
window.radius = refined_radius

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Step 11 — Post-pass (optional)
If multiple windows exist per connection:

Reject overlapping spheres
Keep smallest radius first

title: Design goal (fastest approach)
text:
Final note
This algorithm is geometry-first, topology-constrained, which is exactly what your problem requires. It is also the fastest possible approach given your current inputs because it:

avoids full-interface scans,
avoids medial-axis construction,
and works entirely in local neighborhoods.

If you want, I can also:

convert this into Rust-like pseudocode
or define unit tests to validate correctness under periodic wrapping.

title: Releases and citing mofography
text:
Cite a released tag YYYY.MM.DD.N from the mofography releases page, not an arbitrary checkout of master. For reproducibility, record the tag name and the full git commit hash shown on that release.




Tags look like 2026.10.09.1 (year, month, day, same-day increment).
Second release on the same calendar day: 2026.10.09.2, and so on.
Tags are annotated git tags on the commit you want others to reproduce.
versioneer (setup.cfg, PEP 440) derives mofography.__version__ from the nearest tag.





Merge or commit everything that should be in the release; working tree clean (git status shows no modifications you care about).
Run tests you rely on for the paper or milestone.
Update CITATION.cff: set version to the new tag string (e.g. 2026.10.09.1).
Commit the CITATION.cff bump (if not already on the release commit).
Create an annotated tag on that commit:
git tag -a 2026.10.09.1 -m "mofography 2026.10.09.1 — <short reason>"
Push the commit and tag to the canonical remote:
git push org master
git push org 2026.10.09.1
Open a GitHub Release from the tag; paste a short note (paper, breaking changes, install hint).
Verify from a clean checkout at the tag:
git checkout 2026.10.09.1
python -c "import mofography as m; print(m.__version__, m.__git_revision__)"
Expect __version__ to match the tag (not 0+untagged… or .dirty).





Software name: mofography
Version: tag string, e.g. 2026.10.09.1
URL: https://github.com/mofography/mofography
Commit: full hash from the release (or mofography.__git_revision__ at that tag)
Optional: copy the metadata block from CITATION.cff after updating version




Use the tag and commit from the release you actually ran, not master. Below uses release 2026.10.09.1 (commit f873e50) as a template—swap version/hash when citing a newer release.



Pore segmentation, graph construction, and visualization were performed with mofography version 2026.10.09.1 (Gopalan; https://github.com/mofography/mofography; release tag 2026.10.09.1, commit f873e50effd0bbe7d5a00ec3517394f96766a91b).





mofography v2026.10.09.1 — https://github.com/mofography/mofography/releases/tag/2026.10.09.1





Open-source software: We use mofography (v2026.10.09.1), a Python package for pore analysis in nanoporous materials, obtained from the canonical repository https://github.com/mofography/mofography at release tag 2026.10.09.1 (commit f873e50). Interactive 3D outputs are generated with the project web application; archived analysis uses the tagged source code only.




\bibitem{gopalan2026mofography}
A.~Gopalan,
\textit{mofography} (version 2026.10.09.1),
\url{https://github.com/mofography/mofography},
release tag 2026.10.09.1, commit f873e50effd0bbe7d5a00ec3517394f96766a91b,
2026.
After Zenodo is enabled, add doi = {...} to that entry and cite the version DOI in addition to (or instead of) the raw GitHub URL, per journal rules.



Collaborators do not need to edit CITATION.cff to write a paper. It is the machine-readable record of the same metadata:

At a release: https://github.com/mofography/mofography/blob/2026.10.09.1/CITATION.cff

GitHub shows a “Cite this repository” widget on the repo home when CITATION.cff is on the default branch.

To generate BibTeX from the file locally: Citation File Format tools or cffconvert -i CITATION.cff -f bibtex (if cffconvert is installed).




The repo does not ship large Three.js HTML snapshots under examples/viz_outputs/ (they go stale quickly). Use the mofography web app (local or public demo on Hugging Face) to build and download current HTML, or regenerate with the examples/gen_*_threejs.py scripts when you need a file on disk.



Until mofography/mofography is public: cite GitHub release tag + commit (e.g. 2026.10.09.1, f873e50). That is enough for the manuscript and for collaborators.
After arXiv (or when you intentionally open the org repo): archive releases on Zenodo so journals can cite a DOI. Zenodo does not replace tagging; it snapshots each GitHub Release you already cut.



Make https://github.com/mofography/mofography public (only when you are ready).
Log in to zenodo.org with GitHub; grant access if prompted.
Zenodo → Account → GitHub → enable sync → turn on repository mofography/mofography.
For release 2026.10.09.1 (or the release tied to the paper): either create a new GitHub Release (already done) or use Zenodo’s “Create DOI” for that release if the integration offers a retry.
Open the new Zenodo deposit → review title, authors, license (BSD-3-Clause), version string → Publish.
Copy the version DOI (and note the concept DOI for “all versions of mofography”).
Add the version DOI to the paper SI / software note; optionally add doi: to CITATION.cff on a future release tag.
Tell collaborators: “Paper code = mofography 2026.10.09.1; archival DOI = …”





Your paper: cite the version you used (2026.10.09.1) and, once available, that version’s Zenodo DOI.
Future users: cite their release tag (and DOI for that tag). Zenodo’s concept DOI points at the software family; the version DOI is what reproducibility needs.

References: GitHub–Zenodo, Zenodo GitHub guide.

title: Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
text:
Detecting pore interconnectivity and accessibility using probe molecules




Winding Number Method: - Foster, M.P., et al. (2020). “Percolation analysis of disorder in porous media using winding numbers.” Scientific Reports, 80(11), 6425-6432.
@article{foster2020percolation,
  title={Percolation analysis of disorder in porous media using winding numbers},
  author={Foster, M. P. and others},
  journal={Scientific Reports},
  volume={80},
  number={11},
  pages={6425--6432},
  year={2020}
}






Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) is the maximum probe size at which a spherical molecule can pass through a porous material from one side of the unit cell to the opposite side.
Percolation refers to whether there exists a continuous path through the pore network from one side of the material to the opposite side.



MOFography computes three important pore diameter metrics:

Largest Cavity Diameter (LCD):

The diameter of the largest spherical cavity in the material
Represents the maximum void space available
Simply: 2 × max(distance_grid)

Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD):

The largest spherical probe that can traverse the material
Limited by the narrowest windows along percolating paths
Determined by testing percolation at different probe sizes

Directional Free Sphere Diameter (DFSD):

The largest sphere that can pass through percolating regions only
Considers only regions that are part of percolating clusters at the PLD
Always ≤ LCD


Key relationships:
PLD ≤ DFSD ≤ LCD




Transport Properties 📊

PLD determines what molecules can diffuse through material
Percolation predicts if diffusion is possible
Critical for gas storage, separation, catalysis

Accessibility Analysis 🔑

Not all pores are accessible to all probe sizes
Some pockets may only allow small molecules
Understanding size distribution of accessible pores
Identifying pore bottlenecks

Disorder Characterization 🔬

Percolation behavior relates to material disorder
Winding numbers quantify topological complexity
Distinguish ordered vs disordered materials

Graph-Based Analysis 🕸️

Works on pore graphs (not grids)
Much faster than voxel-based methods
Accounts for periodic boundary conditions
Provides accurate characterization

Materials Screening 🎚️

Compare different materials systematically
Identify candidate materials for specific applications
Optimize pore architecture design







This is an INTERMEDIATE tutorial, not a beginner guide!
✅ What this tutorial covers: - Computing LCD, PLD, and DFSD using the winding percolation method - Computing percolation history across probe sizes - Understanding connected components in periodic pore graphs - Interpreting PLD, LCD, and DFSD results - Visualizing percolating clusters at different probe sizes
❌ What this tutorial does NOT cover: - Basic periodic segmentation - see Periodic Segmentation Quick Start - Distance grid computation - see Distance Grid Tutorial - Pore graph construction basics - see Pore Graph Tutorial - Surface area and void volume calculations - Energy-based percolation - Advanced clustering algorithms
🔗 Prerequisites: 1. Complete Periodic Segmentation Quick Start 2. Complete Distance Grid Tutorial 3. Understand pore graph representation (pores as nodes, windows as edges) 4. Basic understanding of periodic boundary conditions 5. MOFography installed with all modules




Load Structure
    ↓
Generate Distance Grid
    ↓
Run Periodic Segmentation → Get pore graph
    ↓
Compute Percolation History → Get PLD
    ↓
Compute LCD, PLD, DFSD
    ↓
Visualize Percolating Clusters




import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Setup paths
repo_root = Path('/path/to/mofography')
path_to_cif = repo_root / 'examples' / 'TestCIFs' / 'NU-1000_S1.cif'
What is this? - Importing all necessary libraries - Configuring paths for reproducibility




Let’s compute all three pore diameter metrics (LCD, PLD, DFSD) in one go:
# Load structure
mat_atoms = read(str(path_to_cif))
print(f"✅ Loaded structure: {mat_atoms.get_chemical_formula()}")

# Define parameters
kwargs = dict(
    spacing=0.5,              # Grid spacing (Angstroms)
    mask_thickness=0.05,       # Void space threshold
    h=0.2,                    # Smoothing parameter
    threshold_abs=1.5,        # Absolute threshold for segmentation
    minimum_window_separation=1.5,
    wall_thickness=0.08,
    extra_padding=5.0,
)

# Compute LCD, PLD, DFSD in one call
lcd, pld, dfsd, results = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(
    mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
    kwargs=kwargs
)

print(f"\n✅ Pore diameters computed!")
print(f"   LCD (Largest Cavity Diameter): {lcd:.2f} Å")
print(f"   PLD (Pore Limiting Diameter): {pld:.2f} Å")
print(f"   DFSD (Directional Free Sphere Diameter): {dfsd:.2f} Å")
What just happened? - get_pore_dia_mgr_winding() computed the complete workflow - LCD: Maximum distance in the grid × 2 - PLD: Maximum probe radius that percolates × 2 - DFSD: Maximum distance in percolating regions only × 2 - results: Dictionary containing segmentation outputs, percolation history, and cluster information
Understanding the metrics:








Metric
Definition
Physical Meaning




LCD
2 × max(distance_grid)
Largest spherical cavity anywhere


PLD
2 × max_percolating_radius
Largest sphere that can traverse the material


DFSD
2 × max(distance in percolating regions)
Largest cavity accessible via percolating paths







The percolation history shows how percolation changes as we test different probe sizes:
# Get detailed percolation history
percolation_history, pld_locations, final_clusters = mgr.compute_percolation_history_winding(
    results=results,
    step=0.1,  # Probe size step size (Angstroms)
    min_threshold=kwargs['mask_thickness'],
)

print(f"\n✅ Percolation history computed!")
print(f"   Number of probe sizes tested: {len(percolation_history)}")

# Show first few and last entries
print(f"\nFirst 3 entries (small probes):")
for i, (threshold, axis_clusters) in enumerate(percolation_history[:3]):
    percolating_axes = [ax for ax, clusters in axis_clusters.items() if clusters]
    print(f"  {threshold:.2f} Å: Percolating in {percolating_axes}")

print(f"\nLast 3 entries (large probes):")
for i, (threshold, axis_clusters) in enumerate(percolation_history[-3:]):
    percolating_axes = [ax for ax, clusters in axis_clusters.items() if clusters]
    print(f"  {threshold:.2f} Å: Percolating in {percolating_axes}")

print(f"\nFinal PLD threshold: {percolation_history[-1][0]:.2f} Å")
Understanding the output:
percolation_history is a list of tuples, where each tuple contains: 1. Probe radius (in Ångstroms) 2. axis_clusters: Dictionary with keys ‘x’, ‘y’, ‘z’ mapping to lists of clusters 3. Each cluster is a list of region labels
Key patterns to observe: - At small probe sizes: All regions accessible, single large cluster per axis - As probe size increases: Windows close, clusters split and shrink - At PLD: Last probe size where any percolation exists




Let’s examine the final percolating clusters in detail:
# Get final percolation status
final_threshold, final_axis_clusters = percolation_history[-1]

print(f"\n=== Final Percolating Clusters (at {final_threshold:.2f} Å) ===")

for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']:
    clusters = final_axis_clusters[axis]
    print(f"\n{axis.upper()}-axis:")
    if clusters:
        print(f"  Number of percolating clusters: {len(clusters)}")
        for i, cluster_regions in enumerate(clusters, 1):
            print(f"    Cluster {i}: {len(cluster_regions)} regions")
            print(f"      Region labels: {cluster_regions}")
    else:
        print(f"  No percolation")

# Check full percolation
x_perc = len(final_axis_clusters['x']) > 0
y_perc = len(final_axis_clusters['y']) > 0
z_perc = len(final_axis_clusters['z']) > 0

print(f"\n=== Percolation Summary ===")
print(f"X-axis: {'✅ Percolating' if x_perc else '❌ Not percolating'}")
print(f"Y-axis: {'✅ Percolating' if y_perc else '❌ Not percolating'}")
print(f"Z-axis: {'✅ Percolating' if z_perc else '❌ Not percolating'}")

if x_perc and y_perc and z_perc:
    print(f"\n✅ Material is FULLY PERCOLATING in all directions!")
    print(f"   PLD = {pld:.2f} Å")
else:
    print(f"\n⚠️ Material is NOT fully percolating")
Key insight: - Fully percolating materials (all 3 axes) allow molecular transport from any direction - Partially percolating materials have restricted access (1D or 2D channels) - Non-percolating materials have isolated pores with no end-to-end paths




Now let’s visualize the percolating clusters in 3D, exactly as shown in the notebook:
# First, let's look at what the percolating cluster metadata contains
print("\nFinal cluster metadata:")
for cluster_id, cluster_data in final_clusters.items():
    print(f"\nCluster {cluster_id}:")
    print(f"  Regions: {cluster_data['regions']}")
    print(f"  Nodes: {cluster_data['nodes']}")
    print(f"  Percolating axes: {cluster_data['axes']}")

# Prepare visualization data
dgrid = results['dgrid']
regions = results['regions']
maxima = results['maxima']

# Build the pore graph for visualization
from mofography.winding_percolation import make_directed_graph_from_segmentation_results
G = make_directed_graph_from_segmentation_results(results)

# Plot the pore graph (RAG)
rag_trace = mgr.plot_rag(G, name='Pore Graph')

# Plot percolated clusters
percolated_cluster_meshes = mgr.plot_percolated_cluster_meshes(
    percolation_history=percolation_history,
    dgrid=dgrid,
    regions=regions,
    mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
    isovalue=np.min([pld/2 - 0.25, 1.75]),
    stylize=True,
    probe_radius=percolation_history[-1][0]
)

# Plot unit cell, maxima, and PLD locations
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)
maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima(dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms, show_spheres=False, sphere_opacity=0.85)
pld_traces = mgr.plot_pld_locations(dgrid, results['pld_locations'], mat_atoms,
                                     show_spheres=False, sphere_opacity=0.85,
                                     marker_size=10, marker_color='limegreen')

# Create the combined figure
fig = go.Figure(data=[cell_trace, rag_trace, maxima_trace, pld_traces] + percolated_cluster_meshes,
                layout=mgr.epic_layout)
fig.show(renderer='png')
What you’re seeing: - Each colored region represents a percolating cluster - Different colors = different clusters - The probe can pass through any connected region of the same color - Gray regions are inaccessible at this probe size - Green dots mark PLD locations (where distance equals PLD) - The pore graph shows the network structure



Percolating clusters visualization


Example: Percolating clusters shown at the PLD threshold. This matches the visualization from pld_and_percolation.ipynb.




Let’s visualize how percolation changes at different probe sizes:
# Select 3 representative probe sizes
probe_indices = [0, len(percolation_history)//2, len(percolation_history)-1]

for idx in probe_indices:
    threshold, axis_clusters = percolation_history[idx]

    print(f"\n=== Probe size: {threshold:.2f} Å ===")

    # Count total percolating regions
    total_regions = 0
    for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']:
        n_clusters = len(axis_clusters[axis])
        n_regions = sum(len(c) for c in axis_clusters[axis])
        total_regions += n_regions
        print(f"  {axis}-axis: {n_clusters} clusters, {n_regions} regions")

    # Visualize
    cluster_traces = mgr.plot_percolated_cluster_meshes(
        percolation_history=percolation_history,
        dgrid=dgrid,
        regions=regions,
        mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
        isovalue=threshold + 0.5,
        probe_radius=threshold,
        stylize_cluster=True,
    )

    fig = go.Figure(
        data=[mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)] + cluster_traces,
        layout=mgr.epic_layout
    )
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Percolation at {threshold:.2f} Å probe radius")
    fig.show()
What to observe: 1. Small probe: Most regions connected, large percolating clusters 2. Medium probe: Some windows closed, smaller clusters 3. PLD probe: Only the narrowest accessible paths remain




The get_pore_dia_mgr_winding() function is designed for high-throughput screening. For example, you can compare pore diameters across hundreds of materials:
# Example workflow for comparing multiple materials
materials = ['NU-1000', 'IRMOF-1', 'HKUST-1']

results_list = []
for name in materials:
    path_to_cif = repo_root / 'examples' / 'TestCIFs' / f'{name}.cif'
    mat_atoms = read(str(path_to_cif))

    # Compute all three metrics
    lcd, pld, dfsd, _ = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(

title: Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
text:
Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) is the maximum probe size at which a spherical molecule can pass through a porous material from one side of the unit cell to the opposite side.
Percolation refers to whether there exists a continuous path through the pore network from one side of the material to the opposite side.



MOFography computes three important pore diameter metrics:

Largest Cavity Diameter (LCD):

The diameter of the largest spherical cavity in the material
Represents the maximum void space available
Simply: 2 × max(distance_grid)

Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD):

The largest spherical probe that can traverse the material
Limited by the narrowest windows along percolating paths
Determined by testing percolation at different probe sizes

Directional Free Sphere Diameter (DFSD):

The largest sphere that can pass through percolating regions only
Considers only regions that are part of percolating clusters at the PLD
Always ≤ LCD


Key relationships:
PLD ≤ DFSD ≤ LCD




Transport Properties 📊

PLD determines what molecules can diffuse through material
Percolation predicts if diffusion is possible
Critical for gas storage, separation, catalysis

Accessibility Analysis 🔑

Not all pores are accessible to all probe sizes
Some pockets may only allow small molecules
Understanding size distribution of accessible pores
Identifying pore bottlenecks

Disorder Characterization 🔬

Percolation behavior relates to material disorder
Winding numbers quantify topological complexity
Distinguish ordered vs disordered materials

Graph-Based Analysis 🕸️

Works on pore graphs (not grids)
Much faster than voxel-based methods
Accounts for periodic boundary conditions
Provides accurate characterization

Materials Screening 🎚️

Compare different materials systematically
Identify candidate materials for specific applications
Optimize pore architecture design

import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Setup paths
repo_root = Path('/path/to/mofography')
path_to_cif = repo_root / 'examples' / 'TestCIFs' / 'NU-1000_S1.cif'
What is this? - Importing all necessary libraries - Configuring paths for reproducibility

title: Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
text:
Let’s compute all three pore diameter metrics (LCD, PLD, DFSD) in one go:
# Load structure
mat_atoms = read(str(path_to_cif))
print(f"✅ Loaded structure: {mat_atoms.get_chemical_formula()}")

# Define parameters
kwargs = dict(
    spacing=0.5,              # Grid spacing (Angstroms)
    mask_thickness=0.05,       # Void space threshold
    h=0.2,                    # Smoothing parameter
    threshold_abs=1.5,        # Absolute threshold for segmentation
    minimum_window_separation=1.5,
    wall_thickness=0.08,
    extra_padding=5.0,
)

# Compute LCD, PLD, DFSD in one call
lcd, pld, dfsd, results = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(
    mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
    kwargs=kwargs
)

print(f"\n✅ Pore diameters computed!")
print(f"   LCD (Largest Cavity Diameter): {lcd:.2f} Å")
print(f"   PLD (Pore Limiting Diameter): {pld:.2f} Å")
print(f"   DFSD (Directional Free Sphere Diameter): {dfsd:.2f} Å")
What just happened? - get_pore_dia_mgr_winding() computed the complete workflow - LCD: Maximum distance in the grid × 2 - PLD: Maximum probe radius that percolates × 2 - DFSD: Maximum distance in percolating regions only × 2 - results: Dictionary containing segmentation outputs, percolation history, and cluster information
Understanding the metrics:








Metric
Definition
Physical Meaning




LCD
2 × max(distance_grid)
Largest spherical cavity anywhere


PLD
2 × max_percolating_radius
Largest sphere that can traverse the material


DFSD
2 × max(distance in percolating regions)
Largest cavity accessible via percolating paths

title: Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
text:
The percolation history shows how percolation changes as we test different probe sizes:
# Get detailed percolation history
percolation_history, pld_locations, final_clusters = mgr.compute_percolation_history_winding(
    results=results,
    step=0.1,  # Probe size step size (Angstroms)
    min_threshold=kwargs['mask_thickness'],
)

print(f"\n✅ Percolation history computed!")
print(f"   Number of probe sizes tested: {len(percolation_history)}")

# Show first few and last entries
print(f"\nFirst 3 entries (small probes):")
for i, (threshold, axis_clusters) in enumerate(percolation_history[:3]):
    percolating_axes = [ax for ax, clusters in axis_clusters.items() if clusters]
    print(f"  {threshold:.2f} Å: Percolating in {percolating_axes}")

print(f"\nLast 3 entries (large probes):")
for i, (threshold, axis_clusters) in enumerate(percolation_history[-3:]):
    percolating_axes = [ax for ax, clusters in axis_clusters.items() if clusters]
    print(f"  {threshold:.2f} Å: Percolating in {percolating_axes}")

print(f"\nFinal PLD threshold: {percolation_history[-1][0]:.2f} Å")
Understanding the output:
percolation_history is a list of tuples, where each tuple contains: 1. Probe radius (in Ångstroms) 2. axis_clusters: Dictionary with keys ‘x’, ‘y’, ‘z’ mapping to lists of clusters 3. Each cluster is a list of region labels
Key patterns to observe: - At small probe sizes: All regions accessible, single large cluster per axis - As probe size increases: Windows close, clusters split and shrink - At PLD: Last probe size where any percolation exists

title: Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
text:
Let’s examine the final percolating clusters in detail:
# Get final percolation status
final_threshold, final_axis_clusters = percolation_history[-1]

print(f"\n=== Final Percolating Clusters (at {final_threshold:.2f} Å) ===")

for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']:
    clusters = final_axis_clusters[axis]
    print(f"\n{axis.upper()}-axis:")
    if clusters:
        print(f"  Number of percolating clusters: {len(clusters)}")
        for i, cluster_regions in enumerate(clusters, 1):
            print(f"    Cluster {i}: {len(cluster_regions)} regions")
            print(f"      Region labels: {cluster_regions}")
    else:
        print(f"  No percolation")

# Check full percolation
x_perc = len(final_axis_clusters['x']) > 0
y_perc = len(final_axis_clusters['y']) > 0
z_perc = len(final_axis_clusters['z']) > 0

print(f"\n=== Percolation Summary ===")
print(f"X-axis: {'✅ Percolating' if x_perc else '❌ Not percolating'}")
print(f"Y-axis: {'✅ Percolating' if y_perc else '❌ Not percolating'}")
print(f"Z-axis: {'✅ Percolating' if z_perc else '❌ Not percolating'}")

if x_perc and y_perc and z_perc:
    print(f"\n✅ Material is FULLY PERCOLATING in all directions!")
    print(f"   PLD = {pld:.2f} Å")
else:
    print(f"\n⚠️ Material is NOT fully percolating")
Key insight: - Fully percolating materials (all 3 axes) allow molecular transport from any direction - Partially percolating materials have restricted access (1D or 2D channels) - Non-percolating materials have isolated pores with no end-to-end paths

title: Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
text:
Now let’s visualize the percolating clusters in 3D, exactly as shown in the notebook:
# First, let's look at what the percolating cluster metadata contains
print("\nFinal cluster metadata:")
for cluster_id, cluster_data in final_clusters.items():
    print(f"\nCluster {cluster_id}:")
    print(f"  Regions: {cluster_data['regions']}")
    print(f"  Nodes: {cluster_data['nodes']}")
    print(f"  Percolating axes: {cluster_data['axes']}")

# Prepare visualization data
dgrid = results['dgrid']
regions = results['regions']
maxima = results['maxima']

# Build the pore graph for visualization
from mofography.winding_percolation import make_directed_graph_from_segmentation_results
G = make_directed_graph_from_segmentation_results(results)

# Plot the pore graph (RAG)
rag_trace = mgr.plot_rag(G, name='Pore Graph')

# Plot percolated clusters
percolated_cluster_meshes = mgr.plot_percolated_cluster_meshes(
    percolation_history=percolation_history,
    dgrid=dgrid,
    regions=regions,
    mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
    isovalue=np.min([pld/2 - 0.25, 1.75]),
    stylize=True,
    probe_radius=percolation_history[-1][0]
)

# Plot unit cell, maxima, and PLD locations
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)
maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima(dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms, show_spheres=False, sphere_opacity=0.85)
pld_traces = mgr.plot_pld_locations(dgrid, results['pld_locations'], mat_atoms,
                                     show_spheres=False, sphere_opacity=0.85,
                                     marker_size=10, marker_color='limegreen')

# Create the combined figure
fig = go.Figure(data=[cell_trace, rag_trace, maxima_trace, pld_traces] + percolated_cluster_meshes,
                layout=mgr.epic_layout)
fig.show(renderer='png')
What you’re seeing: - Each colored region represents a percolating cluster - Different colors = different clusters - The probe can pass through any connected region of the same color - Gray regions are inaccessible at this probe size - Green dots mark PLD locations (where distance equals PLD) - The pore graph shows the network structure



Percolating clusters visualization


Example: Percolating clusters shown at the PLD threshold. This matches the visualization from pld_and_percolation.ipynb.

title: Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) and Percolation
text:
Let’s visualize how percolation changes at different probe sizes:
# Select 3 representative probe sizes
probe_indices = [0, len(percolation_history)//2, len(percolation_history)-1]

for idx in probe_indices:
    threshold, axis_clusters = percolation_history[idx]

    print(f"\n=== Probe size: {threshold:.2f} Å ===")

    # Count total percolating regions
    total_regions = 0
    for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']:
        n_clusters = len(axis_clusters[axis])
        n_regions = sum(len(c) for c in axis_clusters[axis])
        total_regions += n_regions
        print(f"  {axis}-axis: {n_clusters} clusters, {n_regions} regions")

    # Visualize
    cluster_traces = mgr.plot_percolated_cluster_meshes(
        percolation_history=percolation_history,
        dgrid=dgrid,
        regions=regions,
        mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
        isovalue=threshold + 0.5,
        probe_radius=threshold,
        stylize_cluster=True,
    )

    fig = go.Figure(
        data=[mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)] + cluster_traces,
        layout=mgr.epic_layout
    )
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Percolation at {threshold:.2f} Å probe radius")
    fig.show()
What to observe: 1. Small probe: Most regions connected, large percolating clusters 2. Medium probe: Some windows closed, smaller clusters 3. PLD probe: Only the narrowest accessible paths remain

title: 🌟 Periodic Segmentation Quick Start
text:
A beginner-friendly introduction to analyzing pore networks in crystalline nanoporous materials using MOFography




MOFography is a powerful Python package for analyzing pore networks in crystalline materials like MOFs, COFs, and zeolites.
📖 Full Paper: MOFography: Decoupling Long-Range and Short-Range Influences in Nanoporous Materials via Graph-Based Pore Network Analysis (Coming soon!)
@article{mofography2024,
  title={MOFography: Decoupling Long-Range and Short-Range Influences in Nanoporous Materials via Graph-Based Pore Network Analysis},
  author={[Author names]},
  journal={ChemRxiv},
  year={2024},
  doi={https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-xxxxx}
}




At its core, MOFography breaks down the complex cavities of nanoporous materials into manageable, convex segments centered around local maxima in the distance field. By carefully accounting for periodic boundary conditions (PBC), it constructs a pore graph (also called a Region Adjacency Graph or RAG) that represents the pore network as an interconnected network of pockets.


Traditional textural properties (surface area, pore volume, pore size distribution) provide valuable bulk insights but cannot capture the spatial relationships between pores. MOFography’s graph-based approach:

Decouples Influences 🔀

Short-range: Local pore geometry (size, shape, chemistry)
Long-range: How pores connect and arrange throughout the material

Flexible & Compact 📦

Graphs are much more compact than 3D grids
Easy to manipulate, query, and analyze
Perfect for network theory algorithms

ML-Ready 🤖

Natural input for graph neural networks (GNNs)
Features can be extracted at node, edge, or graph level
Enables transfer learning across materials

Physically Interpretable 🧠

Each node = a real pore you can visualize
Each edge = a real window for molecular transport
Graph properties map to material behavior







This is a QUICK START tutorial, not a comprehensive guide!
✅ What this tutorial covers: - The basic periodic segmentation workflow - How to get started quickly with your own material - Important parameters and what they mean - Key outputs and how to interpret them - Basic visualization using Plotly
❌ What this tutorial does NOT cover: - Detailed algorithmic nuances of each step - Advanced parameter tuning strategies - All available outputs and their uses - Advanced analysis (percolation, path finding, ML applications) - Performance optimization tricks
🔗 For deeper understanding, we strongly recommend going through the series of Basic and Advanced tutorials listed in the README. Each tutorial focuses on specific aspects in detail.




Before we dive into the new workflow, it’s worth mentioning the legacy approach that MOFography used to use:
The Old Way (Legacy): 1. Compute distance grid → Find local maxima → Regular watershed segmentation 2. Get split pores at unit cell boundaries 3. Use apply_pbc() to manually merge periodic images 4. Compute connections separately
Problems with the old approach: - ❌ Manual post-processing required - ❌ Error-prone (easy to miss merges) - ❌ Slower (multiple separate steps) - ❌ Hard to maintain consistent indexing
The New Way (Current): - ✅ One function call: do_periodic_segmentation_rust() - ✅ Handles PBC automatically from the start - ✅ 5-20x faster with Rust backend - ✅ Returns all outputs with consistent indexing
📜 Legacy tutorials (for reference/educational purposes): - PBC considerations - How the old manual merging worked - Region Segmentation - Segmentation methods - Region Adjacency Graph - Working with pore graphs - Connections and Windows - Window detection
These are kept for educational value and for users maintaining legacy code, but new projects should use the periodic segmentation workflow covered in this tutorial.




If you’re working with crystalline nanoporous materials, you’ve encountered a fundamental problem:
Pores don’t respect unit cell boundaries! 😤
Imagine a cubic unit cell with a large pore at each corner. When you segment it, you get 8 separate pore regions at the 8 corners. But wait - these are all actually the same pore, just cut off by the arbitrary boundaries we drew around the unit cell!



Split regions at boundaries


Without PBC: The same pore appears as 8 separate regions at the corners. This is not ideal for the purposes of averaging properties!
Periodic segmentation solves this by expanding the grid to “see” across periodic boundaries, identifying which regions belong together, and merging them correctly.



Merged regions with PBC


With PBC: Regions are correctly merged. The 8 corner pieces are recognized as one pore. Same with opposing faces, sets of 4 parallel edges along each direction etc. you get the idea :) 




By the end of this tutorial, you’ll be able to:

✅ Load a crystalline structure (CIF file)
✅ Compute a distance grid (how far each point is from the nearest atom)
✅ Run periodic segmentation to identify pores and their connections
✅ Trim connections to avoid artifacts from padded regions
✅ Create a pore graph (Region Adjacency Graph) for analysis
✅ Visualize the pore network in 3D

(Note: Pocket type detection is covered in the Pockets Detection tutorial)





Python 3.8+
MOFography installed (uv pip install -e .)
Basic familiarity with Python and NumPy arrays
(Optional) ASE for structure handling





Structure (CIF) → Distance Grid → Periodic Segmentation → Trim Connections → Pore Graph → Visualization




import os
import sys
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read

# Set up paths - adjust for your setup
repo_root = Path('/path/to/mofography')
path_to_cif = repo_root / 'examples' / 'TestCIFs' / 'P1-IRMOF-1.cif'




mat_atoms = read(path_to_cif)

print(f"Loaded structure: {mat_atoms.get_chemical_formula()}")
print(f"  Number of atoms: {len(mat_atoms)}")
print(f"  Unit cell: {mat_atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3]} Angstroms")
What is this? - An ASE Atoms object containing atomic positions, unit cell dimensions, and atomic numbers




# Grid parameters
spacing = 0.5  # Grid spacing in Angstroms

# Segmentation parameters
mask_thickness = 0.05  # Void space threshold (Angstroms)
h = 0.2  # h-maxima persistence (suppress noise)
threshold_abs = 1.5  # Absolute threshold (ignore small maxima)

# Periodic segmentation parameters
minimum_window_separation = 1.5  # Min distance between windows (Angstroms)
wall_thickness = 0.08  # Boundary detection (fraction of cell)
extra_padding = 10  # Extra padding (Angstroms)
Parameter Guide:








Parameter
What it does
Typical range




spacing
Grid resolution (lower = more detailed)
0.3 - 1.0 Å


mask_thickness
Voxels closer to the framework than this are wall (default and recommended: 0.05)
0.05 - 0.15 Å


h
Suppress noise in maxima detection
0.1 - 0.5


threshold_abs
Ignore small maxima
1.0 - 2.0 Å


wall_thickness
PBC boundary detection sensitivity
0.05 - 0.15


extra_padding
Safety margin for large pores
5 - 20 Å



Tip: Start with defaults and adjust only if results don’t look right!




The distance grid is a 3D array where each voxel contains the distance to the nearest atom. This is the foundation for pore analysis.
# Compute distance grid
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing, block_size=50000)

# Apply smoothing
dgrid = mgr.zoom_grid(dgrid, zoom_factor=1).compute()
dgrid = mgr.periodic_gaussian_filter(dgrid, sigma=spacing*2)

# CRITICAL: Convert to float32 for Rust backend
dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)

print(f"Distance grid shape: {dgrid.shape}")
print(f"Distance grid range: {dgrid.min():.2f} to {dgrid.max():.2f} Angstroms")
Understanding the Distance Grid: - 🟢 High values = far from atoms (inside pores) - 🔴 Low values = close to atoms (inside walls/framework) - 🎯 We’re looking for local maxima - the “centers” of pores




One function call does it all!
results = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid,
    mat_atoms,
    spacing=spacing,
    mask_thickness=mask_thickness,
    h=h,
    threshold_abs=threshold_abs,
    minimum_window_separation=minimum_window_separation,
    wall_thickness=wall_thickness,
    extra_padding=extra_padding,
    return_padded_regions=True,
    compute_connections=True
)

print(f"\n✅ Periodic segmentation complete!")
print(f"Found {len(results['maxima_pbc'])} unique periodic maxima")
print(f"Found {len(results['unique_regions'])} unique regions")
print(f"Found {len(results['pbc_groups'])} PBC groups")
print(f"Found {len(results['connections'])} region connections")
What just happened? 1. Padding → Grid expanded to see across periodic boundaries 2. Maxima Detection → Found local maxima (pore centers) in padded grid 3. PBC Grouping → Identified which maxima are periodic images 4. Watershed Segmentation → Assigned each voxel to nearest maximum 5. Connection Detection → Found where regions touch (windows) 6. Reindexing → Organized outputs by importance




# Extract all results
maxima_pbc = results['maxima_pbc']           # One per PBC group
regions_pbc = results['regions_pbc']         # Segmentation WITH PBC merged
regions = results['regions']                 # Segmentation WITHOUT PBC (split)
connections = results['connections']         # Windows between pores
all_maxima = results['all_maxima']           # All periodic images
unique_regions = results['unique_regions']   # Regions influencing unit cell
pbc_groups = results['pbc_groups']           # Lists of periodic image groups

# Maxima influencing the unit cell
maxima = all_maxima[:regions.max()]

print(f"\nmaxima_pbc: {maxima_pbc.shape}  (representative pore centers)")
print(f"regions_pbc: {regions_pbc.shape}, max={regions_pbc.max()}  (merged)")
print(f"regions: {regions.shape}, max={regions.max()}  (split)")
The Output Arrays:








Output
What is it?
Why care?




maxima_pbc
One representative per pore type
Canonical pore centers


regions_pbc
Segmentation with PBC merged
Same pore = same label


regions
Segmentation without PBC
Each piece has different label


all_maxima
All periodic images
For plotting connections


pbc_groups
Which maxima belong together
For pocket type detection


connections
Windows between pores
For pore graph analysis


unique_regions
Regions influencing unit cell
For filtering/trimming



Clever Indexing Trick: Maxima are ordered by importance, so all_maxima[:regions.max()] gives you just the maxima influencing the unit cell! ✨




# Trim to connections that influence the unit cell
connections_trimmed = np.array([
    c for c in connections
    if np.any(np.isin(c[0], unique_regions))
])

print(f"Original connections: {len(connections)}")
print(f"Trimmed connections: {len(connections_trimmed)}")
Why trim? - The full connections list includes connections into padded regions - These can create artifacts in analysis - Trimming ensures we only analyze pores that influence the unit cell




# Create RAG from trimmed connections
rag = mgr.rag_from_connections(connections_trimmed, all_maxima)

print(f"\nPore Graph Statistics:")
print(f"  Nodes (pores): {rag.number_of_nodes()}")
print(f"  Edges (connections): {rag.number_of_edges()}")
What is the RAG? - Nodes: Individual pores - Edges: Windows/connections between pores - Node attributes: Position, volume, shape, etc. - Edge attributes: Window center, radius, type
The RAG is useful for: - 📍 Path finding (percolation analysis) - 📊 Network properties (coordination, clustering) - 🤖 Feature extraction for machine learning




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

# Set up colorscale
cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel

# Update structure with covalent bonds
mat_updated = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)

# Create base traces
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)
frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated, stylize=True)

# Plot merged regions
surface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
    dgrid,
    isovalue=1.5,
    region_labels=regions_pbc,
    ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    name='Pores (PBC merged)',
    stylize=True,
    opacity=0.8
)

# Plot pore centers
maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima(
    dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms,
    name='Pore centers',
    show_spheres=False,
    marker_colorscale=cscale
)

# Plot connections
connections_traces = mgr.plot_connections_as_it_is(
    connections_trimmed,
    all_maxima,
    dgrid.shape,
    mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    plot_disconnected=False,
    show_spheres=False
)

# Combine into figure
fig = go.Figure(
    data=[cell_trace, surface_trace, maxima_trace, *connections_traces, *frame_trace],
    layout=mgr.dark_layout
)

fig.update_layout(
    scene_aspectmode='data',
    title=dict(
        text="IRMOF-1: Pore Network with Connections",
        x=0.5,
        xanchor='center',
        font=dict(size=16, color='white')
    ),
    scene=dict(
        xaxis=dict(title='X (Å)'),
        yaxis=dict(title='Y (Å)'),
        zaxis=dict(title='Z (Å)')
    )
)

fig.show()
Expected Output:



Full pore network visualization


IRMOF-1 pore network showing merged pores (surfaces), pore centers (dots), and connections (lines).











Issue
Solution




Too many/few maxima
Adjust h (higher = fewer) or threshold_abs (higher = fewer)


Regions not merged correctly
Increase extra_padding or check wall_thickness


Missing connections
Decrease minimum_window_separation or increase mask_thickness


Memory error
Increase spacing (lower resolution) or reduce extra_padding


Wrong dtype error
Make sure to do dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)

title: Outputs from the Periodic Segmentation
text:
Let’s quickly review the outputs from the periodic segmentation and provide a quick reference for what each of them means.




maxima_pbc
regions_pbc
maxima_info
regions
pbc_groups
all_maxima
close_or_inside_maxima
unique_regions
regions_padded






In regular segmentation of an image (2D or 3D): - You would start with a distance field - Define a foreground and background using a threshold (mask_thickness) - Find all the local maxima of the distance field present in the foreground - Do segmentation: assign all the points (grid points or voxels) to a unique maxima - Voxels are assigned to maxima such that if you invert the field (maxima become minima) and start a gradient descent from the point, it would end up at that particular minima - Imagine two valleys separated by a mountain: all the rainwater that falls on the left side of the mountain peak would flow and fill up the left valley, and all the rainwater that falls on the right side would flow to the right valley. If rain falls exactly on the mountain peak, it wouldn’t know which valley to go to; such ridge points form the boundary separating the two valleys. By the same principle, we can take a domain and break it down into regions/segments, which in our case become the 3D pockets inside our material.



The issue with this approach for our systems is that we have periodic boundary conditions: - We can compute the distances with PBC, which we are doing anyway - Ideally, local maxima should be exact periodic images of each other. This means if there is a maximum at or near a corner of the unit cell, there should be a maximum at all the corners of the unit cell. Similarly, if there is a maximum at 0.5,0.5,0 face center, there should be a maximum at the 0.5, 0.5, 1 face center as well, and so on (assuming the unit cell is defined over 0 to 1 in all three dimensions). This is not guaranteed just by computing the distance field with PBC, which makes all the downstream post-processing and averaging difficult (which is what we’ve been doing in the old workflow).



Periodic segmentation ensures this by doing the following:



Pad the distance grid by a sufficient amount in all three dimensions
How much padding should you use? I am using enough to complete the largest pocket and then a few more angstroms for security. You can optionally add extra_padding
Values in the padded region: Calculated using wrap mode. This means the values at x>0 are wrapped around to the values at x>1. So value at x=1.1 would be the same as that x=0.1, and so on for all three dimensions. Note that we are talking in fractional coordinates; the actual unit cell may be non-orthogonal, so that is taken care of accordingly.
Now the distance field can see across periodic boundaries, just a little bit using the padded region. Great!





Compute the local maxima on the padded distance field
Detect which one is a periodic image of which
Group them together - These are the pbc_groups. For example:

All the 8 corner maxima will form one group
Opposite face maxima, if any, will form one group
4 opposing edge maxima, if any, will form one group
Anything fully inside the unit cell will form a group of its own, etc.

For each group, pick a maxima that is inside the unit cell (original shape before padding) as the representative. Collection of these representatives is maxima_pbc, which is a numpy array of shape (n_maxima_pbc, 3) where n_maxima is the number of representative maxima found in the unit cell. Of course, n_maxima_pbc = len(pbc_groups). You can think of a pbc_group as the collection of regions that would form a complete pocket if the pocket is chopped up across periodic boundaries. This is super important for averaging properties correctly.
Now, we need a way to keep track of all the local maxima and their relation to the maxima_pbc. That’s where the maxima_info array comes in.




Let’s say we give separate labels 1 to M for all the maxima, including maxima_pbc and their images, including the ones in the padded region. You can relate these maxima to maxima_pbc using simple offsets. - Offsets tell you in which directions to shift the representative maxima (maxima_pbc) to get the labeled maxima. This is tabulated in maxima_info. - A 2D array of shape (N_all_maxima, 7):



Column
Description




maxima_label
Label of the maxima


pbc_x/y/z
Coordinates of the corresponding PBC maxima


offset_x/y/z
Grid shifts to locate the periodic image




To compute the actual indices of a maxima k:
maxima_indices = maxima_info[k-1, 1:4] + maxima_info[k-1, 4:7] * np.array(dgrid.shape)




Note that although a maxima_pbc is inside the unit cell, its periodic image could be in the padded region, sometimes close to the unit cell wall but slightly outside the unit cell (since the grid spacing is not infinitesimal). We need to keep track of this information as well.
Also, we don’t often need all the maxima from the padded grid; pockets and connections fully inside or just close outside the unit cell are enough for most applications. So it would be useful to trim them down quickly. Hence, this information is provided among the outputs:

close_or_inside_maxima: 1D numpy array that lists the indices of all the maxima that are fully inside the unit cell or close to the wall on the outside.
unique_regions: 1D numpy array that lists the indices of all the maxima that have at least one voxel assigned to it inside the unit cell. Now this could include maxima outside the box, often due to noise from the segmentation, or it due to real physical influence where there is a pocket segment in the unit cell, but its maxima is slightly outside the unit boundary (hard to visualize, I know! But imagine cross sectional segments along large zig zag channels, for example).




There is a clever indexing scheme put in place to make the selection of these maxima easier. Maxima are reindexed in the order of decreasing importance:

maxima_pbc get indices 1, 2, ..., N_maxima_pbc
close_or_inside_maxima get the next indices if not already assigned
unique_regions maxima influencing the unit cell get the next indices
Maxima in the padded regions connected to close_or_inside_maxima get indices
Remaining maxima in all_maxima (a.k.a. unlabeled ones in the padded regions) get indices

This indexing convention simplifies downstream analyses greatly. For example, to filter maxima corresponding to unique_regions, you can do:
maxima = all_maxima[:regions.max()] # or 
maxima = all_maxima[:(len(unique_regions)+1)]



Note that some of the information above requires you to know the segmentation. So that is indeed done first, and then the maxima are reindexed to match the above scheme.
Segmentation is done twice on the padded distance field: - Once with maxima_pbc markers: the same marker (say, i) is used for a maxima_pbc and all its images. So you’d get that wrap-around effect for regions across periodic boundaries. - Once with all_maxima: separate markers are used for maxima_pbc and its periodic images, so you would get different labels at the 8 corner regions, even if these maxima belong to the same pbc_group. This is necessary for computing connections to construct the pore graph.
In both cases, you would get a segmentation array of shape (nx+2padding, ny+2padding, nz+2*padding), where the padding is the amount of padding you added to the distance field. From these, you would just grab the central region corresponding to the original unit cell to get regions_pbc and regions, respectively.



Not going to say much about this here, since it’s pretty much the same as in the old workflow, except that we compute them on the regions_padded instead of regions, so we can get the connections in the padded regions as well. If you don’t need these, you have a few options:

Trim down the connections: [c for c in connections if np.all(np.isin(c[0], unique_regions))], meaning keep only those connections where both regions are in the unit cell. You can customize using np.any or using close_or_inside_maxima instead of unique_regions as you need.
You can also ignore the connections from the periodic segmentation workflow and instead just compute them fresh using the unpadded regions array and the distance field, like in the old workflow.
Both of these should give the same results.






Input Preparation: Start with distance grid and ASE atoms object
Padding: Add periodic boundary regions to the distance grid
Maxima Detection: Find local maxima using h_maxima algorithm
Image Identification: Identify periodic images of each maxima
Grouping: Group periodic images into pbc_groups
Representative Selection: Choose one representative per group (maxima_pbc)
Information Array: Create maxima_info with offsets and labels 8.Dual Segmentation: Perform two segmentations with different marker strategies
Extraction: Extract central regions from padded grids
Location importance: Classify maxima by their location relative to unit cell
Reindexing: Smart reindexing by importance priority
Connections: Compute connections between regions using padded regions.
Final Output: Generate all output arrays and data structures





This document explains the periodic segmentation approach for analyzing porous materials with periodic boundary conditions. The key innovations include:
Core Problem: Regular segmentation doesn’t handle periodic boundary conditions properly, leading to inconsistent maxima placement across unit cell boundaries and making downstream analysis difficult.
Solution: Periodic segmentation addresses this by: 1. Padding: Adding wrapped boundary regions to allow the distance field to see across periodic boundaries 2. Grouping: Identifying and grouping periodic images of maxima together (pbc_groups) 3. Representative Selection: Choosing one representative maxima per group (maxima_pbc) for consistent analysis 4. Smart Indexing: Implementing a hierarchical indexing scheme that prioritizes important maxima
Key Outputs: - maxima_pbc: Representative maxima for each periodic group - regions_pbc and regions: Segmented regions with and without periodic wrapping - maxima_info: Detailed mapping between all maxima and their representatives - pbc_groups: Groups of periodic image maxima - Various filtering arrays (close_or_inside_maxima, unique_regions) for different analysis needs
Benefits: This approach enables proper averaging of properties across periodic boundaries and provides a solid foundation for pore network analysis in crystalline porous materials.

title: MC Shell Surface-Area Estimator
text:
Quick reference for compute_surface_area_mc_winding in mofography/compute.py.



The Monte-Carlo shell estimator turns surface area into a counting problem:

Throw N random points inside the unit cell.
Keep the points that land in a thin shell of thickness δ centred on the probe surface (i.e. within δ/2 of the isosurface d(x) = r_probe).
Compute SA = V_cell · (n_shell / N) / δ, then convert Å² → m²/g.

That’s it. Everything else is bookkeeping around step 2 (percolation filtering, region labelling, mass normalisation).




A 2-D surface smeared into a thin 3-D band has a volume proportional to its area:
V_shell  ≈  SA · δ          (in the limit of small δ)
So if you can measure V_shell and you know δ, you get SA = V_shell / δ.
The trick is measuring V_shell without explicitly constructing the surface. The distance grid d(x) (already computed during segmentation) gives us the surface implicitly: every point where d(x) = r_probe is on the probe surface, and every point where |d(x) - r_probe| ≤ δ/2 is in the shell.
Monte Carlo gives the shell volume:
V_shell ≈ V_cell · (n_shell / N)         (fractional volume of the shell)
Combining:
SA = V_cell · p_shell / δ       where   p_shell = n_shell / N



Pseudocode of compute_surface_area_mc in mofography/compute.py:
# 1. Random uniform points in fractional coords
u = np.random.rand(n_samples, 3)                       # (N, 3) in [0, 1)^3
coords = u * (shape - 1)                               # (N, 3) in voxel units

# 2. Interpolate the distance grid at each point
d_samples = map_coordinates(distance_grid, coords, order=1, mode="wrap")

# 3. Define the shell: points whose distance-to-wall is within ±δ/2 of r_probe
half_delta = shell_thickness / 2.0
shell_mask = np.abs(d_samples - probe_radius) <= half_delta
n_shell_total = shell_mask.sum()

# 4. Estimate SA
p_shell = n_shell_total / n_samples
total_surface_area = V_cell * p_shell / shell_thickness * 1e-20 / mass_g
The accessibility version additionally filters samples by whether their region label is in percolating_regions, giving accessible_surface_area from the same samples.












Parameter
Default
What it does
Effect of changing




n_samples
20 000
Number of random points per structure
More samples → lower statistical noise (∝ 1/√N)


shell_thickness (δ)
0.5 Å
Half-width of the band around the probe surface
Thicker → more hits per sample (lower variance) but more bias from averaging


probe_radius
He radius (1.2 Å)
Radius of the fictitious probe molecule
Larger probe → smaller accessible surface





The expected value of the estimator is essentially independent of δ (in the small-δ limit), because p_shell scales linearly with δ and the 1/δ factor cancels. What does depend on δ is the variance and the bias from smoothing:

Thin shell (δ ≈ 0.2 Å): very little bias, but few samples per shell, so the estimate is noisy. Needs n_samples ≈ 50 000+ to reach the same precision.
Default (δ = 0.5 Å): well-matched to a SPACING = 0.5 Å grid; a good default for screening.
Thick shell (δ ≈ 1.0 Å): most samples per shell, but the SA is averaged over a band that is itself a sizable fraction of small pores. Only sensible when the distance field is locally flat (large pores).

The default δ = 0.5 Å is a good choice because it is a few times larger than the grid spacing — so the shell contains a statistically meaningful number of samples — and it is small compared to typical LCD values, so the bias is negligible.




A quick way to confirm that shell_thickness isn’t biasing your results is to re-run the same MOF with two different δ values and check the agreement:
for delta in (0.3, 0.5, 0.7):
    sa = mgr.compute_surface_area_mc_winding(
        results, atoms,
        probe_radius=1.2,
        n_samples=40_000,
        shell_thickness=delta,
    )
    print(f"δ = {delta:.1f} Å  →  SA = {sa['total_surface_area']:.1f} m²/g")
For typical MOFs the three numbers should agree to within a few percent — the MC noise level for 40 000 samples.












Method
Function
Pros
Cons




Mesh
compute_surface_area_mesh_winding
Deterministic; exact (modulo tessellation)
Slow for large grids; needs explicit surface triangulation


MC shell
compute_surface_area_mc_winding
Fast; trivially parallel over n_samples; tunable precision
Stochastic; needs enough samples for low noise



The MC shell method is the natural choice for high-throughput screening, where you can trade a few-percent statistical error for a 10×+ speedup over the mesh method.

Winding-accessible wrapper: mofography/compute.py::compute_surface_area_mc_winding (≈ line 10097)
See also: docs/accessibility_and_surface_area.org for the broader SA/Vol API

He radius (1.2 Å)
Radius of the fictitious probe molecule
Larger probe → smaller accessible surface





The expected value of the estimator is essentially independent of δ (in the small-δ limit), because p_shell scales linearly with δ and the 1/δ factor cancels. What does depend on δ is the variance and the bias from smoothing:

Thin shell (δ ≈ 0.2 Å): very little bias, but few samples per shell, so the estimate is noisy. Needs n_samples ≈ 50 000+ to reach the same precision.
Default (δ = 0.5 Å): well-matched to a SPACING = 0.5 Å grid; a good default for screening.
Thick shell (δ ≈ 1.0 Å): most samples per shell, but the SA is averaged over a band that is itself a sizable fraction of small pores. Only sensible when the distance field is locally flat (large pores).

The default δ = 0.5 Å is a good choice because it is a few times larger than the grid spacing — so the shell contains a statistically meaningful number of samples — and it is small compared to typical LCD values, so the bias is negligible.

title: MC Shell Surface-Area Estimator
text:
A quick way to confirm that shell_thickness isn’t biasing your results is to re-run the same MOF with two different δ values and check the agreement:
for delta in (0.3, 0.5, 0.7):
    sa = mgr.compute_surface_area_mc_winding(
        results, atoms,
        probe_radius=1.2,
        n_samples=40_000,
        shell_thickness=delta,
    )
    print(f"δ = {delta:.1f} Å  →  SA = {sa['total_surface_area']:.1f} m²/g")
For typical MOFs the three numbers should agree to within a few percent — the MC noise level for 40 000 samples.

Fast; trivially parallel over n_samples; tunable precision

The MC shell method is the natural choice for high-throughput screening, where you can trade a few-percent statistical error for a 10×+ speedup over the mesh method.

Rust Segmentation
Show code
# "do_periodic_segmentation_rust_winding": it revised from "do_periodic_segmentation_rust". I deleted line 631-line 643 of "rust_fun.py"(the version in GitHub).

def do_periodic_segmentation_rust_winding(
    dgrid,
    mat_atoms,
    mask_thickness=0.5,
    h=0.2,
    min_distance=1.5,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    return_padded_regions=False,
    spacing=None,
    minimum_window_separation=None,
    wall_thickness=0.05,
    extra_padding=5,
    compactness=0,
    min_region_size=0.001,
    disable_tqdm=False,
    compute_connections=True,
    return_dgrid=False,
    preserve_threshold=3.0,
    smooth_threshold=0.0,
    max_smooth_radius=2.0,
):
    """Perform periodic segmentation on a distance grid to identify pore regions.

    This function implements a comprehensive pore segmentation algorithm that:
    1. Detects local maxima in the distance field
    2. Applies periodic boundary conditions
    3. Performs watershed segmentation
    4. Identifies connections between regions
    5. Returns detailed segmentation results

    :param dgrid: 3D distance grid from dgrid_from_atoms_rust
    :type dgrid: numpy.ndarray
    :param mat_atoms: ASE Atoms object of the material
    :type mat_atoms: ase.Atoms
    :param mask_thickness: Threshold for void space identification
    :type mask_thickness: float
    :param h: Persistence parameter for maxima detection
    :type h: float
    :param min_distance: Minimum distance of separationg required between distinct local maxima
    :type min_distance: float
    :param threshold_abs: Absolute threshold for maxima detection
    :type threshold_abs: float
    :param return_padded_regions: Whether to return padded region arrays
    :type return_padded_regions: bool
    :param spacing: Grid spacing. If None, estimated from dgrid size and cell lengths. Specify for better accuracy.
    :type spacing: float or None
    :param minimum_window_separation: Minimum separation for window connections
    :type minimum_window_separation: float or None
    :param wall_thickness: Thickness of wall regions to exclude
    :type wall_thickness: float
    :param extra_padding: Additional padding for periodic calculations in angstroms. This over and above the standard_padding + 5 A cushion.
    :type extra_padding: float
    :param compactness: Watershed compactness parameter
    :type compactness: float
    :param min_region_size: Minimum region size as fraction of total volume, regions smaller than this in comparison with the *padded_grid* are removed
    :type min_region_size: float
    :param disable_tqdm: Whether to disable progress bars
    :type disable_tqdm: bool
    :param compute_connections: Whether to compute inter-region connections
    :type compute_connections: bool
    :param return_dgrid: Whether to include dgrid in output
    :type return_dgrid: bool
    :return: Dictionary containing segmentation results including maxima, regions, connections, etc.
    :rtype: dict
    """
    import numpy as np

    # from skimage.segmentation import watershed
    from ase.geometry import cellpar_to_cell
    import copy

    # from ase.geometry import complete_cell
    # import sparse
    # from skimage.segmentation import find_boundaries
    # from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
    from time import time

    # from tqdm import tqdm
    import mgr_rust

    logger.info(f"Using {mgr_rust.rayon_num_threads()} threads for parallel processing")
    start_time = time()
    from mofography import (
        compute_wall_cells,
        move_maximum_to_peak,
        process_wall_maxima,
        is_inside_or_close_to_boundary,
        get_fractional_coordinates,
        interpolate_labels,
        find_touching_region_pairs,
        find_end_channel_pairs,
        merge_small_regions,
        merge_small_regions_pbc,
        find_pore_limiting_radius,
        calculate_padding_thickness,
        detect_periodic_maxima_direct,
        get_pbc_groups,
    )

    # print(f"timer started")
    logger.info(f"timer started")
    # h = 0.11
    # note: uncomment these imports when refactoring
    # from .helper import find_touching_region_pairs,compute_wall_cells, move_maximum_to_peak, process_wall_maxima, is_inside_or_close_to_boundary, get_fractional_coordinates, interpolate_labels
    # smooth = false
    if spacing is None:
        logger.warning(
            "warning: no spacing provided. estimating. provide the dgrid spacing, for more accurate calculation!\n"
        )
        spacing = np.min(
            mat_atoms.get_cell_lengths_and_angles()[:3] / (np.array(dgrid.shape) - 1)
        )
        logger.info(f"spacing estimated from dgrid and ase_atoms is {spacing}")

    if minimum_window_separation is None:
        minimum_window_separation = spacing * 3

    logger.info(f"h is {h}")

    # min_distance = 1.1
    #     threshold_abs = 1
    # # merged_maxima, all_maxima = detect_periodic_maxima_dgrid(dgrid, ase_atoms=mat_atoms, spacing=spacing, h=h, threshold_abs=threshold_abs, min_distance=min_distance, sigma_smooth=1.0, cell=cell)
    # dt, merged_maxima, all_maxima =detect_periodic_maxima_direct(
    #     dgrid,
    #     mat_atoms,
    #     spacing,
    #     h=h,
    #     threshold_abs=threshold_abs,
    #     min_distance=min_distance,
    #     # smooth=smooth,
    #     maxima_mask=mask_thickness,
    # )

    cell = cellpar_to_cell(mat_atoms.cell.cellpar()).T
    # merged_maxima, unmerged_maxima, raw_maxima = mgr_rust.detect_maxima_h_morph(dgrid, spacing=spacing, h=h, threshold_abs=threshold_abs, min_distance=min_distance, sigma_smooth=1.0, cell=cell)
    merged_maxima, unmerged_maxima, raw_maxima = (
        mgr_rust.detect_maxima_selective_smoothing_parallel(
            dgrid,
            preserve_threshold=3.0,
            smooth_threshold=6.0,
            max_smooth_radius=2.0,
            h=h,
            threshold_abs=threshold_abs,
            min_distance=min_distance,
            cell=cell,
        )
    )
    dt = dgrid.copy()
    temp = np.ceil(merged_maxima)
    # compute wall cells
    logger.info(
        f"time(s): {np.round(time() - start_time, decimals=2)} computing maxima with pbc\n"
    )
    # computed merged maxima nad regions_pbc!
    # padding_thickness=5
    padding_thickness = calculate_padding_thickness(
        dgrid, mat_atoms, spacing
    ) + np.ceil(extra_padding / spacing).astype(int)
    logger.info(f"padding thickness is {padding_thickness}")
    wall_cells = compute_wall_cells(mat_atoms, spacing, wall_thickness)
    wall_maxima_to_remove = process_wall_maxima(
        merged_maxima,
        dgrid,
        padding_thickness=padding_thickness,
        wall_cells=wall_cells,
        ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    )
    wall_maxima_to_remove = []
    # logger.info("maxima to remove are", wall_maxima_to_remove)
    # optimized_positions = []
    # optimized_values = []
    # original_indices = []
    # for i, pos in enumerate(merged_maxima):
    #     if i not in wall_maxima_to_remove:
    #         # padded_pos = pos + padding_thickness
    #         opt_pos, opt_val = move_maximum_to_peak(pos, dt, padding_thickness)
    #         optimized_positions.append(opt_pos)
    #         optimized_values.append(opt_val)
    #         original_indices.append(i)
    # optimized_positions = np.vstack(optimized_positions)
    # optimized_positions.shape
    # use the rust functions instead
    # * optimize the maxima positions (unused)
    optimized_positions, optimized_values = mgr_rust.move_maxima_to_peaks(
        dt.astype(np.float32), merged_maxima.astype(np.uintp)
    )
    optimized_positions = np.asarray(optimized_positions)

    all_removals = set(wall_maxima_to_remove)
    merged_maxima = np.vstack(
        [m for i, m in enumerate(merged_maxima) if i not in all_removals]
    )

    logger.info(
        f"time(s): {np.round(time() - start_time, decimals=2)} computing regions with pbc \n"
    )
    # compactness = 0
    # compute markers for padded, periodic segmentation
    markers = np.zeros_like(dgrid, dtype=int)
    if len(merged_maxima) > 0:
        maxima_coords = tuple(merged_maxima.T)
        markers[maxima_coords] = np.arange(1, len(merged_maxima) + 1)
    else:
        logger.info("problem: no valid maxima detected after merging.")
    # void mask for segmentation to use the mask_thickness
    void_mask = dgrid > mask_thickness
    padded_grid = np.pad(dt, padding_thickness, mode="wrap")
    padded_markers = np.pad(markers, padding_thickness, mode="wrap")
    padded_void = np.pad(void_mask, padding_thickness, mode="wrap")

    # # run the watershed segmentation using the merged markers.
    # padded_regions = watershed(
    #     -padded_grid,
    #     padded_markers,
    #     mask=padded_void,
    #     compactness=compactness,
    #     connectivity=2,  # 26-connectivity for full 3d
    # )

    # run the watershed segmentation using the merged markers.
    padded_regions = mgr_rust.seeded_watershed_bucket(
        padded_grid.astype(np.float32),
        padded_markers.astype(np.uint32),
        mask=padded_void.astype(np.uint8),
        # # compactness=compactness,
        # connectivity=2,  # 26-connectivity for full 3d
    )

    logger.info(
        f"TIME(s): {np.round(time() - start_time, decimals=2)} Looking to remove regions smaller than {min_region_size} * dgrid.size"
    )
    # clean up the regions_pbc from small regions, remove less than 0.1% of the total size, this is trickier than one would think. We want to find the volume % of just the box, then make our selection to remove, and then pad back up to get the cleaned padded grid.
    padded_regions_box_trimmed = padded_regions[
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
    ]
    padded_regions_box_trimmed_cleaned = merge_small_regions(
        padded_regions_box_trimmed,
        min_size=padded_regions_box_trimmed.size * min_region_size,
    )
    padded_regions_cleaned = np.pad(
        padded_regions_box_trimmed_cleaned, padding_thickness, mode="wrap"
    )

    # padded_regions_cleaned = merge_small_regions(padded_regions, min_size=padded_regions.size*min_region_size)

    unique_padded_regions = np.unique(padded_regions)
    unique_padded_regions_cleaned = np.unique(padded_regions_cleaned)
    removed_labels_pbc = unique_padded_regions[
        ~np.isin(unique_padded_regions, unique_padded_regions_cleaned)
    ]
    logger.info(
        f"Found that labels are too small within the box even with pbc {removed_labels_pbc}"
    )

    # TODO: is this necesary? isnt' everytihng an original maxima this point.
    # only keep removed labels that correspond to original maxima
    max_label = len(merged_maxima)
    removed_maxima_labels = removed_labels_pbc[
        (removed_labels_pbc >= 1) & (removed_labels_pbc <= max_label)
    ]
    if len(removed_maxima_labels) > 0:
        logger.info(f"Removing these small maxima labels:{removed_maxima_labels}")

    # * remove those rows from merged_maxima nd redo segmentations
    merged_maxima = np.delete(merged_maxima, removed_maxima_labels - 1, axis=0)

    if len(removed_maxima_labels) > 0:
        logger.info(
            f"TIME(s): {np.round(time() - start_time, decimals=2)} Redoing segmentation for clean sequential labels in regions pbc"
        )
        markers = np.zeros_like(dgrid, dtype=int)
        if len(merged_maxima) > 0:
            maxima_coords = tuple(merged_maxima.T)
            markers[maxima_coords] = np.arange(1, len(merged_maxima) + 1)
        else:
            logger.info("problem: no valid maxima detected after merging.")
        # void mask for segmentation to use the mask_thickness
        void_mask = dgrid > mask_thickness
        padded_grid = np.pad(dt, padding_thickness, mode="wrap")
        padded_markers = np.pad(markers, padding_thickness, mode="wrap")
        padded_void = np.pad(void_mask, padding_thickness, mode="wrap")

        # run the watershed segmentation using the merged markers.
        padded_regions = mgr_rust.seeded_watershed_bucket(
            padded_grid.astype(np.float32),
            padded_markers.astype(np.uint32),
            mask=padded_void.astype(np.uint8),
            # # compactness=compactness,
            # connectivity=2,  # 26-connectivity for full 3d
        )

    # replace regions_pbc with regions_pbc_cleaned
    # padded_regions=padded_regions_cleaned

    # extract central (unpadded) region to obtain regions_pbc.
    regions_pbc = padded_regions[
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
    ]
    # print("computed merged maxima nad regions_pbc!!")

    #
    logger.info(
        f"time(s): {np.round(time() - start_time, decimals=2)} computing maxima and regions without pbc\n"
    )

    # step 2: get unmerged maxima info using valid maxima
    original_shape = np.array(dgrid.shape)
    padded_shape = np.array(padded_grid.shape)

    new_maxima_info_list = []
    counter = 1
    for m in merged_maxima:
        m_pad = m + padding_thickness
        offset_ranges = [
            range(-((p - 1) // o), (p - 1) // o + 1)
            for p, o in zip(padded_shape, original_shape)
        ]
        for offs in np.array(np.meshgrid(*offset_ranges)).T.reshape(-1, 3):
            candidate = m_pad + offs * original_shape
            if np.all(candidate >= 0) and np.all(candidate < padded_shape):
                candidate_unpadded = candidate - padding_thickness
                offset = candidate_unpadded // original_shape
                image_coord = np.mod(candidate_unpadded, original_shape)
                new_maxima_info_list.append(
                    [
                        counter,
                        image_coord[0],
                        image_coord[1],
                        image_coord[2],
                        offset[0],
                        offset[1],
                        offset[2],
                    ]
                )
                counter += 1

    maxima_info = np.array(new_maxima_info_list, dtype=int)

    # rust version goes here--
    # maxima_info = mgr_rust.build_maxima_info(merged_maxima.astype(np.uintp), np.array(dgrid.shape, dtype=np.uintp), int(padding_thickness))
    # maxima_info = np.asarray(maxima_info, dtype=int)

    # print(maxima_info)
    # merged_maxima
    # create unmerged markers and regions using valid maxima
    unmerged_markers = np.zeros_like(padded_grid, dtype=int)
    for info in maxima_info:
        # warn: should we add the offset times shape here?  fixed
        pos = info[1:4] + padding_thickness + info[4:7] * original_shape
        unmerged_markers[tuple(pos)] = info[0]

    # # compute unmerged regions
    #     unmerged_padded_regions = watershed(
    #         -padded_grid,
    #         unmerged_markers,
    #         mask=padded_void,
    #         compactness=compactness,
    #         connectivity=2,
    #     )

    # compute unmerged regions
    unmerged_padded_regions = mgr_rust.seeded_watershed_bucket(
        padded_grid.astype(np.float32),
        seeds=unmerged_markers.astype(np.uint32),
        mask=padded_void.astype(np.uint8),
        # compactness=compactness,
        # connectivity=2,
    )

    # grab the central block
    unmerged_regions = unmerged_padded_regions[
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
        padding_thickness:-padding_thickness,
    ]

    logger.info(
        f"time(s): { np.round(time() - start_time, decimals=2) } computed regions without pbc\n"
    )
    endchannel_pairs = find_end_channel_pairs(
        regions_pbc, unmerged_regions, size_ratio=0.3
    )
    # so we need to replace only if the removed label is far outside the unit cell
    wall_region_thicknesses = compute_wall_cells(
        mat_atoms, spacing, wall_thickness=wall_thickness
    )
    # let's start by keeping only those maxima that are there in the regions array
    maxima_indices = maxima_info[:, 1:4] + maxima_info[:, 4:7] * np.array(dgrid.shape)
    # get location classifications for all maxima
    inside_close_outside = is_inside_or_close_to_boundary(
        maxima_indices, dgrid.shape, wall_region_thicknesses
    )
    # create a boolean mask for maxima that are either inside or close_outside
    valid_maxima_mask = np.array(
        [loc in ["inside", "close_outside"] for loc in inside_close_outside]
    )
    # find the core maxima ids (region labels), don't forget to add 1 to get label from index
    valid_maxima_ids = np.where(valid_maxima_mask)[0] + 1

    for p in endchannel_pairs:
        # print(f"Trying to replace {p[0]} with {p[1]}")

    """Perform periodic segmentation on a distance grid to identify pore regions.
