    :type h: float
    :param min_distance: Minimum distance of separationg required between distinct local maxima
    :type min_distance: float
    :param threshold_abs: Absolute threshold for maxima detection
    :type threshold_abs: float
    :param preserve_threshold: Distance cutoff (Å) below which maxima are untouched during smoothing
    :type preserve_threshold: float
    :param smooth_threshold: Distance threshold (Å) above which maxima are always smoothed

    :type extra_padding: float
    :param compactness: Watershed compactness parameter

    :param min_region_size: Minimum region size as fraction of total volume, regions smaller than this in comparison with the *padded_grid* are removed

        missing_regions = set(range(0, regions.max())) - set(np.unique(regions))
        missing_regions_pbc = set(range(0, regions_pbc.max())) - set(
            np.unique(regions_pbc)
        )

        if len(missing_regions) > 0:
            logger.warning(f"Potential inconsistency in indexing!:")
            logger.info(f"mising seq indices in regions: {missing_regions}")
            logger.info(f"mising seq indices in regions_pbc: {missing_regions_pbc}")
        # outputs=dict(maxima_pbc=merged_maxima, regions_pbc=regions_pbc, maxima_info=maxima_info_copy_copy, regions=regions,conections=connections_list_copy, pbc_groups=pbc_groups, close_or_inside_maxima=valid_maxima_indices, close_or_inside_regions= valid_maxima_ids, unique_regions = unique_regions)
        all_maxima = maxima_info_copy_copy[:, 1:4] + maxima_info_copy_copy[
            :, 4:7
        ] * np.array(dgrid.shape)
        outputs = dict(
            dgrid=dgrid,
            maxima_pbc=merged_maxima,
            regions_pbc=regions_pbc,
            maxima_info=maxima_info_copy_copy,
            regions=regions,
            connections=connections_list_copy,
            pbc_groups=pbc_groups,
            close_or_inside_maxima=valid_maxima_indices,
            close_or_inside_regions=valid_maxima_ids,
            unique_regions=unique_regions,
            maxima_pbc_dict=merged_maxima_indices,
            all_maxima=all_maxima,
            maxima_relative_locations=np.array(inside_close_outside),
        )
        # we need to save the input params to the results, for future reference.
        outputs["input_params"] = {
            "mask_thickness": mask_thickness,
            "h": h,
            "min_distance": min_distance,
            "threshold_abs": threshold_abs,
            "spacing": spacing,
            "minimum_window_separation": minimum_window_separation,
            "compactness": compactness,
            "wall_thickness": wall_thickness,
            "extra_padding": extra_padding,
            "padding_thickness": padding_thickness,
            "min_region_size": min_region_size,
        }
        if return_padded_regions:
            outputs["regions_padded"] = regions_padded_copy

    if return_dgrid:
        outputs["dgrid"] = dgrid
    logger.info(
        f"TIME(s): {
            np.round(time() - start_time, decimals=2)
        } Padded segmentation workflow complete :) \n"
    )
    return outputs

title: Pore graph (region adjacency graph)
text:
A segmentation gives you pockets and the windows between them. The pore graph (also called the region adjacency graph, RAG) turns that into a networkx graph: pockets are nodes and windows are edges. This page builds the graph two ways, reads its attributes, and plots it on top of the framework.
It assumes you have seen the Quick start. Parameter defaults and safe ranges are on Tuning and safe ranges.

title: Pore graph (region adjacency graph)
text:
Structure, grid, and segmentation


Show code
import numpy as np
from ase.io import read
import mofography as mgr

spacing = 0.5
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing).astype(np.float32)

title: Pore graph (region adjacency graph)
text:
Building the graph
There are two ways to build the graph from a segmentation.








Option
Function
What you get




1
get_rag_from_regions_and_grid
The compact graph: one node per PBC-merged pocket (8 for IRMOF-1), built from the regions and the distance grid. Use it when you want one node per pocket for analysis.


2
rag_from_connections
Go-to builder. One node per maximum including the periodic images in the padded cell (125 for IRMOF-1), with edges taken directly from the detected windows. It is what the Quick start uses, and it lets you control which windows become edges.









Note



Option 1 needs regions_pbc and maxima_pbc from the same segmentation, with one maximum per region. It fails on the unmerged regions array, whose region count does not match the maxima.



Option 1: from regions and the grid


Show code
rag = mgr.get_rag_from_regions_and_grid(regions, dgrid, atoms, maxima)
print(rag.number_of_nodes(), "nodes,", rag.number_of_edges(), "edges")


8 nodes, 12 edges




Option 2: from the window list
seg["connections"] holds the windows. See Connections and windows for how they are detected.


Show code
rag_c = mgr.rag_from_connections(seg["connections"], seg["all_maxima"])
print(rag_c.number_of_nodes(), "nodes (with periodic images),", rag_c.number_of_edges(), "edges")


125 nodes (with periodic images), 54 edges

title: Pore graph (region adjacency graph)
text:
Visualizing the pore graph
To draw the graph, use plot_connections_as_it_is. It plots the detected connections (seg["connections"]) and the pockets they join, including the periodic images, so what you see is exactly what the graph was built from. Like every other mofography plotting function it returns traces, so it combines with the framework, cell, surface, and maxima traces. Build those first:


Show code

# isovalue is a distance from the framework (Å); keep it well above mask_thickness (0.05)
surface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
    dgrid, isovalue=1.75, ase_atoms=atoms_bonded, opacity=0.7,
    region_labels=regions, cscale=cscale, stylize=True,
)
maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima(dgrid, maxima, ase_atoms=atoms_bonded)
connections_traces = mgr.plot_connections_as_it_is(
    seg["connections"], seg["all_maxima"], dgrid.shape, atoms_bonded
)

Cell Matrix Completion: The cell matrix is completed from the atomic structure to ensure proper periodic boundary conditions. 3. text:
Define functions

Compute pore sizes for psd


Show code

def compute_pore_sizes_for_psd(atoms, dgrid=None,  num_samples=50000, spacing=0.25, blocksize=500):
    """
    Computes the pore sizes from an atomic structure using Voronoi tessellation and DGrid interpolation, to be histogrammed to get the Pore Size Distribution (PSD).

    This function follows these steps:
    1. **DGrid Generation**: If a precomputed DGrid is not provided, a new DGrid is generated from the atomic structure using the specified spacing.
    2. **Cell Matrix Completion**: The cell matrix is completed from the atomic structure to ensure proper periodic boundary conditions.
    3. **Voronoi Tessellation**: A box is created from the cell matrix, and the Voronoi tessellation is computed based on the atomic positions.
    4. **Fractional Coordinates Extraction**: The fractional coordinates of the Voronoi nodes are extracted from the tessellation results.
    5. **DGrid Interpolation**: An interpolator for the DGrid is created to facilitate the calculation of node radii.
    6. **Node Radii Calculation**: The radii of the Voronoi nodes are calculated using the interpolator.
    7. **Random Sampling Points Generation**: A specified number of random sampling points are generated in fractional coordinates.
    8. **Accessibility Filtering**: The accessible sampling points are filtered based on the DGrid interpolation results.
    9. **Sample Point Radii Calculation**: The radii for the accessible sampling points are obtained using the DGrid interpolator.
    10. **Distance Calculation**: For each block of sample points, the distances to the Voronoi nodes are calculated, and valid radii are determined.
    11. **Result Compilation**: The maximum valid radii and the sample block radii are combined to produce the final pore sizes.
    12. **Dask Processing**: The calculations are parallelized using Dask to handle large datasets efficiently.

    Parameters:
    - atoms (Atoms): The ASE Atoms object containing atomic structure data.
    - dgrid (DGrid, optional): Precomputed DGrid. If None, it will be computed using the default spacing.
    - num_samples (int): The number of random sampling points to generate. Default is 50000.
    - spacing (float): The spacing for the DGrid computation. Default is 0.25.
    - blocksize (int): The size of the blocks for Dask array processing. Default is 1000. If you have less RAM, and is 
    getting a seg fault as a result, please reduce this number or the num_samples.

    Returns:
    - pore_sizes (ndarray): An array of computed pore sizes.
    """
    def print_stat(data):
        """Compute and print basic statistics of a numpy array."""
        max_value = np.max(data)
        min_value = np.min(data)
        mean_value = np.mean(data)
        variance_value = np.var(data)
        # print(f"Name of variable: )
        print(f"shape: {data.shape}")
        
        print(f"Max: {max_value}")
        print(f"Min: {min_value}")
        print(f"Mean: {mean_value}")
        print(f"Variance: {variance_value}")


    import numpy as np 
    import dask.array as da
    from ase.geometry import complete_cell
    from freud.locality import Voronoi 
    from freud.box import Box 
    import mofography as mgr
    # Generate a DGrid from the atomic structure if not provided
    if dgrid is None:
        dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=spacing)

    # Complete the cell matrix from the atomic structure
    cell = complete_cell(atoms.get_cell().T)

    # Create a box for the Voronoi tessellation
    box = Box.from_matrix(cell)

    # Initialize and compute the Voronoi tessellation
    voro = Voronoi()
    voro.compute((box, atoms.get_positions()))

    # Get the fractional coordinates of the Voronoi nodes
    nodes_fractional = mgr.get_fractional_coordinates(np.vstack(voro.polytopes), atoms)

    # Create an interpolator for the DGrid
    dgrid_interpolator = mgr.interpolate_dgrid(dgrid)

    # Calculate the node radii using the interpolator
    node_radii = dgrid_interpolator(nodes_fractional % 1)

    print('==================================================')
    # Print statistics of the node radii
    print('Statistics on sphere sizes at Voronoi nodes \n(-ve values mean inside framework atoms)')
    print_stat(node_radii)

    print('==================================================')
    # Generate random sampling points in fractional coordinates
    sample_points_fractional = np.random.random((num_samples, 3))
    print('Statistics on sphere sizes at all sampling points \n(-ve values mean inside framework atoms)')
    print_stat(dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_fractional%1))
    print('==================================================')
    # Filter accessible sampling points based on DGrid interpolation
    sample_points_accessible = sample_points_fractional[dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_fractional) > 0]

    # Get the radii for the accessible sampling points
    sample_point_radii = dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_accessible)

    # Print statistics of the sample point radii
    print('Statistics on sphere sizes at sampling points in the void space')
    print_stat(sample_point_radii)

    print('==================================================')
    def points_to_nodes_distances(sample_points_block, nodes_fractional, cell=cell):
        """
        Calculate distances from sample points to Voronoi nodes and determine valid radii.
        This function will be applied to each block of sample points, to be parallelized using Dask.
        
        Parameters:
        - sample_points_block (ndarray): Block of sample points in Cartesian coordinates.
        - nodes_fractional (ndarray): Fractional coordinates of the Voronoi nodes.
        - cell (ndarray): The cell matrix for coordinate transformation.

        Returns:
        - result (ndarray): An array of valid radii for the sample points.
        """
        # Calculate the difference between sample points and nodes
        diff = np.expand_dims(sample_points_block, axis=1) - np.expand_dims(nodes_fractional, axis=0)
        diff = (diff - np.round(diff)).reshape(-1, 3)  # Wrap around periodic boundaries
        diff = np.dot(cell, diff.T).T  # Transform to Cartesian coordinates
        diff = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=1).reshape(-1, nodes_fractional.shape[0])  # Compute distances

        # Print statistics of the distances
        # print_stat(diff)

        # Create a mask for valid node radii
        mask = node_radii > diff
        valid_radii = np.where(mask, node_radii, -np.inf)  # Replace invalid radii with -inf
        max_valid_radii = np.max(valid_radii, axis=1)  # Get the maximum valid radii

        # Print statistics of the maximum valid radii
        # print_stat(max_valid_radii)

        # Get the radii for the sample block
        sample_block_radii = dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_block)

        # Combine sample block radii and maximum valid radii
        result = np.array([s if np.logical_and(m != -np.inf, s > m) else m for s, m in zip(sample_block_radii, max_valid_radii)])

        return result * 2  # Return the result scaled by a factor of 2 converting radii to diameters

    # Create a Dask array from the accessible sample points
    sample_points_da = da.from_array(sample_points_accessible, chunks=(blocksize, 3))

    # Map the distance calculation function over the Dask array
    pore_sizes = sample_points_da.map_blocks(
        points_to_nodes_distances,
        nodes_fractional=nodes_fractional,
        cell=cell,
        chunks=(blocksize,),
        dtype='float32',
        drop_axis=1
    ).compute()  # Compute the result
    print('For trustworthy sampled points')
    # Print statistics of the computed pore sizes
    print_stat(pore_sizes[np.isfinite(pore_sizes)])  # Only print finite values
    print('==================================================')
    return pore_sizes  # Return the computed pore sizes




Show code

def compute_pore_sizes_for_psd(atoms, dgrid=None,  num_samples=50000, spacing=0.25, blocksize=500, probe_radius=0.0):
    """
    Computes the pore sizes from an atomic structure using Voronoi tessellation and DGrid interpolation, to be histogrammed to get the Pore Size Distribution (PSD).

    This function follows these steps:
    1. **DGrid Generation**: If a precomputed DGrid is not provided, a new DGrid is generated from the atomic structure using the specified spacing.
    2. **Cell Matrix Completion**: The cell matrix is completed from the atomic structure to ensure proper periodic boundary conditions.
    3. **Voronoi Tessellation**: A box is created from the cell matrix, and the Voronoi tessellation is computed based on the atomic positions.
    4. **Fractional Coordinates Extraction**: The fractional coordinates of the Voronoi nodes are extracted from the tessellation results.
    5. **DGrid Interpolation**: An interpolator for the DGrid is created to facilitate the calculation of node radii.
    6. **Node Radii Calculation**: The radii of the Voronoi nodes are calculated using the interpolator.
    7. **Random Sampling Points Generation**: A specified number of random sampling points are generated in fractional coordinates.
    8. **Accessibility Filtering**: The accessible sampling points are filtered based on the DGrid interpolation results.
    9. **Sample Point Radii Calculation**: The radii for the accessible sampling points are obtained using the DGrid interpolator.
    10. **Distance Calculation**: For each block of sample points, the distances to the Voronoi nodes are calculated, and valid radii are determined.
    11. **Result Compilation**: The maximum valid radii and the sample block radii are combined to produce the final pore sizes.
    12. **Dask Processing**: The calculations are parallelized using Dask to handle large datasets efficiently.

    Parameters:
    - atoms (Atoms): The ASE Atoms object containing atomic structure data.
    - dgrid (DGrid, optional): Precomputed DGrid. If None, it will be computed using the default spacing.
    - num_samples (int): The number of random sampling points to generate. Default is 50000.
    - spacing (float): The spacing for the DGrid computation. Default is 0.25.
    - blocksize (int): The size of the blocks for Dask array processing. Default is 1000. If you have less RAM, and is 
    getting a seg fault as a result, please reduce this number or the num_samples.

    Returns:
    - pore_sizes (ndarray): An array of computed pore sizes.
    """
    def print_stat(data):
        """Compute and print basic statistics of a numpy array."""
        max_value = np.max(data)
        min_value = np.min(data)
        mean_value = np.mean(data)
        variance_value = np.var(data)
        # print(f"Name of variable: )
        print(f"shape: {data.shape}")
        
        print(f"Max: {max_value}")
        print(f"Min: {min_value}")
        print(f"Mean: {mean_value}")
        print(f"Variance: {variance_value}")


    import numpy as np 
    import dask.array as da
    from ase.geometry import complete_cell
    from freud.locality import Voronoi 
    from freud.box import Box 
    import mofography as mgr
    # Generate a DGrid from the atomic structure if not provided
    if dgrid is None:
        dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=spacing)

    # Complete the cell matrix from the atomic structure
    cell = complete_cell(atoms.get_cell().T)

    # Create a box for the Voronoi tessellation
    box = Box.from_matrix(cell)

    # Initialize and compute the Voronoi tessellation
    voro = Voronoi()
    voro.compute((box, atoms.get_positions()))

    # Get the fractional coordinates of the Voronoi nodes
    nodes_fractional = mgr.get_fractional_coordinates(np.vstack(voro.polytopes), atoms)

    # Create an interpolator for the DGrid
    dgrid_interpolator = mgr.interpolate_dgrid(dgrid)

    # Calculate the node radii using the interpolator
    node_radii = dgrid_interpolator(nodes_fractional % 1)

    print('==================================================')
    # Print statistics of the node radii
    print('Statistics on sphere sizes at Voronoi nodes \n(-ve values mean inside framework atoms)')
    print_stat(node_radii)

    print('==================================================')
    # Generate random sampling points in fractional coordinates
    sample_points_fractional = np.random.random((num_samples, 3))
    print('Statistics on sphere sizes at all sampling points \n(-ve values mean inside framework atoms)')
    print_stat(dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_fractional%1))
    print('==================================================')
    # Filter accessible sampling points based on DGrid interpolation
    sample_points_accessible = sample_points_fractional[dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_fractional) > probe_radius]

    # Get the radii for the accessible sampling points
    sample_point_radii = dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_accessible) - probe_radius

    # Print statistics of the sample point radii
    print('Statistics on sphere sizes at sampling points in the void space')
    print('Sample point radii =', sample_point_radii)
    print_stat(sample_point_radii)

    print('==================================================')
    def points_to_nodes_distances(sample_points_block, nodes_fractional, cell=cell):
        """
        Calculate distances from sample points to Voronoi nodes and determine valid radii.
        This function will be applied to each block of sample points, to be parallelized using Dask.
        
        Parameters:
        - sample_points_block (ndarray): Block of sample points in Cartesian coordinates.
        - nodes_fractional (ndarray): Fractional coordinates of the Voronoi nodes.
        - cell (ndarray): The cell matrix for coordinate transformation.

        Returns:
        - result (ndarray): An array of valid radii for the sample points.
        """
        # Calculate the difference between sample points and nodes
        diff = np.expand_dims(sample_points_block, axis=1) - np.expand_dims(nodes_fractional, axis=0)
        diff = (diff - np.round(diff)).reshape(-1, 3)  # Wrap around periodic boundaries
        diff = np.dot(cell, diff.T).T  # Transform to Cartesian coordinates
        diff = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=1).reshape(-1, nodes_fractional.shape[0])  # Compute distances

        # Print statistics of the distances
        # print_stat(diff)

        # Create a mask for valid node radii
        mask = (node_radii - probe_radius)> diff
        valid_radii = np.where(mask, node_radii - probe_radius, -np.inf)  # Replace invalid radii with -inf
        max_valid_radii = np.max(valid_radii, axis=1)  # Get the maximum valid radii

        # Print statistics of the maximum valid radii
        # print_stat(max_valid_radii)

        # Get the radii for the sample block
        sample_block_radii = dgrid_interpolator(sample_points_block) - probe_radius

        # Combine sample block radii and maximum valid radii
        result = np.array([s if np.logical_and(m != -np.inf, s > m) else m for s, m in zip(sample_block_radii, max_valid_radii)])

        return result * 2  # Return the result scaled by a factor of 2 converting radii to diameters

    # Create a Dask array from the accessible sample points
    sample_points_da = da.from_array(sample_points_accessible, chunks=(blocksize, 3))

    # Map the distance calculation function over the Dask array
    pore_sizes = sample_points_da.map_blocks(
        points_to_nodes_distances,
        nodes_fractional=nodes_fractional,
        cell=cell,
        chunks=(blocksize,),
        dtype='float32',
        drop_axis=1
    ).compute()  # Compute the result
    print('For trustworthy sampled points')
    # Print statistics of the computed pore sizes
    print_stat(pore_sizes[np.isfinite(pore_sizes)])  # Only print finite values
    print('==================================================')
    return pore_sizes  # Return the computed pore sizes

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

def get_pore_size_distribution_trace(distances, normalize=False, cumulative=False):
    # if normalize:
        # distances = distances / np.max(distances)
    
    # Create histogram data
    hist, bin_edges = np.histogram(distances, bins=np.linspace(0,100, 200), density=normalize)

    if cumulative:

    trace = go.Scatter(
        x=binC, 
        y=hist,

        name='Pore Size Distribution',
        line=dict(width=2)
    )

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
text:
In this notebook we will
The winding method works on the pore graph: nodes are pockets, edges are windows carrying a periodic cell offset. A cluster percolates along an axis if it contains a cycle whose accumulated offset (winding number) is non-zero along that axis. This is exact for contorted channels that wrap around the cell obliquely. See Face merging vs winding and Accessibility for the background.
Prerequisites: distance grid and region segmentation.

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
text:
Imports


Show code
import warnings, logging
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
logging.disable(logging.WARNING)
import numpy as np
from ase.io import read
import mofography as mgr

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
text:
Segment the structure
The winding functions take the periodic segmentation seg (with its distance grid), so we build it once and reuse it.
The example structure is NU-1000 (examples/TestCIFs/NU-1000_S1.cif), a mesoporous MOF with large hexagonal channels along z, at grid spacing 0.5 Å.


Show code
atoms = read("../examples/TestCIFs/NU-1000_S1.cif")   # NU-1000 (examples/TestCIFs)
spacing = 0.5
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid.astype(np.float32), atoms,
    mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
    spacing=spacing, compute_connections=True, return_dgrid=True, disable_tqdm=True,
)
print("pockets (PBC-grouped):", len(seg["maxima_pbc"]))


pockets (PBC-grouped): 11

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
text:
LCD, PLD and LIS (winding)
get_pore_dia_mgr_winding is the one-call entry point. It returns (lcd, pld, lis, dgrid), all diameters in Å. PLD is the largest probe diameter for which a percolating winding cycle exists; LIS is the largest included sphere along the percolating pathways. (Older code calls the third value dfsd.)

There is no function called compute_pore_diameters_winding; get_pore_dia_mgr_winding is the actual name.



Show code
lcd, pld, lis, _ = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(results=seg, mat_atoms=atoms, include_dangling=True)
print(f"LCD = {lcd:.3f} Å   PLD = {pld:.3f} Å   LIS = {lis:.3f} Å")


LCD = 29.415 Å   PLD = 28.815 Å   LIS = 29.415 Å

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
text:
Percolation history (winding)
compute_percolation_history_winding sweeps the probe radius and returns (percolation_history, pld_locations, final_clusters). Each history entry is (probe_radius, {'x': [...], 'y': [...], 'z': [...]}), where each axis lists the percolating clusters (lists of pocket labels). step is the sweep step in Å (probe radius).


Show code
hist, pld_locations, clusters = mgr.compute_percolation_history_winding(seg, step=0.1)
print("entries:", len(hist), " first probe radius:", hist[0][0], " last:", round(hist[-1][0], 2))
print("percolating clusters at the last probe radius (pockets per cluster):")
for axis, cl in hist[-1][1].items():
    print(" ", axis, [len(x) for x in cl])


entries: 145  first probe radius: 0.0  last: 14.4
percolating clusters at the last probe radius (pockets per cluster):
  x []
  y []
  z [8]


The last entry is the largest probe radius for which some axis still percolates; PLD/2 should match it to within the sweep step. For NU-1000 the last radius is about 14.4 Å (PLD about 28.8 Å), and only the z axis still percolates: the large channels run along z, and the narrower connections in the xy plane close at smaller probes.


Show code
print(f"PLD/2 = {pld/2:.3f} Å, last percolating radius = {hist[-1][0]:.3f} Å")
assert abs(pld/2 - hist[-1][0]) <= 0.1 + 1e-6


PLD/2 = 14.407 Å, last percolating radius = 14.400 Å

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
section: Visualize the percolating clusters at the PLD probe
text:
Visualize the percolating clusters at the PLD probe
The percolation history is ordered by increasing probe radius, so its last entry, hist[-1], is the largest probe that still percolates. That radius is the pore limiting radius (PLD/2), and the cluster stored there is what you see below: the last percolating cluster, the pores and windows that stay connected across the cell at the PLD probe. A slightly larger probe breaks it.


Show code
import plotly.graph_objects as go
traces = list(mgr.plot_percolated_cluster_meshes(
    hist, seg["dgrid"], seg["regions"], atoms,
    isovalue=1.0, stylize=True, probe_radius=hist[-1][0],
))
cell = mgr.plot_cell(atoms)
traces += list(cell) if isinstance(cell, (list, tuple)) else [cell]
fig = go.Figure(traces)
fig.update_layout(scene_aspectmode="data", height=600, margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=0, b=0))
fig
fig.write_image("tutorial_images/pld_percolation_clusters.png", width=1000, height=700)  # static preview for the docs

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
section: Comparison only: face merging (older, less accurate)
text:
Comparison only: face merging (older, less accurate)
Before the winding method, percolation was decided on the labelled voxel grid by merging labels across periodic faces (the same idea as PoreBlazer-style voxel sweeps). It cannot see paths that leave the cell, wrap around and re-enter, and it is tied to voxel contiguity, so it is less accurate on contorted frameworks. It is kept here only for comparison; use the winding functions above for real work.
On NU-1000 the two differ by only about 0.2 Å in PLD (29.0 vs 28.8 Å), which is the size of a grid step effect at spacing 0.5 Å. The gap grows on frameworks whose channels wrap obliquely.


Show code
lcd_f, pld_f, lis_f, _ = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr(atoms, kwargs=dict(spacing=spacing))   # face merging
rows = [("winding (standard)", lcd, pld, lis), ("face merging (legacy)", lcd_f, pld_f, lis_f)]
for name, a, b, c in rows:
    print(f"{name:<24s} LCD {a:7.3f}  PLD {b:7.3f}  LIS {c:7.3f}  Å")
print(f"PLD difference (face - winding): {pld_f - pld:+.3f} Å")


winding (standard)       LCD  29.415  PLD  28.815  LIS  29.415  Å
face merging (legacy)    LCD  29.615  PLD  29.002  LIS  29.615  Å
PLD difference (face - winding): +0.187 Å

title: PLD and percolation (winding method)
text:
Summary

Use get_pore_dia_mgr_winding for LCD / PLD / LIS and compute_percolation_history_winding for the percolation history.
Winding numbers detect true periodic percolation, including oblique wrap-around channels.
Face merging (get_pore_dia_mgr, lattice histories) is retained only to compare with voxel-based tools.

title: Download a subset from MOFDB and Quick Cluster
text:
In this tutorial, we see how to download a subset of structures from the MOFDB database using a wrapper function in mofography. MOFDB is a large database of nanoporous materials, including MOFs and zeolites that is hosted by Northwestern University. https://mof.tech.northwestern.edu/
For a lot of the materials workflows, it is very convenient to have a subset of structures to be used as a starting point, and to be saved as a pandas dataframe, that some of the textural properties of the material along with its crystallographic information. However, downloading large datasets can be cumbersome. Hence, mofography provides a wrapper that can do this asynchronously, meaning, the pages and pages of your search results will be downloaded in parallel, saving a lot of time. Note that at the time of writing, MOFDB itself has a python API that does this, https://github.com/n8ta/mofdb-client, the comparison of speeds of the two codes is not tested, but you are welcome to test it out as well.
Note that in order to avoid excessive strain on the MOFDB website, it is recommended you save the downloaded dataset locally (we will show this at the end) instead of downloading it every time.
Once we have the dataset, we can create ASE atoms objects from it, pick one or more at random and perform a mofography workflo. In this example, we simply perform the quick cluster workflow, but feel free to build one of your own. If you don’t remember what the Quick Cluster workflow does, please go check out the Quick Cluster notebook in the tutorials.

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
In this notebook:
The same code scales to an HPC or cloud cluster by swapping the LocalCluster() for a SLURMCluster or KubeCluster. See the Dask docs for details.
Show code
# --- General imports --------------------------------------------------------
import os
import sys
import shutil
import tarfile
import pickle
from io import BytesIO
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

# --- ASE + mofography --------------------------------------------------------
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
from mofography.cif_io import read_cif_to_ase  # fast Rust CIF reader (returns ase.Atoms)
from ase.build import make_supercell
from ase.geometry import complete_cell

# --- Dask for HTS ------------------------------------------------------------
import dask
from dask import delayed
from dask.distributed import Client, LocalCluster, progress

# --- Notebook hygiene --------------------------------------------------------
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=DeprecationWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning, module="pymatgen")

# --- Path to the repo / docs folder (works from any cwd) --------------------
# Adjust REPO_ROOT to point at your local mofography clone. The default
# assumes the notebook lives at <repo>/docs/hts_using_mofography.ipynb.
REPO_ROOT = Path(mgr.__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DOCS_DIR  = REPO_ROOT / "docs"
TESTCIF_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "examples" / "TestCIFs"
sys.path.insert(0, str(REPO_ROOT))

print(f"mofography version: {mgr.__version__ if hasattr(mgr, '__version__') else 'dev'}")
print(f"REPO_ROOT           = {REPO_ROOT}")
print(f"TESTCIF_DIR         = {TESTCIF_DIR}  ({len(list(TESTCIF_DIR.glob('*.cif')))} CIFs)")

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
1. Load the dataset
The original notebook pulled a pre-built MOFdb feather file. To make this tutorial self-contained we read a small set of CIFs directly from examples/TestCIFs/. Drop your own CIFs into a folder of your choice and point cif_dir at it.
For very large datasets (1000+ structures) it is much faster to pre-pack the CIFs into a compressed Parquet dataframe first — see hts_periodic_seg_benchmark.ipynb for the same trick used in batch benchmarking.


Show code
# Pick a small set of test MOFs for the demo. The first is the canonical
# IRMOF-1; the rest are pulled from examples/TestCIFs/. Replace with your own
# folder if you have one.
cif_dir = TESTCIF_DIR
all_cifs = sorted(cif_dir.glob("*.cif"))

# Use a small, diverse subset so the demo runs in a few minutes on a laptop.
demo_stems = ["IRMOF-1", "UiO-66-RASPA", "ZIF-8-RASPA", "NU-1000_S1", "P1-Cu-BTC"]
cif_paths = [cif_dir / f"{stem}.cif" for stem in demo_stems if (cif_dir / f"{stem}.cif").exists()]
# Fall back to the first five available CIFs if the canonical set is missing.
if not cif_paths:
    cif_paths = all_cifs[:5]

print(f"Loading {len(cif_paths)} CIFs:")
for p in cif_paths:
    print(f"  {p.name}")




Show code
# Read CIFs into ASE Atoms objects. We attach the stem to atoms.info['name']
# so the saved output files keep their material name.
def load_cif_to_atoms(cif_path: Path):
    atoms = read_cif_to_ase(cif_path)  # Rust CIF reader, much faster than ase.io.read over many files
    atoms.info["name"] = cif_path.stem
    return atoms

iza_atoms = [load_cif_to_atoms(p) for p in cif_paths]
for a in iza_atoms:
    print(f"  {a.info['name']:<20s}  {len(a):>4d} atoms  cell={a.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(1)}")

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
2. Single-material workflow (new merged API)
The new API collapses what used to be five separate calls (dgrid_from_atoms_cpu → regions_from_dgrid → apply_pbc → get_rag_from_regions_and_grid → get_connections_for_rag) into two:
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5).astype(np.float32)
seg   = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(dgrid, atoms, ...)
The seg dict returns everything you used to assemble by hand: regions, PBC-merged regions, maxima, PBC groups, connections, and the input parameters used. See pbc_considerations.qmd for the full key reference.

Don’t use dgrid_from_atoms_gpu or dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb. They are known to mis-handle non-orthorhombic cells. The *_rust backends are correct for all cell types.



Show code
# Pick one material and run the new merged pipeline on it.
mat_atoms = iza_atoms[0]
mat_name  = mat_atoms.info["name"]
print(f"Working on: {mat_name}  ({len(mat_atoms)} atoms)")

# --- Step 1: distance grid (Rust exact) --------------------------------------
spacing = 0.5
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing)
dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)        # Rust kernel requires float32
print(f"dgrid shape={dgrid.shape}  void_max={dgrid.max():.2f} Å  size={dgrid.nbytes/1e6:.1f} MB")




Show code
# --- Step 2: periodic segmentation (one call) ------------------------------
seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid, mat_atoms,
    mask_thickness=0.05,
    h=0.2,
    min_distance=1.5,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    spacing=spacing,
    compute_connections=True,    # also fill seg['connections']
    extra_padding=5.0,           # default halo
    watershed_backend="rust_det", # default; see Section 9 for alternatives
    disable_tqdm=True,
)
print("Segmentation keys:")
for k, v in seg.items():
    if hasattr(v, "shape"):
        print(f"  {k:30s} ndarray  shape={v.shape}  dtype={v.dtype}")
    elif isinstance(v, (list, tuple, set)):
        print(f"  {k:30s} {type(v).__name__:6s}  ({len(v)} items)")
    elif isinstance(v, dict):
        print(f"  {k:30s} dict    ({len(v)} entries)")
    else:
        print(f"  {k:30s} {type(v).__name__}")

print()
print(f"  Pockets (PBC-merged): {len(seg['maxima_pbc'])}")
print(f"  Unique regions:       {len(seg['unique_regions'])}")
print(f"  PBC groups:           {len(seg['pbc_groups'])}")

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
3. Pocket type detection (HTS feature)
The interactive app exposes pocket type detection on every saved material. The same call works in Python: assign_pocket_types clusters pockets by their environment (peak probe radius, framework fingerprint, connectivity) using env_cluster by default.
enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds should be run once before typing so the per-pocket PSD sampling cost is paid only once. Both modify the dict in place by default.


Show code
# Cache pocket PSDs and assign types. This is exactly the call the
# Streamlit "Pocket types" panel makes.
seg = mgr.enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds(seg, mat_atoms)
print(f"pocket_psds cached:   {seg.get('pocket_psds') is not None}")
print(f"probe radius used:    {seg.get('pocket_psd_probe_radius_a'):.2f} Å")

typed = mgr.assign_pocket_types(seg, mat_atoms, method="env_cluster")
print(f"\nPocketTypingResult.ok = {typed.ok}  (method={typed.method})")
print(f"  n_types:   {typed.n_types}")
print(f"  n_pockets: {typed.n_pockets}")
print()
for t in typed.type_summary:
    print(f"  type {t['type_id']}: n={t['n_pockets']:<3d}  "
          f"max_r ∈ [{t['max_r_min_a']:.2f}, {t['max_r_max_a']:.2f}] Å  "
          f"vol ∈ [{t['volume_min_a3']:.0f}, {t['volume_max_a3']:.0f}] Å³")

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
4. Accessibility — LCD / PLD / DFSD
Once the segmentation is done, get_pore_dia_mgr_winding runs the winding-number percolation sweep to compute the largest cavity diameter (LCD), the pore-limiting diameter (PLD), and the dominant flat surface diameter (DFSD). This is the same routine the app runs on the Accessibility tab.
The sweep also stores a per-radius percolation_history that is saved into the results .npz (and into the *_pore_dia.csv we build later).


Show code
from mofography import get_pore_dia_mgr_winding

# get_pore_dia_mgr_winding returns (lcd, pld, dfsd, percolation_grid).
lcd, pld, dfsd, _perco_grid = get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(
    mat_atoms, dgrid=dgrid,
    kwargs=dict(seg=seg, spacing=spacing, extra_padding=5.0, disable_tqdm=True),
)
print(f"LCD  = {lcd:.3f} Å")
print(f"PLD  = {pld:.3f} Å")
print(f"DFSD = {dfsd:.3f} Å")

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
5. Visualize the single material
show_mof_plotly is the canonical figure used by the web app. Pass the typed_result to colour the cavity surface by pocket type.


Show code
fig = mgr.show_mof_plotly(seg, mat_atoms, typed_result=typed, stylize=True)
fig.update_layout(title=f"{mat_name} — pocket types (env_cluster)")
# NB: fig.show() is interactive; the rendered HTML in _freeze/ embeds a PNG snapshot
# of the same scene so the static build stays light. We avoid fig.write_html() here
# because Plotly HTML embeds the whole grid as JSON (~4 MB per material) and is the
# reason the previous version of this notebook ballooned to 9.2 MB.
fig.show()

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
6. Wrap the workflow for Dask
The new merged API makes the per-material wrapper much smaller than the old multi-step function. We return the segmentation dict and the typing result together so downstream code (savers, RAG builder) doesn’t have to re-thread inputs through the dask graph.


Show code
import time

# Per-material HTS worker. The Rust dgrid + segmentation pair is the hot
# path; pocket-typing is optional and slightly slower (extra PSD sampling).
def run_one(mat_atoms, *,
            spacing=0.5,
            do_pocket_typing=True,
            do_pore_dia=True,
            watershed_backend="rust_det",
            extra_padding=5.0,
            ):
    """Compute the segmentation, pocket types, and pore diameters for one MOF.

    Returns a dict ready to be saved to .npz, or None on failure.
    """
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing)
        dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)
        seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
            dgrid, mat_atoms,
            mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
            spacing=spacing, compute_connections=True,
            extra_padding=extra_padding, watershed_backend=watershed_backend,
            disable_tqdm=True,
        )

        typed = None
        if do_pocket_typing:
            seg = mgr.enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds(seg, mat_atoms)
            typed = mgr.assign_pocket_types(seg, mat_atoms, method="env_cluster")

        pore_dia = None
        if do_pore_dia:
            _lcd, _pld, _dfsd, _perco = get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(
                mat_atoms, dgrid=dgrid,
                kwargs=dict(seg=seg, spacing=spacing, extra_padding=extra_padding, disable_tqdm=True),
            )
            pore_dia = {
                "lcd":  float(_lcd),
                "pld":  float(_pld),
                "dfsd": float(_dfsd),
                "history_points": int(_perco.size),
            }

        return {
            "name":           mat_atoms.info.get("name", "unknown"),
            "num_atoms":      int(len(mat_atoms)),
            "cellpar":        np.asarray(mat_atoms.cell.cellpar(), dtype=np.float64),
            "dgrid_shape":    np.asarray(dgrid.shape, dtype=np.int32),
            "maxima_pbc":     np.asarray(seg["maxima_pbc"]),
            "regions_pbc":    np.asarray(seg["regions_pbc"]),
            "pbc_groups":     seg["pbc_groups"],
            "connections":    seg["connections"],
            "n_pockets":      int(len(seg["maxima_pbc"])),
            "n_regions":      int(len(seg["unique_regions"])),
            "pocket_types":   typed.n_types        if typed is not None and typed.ok else 0,
            "pocket_summary": typed.type_summary  if typed is not None and typed.ok else None,
            "pore_dia":       pore_dia,
            "wall_seconds":   float(time.perf_counter() - t0),
        }
    except Exception as exc:
        return {"name": mat_atoms.info.get("name", "unknown"), "error": repr(exc)}

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
7. Build the delayed futures
Each material becomes one delayed task. With Dask’s threaded scheduler this also lets us overlap the file I/O on the front end (CIF reads) with the Rust dgrid/segmentation work on the back end.


Show code
delayed_futures = [delayed(run_one)(a) for a in iza_atoms]
print(f"{len(delayed_futures)} delayed tasks queued.")

# Smoke-test the wrapper on the first material *before* starting the cluster.
# This is the canonical "test one to make sure it works" step from the
# original notebook — it surfaces import / API errors without spinning up
# Dask.
print()
print("--- test one ---")
first = delayed_futures[0].compute()
print(f"name      : {first['name']}")
print(f"n_pockets : {first['n_pockets']}")
print(f"n_types   : {first['pocket_types']}")
print(f"pore_dia  : {first['pore_dia']}")
print(f"wall      : {first['wall_seconds']:.2f} s")

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
8. Start a local Dask cluster
LocalCluster() gives one process per CPU core by default. On a laptop that’s usually 4–16 workers; on an HPC use SLURMCluster instead and set n_workers = # cores on one node so data transfer stays local.


Show code
# Shutdown any prior cluster (idempotent — fine to re-run).
try:
    client.close()
    cluster.close()
except (NameError, AttributeError):
    pass

cluster = LocalCluster(n_workers=min(4, os.cpu_count() or 1), threads_per_worker=1)
client  = Client(cluster)
print("Dashboard link:", client.dashboard_link)

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
9. Persist the workflow
dask.persist submits every task to the cluster and returns the running futures. We then attach a progress bar so you can watch the queue drain.


Show code
futures = dask.persist(*delayed_futures)
progress(futures)

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
10. Collect the results
We pull each future’s result with a None fallback for any that errored. Dask’s progress(futures) cell above should be fully done before you run this.


Show code
collected = client.compute(futures)
results = [f.result() if f.status == "finished" else None for f in collected]
n_ok    = sum(r is not None for r in results)
n_fail  = sum(r is None for r in results)
print(f"finished: {n_ok}/{len(results)}   failed: {n_fail}")
print()
for r in results:
    if r is None:
        print("  <None>")
    elif "error" in r:
        print(f"  {r['name']:<20s}  ERROR: {r['error']}")
    else:
        print(f"  {r['name']:<20s}  pockets={r['n_pockets']:>2d}  "
              f"types={r['pocket_types']:>2d}  "
              f"PLD={r['pore_dia']['pld']:.2f} Å  wall={r['wall_seconds']:.1f} s")

title: High-Throughput Processing using Mofography and Dask
text:
11. Save options
The interactive app stores per-material results under hts_output/<stem>/ with a small set of canonical files. We replicate that layout here so the hts_output/ folder can be opened by the Streamlit app for browsing or by the mgrcli CLI for downstream work (mgrcli aggregate ...).
The four canonical files per material are:







File
Contents




<stem>_results.npz
Full segmentation dict (dgrid, regions, maxima, connections, typing)


<stem>_pore_dia.csv
LCD, PLD, DFSD + history point count


<stem>_psd_psd_uniform.csv
Globally sampled pore-size distribution


<stem>_psd_psd_pockets.csv
Per-pocket probe-occupiable PSDs


<stem>_rag_clustered.pkl
NetworkX region-adjacency graph (RAG)



We build the same files here, then tar -czf the whole folder at the end so a 1000-MOF HTS run ships as a single archive.


Show code
# Point the output at the repo's docs/hts_output folder so the rendered
# HTML can be browsed without a separate demo step.
hts_root = DOCS_DIR / "hts_output"
hts_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# We re-run each material to produce the full output set. The `run_one`
# wrapper above returns a *summary* dict; here we write a richer saver
# that mirrors the Streamlit / mgrcli output format.
def save_one(mat_atoms, out_dir, *, spacing=0.5, do_pocket_typing=True, do_pore_dia=True):
    """Run the full pipeline and save all canonical files under out_dir."""
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    stem = mat_atoms.info.get("name", out_dir.name)

    dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing).astype(np.float32)
    seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
        dgrid, mat_atoms, mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5,
        threshold_abs=1.5, spacing=spacing, compute_connections=True,
        extra_padding=5.0, watershed_backend="rust_det", disable_tqdm=True,
    )

    typed = None
    if do_pocket_typing:
        seg = mgr.enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds(seg, mat_atoms)
        typed = mgr.assign_pocket_types(seg, mat_atoms, method="env_cluster")

    _lcd, _pld, _dfsd, _perco = get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(
        mat_atoms, dgrid=dgrid,
        kwargs=dict(seg=seg, spacing=spacing, extra_padding=5.0, disable_tqdm=True),
    )
    pore_dia = {"lcd": float(_lcd),
                "pld": float(_pld),
                "dfsd": float(_dfsd),
                "history_points": int(_perco.size)}

    # --- 1) <stem>_results.npz ---------------------------------------------
    save_dict = {
        "dgrid":            dgrid,
        "maxima_pbc":       np.asarray(seg["maxima_pbc"]),
        "regions_pbc":      np.asarray(seg["regions_pbc"]),
        "pbc_groups":       np.asarray(seg["pbc_groups"], dtype=object),
        "connections":      np.asarray(seg["connections"], dtype=object),
        "lcd":              pore_dia["lcd"],
        "pld":              pore_dia["pld"],
        "dfsd":             pore_dia["dfsd"],
        "n_pockets":        int(len(seg["maxima_pbc"])),
        "n_regions":        int(len(seg["unique_regions"])),
    }
    if typed is not None and typed.ok:
        save_dict["regions_cluster"]      = np.asarray(typed.regions_cluster)
        save_dict["pocket_types_detected"]= typed.n_types
        save_dict["pocket_typing_method"] = typed.method
        save_dict["pocket_type_summary"]  = np.asarray(typed.type_summary, dtype=object)
        save_dict["pocket_rep_to_type"]   = np.asarray(typed.rep_to_type)
    np.savez_compressed(out_dir / f"{stem}_results.npz", **save_dict)

    # --- 2) <stem>_pore_dia.csv --------------------------------------------
    pd.DataFrame(
        [
            ("LCD", pore_dia["lcd"],  "Å"),
            ("PLD", pore_dia["pld"],  "Å"),
            ("DFSD", pore_dia["dfsd"], "Å"),
            ("Percolation history points", pore_dia["history_points"], "count"),
        ],
        columns=["Metric", "Value", "Unit"],
    ).to_csv(out_dir / f"{stem}_pore_dia.csv", index=False)

    # --- 3) PSDs (uniform + pocketwise) -----------------------------------
    # compute_pocket_psds_for_segmentation is the same call used by
    # enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds; we just write the result out.
    if do_pocket_typing and "pocket_psds" in seg:
        # pocket_psds is dict[region_label -> {bin_centers, hist, num_samples, ...}]
        psd_pockets = seg["pocket_psds"]
        rows = []
        for region_label, p in psd_pockets.items():
            centers = p["bin_centers"]
            counts  = p["hist"]
            bw = float(centers[1] - centers[0]) if len(centers) > 1 else 0.25
            for b, c in zip(centers, counts):
                rows.append({
                    "region_label": int(region_label),
                    "bin_start":    float(b) - bw / 2,
                    "bin_end":      float(b) + bw / 2,
                    "bin_center":   float(b),
                    "count":        int(c),
                })
        if rows:
            pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv(out_dir / f"{stem}_psd_psd_pockets.csv", index=False)

    from mofography.rust_fun import compute_pore_sizes_uniform_rust
    _pts, pore_sizes = compute_pore_sizes_uniform_rust(
        dgrid, mat_atoms, num_samples_total=20000,
    )
    _bins = np.linspace(0, 50, 200)
    _hist, _edges = np.histogram(pore_sizes * 2, bins=_bins)
    pd.DataFrame({
        "bin_start":  _edges[:-1],
        "bin_end":    _edges[1:],
        "bin_center": (_edges[:-1] + _edges[1:]) / 2,
        "count":      _hist,
    }).to_csv(out_dir / f"{stem}_psd_psd_uniform.csv", index=False)

    # --- 4) RAG pickle -----------------------------------------------------
    from mofography.compute import rag_from_connections
    maxima = seg["maxima_pbc"]
    rag = rag_from_connections(seg["connections"], maxima)
    with open(out_dir / f"{stem}_rag_clustered.pkl", "wb") as f:
        pickle.dump(rag, f)

    return {"name": stem, "out_dir": str(out_dir), "pore_dia": pore_dia}

12. Tar on done
For large HTS runs (100+ materials) the per-material folder layout is annoying to ship. The tar-on-done helper bundles the whole hts_output/ folder into a single .tar.gz and (optionally) moves it to a release location. The Streamlit app can read straight from a tarball, so this is also the format the HTS tab expects when ingesting a completed run from another machine.


Show code
def tar_on_done(hts_root: Path, archive_path: Path, *, glob="*"):
    """Bundle hts_root into a gzipped tarball. Returns the archive path.

    `glob` lets you restrict the bundle (e.g. glob='IRMOF-1*' to ship one MOF).
    """
    archive_path = Path(archive_path)
    archive_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    if archive_path.exists():
        archive_path.unlink()
    with tarfile.open(archive_path, "w:gz") as tf:
        for sub in sorted(hts_root.glob(glob)):
            if sub.is_dir():
                tf.add(sub, arcname=sub.name)
    return archive_path

archive = REPO_ROOT / "outputs" / "hts_using_mofography_demo.tar.gz"
archive.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
tar_on_done(hts_root, archive)

print(f"Archived {hts_root} -> {archive}  ({archive.stat().st_size/1024:.1f} KB)")
print()
# List the contents to confirm.
with tarfile.open(archive, "r:gz") as tf:
    for m in tf.getmembers()[:12]:
        print(f"  {m.size:>9,d}  {m.name}")
    if len(tf.getmembers()) > 12:
        print(f"  ... ({len(tf.getmembers()) - 12} more)")

text:
13. Watershed backend comparison (mini-tutorial)
do_periodic_segmentation_rust ships with four watershed backends. They all return the same segmentation keys; the differences are determinism, speed, and the order in which basins are explored (which can shift the integer labels of equal-volume pockets).









Backend
Determinism
Speed
When to use




rust_det
✅ (default)
fast
Web app default. Stable labels, good for HTS re-runs.


rust_det_parallel
✅ (deterministic by basin)
fastest on big cells
Drop-in for rust_det when scaling past ~1 M voxels.


rust_bucket
⚠️ basin order varies
fastest on small cells
Legacy. Keep for parity checks; don’t trust label IDs.


skimage
✅
slowest (Python)
Pure-Python cross-check. Requires scikit-image.



The cell below re-runs the segmentation for IRMOF-1 with each backend and compares (a) wall time, (b) number of PBC-merged pockets, and (c) the label mapping. For most MOFs the basin count is identical across backends; label IDs can differ but pocket_psd_probe_radius_a and type_summary are backend-invariant (the env_cluster typing reads pocket_psds, not labels).


Show code
backends = ["rust_det", "rust_det_parallel", "rust_bucket", "skimage"]
rows = []
seg_dicts = {}

for b in backends:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        s = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
            dgrid, mat_atoms,
            mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
            spacing=spacing, compute_connections=True, extra_padding=5.0,
            watershed_backend=b, disable_tqdm=True,
        )
        ok = True
        err = ""
    except Exception as exc:
        ok = False
        err = repr(exc)
        s = None
    dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
    if ok:
        rows.append({
            "backend":      b,
            "wall_s":       dt,
            "n_pockets":    int(len(s["maxima_pbc"])),
            "n_regions":    int(len(s["unique_regions"])),
            "n_pbc_groups": int(len(s["pbc_groups"])),
        })
        seg_dicts[b] = s
    else:
        rows.append({"backend": b, "wall_s": dt, "error": err})

cmp_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Backend comparison on IRMOF-1 (single core, same dgrid):")
print(cmp_df.to_string(index=False))




Show code
# Cross-check: do all backends agree on the *physical* number of pockets
# (maxima_pbc)? For most cells they should.
if len(seg_dicts) > 1:
    pock_counts = {b: len(s["maxima_pbc"]) for b, s in seg_dicts.items()}
    print("Pocket counts per backend:", pock_counts)
    if len(set(pock_counts.values())) == 1:
        print("  ✓ All backends agree on the number of pockets.")
    else:
        print("  ✗ Backend counts differ — investigate the basin-ordering difference.")

text:
14. Conclusions and next steps
In this notebook we:

Loaded a small MOF set from examples/TestCIFs/ (no MOFdb token required).
Computed the full segmentation in two API calls per material (dgrid_from_atoms_rust → do_periodic_segmentation_rust).
Added pocket-type detection with enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds + assign_pocket_types (the HTS feature exposed on the app’s Pocket types tab).
Computed accessibility metrics (LCD/PLD/DFSD) with the winding percolation sweep.
Parallelized the workflow with Dask delayed and a LocalCluster.
Saved every material to the canonical hts_output/<stem>/ layout (_results.npz, _pore_dia.csv, PSD CSVs, RAG pickle).
Bundled the whole run as a single tar.gz for shipping (tar_on_done).
Compared the four watershed backends on a single material.

Exercises

HPC run. Swap LocalCluster() for SLURMCluster and point the same run_one at a 10k-MOF dataset on your cluster’s scratch.
Re-run on change. Persist the futures list and re-compute() only the materials whose CIF mtime changed (skip already-processed stems).
CLI parity. Compare the .npz keys here with the mgrcli process output on the same CIF (the CLI saves a superset including RAG-as-arrays, timing, and accessibility method flags). See cli_quickstart.qmd.
Backend sensitivity. Re-run the comparison on a MOF with many tiny cages (e.g. ZIF-8) and see whether the basin-order difference matters for assign_pocket_types.

title: Graph Convolution on RAGs to predict adsorption isotherms
text:
NOte: Only works with Numpy 1.23.* for now, will fix soon.
In this notebook, we will start from scratch, create a dataset of pore graphs, learn a graph embedding for these pore graphs using Graph Convolutional Net, trained such that the embedding will accurately predict (or try to) hydrogen adsorption of the IZA dataset based on the data pre tabulated in MOFDB. Once we have a working model, we will estimate it’s accuracy, and also do hyper parameter tuning using Bayesian Optimization as implemented in Optuna. Then we can try to grab a bunch of CoRE MOFs and try to see how well the model can predict the hydrogen isotherms. In theory, the embedding learned this way is pretty much a latent space for you to use as an input for other more complex adsorption applications.
This tutorial is really really long, since we are building the dataset from scratch. Once you have the dataset, next time you run it, you can load up the pickle file and resume the workflow from there, that should be much faster.
Here are the approximate steps in this monstrosity 1. Make imports and set paths 2. Load the IZA dataset from MOFDB 3. Create RAGs, - compute dgrid - compute regions and maxima - compute pbc - compute connections - compte rag - add maxima and pbc to rag - add energy interpolator to rag 4. Do clustering of pockets on the pore graphs using energy values using precalculated interpolators 5. Add energy histograms to pore graphs keeping the bins the same across materials (of course, we need this to do machine learning) 6. Define Graph convolutional network that outputs the embeddings using Deep Graph Library 7. Train the model to predict adsorption at the highest pressure point 8. Estimate and plot the parity 10. Train the model to predict adsorption at all 8 pressures 11. Estimate and plot the average error and std deviation at each pressure point 12. Hyperparameter tuning We wil tune the learning rate, number of hidden units, droput ratio, weigh decay ratio, and the choice of activation function using Optuna as a black box 13. Predict isotherms for a new set of pore graphs like coremofs for example, compiling this dataset is left as an excercise to the reader. the code for predicting is here.
Unlike usual tutorials, I am not quite going into the details of each step, you can ask chat gpt is something is unclear.
PS: The reason for splitting up the dataset creation workflow is to avoid memory bottlenecks while passing around large energy interpolators or accidentally running the energ calculation over a single core instead of in parallel due to poor distribution. Just follow along and you shall be fine (mostly).

def regions_maxima_radii_from_dgrid(dgrid, mask_thickness = 1.0):
    regions, maxima = mgr.regions_from_dgrid(dgrid, mask_thickness = mask_thickness)
    maxima_radii = dgrid[tuple(maxima.T )]
    return regions, maxima, maxima_radii


def make_rag_upto_pbc(regions, dgrid, maxima,maxima_radii, mat_atoms, pbc_groups):
    connections = mgr.connections_from_regions_and_dgrid(regions, dgrid, maxima, mat_atoms)
    rag = mgr.rag_from_connections(connections, maxima, only_use_internal=False)
    shape = dgrid.shape
    rag = mgr.add_maxima_to_rag(rag, maxima, maxima_radii, shape, mat_atoms)
    rag = mgr.add_pbc_to_rag(rag, pbc_groups)
    props = regionprops(regions)
    rag = mgr.add_centroids_to_rag_with_pbc(rag,props, pbc_groups, mat_atoms, regions.shape)
    # einterp = make_einterp(mat_atoms)
    # rag = mgr.add_vdw_hist_to_rag(rag, regions, energy_interpolator=einterp, use_pbc=True, pbc_groups = pbc_groups)
    rag = mgr.add_pbc_to_rag(rag, pbc_groups)
    rag.graph['dgrid'] = dgrid
    rag.graph['regions'] = regions
    rag.graph['maxima'] = maxima
    rag.graph['ase_atoms'] = mat_atoms
    rag.graph['connections'] = connections
    rag.graph['pbc_groups'] = pbc_groups
    rag.graph['einterp'] = einterp
    return rag
def make_einterp(mat_atoms):
    egrid = mgr.egrid_from_atoms2(mat_atoms, spacing=0.5, probe_symbol='He', precompute=False)
    # einterp = mgr.interpolate_dgrid(egrid)
    einterp = mgr.get_energy_interpolator(egrid)
    return einterp

title: Graph Convolution on RAGs to predict adsorption isotherms
text:
Hyperparameter optimization
Let’s do some hyper parameter tuning using Optuna, since, graph netwroks are notorious for over fitting and given our small dataset, we probably overfit the heck out of it. I am doing only 50 trials, you can do more


Show code
class GCN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_feats, hidden_size, num_classes, dropout, activation):
        super(GCN, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = GraphConv(in_feats, hidden_size, activation=activation)
        self.conv2 = GraphConv(hidden_size, num_classes)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)

    def forward(self, g, features):
        x = self.conv1(g, features)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = self.conv2(g, x)
        return x
import optuna

def objective(trial):
    # Suggest values for the hyperparameters
    hidden_size = trial.suggest_int('hidden_size', 16, 128)
    lr = trial.suggest_loguniform('lr', 1e-5, 1e-1)
    dropout = trial.suggest_uniform('dropout', 0.0, 1.0)
    weight_decay = trial.suggest_loguniform('weight_decay', 1e-9, 1e-3)
    activation_name = trial.suggest_categorical('activation', ['relu', 'tanh', 'sigmoid'])
    activation = getattr(F, activation_name)

    # Initialize the model and optimizer
    model = GCN(features.size(1), hidden_size, 8, dropout, activation)
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)

    # Training loop
    for epoch in range(1000):
        model.train()
        embeddings = model(batched_graph, features)
        batched_graph.ndata['h'] = embeddings
        logits = dgl.mean_nodes(batched_graph, 'h')
        loss = F.mse_loss(logits, labels, reduction='mean')
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        # Handle pruning based on the intermediate value.
        if trial.should_prune():
            raise optuna.exceptions.TrialPruned()

    return loss.item()

study = optuna.create_study(direction='minimize', pruner=optuna.pruners.HyperbandPruner())
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50)

print('Best trial:')
trial = study.best_trial
print('  Value: ', trial.value)
print('  Params: ')
for key, value in trial.params.items():
    print('    {}: {}'.format(key, value))

def dgrid_and_frameindex_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb(ase_atoms, radii=None, spacing=0.2, block_size=20000):
    """
    Similar to dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb but returns both the distance grid and the indices
    of the closest framework atoms for each grid point.

    :param ase_atoms: ASE Atoms object containing the framework structure
    :param radii: Array of atomic radii for each atom. If None, uses default vdW radii
    :param spacing: Grid spacing in Angstroms, defaults to 0.2
    :param block_size: Size of blocks for parallel processing, defaults to 20000
    :return: Tuple of (distance_grid, argmin_grid) where:
            - distance_grid is a 3D array of minimum distances to framework surface
            - argmin_grid is a 3D array of indices of closest framework atoms
    """
     # data    = read(path_to_cif)

    
    from ase.io import read
    import numpy as np
    import dask.array as da
    import pandas as pd
    from tqdm import tqdm
    import ase

                "Rf": np.nan,
                "Db": np.nan,
                "Sg": np.nan,
                "Bh": np.nan,
                "Hs": np.nan,
                "Mt": np.nan,
                "Ds": np.nan,
                "Rg": np.nan,
                "Cn": np.nan,
                "Nh": np.nan,
                "Fl": np.nan,
                "Mc": np.nan,
                "Lv": np.nan,
                "Ts": np.nan,
                "Og": np.nan,})
    radii = (vdw_radii[ase_atoms.get_chemical_symbols()].values / 100.0).reshape(-1, 1)

    fpoints = ase_atoms.get_scaled_positions() - 0.5
    cell = (ase.geometry.complete_cell(ase_atoms.get_cell())).T

    [nx, ny, nz] = (ase_atoms.cell.cellpar()[0:3] / spacing).astype(int) + 1
    gpoints = (da.stack(
        da.meshgrid(
            np.linspace(-0.5, 0.5, nx),
            np.linspace(-0.5, 0.5, ny),
            np.linspace(-0.5, 0.5, nz),
            indexing="ij",
        ),
        -1,
    ).reshape(-1, 3).rechunk(block_size, 3))

    def gpd_np_with_argmin(points, fpoints=fpoints, cell=cell, radii=radii):
        diff = np.expand_dims(points, axis=1) - np.expand_dims(fpoints, axis=0)
        diff = (diff - np.around(diff)).reshape(-1, 3)
        diff = np.dot(cell, diff.T).T
        distances = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=1).reshape(-1, fpoints.shape[0]) - radii.T
        min_distances = np.min(distances, axis=1)
        argmin_indices = np.argmin(distances, axis=1)
        return np.column_stack((min_distances, argmin_indices))

    # Map the function across blocks and compute both grids
    combined = gpoints.map_blocks(
        gpd_np_with_argmin,
        chunks=(block_size, 2),
        dtype=np.float32,
    ).compute()

    # Separate the results into distance grid and argmin grid
    dgrid = combined[:, 0].reshape(nx, ny, nz)
    argmin_grid = combined[:, 1].astype(np.int32).reshape(nx, ny, nz)

    return dgrid, argmin_grid

Looks good enough, the linker is detecte correctly by MOFId.


Find linkers in the framework
We can match a given pattern (subgraph) to a larger graph, with additional criteria on nodes and/or linkers using subgraph isomorphism algorithms in networkx. Check out the functional groups tutorial https://github.com/Shi-Research-Group/mofography/blob/master/docs/detect_functional_groups_in_dataset.ipynb for additional example of the same.
Let’s use subgraph isomorphism to find the indices aof all the linker atoms in the MOF like this:


Show code
from networkx.algorithms import isomorphism
node_matcher = isomorphism.categorical_node_match('element', 'C')
matcher = isomorphism.GraphMatcher(mof_sgraph, linker_sgraph, node_match=node_matcher)
isomorphic_subgraphs = list(matcher.subgraph_isomorphisms_iter())


In theory, you could match the edge bond_type or bond_order as well, but, if the framework distances are not spot on, the bond_order calculated might be wrong, and you might miss matches. So that’s not included here. We are just matching groups of connected element types only.

Conclusions
So here’s what we did in this document: - Grabbed a cif file - Compute the distance and frame indices grid - Picked a region - Found some atoms that are directly responsible for the distances in that region - Decomposed the MOF into building blocks using MOFId - Found matching patterns (linkers) in the framework using subgraph isomorphism - Found the indices of the linkers that include the atoms we identfied earlier. - Visualized the said linkers only, around our region of interest.

title: Pore diameters with the winding method: parity with Zeo++
text: In this notebook we take the IZA zeolite dataset from MOFDB and compare the LCD and PLD tabulated there (Zeo++) with the values computed by mofography’s winding-number percolation (get_pore_dia_mgr_winding, the standard method), and make parity plots. The older face-merging method is run at the end for comparison only.

title: Pore diameters with the winding method: parity with Zeo++
text:
Pore diameter calculation (winding method)
get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(mat_atoms, kwargs=...) takes a distance grid (computed with dgrid_from_atoms_rust, as float32), builds the periodic segmentation and the pore graph, then returns (lcd, pld, lis, dgrid) (diameters in Å). LIS (largest included sphere along percolating pathways) is what older code calls DFSD. We run it over the whole dataset with dask. (There is no compute_pore_diameters_winding function; this is the one-call entry point.)


Show code
def get_pore_dia_winding(mat_atoms):
    spacing = 0.5
    # pass a float32 dgrid: the Rust segmentation rejects float64 grids
    dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing).astype(np.float32)
    lcd, pld, lis, _ = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(mat_atoms, dgrid=dgrid, kwargs=dict(spacing=spacing))
    return lcd, pld, lis

def safe_result(f):
    # blocks until the task finishes; failed structures become None
    try:
        return f.result()
    except Exception:
        return None

client = Client(processes=True)
futures = client.compute([delayed(get_pore_dia_winding)(a) for a in iza_atoms])
iza_pore_dias = [safe_result(f) for f in futures]
n_ok = sum(d is not None for d in iza_pore_dias)
print(f"{n_ok}/{len(iza_pore_dias)} structures finished")

# Create subplots
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) LCD", "(b) PLD"),
                    horizontal_spacing=0.1)

fig.add_trace(

)

# PLD subplot
fig.add_trace(

)
fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=[0, max(pld_zeo)+3],
        y=[0, max(pld_zeo)+3],
        mode='lines',
        line=dict(color='black', width=1, dash='dash'),
        name='PLD Parity Line'
    ),
    row=1, col=2
)

# Update layout for both subplots
fig.update_layout(
    template='simple_white',
    showlegend=False,
    font=dict(family='Arial'),
    width=1200,
    height=600,
    autosize=False,
)

# Update x and y axes for both subplots
for i in [1, 2]:
    fig.update_xaxes(
        title=dict(text='MOFography (\u212b)', font=dict(size=14)),
        tickfont=dict(size=12),
        mirror=True,

def remove_nan_pairs(arr1, arr2):
    arr1 = np.array(arr1, dtype=float)
    arr2 = np.array(arr2, dtype=float)
    mask = ~np.isnan(arr1) & ~np.isnan(arr2)
    return arr1[mask], arr2[mask]

# Remove NaN entries and compute R² and MAE for LCD
lcd_zeo_clean, lcd_mgr_clean = remove_nan_pairs(lcd_zeo, lcd_mgr)

title: Pore diameters with the winding method: parity with Zeo++
section: Comparison only: face merging (older, less accurate)
text:
Comparison only: face merging (older, less accurate)
The previous percolation method labels the voxel grid and merges labels across periodic faces (get_pore_dia_mgr). It is the closer analogue of voxel-sweep tools such as PoreBlazer and is less accurate than the winding method on contorted frameworks, because it cannot follow paths that wrap around the cell obliquely. It is shown here only to compare against the winding results above; do not use it for new work.


Show code
def get_pore_dia_face_merging(mat_atoms):
    lcd, pld, lis, _ = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr(mat_atoms, kwargs=dict(spacing=0.5))
    return lcd, pld, lis

futures_fm = client.compute([delayed(get_pore_dia_face_merging)(a) for a in iza_atoms])
iza_fm = [safe_result(f) for f in futures_fm]

def mae_vs_zeo(dias, col, idx):
    x = np.array([d[idx] if d is not None else np.nan for d in dias], dtype=float)
    y = iza_df[col].values.astype(float)
    m = ~np.isnan(x) & ~np.isnan(y)
    return mean_absolute_error(y[m], x[m]), r2_score(y[m], x[m])

print(f"{'method':<22s} {'LCD MAE':>8s} {'LCD R2':>8s} {'PLD MAE':>8s} {'PLD R2':>8s}")
for name, dias in [("winding (standard)", iza_pore_dias), ("face merging (legacy)", iza_fm)]:
    lm, lr = mae_vs_zeo(dias, "lcd", 0); pm, pr = mae_vs_zeo(dias, "pld", 1)
    print(f"{name:<22s} {lm:8.3f} {lr:8.3f} {pm:8.3f} {pr:8.3f}")
client.close()


method                  LCD MAE   LCD R2  PLD MAE   PLD R2
winding (standard)        0.213    0.956    0.169    0.983
face merging (legacy)     0.194    0.957    0.257    0.960

title: Pore diameters with the winding method: parity with Zeo++
text:
Conclusions

Computed LCD and PLD for the 216 all-silica IZA zeolites with the winding method and compared them with the Zeo++ values tabulated in MOFDB.
Face merging was run for comparison only; the winding method is the standard.
Mofography uses a 0.5 Å grid here; finer grids give higher accuracy.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
text:
Every connection in a periodic segmentation is a window — a narrow passage between two pore regions. The natural question is: “How wide is that window?” Most tools answer with the local pore-limiting diameter (PLD) along the pocket-to-pocket connection. mofography goes one step further: it attaches a direction-invariant, element-weighted fingerprint of the framework atoms that ring each window centre. Diameter + chemistry give a multi-modal description of each aperture — useful when diameter alone hides important distinctions.
This tutorial covers:

Window shell fingerprints — what the 118-element vector captures and how it is built.
Window fingerprint expansion — a BFS that rescues watershed regions behind slightly sub-probe windows when the local framework shell looks like the rest of the open mouth.
Effect on textural properties — how the bridging changes accessible surface area and void volume on IRMOF-1, and when you should (and should not) turn it on.
Mechanism A / B / C / D failure modes — what each one is, what fingerprinting does (and does not) fix, and where to look when you suspect each. If you have not done so, please complete the Connections and Windows tutorial first — it explains the basic seg['connections'] 5-tuple and the difference between internal and periodic windows. This page assumes that knowledge.
