title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
text:
Why fingerprints exist
A single PLD number tells you how wide a window is. It does not tell you what is around it:

Two windows of diameter 3.8 Å may be ringed by different framework chemistry (e.g. Si/Al vs carboxylate pillars).
Two windows of diameter 5.0 Å may sit in different topology contexts (8-ring in a zeolite vs the 4-ring of a MOF).

For percolation at a near-PLD probe radius, this distinction matters more than the absolute size. If a candidate sub-probe window is at a position whose framework shell looks the same as an already-open mouth, the probability that it is the same physical aperture — undercounted by the grid — is high. If the framework shell looks completely different, the throat probably is different too, and the user’s probe should still gate access.
That idea is the entire basis of the BFS expansion in _expand_percolating_labels_with_window_fingerprint.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
text:
Imports


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np
import networkx as nx
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
import logging

# Quiet the segmentation chatter
logging.getLogger("mofography").setLevel(logging.WARNING)

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
text:
Step 1: Periodic segmentation with windows
We use IRMOF-1 because it has a tight distribution of window sizes near its PLD — the perfect regime to show the bridging effect.


Show code
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
spacing = 0.5                                            # Å

dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
dgrid_f32 = dgrid.astype(np.float32)                     # Rust kernel requires float32

seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid_f32, atoms,
    spacing=spacing,
    mask_thickness=0.05,
    h=0.2,
    min_distance=1.5,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    minimum_window_separation=1.5,
    wall_thickness=0.05,
    extra_padding=5,
    compute_connections=True,                            # <-- windows come back in seg['connections']
    watershed_backend="rust_det",
    disable_tqdm=True,
    return_dgrid=True,
    return_padded_regions=True,
)
seg["mat_atoms"] = atoms                                 # needed by the fingerprint annotator
print(f"Pockets (PBC-grouped): {len(seg['maxima_pbc'])}")
print(f"Unique regions:        {len(seg['unique_regions'])}")
print(f"Window connections:    {len(seg['connections'])}")


Pockets (PBC-grouped): 8
Unique regions:        27
Window connections:    300


The key point: compute_connections=True (default) makes the same call return the regions, the maxima, and the window list together.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
text:
Step 2: Inspect seg['connections']
Each entry of seg['connections'] is a 5-element numpy array:



Index
Meaning




c[0]
The two region labels the window connects


c[1]
Confirmation flag (always True for a detected window)


c[2]
'internal' or 'periodic'


c[3]
Window centroid coordinates, shape (1, 3)


c[4]
Window radius in Å, shape (1,)



The detailed walkthrough of the 5-tuple lives in the Connections and Windows tutorial. Here we just need two things: a connections list with internal and periodic windows, and a unique_regions set that filters out padding artefacts.


Show code
connections = seg["connections"]
unique_regions = seg["unique_regions"]

# Keep only windows that touch at least one unit-cell region
connections_trimmed = [
    c for c in connections
    if np.any(np.isin(c[0], unique_regions))
]

internal = [c for c in connections_trimmed if c[2] == "internal"]
periodic = [c for c in connections_trimmed if c[2] == "periodic"]
print(f"Unit-cell windows:  {len(connections_trimmed)} (internal={len(internal)}, periodic={len(periodic)})")


Unit-cell windows:  108 (internal=54, periodic=54)


Each window is essentially a centroid of the touching boundary between two regions. The list already carries a window_radius; what we want to do now is add a shell fingerprint to each one.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 3: Build the canonical pore graph
text:
Step 3: Build the canonical pore graph
The connections list contains two directed entries per canonical window (one for each traversal direction). The standard pore-graph view collapses these to a networkx.MultiDiGraph keyed by canonical edge identity:


Show code
graph = mgr.make_directed_graph_from_segmentation_results(seg, dgrid=dgrid_f32)
print(f"Pore graph: {graph.number_of_nodes()} nodes, {graph.number_of_edges()} edges")

# Each edge carries a window_radius (the maximum over periodic images on that canonical edge).
wrs = sorted({float(d.get("window_radius", 0.0)) for _, _, d in graph.edges(data=True)})
print(f"Window radius range: {wrs[0]:.3f} ... {wrs[-1]:.3f} Å  (N unique = {len(wrs)})")


Pore graph: 8 nodes, 24 edges
Window radius range: 3.678 ... 3.957 Å  (N unique = 3)


For IRMOF-1 the windows come in a tight 3.68–3.96 Å band — close to the framework’s PLD, which is exactly where the fingerprinting rescue is most useful.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 4: Annotate graph edges with shell fingerprints
text:
Step 4: Annotate graph edges with shell fingerprints
annotate_graph_edges_with_window_fingerprints walks every graph edge, computes a window centre from the edge data, and stamps an element-weighted vector onto the edge:

a shell of radius shell_radius (default 3.5 Å) around the centre,
weighted by 1 / max(dist, 1e-3) so nearer atoms dominate,
placed into a 118-slot vector (one slot per atomic number 1–118),
L2-normalized so cosine similarity is meaningful.

The result is stored on each edge as window_fp_vec (the tuple) and window_fp_ready (boolean). The window centre in fractional coordinates is also stored as window_frac_pos.


Show code
mgr.annotate_graph_edges_with_window_fingerprints(
    graph, seg, atoms=atoms, shell_radius=3.5
)

# Inspect the first few edges
print(f"{'edge':>14s}  {'wr [Å]':>7s}  {'ready':>6s}  {'nonzero slots (Z)':>30s}")
print("-" * 65)
for u, v, k, data in list(graph.edges(keys=True, data=True))[:6]:
    wr = float(data.get("window_radius", 0.0))
    ready = bool(data.get("window_fp_ready", False))
    if ready:
        v_fp = np.asarray(data["window_fp_vec"])
        nz = np.flatnonzero(v_fp)
        z_list = ", ".join(f"Z={int(i+1)}" for i in nz)
    else:
        z_list = "(no atoms in shell)"
    print(f"({u:>2d},{v:>2d},{k:>2d})  {wr:7.3f}  {ready!s:>6s}  {z_list:>30s}")


          edge   wr [Å]   ready               nonzero slots (Z)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
( 2, 4, 0)    3.678    True             Z=1, Z=6, Z=8, Z=30
( 2, 4, 1)    3.678    True             Z=1, Z=6, Z=8, Z=30
( 2, 3, 0)    3.710    True                        Z=1, Z=6
( 2, 3, 1)    3.710    True                        Z=1, Z=6
( 4, 6, 0)    3.678    True             Z=1, Z=6, Z=8, Z=30
( 4, 6, 1)    3.678    True             Z=1, Z=6, Z=8, Z=30


For IRMOF-1 every window lands on the same set of non-zero slots — Z=6 (C), Z=8 (O), Z=30 (Zn), Z=1 (H) — which is exactly what we expect: a carboxylate linker + Zn₄O node + benzene ring + terminating H.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 5: What the fingerprint actually captures
text:
Step 5: What the fingerprint actually captures
The vector is direction-invariant: whether you walk the graph edge from u → v or v → u, the centre and the shell are the same, so the fingerprint is the same. That makes cosine similarity a meaningful distance.
Let’s confirm that on IRMOF-1:


Show code
# Cosine between two windows on the same canonical edge (different periodic images
# at the same physical throat — fingerprints should be essentially identical).
def cosine(a, b):
    a, b = np.asarray(a), np.asarray(b)
    denom = float(np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
    return float(np.dot(a, b) / denom) if denom > 1e-12 else 0.0

ready_edges = [
    (u, v, k, data["window_fp_vec"], float(data["window_radius"]))
    for u, v, k, data in graph.edges(keys=True, data=True)
    if data.get("window_fp_ready")
]

# Same canonical (u, v), two different periodic images (different keys)
pairs = {}
for e in ready_edges:
    pairs.setdefault((e[0], e[1]), []).append(e)
canon_with_two = next((grp for grp in pairs.values() if len(grp) >= 2), None)
if canon_with_two is not None:
    a, b = canon_with_two[0], canon_with_two[1]
    print(f"Same canonical edge, two periodic images: "
          f"({a[0]},{a[1]},{a[2]}) and ({b[0]},{b[1]},{b[2]}); "
          f"cos = {cosine(a[3], b[3]):.4f}")

# Two different edges at the same radius
e0 = ready_edges[0]
same_wr = [e for e in ready_edges if abs(e[4] - e0[4]) < 1e-6 and e[3] is not e0[3]]
if same_wr:
    e1 = same_wr[0]
    print(f"Different edge, same wr={e1[4]:.3f}: cos = {cosine(e0[3], e1[3]):.4f}")

# The most different edge
def farthest_cosine(ref, others):
    ref_v = np.asarray(ref[3])
    return max(others, key=lambda e: 1.0 - cosine(ref_v, e[3]))

far = farthest_cosine(e0, [e for e in ready_edges if e[3] is not e0[3]])
print(f"Farthest pair: ({e0[0]},{e0[1]},{e0[2]}) wr={e0[4]:.3f} "
      f"vs ({far[0]},{far[1]},{far[2]}) wr={far[4]:.3f}: cos = {cosine(e0[3], far[3]):.4f}")


Same canonical edge, two periodic images: (2,4,0) and (2,4,1); cos = 0.9998
Different edge, same wr=3.678: cos = 0.9998
Farthest pair: (2,4,0) wr=3.678 vs (5,6,0) wr=3.710: cos = 0.3967


In IRMOF-1 every window fingerprints the same chemistry (Zn, O, C, H) at slightly different distances, so all pairwise cosines are very close to 1. That’s the easy case. On more complex materials — a zeolite with 8-ring and 6-ring windows of similar diameter, or a MOF with carboxylate and pyridyl linkers — the cosine separates the two families cleanly.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 6: Percolation at a near-PLD probe
text:
Step 6: Percolation at a near-PLD probe
Now the core question: what does fingerprinting actually do at a probe radius near the PLD?
percolating_region_labels_at_probe_winding is the central entry point. It runs the standard winding percolation at probe_radius, then optionally calls _expand_percolating_labels_with_window_fingerprint to add neighbour regions whose connecting window is slightly sub-probe but whose shell matches an open mouth.


Show code
def percolating_labels(seg, probe, fp_on=False, subprobe_gap=0.5):
    kwargs = {"window_fp_for_accessible": fp_on, "window_fp_subprobe_gap": subprobe_gap}
    return mgr.percolating_region_labels_at_probe_winding(seg, probe, kwargs=kwargs)


Sweep probe radius and watch the difference:


Show code
print(f"{'probe [Å]':>10s}  {'strict':>7s}  {'+FP':>5s}  {'+FP adds':>9s}")
print("-" * 42)
for probe in [3.5, 3.6, 3.65, 3.7, 3.75, 3.8, 3.9, 4.0]:
    strict = percolating_labels(seg, probe, fp_on=False)
    fp     = percolating_labels(seg, probe, fp_on=True)
    diff = sorted(fp - strict)
    print(f"{probe:10.2f}  {len(strict):7d}  {len(fp):5d}  {len(diff):9d}  "
          f"{diff[:6]}")


 probe [Å]   strict    +FP   +FP adds
------------------------------------------
      3.50       27     27          0  []
      3.60       27     27          0  []
      3.65       27     27          0  []
      3.70       26     27          1  [4]
      3.75       20     26          6  [2, 6, 7, 12, 19, 20]
      3.80       20     26          6  [2, 6, 7, 12, 19, 20]
      3.90       20     20          0  []
      4.00        0      0          0  []


You should see:

Below the smallest window (probe ≪ 3.68 Å): no percolation either way.
Near the PLD (probe ≈ 3.7–3.8 Å): strict percolation drops because the smallest windows are just below the probe, but window FP rescues those regions whose sub-probe throats share a shell with an open mouth.
At/above the largest window (probe ≳ 3.96 Å): every window passes the strict threshold, so the FP expansion has nothing to add.

The window FP does not force a percolation that does not exist — it only bridges sub-probe gaps whose size is within window_fp_subprobe_gap (default 0.5 Å) and whose shell cosine is above window_fp_sim_thresh (default 0.88) of an open mouth. Windows that are too small, or look chemically different, stay closed.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 7: Why the expansion fires — walking a single BFS step
text:
Step 7: Why the expansion fires — walking a single BFS step
The mechanism is concrete. Let’s track one sub-probe edge that gets bridged and confirm the three gates that let it through:


Show code
# Pick a probe in the interesting regime
probe = 3.75
subprobe_gap = 0.5
sim_thresh = 0.88
ref_tol = 0.12

# Build the per-edge view used internally
percolating_strict = percolating_labels(seg, probe, fp_on=False)
percolating_nodes_strict = set()
for node, labels in mgr.build_base_region_labels_from_results(seg).items():
    if set(labels).intersection(percolating_strict):
        percolating_nodes_strict.add(int(node))

# Reference edges = those incident on a strict-percolating node whose window_radius >= probe - ref_tol
ref_edges = []
for u, v, k, data in graph.edges(keys=True, data=True):
    if int(u) not in percolating_nodes_strict and int(v) not in percolating_nodes_strict:
        continue
    wr = float(data.get("window_radius", 0.0))
    if wr < probe - ref_tol:
        continue
    if not data.get("window_fp_ready"):
        continue
    ref_edges.append((int(u), int(v), int(k), data, wr))
print(f"Reference edges (strict-percolating, wr >= {probe-ref_tol:.2f}): {len(ref_edges)}")

# Candidate edges = sub-probe but within subprobe_gap, that the BFS will consider
candidate_count = 0
bridged = []
for u, v, k, data in graph.edges(keys=True, data=True):
    wr = float(data.get("window_radius", 0.0))
    gap = probe - wr
    if gap <= 0 or gap > subprobe_gap:
        continue
    if not data.get("window_fp_ready"):
        continue
    candidate_count += 1
    cvec = np.asarray(data["window_fp_vec"])
    # match against any reference
    best = None
    for _, _, _, ref_data, rwr in ref_edges:
        rvec = np.asarray(ref_data["window_fp_vec"])
        if rwr - wr > subprobe_gap:
            continue
        cos = cosine(cvec, rvec)
        if cos >= sim_thresh and (best is None or cos > best[1]):
            best = (rwr, cos)
    if best is not None:
        bridged.append((u, v, k, wr, best[0], best[1]))
print(f"Candidate sub-probe edges:        {candidate_count}")
print(f"  Bridged by FP (cos >= {sim_thresh}): {len(bridged)}")
print()
print(f"{'edge':>14s}  {'wr [Å]':>7s}  {'gap':>5s}  {'ref_wr [Å]':>10s}  {'cosine':>7s}")
print("-" * 56)
for u, v, k, wr, rwr, c in bridged[:8]:
    print(f"({u:>2d},{v:>2d},{k:>2d})  {wr:7.3f}  {probe-wr:5.2f}  {rwr:10.3f}  {c:7.4f}")

Candidate sub-probe edges:        18

--------------------------------------------------------
( 2, 3, 0)    3.710   0.04       3.710   1.0000
( 2, 3, 1)    3.710   0.04       3.710   1.0000
( 5, 7, 0)    3.710   0.04       3.710   1.0000

The three gates you should see in action:

Sub-probe gap — probe − wr ≤ window_fp_subprobe_gap (default 0.5 Å). Windows that are much smaller than the probe stay closed regardless of chemistry.
Reference gap — wr_ref − wr_cand ≤ window_fp_subprobe_gap (one-sided). A candidate window must not be much smaller than a reference open mouth either — this is the Mechanism D guard that stops the FP from over-bridging to genuinely smaller annex apertures.
Shell cosine — cosine(cvec, rvec) ≥ window_fp_sim_thresh (default 0.88). The local framework shell must look like an open mouth.

Together they are the entire fingerprint expansion policy.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 8: Effect on accessible void volume and surface area
text:
Step 8: Effect on accessible void volume and surface area
The standard compute_void_volume_from_results and compute_surface_area_mc / compute_surface_area_mesh entry points accept window_fp_for_accessible and an optional winding_kwargs dict. The defaults are window_fp_for_accessible=True, which is the recommended setting for production runs.


Show code
fp_kwargs = {
    "window_fp_for_accessible": True,
    "window_fp_shell_radius": 3.5,
    "window_fp_sim_thresh": 0.88,
    "window_fp_subprobe_gap": 0.5,
}

def sa(atoms, seg, probe, fp):
    return mgr.compute_surface_area_mc(
        seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe,
        window_fp_for_accessible=fp, accessibility_method="winding",
        winding_kwargs=fp_kwargs if fp else None,
    )

def vv(atoms, seg, probe, fp):
    return mgr.compute_void_volume_from_results(
        seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe,
        window_fp_for_accessible=fp, accessibility_method="winding",
        winding_kwargs=fp_kwargs if fp else None,
    )

print(f"{'probe [Å]':>10s}  {'VV strict':>10s}  {'VV +FP':>9s}  {'ΔVV':>8s}  "
      f"{'SA strict':>11s}  {'SA +FP':>9s}  {'ΔSA':>9s}")
print("-" * 78)
for probe in [3.5, 3.6, 3.65, 3.7, 3.75, 3.8, 3.9, 4.0]:
    vv_strict = vv(atoms, seg, probe, fp=False)
    vv_fp     = vv(atoms, seg, probe, fp=True)
    sa_strict = sa(atoms, seg, probe, fp=False)
    sa_fp     = sa(atoms, seg, probe, fp=True)
    dV = vv_fp["accessible_void_volume"] - vv_strict["accessible_void_volume"]
    dS = sa_fp["accessible_surface_area"] - sa_strict["accessible_surface_area"]
    print(f"{probe:10.2f}  {vv_strict['accessible_void_volume']:10.4f}  "
          f"{vv_fp['accessible_void_volume']:9.4f}  {dV:+8.4f}  "
          f"{sa_strict['accessible_surface_area']:11.2f}  "
          f"{sa_fp['accessible_surface_area']:9.2f}  {dS:+9.2f}")


 probe [Å]   VV strict     VV +FP       ΔVV    SA strict     SA +FP        ΔSA
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      3.50      0.2184     0.2184   +0.0000      1946.71    1852.32     -94.39
      3.60      0.1956     0.1956   +0.0000      1784.91    1722.54     -62.36
      3.65      0.1902     0.1902   +0.0000      1634.90    1729.29     +94.39
      3.70      0.1717     0.1798   +0.0081      1511.86    1670.29    +158.43
      3.75      0.0685     0.1605   +0.0921       608.45    1439.39    +830.93
      3.80      0.0667     0.1542   +0.0875       606.77    1346.69    +739.92
      3.90      0.0583     0.0583   +0.0000       542.72     527.55     -15.17
      4.00      0.0000     0.0000   +0.0000         0.00       0.00      +0.00


On IRMOF-1 at probe = 3.75 Å, window FP roughly doubles the accessible void volume and surface area. The strict reading misses an entire ring of small-cage regions because the smallest windows are just under the probe; the FP reads them as the same aperture (the cosine is essentially 1) and adds them.
This is the expected behaviour for a Mechanism B failure (defined below): the user’s probe and the grid are slightly mis-aligned, and the FP closes the gap on the user’s behalf.

Numerical note. Because we passed winding_kwargs only when fp=True, the legacy reader is bit-for-bit comparable — the only difference is whether the FP expansion fires. If you want to compare against the lattice / Zeo++-style definition, use accessibility_method="lattice" (the FP is winding-only).

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 9: Tweak the parameters and watch the policy change
text:
Step 9: Tweak the parameters and watch the policy change
winding_kwargs is the single dict that controls fingerprint behaviour. Every entry has a default; the table in docs/window_fingerprinting.org lists them. Two are worth playing with interactively:

window_fp_subprobe_gap (default 0.5 Å) — how far below the probe a window can sit and still be bridged. Lower it to make the policy stricter; raise it to be more permissive.
window_fp_sim_thresh (default 0.88) — minimum cosine to a reference open mouth. Lower to be more permissive (less chemistry discrimination); raise to require tighter matches.



Show code
probe = 3.75
print(f"{'subprobe_gap':>14s}  {'sim_thresh':>11s}  {'regions':>8s}  {'VV':>8s}")
print("-" * 50)
for gap in [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]:
    for sim in [0.80, 0.88, 0.95]:
        kwargs = {
            "window_fp_for_accessible": True,
            "window_fp_subprobe_gap": gap,
            "window_fp_sim_thresh": sim,
        }
        labels = mgr.percolating_region_labels_at_probe_winding(seg, probe, kwargs=kwargs)
        result = mgr.compute_void_volume_from_results(
            seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe,
            window_fp_for_accessible=True, accessibility_method="winding",
            winding_kwargs=kwargs,
        )
        print(f"{gap:14.2f}  {sim:11.2f}  {len(labels):8d}  "
              f"{result['accessible_void_volume']:8.4f}")


  subprobe_gap   sim_thresh   regions        VV
--------------------------------------------------
          0.20         0.80        26    0.1605
          0.20         0.88        26    0.1605
          0.20         0.95        26    0.1605
          0.50         0.80        26    0.1605
          0.50         0.88        26    0.1605
          0.50         0.95        26    0.1605
          0.80         0.80        26    0.1605
          0.80         0.88        26    0.1605
          0.80         0.95        26    0.1605


In this sweep on IRMOF-1 the values stay similar because every window fingerprints the same Zn/O/C/H chemistry. The parameters matter much more on materials where windows have different local framework environments (zeolites, MOFs with mixed linkers).

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 10: Mechanism A / B / C / D failure modes
text:
Step 10: Mechanism A / B / C / D failure modes
The fingerprint expansion is a targeted fix. It is useful for some failure modes and useless for others. The four labelled failure modes in the literature are:

Mechanism A — PLD threshold / no percolation seed (FP cannot help)

MGR PLD is just below the requested probe, so no window opens; no percolating mouth exists.
The BFS in _expand_percolating_labels_with_window_fingerprint returns immediately because percolating_labels is empty.
Policy: do not silently widen the probe. The user-set probe radius stays strict. This is a separate PLD / graph-edge calibration problem.



Show code
# Above the largest window in IRMOF-1, strict winding has no percolation at all,
# and the FP expansion has nothing to start from.
probe_above_pld = 5.0
strict = percolating_labels(seg, probe_above_pld, fp_on=False)
fp     = percolating_labels(seg, probe_above_pld, fp_on=True)
print(f"probe {probe_above_pld} Å: strict={len(strict)} regions, +FP={len(fp)} regions  (Mechanism A: still zero)")


probe 5.0 Å: strict=0 regions, +FP=0 regions  (Mechanism A: still zero)




Mechanism B — watershed / graph window gating (FP helps)

A region is reachable only through a window whose window_radius is slightly below the probe (grid undershoot, watershed placement, mask thickness).
The BFS bridges it when the sub-probe gap ≤ window_fp_subprobe_gap and the shell matches an open mouth.
This is the failure mode the FP expansion is designed to fix. Step 8 above demonstrates it on IRMOF-1.



Mechanism C — dead-end annex pockets (FP does not help)

The annex is reached through a window with window_radius ≈ 0.6–0.8 Å and pocket_radius ≈ 2 Å — much below the probe.
The sub-probe gap exceeds window_fp_subprobe_gap (default 0.5 Å), so the BFS rejects the bridge. The annex is correctly excluded at a 1.2 Å probe — a 1.2 Å sphere cannot pass a 0.7 Å throat even if the annex interior is wide.
Mofography counts void only in regions graph-reachable from percolating mouths. Zeo++ uses a geometric accessibility (every voxel with dgrid > probe on a percolating mask) and includes annex void regardless of whether a probe can fit through.
Policy: treat a large Zeo++ excess with good PLD agreement and intact main-path winding as expected conservative bias, not a Mofography bug. The CoRE-2000 screen documents several UDEMEW-like cases.



Mechanism D — FP over-bridge to annex apertures (FP can hurt; the one-sided gate fixes it)

Before the fix, FP could bridge a candidate whose shell cosine was high but whose window_radius was much smaller than the reference open mouth (an annex throat on the same framework shell but at a different aperture size).
Fix: _window_fp_matches_reference_edges uses a one-sided wr_ref − wr_cand ≤ window_fp_ref_minus_cand_tol gate (default = subprobe_gap = 0.5 Å). It blocks annex bridges with Δwr ≈ 0.7–0.8 Å while preserving Mechanism B grid undershoot (Δwr ≈ 0.4–0.5 Å). See docs/window_fingerprinting.org for the XALDOE case study.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 11: When to use window FP
text:
Step 11: When to use window FP







Scenario
Recommendation




Production accessible SA / void volume
Leave window_fp_for_accessible=True (default). The default tuning is calibrated for CoRE-2000 / typical MOFs.


Strict probe-gated comparison vs Zeo++
Pass window_fp_for_accessible=False. Use this when you want to audit Mofography’s graph-reachable definition explicitly.


LIS (largest included sphere)
FP is off by default for LIS. Enable window_fp_for_lis=True only when validating a specific outlier — it is experimental.


A material with very different window chemistries (e.g. mixed-linker MOF)
Consider raising window_fp_sim_thresh (e.g. 0.95) to require tighter matches.


A material with very small framework atoms (zeolites)
Default shell_radius=3.5 Å is calibrated for organic / metal-organic frameworks. On pure siliceous zeolites the shell often contains only Si/O; cosine between two windows of the same ring is essentially 1 and the gate barely fires.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
section: Step 12: What fingerprinting does not change
text:
Step 12: What fingerprinting does not change
annotate_graph_edges_with_window_fingerprints does not change where the windows are or how wide they are. It only adds metadata.

title: Window Fingerprinting for Accessible Textural Properties
text:
Summary







Concept
What it does




Window shell fingerprint
118-element vector of framework atoms within shell_radius (default 3.5 Å) of a window centre, weighted by 1/d, L2-normalized. Direction-invariant.


annotate_graph_edges_with_window_fingerprints
Stamps window_fp_vec and window_fp_ready onto every edge of the canonical pore graph.


BFS expansion
Adds neighbour regions behind sub-probe windows when (a) probe − wr ≤ window_fp_subprobe_gap, (b) wr_ref − wr_cand ≤ window_fp_ref_minus_cand_tol (one-sided), and (c) cosine(fp_cand, fp_ref) ≥ window_fp_sim_thresh.


Effect on accessible SA / VV
Largest impact at probes just above the smallest window_radius in the structure; no impact when the probe is far from the PLD.


Mechanism A
No percolating mouth exists; FP cannot help.


Mechanism B
Sub-probe window with matching shell; FP can help.


Mechanism C
Annex dead-end with much smaller throat; FP deliberately does not help.


Mechanism D
FP would over-bridge to an annex; the one-sided reference gate prevents it.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
The distance grid that every MOFography analysis starts from is built by subtracting a per-atom van der Waals (VDW) radius from the distance to each atom. That means the choice of VDW table is a fundamental modelling decision — not just a bookkeeping detail.
This tutorial:

Introduces the three VDW tables most commonly used in MOF characterisation: Bondi (1964), CRC / Mendeleev, and Alvarez (2013).
Shows how to load each table with the mofography.vdw_radii API.
Compares the per-element values for the seven most common MOF elements.
Runs a full periodic segmentation of IRMOF-1 with each table and compares maxima count, pocket sizes, and the Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD).
Explains the audit trail that do_periodic_segmentation_rust records in seg['input_params'].

Bottom line: Bondi/CRC is the recommended default. Switching to a different table is a deliberate modelling choice — record the choice in vdw_radii_set= so it lives on the segmentation result for the next person to read.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
The distance grid that every MOFography analysis starts from is built by subtracting a per-atom van der Waals (VDW) radius from the distance to each atom. That means the choice of VDW table is a fundamental modelling decision — not just a bookkeeping detail.
This tutorial:

Introduces the three VDW tables most commonly used in MOF characterisation: Bondi (1964), CRC / Mendeleev, and Alvarez (2013).
Shows how to load each table with the mofography.vdw_radii API.
Compares the per-element values for the seven most common MOF elements.
Runs a full periodic segmentation of IRMOF-1 with each table and compares maxima count, pocket sizes, and the Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD).
Explains the audit trail that do_periodic_segmentation_rust records in seg['input_params'].

Bottom line: Bondi/CRC is the recommended default. Switching to a different table is a deliberate modelling choice — record the choice in vdw_radii_set= so it lives on the segmentation result for the next person to read.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Why VDW radii matter
The distance grid answers the question “what is the radius of the largest sphere that fits here, minus a probe?” — but which largest sphere? The answer depends on how big you say each atom is.
# Conceptual: dgrid[x,y,z] = min_i( dist(x,y,z, atom_i) - vdw_radii[i] )
Two MOFs with identical geometry but different VDW assignments can have very different accessible volumes:

A larger metal radius (Zn, Cu, Zr) shrinks the corners and channels the metal sits in.
A larger H radius tightens pore openings near organic linkers.
A larger C/N/O radius shrinks the linker envelope.

The downstream impact:








Step
Sensitive to VDW?
How?




Distance grid
✅ directly
The per-atom offset


maxima_info peak radius
✅
Peaks shift toward/away from framework


Pore maxima count
✅ indirectly
Aggressive VDW radii merge small maxima into bigger ones


Pocket volumes
✅
Tighter radii → smaller pocket volumes


Window radii / PLD
✅
Tighter radii → smaller windows


Pocket type count
✅
Tightening one family can merge two cage types

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
The three VDW tables
mofography.vdw_radii ships with two tables out of the box and supports a third as a custom array:










Table
radii_set token
Origin
Coverage
Philosophy




Bondi / CRC
"bondi" (alias "bondi_crc_fallback")
Bondi (1964), CRC Handbook, with Mendeleev fill
All 118 elements
Conservative, sparse, the de facto MOF default


CRC / Mendeleev
"crc" (alias "mendeleev")
Mendeleev vdw_radius column
All 118 elements
Larger values for transition metals


Alvarez (2013)
"alvarez" (custom array)
Alvarez, “A cartography of the van der Waals territories”, Dalton Trans. 2013
Most elements
Larger values for metals; explicitly modern




Why three tables? Bondi is 60 years old and was calibrated on a small set of organic molecules. CRC/Mendeleev is a database consolidation that pulls many more measurements. Alvarez is the most recent systematic derivation, with explicit attention to coordination environment. For MOFs — which mix light organics with transition metals — the differences are non-trivial, especially for the metals.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Imports


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from mofography.vdw_radii import (
    default_vdw_radii_angstrom,    # Bondi / CRC
    mendeleev_vdw_radii_angstrom,  # CRC / Mendeleev
    typing_vdw_radii_angstrom,     # Bondi/CRC + Mendeleev fill for NaN entries
)
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Step 1: Per-element radii table
The most direct way to feel the difference is to look at common MOF elements. We build a one-atom-per-symbol Atoms object so we can pull each table’s value for the same element in a single call.


Show code
from ase import Atoms

# One atom of each element of interest
PROBE = Atoms(
    symbols=["H", "C", "N", "O", "Zn", "Cu", "Zr"],
    positions=[(i * 3.0, 0, 0) for i in range(7)],
    cell=[30, 5, 5],
    pbc=True,
)

bondi = default_vdw_radii_angstrom(PROBE)
mend = mendeleev_vdw_radii_angstrom(PROBE)

# Alvarez (2013) — picometers, vendored here for self-containment
ALVAREZ_PM = {
    "H": 120.0, "C": 177.0, "N": 166.0, "O": 150.0, "F": 146.0,
    "Cu": 238.0, "Zn": 239.0, "Zr": 252.0,
}
alvarez = np.array([ALVAREZ_PM.get(s, 170.0) for s in PROBE.get_chemical_symbols()]) / 100.0


Now lay them out side by side:


Show code
print(f"{'Element':>8} {'Bondi/CRC (Å)':>14} {'CRC/Mendeleev (Å)':>19} {'Alvarez (Å)':>13} {'Δ(A-B)':>8} {'Δ(C-B)':>8}")
print("-" * 76)
for i, sym in enumerate(PROBE.get_chemical_symbols()):
    a, b, c = bondi[i], mend[i], alvarez[i]
    print(f"{sym:>8} {a:>14.2f} {b:>19.2f} {c:>13.2f} {b-a:>+8.2f} {c-a:>+8.2f}")


 Element  Bondi/CRC (Å)   CRC/Mendeleev (Å)   Alvarez (Å)   Δ(A-B)   Δ(C-B)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
       H           1.20                1.10          1.20    -0.10    +0.00
       C           1.70                1.70          1.77    +0.00    +0.07
       N           1.55                1.55          1.66    +0.00    +0.11
       O           1.52                1.52          1.50    +0.00    -0.02
      Zn           1.73                2.01          2.39    +0.28    +0.66
      Cu           1.70                1.96          2.38    +0.26    +0.68
      Zr           2.12                2.23          2.52    +0.11    +0.40


Take-aways for the common MOF elements:

H, N, O — close to identical across the three tables (≤ 0.1 Å spread).
C — Bondi and CRC agree at 1.70 Å; Alvarez is 1.77 Å (+0.07 Å, slightly larger).
Zn — biggest spread: Bondi 1.73 Å, CRC 2.01 Å (+0.28), Alvarez 2.39 Å (+0.66). This is the element where your table choice matters most.
Cu, Zr — same pattern as Zn: Bondi smaller, CRC larger, Alvarez largest.

The metal spread is the practical reason the table matters: a Zn- or Cu-paddlewheel node’s environment looks very different under Bondi versus Alvarez. A Bondi-radii dgrid over-counts the void around a Zn₄O node, while Alvarez under-counts it (or matches experiment better, depending on whose measurement you trust).

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Step 2: The vdw_radii_set audit-trail parameter
do_periodic_segmentation_rust does not recompute the distance grid — it expects you to pass an already-built dgrid. The vdw_radii_set and vdw_radii_angstrom parameters are record-only: they stamp the result with provenance so that future readers know which table was used.








Parameter
Default
Meaning




vdw_radii_set
"bondi_crc_fallback"
A short tag ("bondi", "crc", "mendeleev", "alvarez", "array", …) describing the table


vdw_radii_angstrom
None
The actual per-atom radii used (Å). If passed without vdw_radii_set, the tag becomes "array"



The recorded value lands in seg['input_params'] under the same key, together with a per-symbol radii map:
seg['input_params']['vdw_radii_set']         # → "bondi_crc_fallback" | "crc" | "alvarez" | ...
seg['input_params']['vdw_radii_by_symbol']   # → {"Zn": 1.73, "O": 1.52, ...}
This is the only place the table choice is recorded — the segmentation result itself is otherwise agnostic to which table built the dgrid.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
section: Step 3: Load IRMOF-1 and pick a grid spacing
text:
Step 3: Load IRMOF-1 and pick a grid spacing
We use IRMOF-1 because it is well-characterised (two cage families, simple cubic) and contains the four elements where the tables disagree most: C, H, O, Zn.


Show code
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
print(f"Atoms: {len(atoms)}  ({atoms.get_chemical_formula()})")
print(f"Cell:  {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)} Å (cubic)")

spacing = 0.5  # Å — the canonical default


Atoms: 424  (C192H96O104Zn32)
Cell:  [25.83 25.83 25.83] Å (cubic)

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
section: Step 4: Build a distance grid for each table
text:
Step 4: Build a distance grid for each table
For each table, we build a separate dgrid using dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing, radii=...). The default dgrid (no radii argument) uses default_vdw_radii_angstrom, i.e. Bondi/CRC.


Show code
# Bondi/CRC: dgrid_from_atoms_rust uses this by default
dgrid_bondi = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)

# CRC / Mendeleev: pass the explicit radii array
radii_crc = mendeleev_vdw_radii_angstrom(atoms)
dgrid_crc = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing, radii=radii_crc)

# Alvarez: same pattern, custom array
radii_alvarez = np.array([ALVAREZ_PM.get(s, 170.0) for s in atoms.get_chemical_symbols()]) / 100.0
dgrid_alvarez = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing, radii=radii_alvarez)

print(f"bondi    dgrid: shape={dgrid_bondi.shape}, void max={dgrid_bondi.max():.2f} Å, "
      f"void voxels (d>1): {(dgrid_bondi > 1.0).sum():,}")
print(f"crc      dgrid: shape={dgrid_crc.shape}, void max={dgrid_crc.max():.2f} Å, "
      f"void voxels (d>1): {(dgrid_crc > 1.0).sum():,}")
print(f"alvarez  dgrid: shape={dgrid_alvarez.shape}, void max={dgrid_alvarez.max():.2f} Å, "
      f"void voxels (d>1): {(dgrid_alvarez > 1.0).sum():,}")


bondi    dgrid: shape=(52, 52, 52), void max=7.54 Å, void voxels (d>1): 83,608
crc      dgrid: shape=(52, 52, 52), void max=7.54 Å, void voxels (d>1): 84,136
alvarez  dgrid: shape=(52, 52, 52), void max=7.47 Å, void voxels (d>1): 81,440


You should see:

The void-max is slightly smaller for Alvarez than for Bondi (because the larger Zn and C radii push the dgrid down).
The void-voxel count is roughly constant — the topology of IRMOF-1 is robust, but the per-voxel probe radius drops.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
section: Step 5: Run periodic segmentation with each dgrid
text:
Step 5: Run periodic segmentation with each dgrid
For each dgrid, we call do_periodic_segmentation_rust and record the table choice via vdw_radii_set=. The function uses the dgrid as-is; the recording is what makes the segmentation reproducible.


Show code
def run_seg(dgrid, atoms, *, vdw_set, radii_for_audit=None):
    dgrid_f32 = dgrid.astype(np.float32)
    return mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
        dgrid_f32, atoms,
        mask_thickness=0.05,
        h=0.2,
        min_distance=1.5,
        threshold_abs=1.5,
        spacing=spacing,
        compute_connections=True,
        watershed_backend="rust_det",
        disable_tqdm=True,
        vdw_radii_set=vdw_set,
        vdw_radii_angstrom=radii_for_audit,
    )

seg_bondi = run_seg(dgrid_bondi, atoms, vdw_set="bondi")
seg_crc = run_seg(dgrid_crc, atoms, vdw_set="crc", radii_for_audit=radii_crc)
seg_alvarez = run_seg(dgrid_alvarez, atoms, vdw_set="alvarez", radii_for_audit=radii_alvarez)

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Step 6: Compare results

Maxima count (pore count)
The first sanity check — the topology of IRMOF-1 (cubic, with 8 cages per unit cell) should be preserved across all three tables.


Show code
print(f"{'Table':<10} {'maxima_pbc':>12} {'all_maxima':>12}")
print("-" * 36)
for name, seg in [("bondi", seg_bondi), ("crc", seg_crc), ("alvarez", seg_alvarez)]:
    print(f"{name:<10} {len(seg['maxima_pbc']):>12} {len(seg['all_maxima']):>12}")


Table        maxima_pbc   all_maxima
------------------------------------
bondi                 8          125
crc                   8          125
alvarez               8          125


For IRMOF-1 all three tables should report 8 PBC-grouped maxima — the topology is robust.


Pocket size distribution
The peak probe radius at each maximum is the most direct measure of “how big is this pocket” — it is the dgrid value at the maximum voxel. Tighter VDW radii → smaller peak radius.


Show code
print(f"{'Table':<10} {'min peak r (Å)':>16} {'mean peak r (Å)':>18} {'max peak r (Å)':>16}")
print("-" * 64)
for name, dgrid, seg in [
    ("bondi", dgrid_bondi, seg_bondi),
    ("crc", dgrid_crc, seg_crc),
    ("alvarez", dgrid_alvarez, seg_alvarez),
]:
    # maxima_pbc are (N, 3) integer voxel indices into the dgrid
    m = seg["maxima_pbc"]
    peaks = dgrid[m[:, 0], m[:, 1], m[:, 2]]
    print(f"{name:<10} {peaks.min():>16.3f} {peaks.mean():>18.3f} {peaks.max():>16.3f}")


Table        min peak r (Å)    mean peak r (Å)   max peak r (Å)
----------------------------------------------------------------
bondi                 5.284              6.357            7.538
crc                   5.384              6.407            7.538
alvarez               5.284              6.322            7.468


For IRMOF-1, Alvarez gives the smallest peak radii (largest metals → tightest dgrid). Bondi and CRC land close to each other, with CRC slightly larger because its bigger Zn radius pushes the maxima toward the cage centers. The Bondi-to-Alvarez spread is on the order of 0.1 Å — exactly the regime where it changes whether a small probe (N₂, CO₂) can fit through a window.


Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD)
PLD = 2 × the smallest window radius. It is the hard upper bound on the size of a spherical molecule that can diffuse through the material.


Show code
def compute_pld(seg):
    """Smallest window diameter in the unit cell."""
    if not seg["connections"]:
        return float("nan")
    unique = set(seg["unique_regions"])
    diams = []
    for c in seg["connections"]:
        # c[0] = (region_a, region_b); c[2] in {"internal", "periodic"}
        if np.any(np.isin(c[0], list(unique))):
            diams.append(2.0 * float(c[4][0]))
    return min(diams) if diams else float("nan")

print(f"{'Table':<10} {'PLD (Å)':>12} {'# unit-cell windows':>22}")
print("-" * 48)
for name, seg in [("bondi", seg_bondi), ("crc", seg_crc), ("alvarez", seg_alvarez)]:
    n_uc = sum(1 for c in seg["connections"] if np.any(np.isin(c[0], list(seg["unique_regions"]))))
    print(f"{name:<10} {compute_pld(seg):>12.3f} {n_uc:>22}")


Table           PLD (Å)    # unit-cell windows
------------------------------------------------
bondi             7.356                    108
crc               7.358                    108
alvarez           7.218                    108


The PLD for IRMOF-1 is ~7.3 Å for Bondi and CRC, dropping to ~7.2 Å for Alvarez. The metal-heavy Alvarez table tightens the windows most. For MOFs with a single gating window (e.g. ZIF-8, MOF-74), a 0.1 Å change in PLD is the difference between “passes N₂ at 77 K” and “doesn’t”.


Volume comparison
The connected-pore volume also tracks the VDW table directly.


Show code
def void_volume(dgrid, spacing):
    return float((dgrid > 1.0).sum()) * (spacing ** 3)

print(f"{'Table':<10} {'void volume (Å³)':>18} {'relative to bondi':>20}")
print("-" * 52)
v_b = void_volume(dgrid_bondi, spacing)
for name, dgrid in [("bondi", dgrid_bondi), ("crc", dgrid_crc), ("alvarez", dgrid_alvarez)]:
    v = void_volume(dgrid, spacing)
    print(f"{name:<10} {v:>18.1f} {v / v_b:>20.4f}")


Table        void volume (Å³)    relative to bondi
----------------------------------------------------
bondi                 10451.0               1.0000
crc                   10517.0               1.0063
alvarez               10180.0               0.9741


The relative volumes should differ by 1–3 % for IRMOF-1 (a robust MOF); for MOFs with narrow channels the spread is larger.

text:
Step 7: The audit trail
Every segmentation result carries the table choice. The same seg dict from above can answer “what radii were used to build this?” years later.


Show code

    ip = seg["input_params"]
    print(f"\n{name} audit:")
    print(f"  vdw_radii_set:         {ip.get('vdw_radii_set')}")
    print(f"  vdw_radii_by_symbol:   {ip.get('vdw_radii_by_symbol')}")



bondi audit:
  vdw_radii_set:         bondi_crc_fallback
  vdw_radii_by_symbol:   {'Zn': 1.73, 'O': 1.52, 'C': 1.7, 'H': 1.2}

crc audit:
  vdw_radii_set:         crc
  vdw_radii_by_symbol:   {'Zn': 2.01, 'O': 1.52, 'C': 1.7, 'H': 1.1}

alvarez audit:
  vdw_radii_set:         alvarez
  vdw_radii_by_symbol:   {'Zn': 2.39, 'O': 1.5, 'C': 1.77, 'H': 1.2}


The same field is what pocket_typing reads to decide which max_r calibration to use, so the audit trail is also functional, not just cosmetic.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Step 8: Visualising the effect
The cleanest visual side-by-side is the isovalue of the dgrid at a fixed probe radius. Lowering the VDW radii is equivalent to raising the isovalue, so the same isosurface at dgrid = 1.5 Å shows less accessible surface for Alvarez than for Bondi.


Show code
# One line per table, one column per probe radius
# (Useful as a quick figure for a paper or report)
import pandas as pd
rows = []
for name, dgrid in [("bondi", dgrid_bondi), ("crc", dgrid_crc), ("alvarez", dgrid_alvarez)]:
    for probe in [1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5]:
        n_vox = int((dgrid > probe).sum())
        rows.append({"table": name, "probe_a": probe, "n_voxels": n_vox,
                     "volume_a3": n_vox * spacing**3})
df = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="table", columns="probe_a", values="volume_a3")
print("Accessible volume (Å³) at each probe radius:")
print(df.round(1))


Accessible volume (Å³) at each probe radius:
probe_a      1.0     1.5     2.0     2.5
table                                   
alvarez  10180.0  8292.0  6485.0  4785.0
bondi    10451.0  8509.0  6638.0  4911.0
crc      10517.0  8638.0  6743.0  5004.0


The pattern: at every probe radius, accessible volume is largest for CRC, smallest for Alvarez, with Bondi in between. The differences are largest at small probe radii (where the VDW table choice matters most for surface area) and shrink at large probes.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Which table to use







Situation
Recommendation




General MOF / ZIF / COF screening
Bondi / CRC — the historical default; matches zeo++ and PoreBlazer


Open-metal MOFs (Cu-paddlewheel, Zn₄O, Zr₆) where metal radius matters most
Alvarez — modern, explicit, metal-friendly


Reproducing an old paper that used Mendeleev
CRC / Mendeleev — match the original


Custom (e.g. UFF, Dreiding)
Pass a per-atom array + vdw_radii_set="array"


Comparing across packages
Always record the choice in vdw_radii_set=



Our default recommendation: Bondi/CRC. It is the de-facto community standard for MOF characterisation, it is what default_vdw_radii_angstrom returns, and it is what most published PLDs / void fractions are quoted against. Switch to Alvarez when the metal chemistry dominates (open-metal sites, large metal nodes) and you want the most modern calibration.

text:
Parameter reference








Parameter (on do_periodic_segmentation_rust)
Default
Effect




vdw_radii_set
"bondi_crc_fallback"
Audit tag — does not recompute the dgrid. One of "bondi", "bondi_crc_fallback", "crc", "mendeleev", "alvarez", "array".


vdw_radii_angstrom
None
Per-atom radii (Å). If passed, recorded under vdw_radii_set="array" (unless you also set the tag explicitly).


(build dgrid with) dgrid_from_atoms_rust(..., radii=...)
Bondi
The actual table the dgrid is built with. Always pass an explicit radii= for non-Bondi tables.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Tips

Always pass radii= when building the dgrid if you want a non-Bondi table. The default is Bondi/CRC, not “auto-detect”.
Always pass vdw_radii_set= when calling the segmentation so the audit trail captures your choice. The same key in seg['input_params'] is what downstream pocket typing reads.
When comparing two segmentations of the same MOF, plot pocket_radius (from maxima_info) and PLD side-by-side. Those two numbers capture >90 % of the practical difference.
Don’t mix tables across steps. If you build a dgrid with Bondi and then pass vdw_radii_set="alvarez", the audit will be wrong. The tag must match the dgrid.

title: Van der Waals Radii and Segmentation
text:
Troubleshooting








Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




ValueError: unknown vdw_radii_set
A typo or unsupported tag
Use one of bondi / bondi_crc_fallback / crc / mendeleev / alvarez / array


Same PLD across all three tables
The dgrid was built with the same table in all three runs (forgot radii=)
Pass radii= explicitly when building each dgrid


Pockets “disappear” under Alvarez
The dgrid is too tight — the h-maxima threshold cuts too many peaks
Lower threshold_abs (e.g. 1.5 → 1.0) and re-run with the same dgrid


vdw_radii_by_symbol shows wrong values
You passed vdw_radii_set but built the dgrid with a different table
Build the dgrid with the matching radii= first

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
Once you have a periodic segmentation (seg dict from do_periodic_segmentation_rust), the next quantity of interest is the probe-accessible surface area and void volume at a chosen probe radius. mofography ships two complementary estimators that share the same percolation analysis pipeline:

Mesh (marching-cubes) — compute_surface_area_mesh_winding. Deterministic; tessellates the level set dgrid = r_probe with skimage.measure.marching_cubes, then measures the mesh area with trimesh. Excellent as a reference, slow on large grids.
Monte-Carlo shell — compute_surface_area_mc_winding. Statistical; samples N random points in the unit cell, counts how many land in a thin shell of thickness δ around the probe surface, and reports SA = V_cell · p_shell / δ. Fast, parallelisable, and tunable for precision.

This tutorial covers:

The full dgrid → seg → SA / void volume pipeline on IRMOF-1.cif.
The Monte-Carlo shell estimator: signature, returned dict, per-region / per-pocket / per-cluster breakdowns.
A side-by-side MC shell vs. marching-cubes mesh comparison.
Void volume via the same accessibility analysis — global, per-region, per-pocket, and a point-probe reference for sanity.
The role of window fingerprinting (window_fp=True) on accessible SA: where the two accessibility modes disagree and why.
A 3-D figure of the unit cell with a translucent dgrid isosurface and the pocket maxima.

If you have not done so, please complete the Distance Grid, Region Segmentation, and Connections and Windows tutorials first — the rest of this page assumes you can build a seg dict in your sleep.

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
Why the MC shell estimator?
The mesh method is exact (modulo tessellation) but two artifacts creep in on coarse grids:

Blocky isosurface — coarse dgrid spacing produces low-poly surfaces; mesh area underestimates the true value.
Region-boundary triangles dropped — faces that straddle region boundaries disappear when the per-region submeshes are built, leading to systematic undercount of surface area at the interfaces between pores.

The MC shell estimator does not build a mesh at all. It directly measures the volume of the thin band around the isosurface — a quantity that is mathematically well-defined even when the discrete mesh is imperfect. In practice the MC shell agrees with Zeo++ better than the marching-cubes mesh does, and the noise floor is set by n_samples (∝ 1/√N).

section: Step 1: Load IRMOF-1 and compute the distance grid
text:
Step 1: Load IRMOF-1 and compute the distance grid
IRMOF-1 is a clean test case: 424 atoms, ~26 Å cubic cell, two cage families, no disordered atoms. The defaults of do_periodic_segmentation_rust produce 8 PBC-grouped pockets.


Show code
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
print(f"IRMOF-1: {len(atoms)} atoms, cell = {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)} Å")

spacing = 0.5                                  # Å — see dgrid_methods.qmd
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)               # cast to float32 — required by do_periodic_segmentation_rust
print(f"dgrid: shape={dgrid.shape}, void max = {dgrid.max():.1f} Å")


IRMOF-1: 424 atoms, cell = [25.83 25.83 25.83] Å
dgrid: shape=(52, 52, 52), void max = 7.5 Å

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
Step 2: Periodic segmentation + percolation history
A single call to do_periodic_segmentation_rust returns a seg dict containing everything the SA / void-volume routines need: the dgrid, the regions_pbc and pbc_groups from the PBC merge, the connections list, and the percolation_history (computed automatically here because compute_connections=True and the percolation stage is on by default).


Show code
seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid, atoms, spacing=spacing,
    mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
    minimum_window_separation=1.5, wall_thickness=0.05, extra_padding=5,
    compute_connections=True, watershed_backend="rust_det", disable_tqdm=True,
)

print(f"Pockets (PBC-grouped):  {len(seg['maxima_pbc'])}")
print(f"Unique regions:         {len(seg['unique_regions'])}")
print(f"Window connections:     {len(seg['connections'])}")
print(f"pbc_groups:             {len(seg['pbc_groups'])} PBC pockets")
print(f"percolation_history:    {'percolation_history' in seg}  (computed lazily if missing)")


Pockets (PBC-grouped):  8
Unique regions:         27
Window connections:     300
pbc_groups:             8 PBC pockets
percolation_history:    False  (computed lazily if missing)

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
Step 3: Pore diameters (LCD, PLD, DFSD)
get_pore_dia_mgr is the single-call helper that returns the three standard diameters. We do this before SA so we can sanity-check the probe radius we feed into the SA routines — it should be smaller than the PLD, otherwise no pocket percolates and accessible SA drops to zero.


Show code
lcd, pld, dfsd, _ = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr(atoms, dgrid=dgrid, kwargs={})
print(f"LCD  (largest cavity diameter):       {lcd:.2f} Å")
print(f"PLD  (pore-limiting diameter):       {pld:.2f} Å")
print(f"DFSD (dominant framework-solvent):   {dfsd:.2f} Å")

probe_radius = 1.2   # helium — well below the PLD, so all pockets percolate
print(f"\nChosen probe_radius = {probe_radius} Å  →  probe < PLD ✓")


LCD  (largest cavity diameter):       15.08 Å
PLD  (pore-limiting diameter):       7.89 Å
DFSD (dominant framework-solvent):   15.08 Å

Chosen probe_radius = 1.2 Å  →  probe < PLD ✓

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
Step 4: Monte-Carlo shell surface area
The signature is:
compute_surface_area_mc_winding(
    results_dict, mat_atoms,
    probe_radius=None,         # default: helium radius (1.2 Å)
    n_samples=20_000,          # MC sample count
    shell_thickness=0.5,       # half-width of the band around the probe surface (Å)
    return_details=False,
    window_fp=True,            # window-fingerprint rescue on accessible side
    winding_kwargs=None,
)
It returns a dict with:







Key
Meaning




total_surface_area
SA over all regions at the probe radius (m²/g), MC estimate.


accessible_surface_area
SA restricted to percolating regions only (m²/g).


accessible_fraction
accessible / total.


by_region
{region_id → SA (m²/g)} for the accessible fragment regions.


by_pocket
{pocket_id → SA (m²/g)} — sums by_region over each PBC pocket.


by_percolated_cluster
{cluster_label → SA (m²/g)} — per percolated cluster at the chosen threshold.


sa_mc_diagnostics
n_samples, shell_thickness, n_shell_hits_total, n_shell_hits_accessible.


probe_radius
The probe actually used.





Show code
sa_mc = mgr.compute_surface_area_mc_winding(
    seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe_radius, n_samples=20000, shell_thickness=0.5
)

print("=" * 60)
print("MC SHELL SURFACE AREA  (IRMOF-1, He probe)")
print("=" * 60)
print(f"  total_surface_area:        {sa_mc['total_surface_area']:>10.1f} m²/g")
print(f"  accessible_surface_area:   {sa_mc['accessible_surface_area']:>10.1f} m²/g")
print(f"  accessible_fraction:       {sa_mc['accessible_fraction']:>10.4f}")
print(f"  probe_radius:              {sa_mc['probe_radius']:>10.2f} Å")
print()
print("  sa_mc_diagnostics:")
for k, v in sa_mc['sa_mc_diagnostics'].items():
    print(f"    {k:>26s}  {v}")


============================================================
MC SHELL SURFACE AREA  (IRMOF-1, He probe)
============================================================
  total_surface_area:            3794.0 m²/g
  accessible_surface_area:       3794.0 m²/g
  accessible_fraction:           1.0000
  probe_radius:                    1.20 Å

  sa_mc_diagnostics:
                     n_samples  20000
               shell_thickness  0.5
            n_shell_hits_total  2251
       n_shell_hits_accessible  2251


The diagnostic n_shell_hits_total is the raw number of n_samples=20000 random points whose interpolated distance from the framework lies within shell_thickness/2 of the probe radius. It is the MC count that gets converted to a surface area. With 20000 samples you expect a few-percent statistical error on total_surface_area.

Per-pocket breakdown
by_pocket is the most useful field for a structural-chemistry report: it gives one SA number per PBC pocket. We sort by descending area and print a small table.

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
Step 5: Mesh surface area (marching-cubes reference)
For a head-to-head comparison we run the mesh method on the same seg dict, same probe radius, same accessibility mode. The two should agree to within a few percent on a clean MOF; the disagreement quantifies how much the mesh is missing at region interfaces.


Show code
sa_mesh = mgr.compute_surface_area_mesh_winding(seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe_radius)

print(f"{'method':<14s}  {'total':>10s}  {'accessible':>12s}  {'frac':>8s}")

section: Step 7: Effect of window_fp on accessible SA
text:
Step 7: Effect of window_fp on accessible SA
window_fp=True (the default) lets the winding accessibility logic rescue watershed regions that are visually accessible but lie behind a sub-probe window. The mechanism is: if the window’s direction-invariant shell fingerprint matches a reference open window (e.g. a window of the same size on a different edge of the same region), the downstream region is treated as percolating. Setting window_fp=False disables that rescue and falls back to strict winding-only percolation.
The impact is structure-specific. On IRMOF-1 (a clean, symmetric framework) the difference is small; on more irregular MOFs with sub-probe windows it can flip the accessibility of an entire pocket.


Show code
sa_fp_on  = mgr.compute_surface_area_mc_winding(seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe_radius, window_fp=True)
sa_fp_off = mgr.compute_surface_area_mc_winding(seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe_radius, window_fp=False)

print(f"{'window_fp':<14s}  {'total':>10s}  {'accessible':>12s}  {'n_pockets':>10s}")

      f"{sa_fp_on['accessible_surface_area']:>12.1f}  {len(sa_fp_on['by_pocket']):>10d}")
print(f"{'False':<14s}  {sa_fp_off['total_surface_area']:>10.1f}  "
      f"{sa_fp_off['accessible_surface_area']:>12.1f}  {len(sa_fp_off['by_pocket']):>10d}")

section: Step 8: MC shell-thickness sweep — bias and variance
text:
Step 8: MC shell-thickness sweep — bias and variance
The expected value of the MC estimator is independent of shell_thickness in the small-δ limit, because p_shell scales linearly with δ and the 1/δ factor cancels. The variance, however, scales with 1/δ: thicker shells contain more samples and the estimate is less noisy. A sweep across δ is a useful diagnostic — agreement to within a few percent confirms the shell-thickness bias is small.


Show code
print(f"{'δ (Å)':>6s}  {'total SA':>10s}  {'shell hits':>12s}  {'hits/sample':>14s}")
print("-" * 50)
for delta in (0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0):
    sa = mgr.compute_surface_area_mc_winding(
        seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe_radius, n_samples=40000, shell_thickness=delta
    )
    hits = sa['sa_mc_diagnostics']['n_shell_hits_total']
    print(f"  {delta:>4.1f}  {sa['total_surface_area']:>10.1f}  {hits:>12d}  "
          f"{hits/40000:>14.4f}")


 δ (Å)    total SA    shell hits     hits/sample
--------------------------------------------------
   0.3      3868.1          2754          0.0688
   0.5      3810.0          4521          0.1130
   0.7      3903.1          6484          0.1621
   1.0      3777.5          8965          0.2241


For IRMOF-1 all four rows should agree within ~3% — the MC noise level for 40 000 samples. If they do not agree, one of two things is happening:

δ is comparable to the probe radius → the shell is sampling curvature that the small-δ approximation cannot resolve. Drop δ to 0.5 or below.
A real feature is being washed out by the shell (e.g. a 1-Å window at a 1.2-Å probe with δ=1.0). Drop δ to 0.3 and re-check.

text:
Step 9: Visualize the accessible pockets
plot_maxima returns a tuple (Scatter3d, Mesh3d) when show_spheres=True — we unpack it and add both traces to a go.Figure. plot_surface_dgrid returns a single Mesh3d trace; we add it directly. Passing select= with the accessible region labels (the keys of by_region) trims the isosurface to the accessible domains, so a blocked pocket would not be drawn.


Show code
n_pockets = int(seg["regions_pbc"].max())
unit_cell_maxima = seg["all_maxima"][:n_pockets]

# Pore maxima as spheres (sphere opacity = 0.6, colour ~ pore radius)
scatter_tr, mesh_tr = mgr.plot_maxima(
    dgrid, unit_cell_maxima, atoms,
    show_spheres=True, sphere_opacity=0.6,
    name=f"Pockets ({n_pockets})",
)

# Translucent dgrid isosurface at the probe radius, trimmed to the accessible regions.
# `by_region` holds the accessible region labels of the un-merged `seg["regions"]`
# (labels of the PBC-merged array would also pull in partial pores).
accessible_labels = list(sa_mc["by_region"])
surf_tr = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
    dgrid, probe_radius, atoms,
    region_labels=seg["regions"], select=accessible_labels,
    opacity=0.35, cscale=px.colors.qualitative.Pastel,
    stylize=True, name=f"accessible isosurface @ {probe_radius} Å",
)

# Faint framework
fw_atoms = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(atoms)
framework_trs = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(
    fw_atoms, stylize=True, kwargs_frame_mesh={"opacity": 0.15},
)

fig = go.Figure(data=[scatter_tr, mesh_tr, surf_tr, *framework_trs])
fig.update_layout(
    scene_aspectmode="data",
    title=dict(
        text=f"IRMOF-1: 8 PBC pockets + accessible SA = {sa_mc['accessible_surface_area']:.0f} m²/g",
        x=0.5, xanchor="center",
    ),
    paper_bgcolor="black",
)

Common pitfalls








Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




accessible_surface_area = 0 at small probe
probe > PLD; nothing percolates
drop probe_radius until it sits well below the PLD


MC and mesh disagree by >10%
shell thickness is too small (δ << spacing) or mesh has resolution artefacts

Mesh misses a region boundary
sub-mesh tessellation drops boundary triangles; this is a real estimator bias

a pocket sits behind a sub-probe window that the fingerprint would normally rescue
either is defensible — interpret as a strict bound; document the choice


by_percolated_cluster keys look like axis_x_cluster_0

point_probe_reference.void_volume_fraction looks very different from accessible_void_volume / cell_volume
the point-probe reference uses a different (purely geometric) convention
use the accessible numbers for the screening-quality value; the point-probe number is a consistency check

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
What’s in the output dict
A single call to compute_surface_area_mc_winding(seg, atoms, probe_radius=1.2) gives you this:
{
  'total_surface_area':       <float, m²/g>,
  'accessible_surface_area':  <float, m²/g>,
  'accessible_fraction':      <float in [0, 1]>,
  'probe_radius':             <float, Å>,
  'by_region':                {region_id (int)            → SA (m²/g)},
  'by_pocket':                {pocket_id (int)            → SA (m²/g)},
  'by_percolated_cluster':    {"axis_X_cluster_N" (str)   → SA (m²/g)},
  'sa_mc_diagnostics': {
      'n_samples':                 <int>,
      'shell_thickness':           <float, Å>,
      'n_shell_hits_total':        <int>,
      'n_shell_hits_accessible':   <int>,
  },
}
A single call to compute_void_volume_from_results_winding(seg, atoms, probe_radius=1.2) gives you this:
{
  'total_void_volume':             <float, cm³/g>,
  'accessible_void_volume':        <float, cm³/g>,
  'by_region':                     {region_id → V (cm³/g)},  # accessible fragments
  'by_region_pbc':                 {region_pbc_label → V (cm³/g)},
  'by_pocket':                     {pocket_id → V (cm³/g)},
  'by_percolated_cluster':         {cluster_label → V (cm³/g)},
  'accessible_fraction':           <float>,
  'probe_radius':                  <float, Å>,
  'num_regions':                   <int>,
  'num_accessible_regions':        <int>,
  'num_pockets':                   <int>,
  'num_accessible_pockets':        <int>,
  'num_percolated_clusters':       <int>,
  'complete_pockets':              <int>,
  'incomplete_pockets':            <int>,
  'flagged_incomplete_pockets':    {pocket_id → {accessible_void_volume, completeness_fraction, missing_regions, accessible_regions}},
  'pocket_completeness_stats':     {total_pockets, complete_pockets, incomplete_pockets, completeness_rate},
  'point_probe_reference':         {surface_area, void_volume, void_volume_fraction},
}
The fields you actually want in a screening report are usually:

Total surface area / void volume — for table 1.
accessible_fraction — for filtering “open” MOFs.
by_pocket — for ranking pockets within a single MOF.
point_probe_reference.void_volume_fraction — for cross-validating against Zeo++.

title: Surface Area & Void Volume — MC Shell Estimator + Window Fingerprints
text:
Summary







Concept
What it does




compute_surface_area_mc_winding
MC shell SA — fast, statistical, robust to mesh artefacts.


compute_surface_area_mesh_winding
Marching-cubes mesh SA — slow, deterministic, tessellation artefacts.


compute_void_volume_from_results_winding
Voxel-counted void volume + per-pocket completeness.


n_samples
MC sample count. 20 000 is the default; 50 000+ for sub-percent noise.


shell_thickness
Half-width of the MC band around the isosurface. 0.5 Å is the canonical default; sweep {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} to confirm bias is small.


window_fp=True
Use window-fingerprint rescue on the accessible side. Default; flip to False for a strict-winding bound.


by_region / by_pocket / by_percolated_cluster
Three granularities of accessible SA / void volume for a single MOF.



Key takeaways:

The MC shell estimator is the right default for high-throughput screening — n_samples=20 000 is fast, gives few-percent accuracy, and does not suffer from mesh artefacts.
A shell-thickness sweep at fixed n_samples is the simplest bias diagnostic: if δ=0.3 and δ=0.7 agree to within a few percent, the bias is small.
window_fp=True (default) is the more permissive accessibility mode; switch to False only when you want the strict-winding bound.
Always sanity-check with the point-probe reference in the void-volume output — it catches segmentation / dgrid mistakes that would otherwise pass unnoticed.

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
Region segmentation breaks the void space of a nanoporous material into discrete pockets, each centered on a local maximum of the distance field. It is the conceptual bridge between the distance grid (a continuous scalar field) and the pore graph (a discrete graph you can analyze with NetworkX).
This tutorial covers the why behind the algorithm: what maxima and watershed do, why periodic boundary conditions (PBC) matter, and which parameters to tune. For the hands-on three-call pipeline, see the Quick Start. For defaults and safe ranges of every parameter, see Tuning and safe ranges.

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
Region segmentation breaks the void space of a nanoporous material into discrete pockets, each centered on a local maximum of the distance field. It is the conceptual bridge between the distance grid (a continuous scalar field) and the pore graph (a discrete graph you can analyze with NetworkX).
This tutorial covers the why behind the algorithm: what maxima and watershed do, why periodic boundary conditions (PBC) matter, and which parameters to tune. For the hands-on three-call pipeline, see the Quick Start. For defaults and safe ranges of every parameter, see Tuning and safe ranges.

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
The Core Question
Segmentation answers: “Which pore does this voxel belong to?”
Imagine the distance field as a landscape:

🎯 Local maxima → pore centers (peaks where a probe would sit)
🏔️ Watershed boundaries → pore walls (ridges between adjacent valleys)
💧 Voxels → assigned to the basin of the nearest maximum




Pockets as watershed basins


This metaphor — pour water into the inverted distance field, label each voxel by which basin it drains into — is exactly what watershed segmentation does.

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
Why We Need Periodic Segmentation
Crystalline materials repeat across unit cell boundaries, but pores don’t respect those boundaries. A large pore sitting at the corner of a cubic cell appears as 8 fragments (one per corner) when you segment without PBC handling. Physically, those 8 fragments are one pore cut off by the box.



Split regions at boundaries


Periodic segmentation solves this by:

Padding the grid so maxima near edges can “see” their periodic images
Identifying which maxima are periodic images of the same pore
Assigning the same label to all images
Trimming back to the original unit cell

The result: the 8 corner pieces merge into a single pore.



Merged regions with PBC

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
Concept 1: Maxima Detection (Finding Pore Centers)
The first step is to find the local maxima of the distance field. These are the pore centers.

The challenge: noise vs. features
A real distance grid has:

Noise from grid discretization (atom responsible for nearest distance can jump abruptly, causing distance values to wobble)
Real features: small pockets, large channels, tunnels
Surface roughness that would spawn spurious maxima if treated as features

A naive “every voxel that’s higher than its 26 neighbors” pass would give you hundreds of fake pockets. We need a selective approach.


h-maxima
The classic tool is h-maxima from scikit-image: keep only those local maxima that stand at least h units above their surroundings. Smaller peaks get suppressed. The parameter h is the persistence — how significant a peak has to be to count.
# Conceptual: keep peak P iff (value(P) - value(any neighbor)) >= h
# Smaller h  ->  more, smaller pockets
# Larger h   ->  fewer, larger pockets



Effect of h on maxima detection




Selective smoothing
MOFography’s Rust backend adds a layer on top of h-maxima: selective smoothing. The idea is to smooth the distance field with a spatially-varying Gaussian kernel that:

Does not smooth small features (distance < preserve_threshold) — they are real pockets
Smooths heavily for large features (distance > smooth_threshold) — this is roughness in channel walls that should not produce maxima
Linearly interpolates the smoothing radius in between

After smoothing, h-maxima runs on the cleaned-up field. The result is cleaner pore centers with fewer spurious ones.
The three smoothing parameters you can tune:








Parameter
Default
Effect




preserve_threshold
3.0 Å
Features below this distance are not smoothed (kept as pockets)


smooth_threshold
6.0 Å
Features above this distance are smoothed at max_smooth_radius


max_smooth_radius
2.0 Å
Cap on the smoothing radius (grid units)

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
Concept 2: Watershed Segmentation
Once maxima are found, watershed segmentation assigns every void-space voxel to one of them.

The water-filling analogy

Take the (inverted) distance field — maxima become valleys
Pour water simultaneously into each valley
Where water from two valleys would meet, raise a “dam” — that is the watershed boundary
When the water covers everything, each voxel is in the basin of exactly one maximum

Equivalently, in MOFography, the watershed assigns each void voxel to the nearest maximum, where “nearest” is geodesic (respecting the topology of the void). The output is a 3D integer array where every void voxel has a region label.



Cross-section of segmentation




With and without PBC
You get two region arrays from the same call:








Array
PBC handling
Use case




regions_pbc
✅ Merged (all periodic images share a label)
Property averaging, visualization, most analyses


regions
❌ Split (each periodic image is its own region)
Detailed pore graph, ML, non-periodic systems



For most analyses of crystalline MOFs, use regions_pbc. The number of unique pores is simply regions_pbc.max().

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
The Single API Call
The whole pipeline — distance grid prep, selective smoothing, maxima detection, PBC grouping, watershed, connection detection — happens inside do_periodic_segmentation_rust(). It takes the distance grid and the ASE atoms, and returns a dictionary of 15 keys.


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np

# Step 1: load the structure
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
print(f"Loaded {atoms.get_chemical_formula()}, {len(atoms)} atoms")
print(f"Cell: {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)} Å")


Loaded C192H96O104Zn32, 424 atoms

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
Parameter Tuning

Most important parameters
These four control the number and shape of the detected pores:








Parameter
Default
Effect




h
0.2 Å
h-maxima persistence. Higher → fewer, larger pockets.


min_distance
1.5 Å
Maxima closer than this get merged. Higher → fewer pockets.


threshold_abs
1.5 Å
Ignore peaks shallower than this. Higher → only large pores.


mask_thickness
0.05 Å
Voxels closer to framework than this are “wall”, not pore. 0.05 is the default and recommended; raise to ~0.15 only to drop wall slivers. Keep it well below the plotting isovalue.





Advanced smoothing parameters
If you see spurious small maxima in the middle of large channels, or you are losing real small pockets, tune the selective-smoothing triad:








Parameter
Default
Effect




preserve_threshold
3.0 Å
Below this distance, smoothing is off (real pockets preserved)


smooth_threshold
6.0 Å
Above this distance, smoothing is at max_smooth_radius


max_smooth_radius
2.0 Å
Cap on smoothing kernel (Å)



Lower smooth_threshold to smooth more aggressively; raise preserve_threshold to protect more small pockets.


PBC handling parameters








Parameter
Default
Effect




extra_padding
5 Å
Extra padding beyond the standard +5 Å, for very large pores


wall_thickness
0.05
Fraction of cell — controls how “wall” is defined near boundaries


minimum_window_separation
auto
Min separation for two windows to count as distinct


watershed_backend
"rust_det"
One of rust_det | rust_bucket | rust_det_parallel | skimage


min_region_size
0.001
Fraction of padded volume — regions smaller than this are dropped





Recipes



Symptom
Try




Too many tiny pockets
Increase h (e.g. 0.2 → 0.4), or increase min_distance


Missing small pockets
Decrease threshold_abs (1.5 → 1.0) or h (0.2 → 0.1)


Spurious maxima in large channels
Decrease smooth_threshold or increase max_smooth_radius


Real small pockets getting smoothed away
Increase preserve_threshold (3.0 → 4.0)


Wall fragments in regions
Increase mask_thickness (0.05 → 0.15; see Tuning)


Out of memory
Use dgrid_from_atoms_rtree_rust (R-tree, less RAM)

title: Region Segmentation in MOFography
text:
Common Pitfalls







Issue
Fix




dgrid dtype error from Rust
dgrid = dgrid_from_atoms_rust(...) already returns float32 — do not pass a float64 grid from Dask.


Wrong unit cell conventions
Use the Rust backend (dgrid_from_atoms_rust) — it handles non-orthogonal cells correctly. Avoid the deprecated _gpu and _cpu_no_aabb variants.


Pore count doesn’t match expectation
Check regions_pbc.max() (not len(maxima_pbc)) — both should agree, but regions_pbc.max() is the ground truth.


Some regions missing from unit cell
Increase extra_padding — large pores may need more room around the cell to be detected.

title: pocket_regions_cluster
text:
go-to Safe accessor for typed region label grid used in surface colouring.
workflow.pocket_regions_cluster(typed_result, seg)
Return the pocket-type region label grid for surface colouring.
assign_pocket_types stores the typed region array as PocketTypingResult.regions_cluster (a numpy.ndarray). The naive typed.regions_cluster or seg.get("regions_pbc") fails with ValueError because numpy arrays have no single boolean truth value.
This helper does the safe is not None check and falls back to the raw PBC-merged region grid from the segmentation dict when pocket typing did not populate the array (e.g. when result.ok is False).
Usage::
from mofography.workflow import assign_pocket_types, pocket_regions_cluster

result  = assign_pocket_types(seg, atoms)
regions = pocket_regions_cluster(result, seg)
surface = plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid, 1.75, select="all",
                             region_labels=regions, ...)

title: get_pore_dia_mgr_winding3
text:
alternate Prunes spill artifact edges on the graph instead of re-segmenting; dev-focused. Use get_pore_dia_mgr_winding instead.
winding_percolation.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding3(
    mat_atoms=None,
    dgrid=None,
    kwargs=None,
    results=None,
    include_dangling=True,
    expand_components=True,
    spill_margin=2.0,
)
Compute pore diameters with spill-edge pruning (no resegmentation).
Identical to get_pore_dia_mgr_winding but instead of re-segmenting with a thicker mask, this version detects and removes spill-over edges from the pore graph. A real constriction must have framework atoms near the window center; spill artifacts float in empty pore space.
Detection: for each edge, compute PBC-aware distance from the window center to the nearest framework atom. If nearest_atom_dist > wr_min + spill_margin, the edge is a spill artifact and is pruned.


mat_atoms : ase.Atoms, optional ASE Atoms object. Required if results is None. dgrid : ndarray, optional Pre-computed distance grid. kwargs : dict, optional Keyword arguments for do_periodic_segmentation_rust. results : dict, optional Pre-computed segmentation results. include_dangling : bool Whether to include dangling edges. expand_components : bool Whether to expand components. spill_margin : float Extra tolerance (Å) beyond window radius for spill detection. Default 2.0 Å covers max(CRC_vdw) + headroom.



tuple[float, float, float, ndarray] (lcd, pld, dfsd, dgrid)
