go-to Finds region connections and window sites on a RAG; used after segmentation in tutorials.
compute.get_connections_for_rag(
    rag,
    region_labels,
    maxima,
    ase_atoms,
    dgrid,
    minimum_window_separation=1.0,
    wall_windows=True,
    wall_thickness=2,
)
Find connections between regions in a region adjacency graph (RAG) and identify window locations.
This function analyzes a RAG to find connections between adjacent regions and identifies the window locations where regions connect. It uses agglomerative clustering to group boundary points into windows and finds the optimal window centers based on distance values.


rag : networkx.Graph Region adjacency graph representing connections between regions region_labels : numpy.ndarray 3D array of region labels where each unique value represents a different region maxima : numpy.ndarray Array containing the maxima points of each region ase_atoms : ase.Atoms ASE Atoms object containing the structure information dgrid : numpy.ndarray 3D array of distance values on the grid minimum_window_separation : float, optional Minimum distance between separate windows, by default 1.0 wall_windows : bool, optional Whether to calculate windows on periodic boundaries, by default True wall_thickness : int, optional Thickness of wall region for finding periodic windows, by default 2

title: get_bond_types

go-to Bin bond orders to single/double/triple with aromatic distance tolerances for plotting.
analyze.get_bond_types(bond_orders, *, bonds=None, ase_atoms=None)
Map continuous bond orders to single / double / triple labels.
With bonds and ase_atoms, applies distance-based aromatic tolerances when pymatgen bond orders sit on bin edges:

triple → double if C–N distance ≤ _AROMATIC_CN_TRIPLE_MAX_DIST (short aromatic C–N misclassified as triple)

The function dgrid_from_atoms_gpu calculates a distance grid based on atomic positions using GPU acceleration.

The ase_atoms parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_gpu function is expected to be an ASE Atoms object, which represents a collection of atoms and their properties. It determines the resolution of the grid where the distances from atoms to grid points are calculated. A smaller spacing value will result in a higher resolution grid with more grid points,
0.2

The block_size parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms_gpu function determines the size of each block used for processing the data. In this function, it is used for chunking the data and processing it in parallel on the GPU. A larger block_size can lead to more efficient, defaults to 10000 (optional)
10000














Name
Type
Description






The function dgrid_from_atoms_gpu returns a 3D numpy array representing a distance grid computed based on the input atomic structure provided in the form of ASE atoms. The distance grid is calculated by computing the minimum distance between each point on the grid and the atoms in the structure, taking into account the atomic radii. The grid is computed using GPU-accelerated calculations for efficiency.

Compute void volume analysis from pre-computed results dictionary with accessibility concerns.
This function takes results from do_periodic_segmentation and compute_percolation_history to provide comprehensive void volume analysis at multiple granularity levels.


results_dict : dict Results dictionary containing at minimum: - ‘distance_grid’: Distance grid array - ‘pbc_groups’: PBC groups dictionary - ‘regions_pbc’: Periodic regions array - Optional: ‘percolation_history’ from compute_percolation_history mat_atoms : ase.Atoms Atomic structure for volume calculation and coordinate transformations. probe_radius : float, optional Probe radius for void volume calculation. If None, uses helium radius. return_details : bool, optional If True, returns detailed intermediate results. Default False. window_fp_for_accessible : bool, optional Winding only: window-fingerprint bridging when True; strict winding when False. winding_kwargs : dict, optional Extra keyword arguments for winding fingerprint bridging (merged over results_dict['winding_kwargs'] when present). accessibility_method : str, optional "winding" (default) or "lattice". lattice_variant : str, optional "v2" or "v1" for lattice accessibility.



dict Dictionary containing: - ‘total_void_volume’: Total void volume of entire structure (cm³/g) - ‘accessible_void_volume’: Total accessible void volume (percolated) (cm³/g) - ‘by_region’: Accessible void volume per individual region (dict) - ‘by_pocket’: Accessible void volume per complete pocket (dict) - ‘by_percolated_cluster’: Accessible void volume per percolated cluster (dict) - ‘accessible_fraction’: Fraction of total void volume that is accessible - ‘probe_radius’: Probe radius used If return_details=True, also includes intermediate results.

title: compute_aromatic_cycles
text:
compute_aromatic_cycles
go-to Main aromatic-ring API; caches cycles on the Atoms object after bond detection.
analyze.compute_aromatic_cycles(
    ase_atoms,
    *,
    force_recompute=False,
    expand_isomorphisms=True,
    default_ring_sizes=None,
    merge_duplicate_sites=True,
    expand_to_unit_cell=True,
)
Detect aromatic cycles and cache the result in ase_atoms.info.
Mirrors mgr.analyze.compute_aromatic_cycles:

Ensures covalent bonds are present (calls :func:update_with_covalent_bonds if needed).
Returns the cached ase_atoms.info["aromatic_cycles"] when force_recompute=False and the info entry is already populated.
Otherwise detects rings (unit-cell chordless search by default), stores the result in ase_atoms.info["aromatic_cycles"], and returns it.

When merge_duplicate_sites is True (default), atoms that share the same element and wrapped fractional coordinates are merged before graph construction. Cycle atom indices are mapped back to the input structure.
When expand_to_unit_cell is True (default), rings are found on the full structure with :func:find_aromatic_cycles_in_unit_cell (sizes default_ring_sizes, default 5–9) so every distinct linker in the cell is highlighted. When False, uses graph cycle detection on a merged or full structure (representative atoms only for merged sites).
Used by :func:~mofography.visualize.plot_aromatic_rings (Plotly) and :func:~mofography.movies.make_aromatic_rings_trace (Three.js) when a pre-computed cycle list is not supplied.

text:
blocking_spheres_overlap_leakage
raspa_helper.blocking_spheres_overlap_leakage(
    results,
    ase_atoms,
    spheres,
    probe_radius,
    *,
    denominator_domain='accessible',
    resolution='coarse',
    sample_spacing=0.5,

    restrict_to_rag_adjacent_accessible=True,
    require_face_neighbor_inaccessible=True,

    atol=0.0001,
    chunk_size=65536,
)
How much blocking spheres intrude into the other void class (leakage).

denominator_domain="accessible" — measure overlap into percolating void (typical when spheres block inaccessible pockets, BlockPockets).
denominator_domain="inaccessible" — measure overlap into non-percolating void (when spheres target accessible regions, InvertBlockPockets).

resolution: "fine" (full segmentation grid), "coarse" (subsample at sample_spacing), or "interface" (accessible interface band only; denominator_domain must be "accessible").
Fine grid spacing defaults to :func:segmentation_spacing_from_results (usually results["input_params"]["spacing"] from periodic segmentation).

title: blocking_spheres_overlap_into_accessible_near_interface
text:
raspa_helper.blocking_spheres_overlap_into_accessible_near_interface(
    results,
    ase_atoms,
    spheres,
    probe_radius,
    *,
    sample_spacing=0.5,
    fine_spacing=None,
    accessible_dgrid_ge_probe=False,
    restrict_to_rag_adjacent_accessible=True,
    require_face_neighbor_inaccessible=True,
    atol=0.0001,
    chunk_size=65536,
)
Cheaper overlap diagnostic: sample coarse grid points (default 0.5 Å) that lie on interface accessible voxels (see :func:accessible_interface_voxel_mask).
Each coarse voxel center is classified by nearest fine-grid voxel (same fractional mapping as :func:mofography.compute.dask_grid_over_atoms).
The reported fraction is only over this interface sample — not over all accessible void. A high percentage here often means the blocking union covers the narrow gasket next to pockets (expected for large including spheres), not that the bulk percolating channel is blocked; compare with :func:blocking_spheres_overlap_into_accessible_regions for a global accessible denominator (much more expensive).
Implemented via :func:blocking_spheres_overlap_leakage (resolution="interface").


sample_spacing : float Spacing (Å) for probe points; coarser => fewer distance evaluations. fine_spacing : float, optional Spacing of results['regions']; inferred if omitted. restrict_to_rag_adjacent_accessible, require_face_neighbor_inaccessible Passed to :func:accessible_interface_voxel_mask.

title: blocking_spheres_largest_including
text:
go-to PBC-consistent Gelb-Gubbins including spheres for inaccessible pockets.
raspa_helper.blocking_spheres_largest_including(
    results,
    ase_atoms,
    region_labels_to_cover,
    radius_scale=1.0,
)
Build a list of RASPA blocking spheres [sx, sy, sz, radius_Å] (fractional center + radius) that covers every voxel in the given segmentation regions.
For each voxel in the selected regions, the largest including sphere (Gelb–Gubbins style) is found: center is the voxel C with maximum dgrid[C] such that PBC-distance(voxel, C) <= dgrid[C]. Many voxels map to the same (center, radius); unique (center, radius) pairs are returned.
Use with region_labels_to_cover = inaccessible region labels to block non-percolating pockets for GCMC.


results : dict Must include regions and dgrid. ase_atoms : ase.Atoms Unit cell for PBC distances. region_labels_to_cover : set of int Region labels whose voxels must be covered by the output spheres. radius_scale : float Multiply each sphere radius by this factor (>= 0).

title: add_centroids_to_rag_with_pbc
text:
compute.add_centroids_to_rag_with_pbc(rag, props, pbc_groups, ase_atoms, shape)
Add PBC-aware centroid_pbc coordinates to RAG nodes for each periodic image group.
The function takes in a graph, a list of properties, a list of groups of nodes that are connected by periodic boundary conditions, an ASE atoms object, and the shape of the image.
The function first makes a copy of the graph. Then, it loops through each group of nodes that are connected by periodic boundary conditions. For each group, it finds the indices of the properties that correspond to the nodes in the group. If there is more than one node in the group, it finds the centroid of the group by taking the circular mean of the coordinates of the nodes in the group. If there is only one node in the group, it finds the centroid of the node by taking the mean of the coordinates of the node. Finally, it adds the centroid of the group

Type

Default

required


pbc_groups

a list of lists, where each list contains the labels of the atoms that are connected by periodic boundary conditions
required

the atoms object from ASE
required

required

threejs_viz.MovieFigure.export_png(
    path,
    *,
    resolution_mult=2,
    width=None,
    height=None,
    wait_ms=1500,
)
Export the current static scene to PNG.
Uses Playwright headless Chromium when installed::
pip install playwright
playwright install chromium
Otherwise raises with instructions to use the in-viewer Export PNG button after .show(renderer="browser").


path Output .png path. resolution_mult Supersampling factor (matches the viewer Export PNG control). width, height Browser viewport in pixels (default 1280×720). wait_ms Milliseconds to wait for WebGL scene load before capture.




threejs_viz.MovieFigure.save_html(path, **kwargs)
Write standalone HTML (alias of :meth:to_html).



threejs_viz.MovieFigure.set_lights(
    ambient=None,
    hemisphere_intensity=None,
    hemisphere_sky=None,
    hemisphere_ground=None,
    dir_key_intensity=None,
    dir_key_position=None,
    dir_fill_intensity=None,
    dir_fill_position=None,
    ssao=None,
    explicit=True,
)
Set Three.js scene lighting (embedded in exported HTML).
When explicit is True (default), the viewer uses these intensities as-is and does not apply the automatic orthographic compensation.


ambient Ambient light intensity (0–1 typical). hemisphere_intensity, hemisphere_sky, hemisphere_ground Hemisphere light settings (sky/ground are hex colours). dir_key_intensity, dir_key_position Key directional light. dir_fill_intensity, dir_fill_position Fill directional light. ssao Enable SSAO. Default: off in orthographic, on in perspective. explicit If True, skip orthographic auto-boost of directional lights.




threejs_viz.MovieFigure.show(
    renderer=None,
    *,
    height=600,
    width='100%',
    port=None,
)
Display the figure.
renderer="notebook" shows inline (iframe srcdoc); "browser" serves on 127.0.0.1 and opens the system browser. Default: inline inside a Jupyter kernel, browser otherwise.



threejs_viz.MovieFigure.to_html(
    path,
    template='threejs_default',
    sidecar=False,
    fps=20.0,
    point_size=0.16,
    pack_binary=False,
    background=None,
)
Write the scene to a standalone HTML file.
background (opt-in; default None keeps the current look) sets the initial viewer background: a solid colour "#0b1d3a", ("linear", c1, c2[, ...]) (left-to-right), ("radial", centre, edge) or {"type": ..., "colors": [...]}. The Bg picker / gradient buttons still work (they override it) and Export PNG captures it (it is drawn in the WebGL scene).
pack_binary=True (opt-in) stores large numeric arrays (positions, indices, colors, radii, sizes) as base64 float32/uint16/uint32 blobs instead of JSON number lists; the viewer decodes them on load. Typically ~3-4x smaller files.

title: Quick start
text: The full mofography pipeline: from a MOF crystal (a) through distance grid, watershed, PBC-aware segmentation, and pore graph construction (paper Figure 2)

title: Quick start
text:
Overview
Two functions do the heavy lifting. Everything else reads their output.

dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing) computes the distance grid (distance from each voxel to the nearest framework surface).
do_periodic_segmentation_rust(dgrid, atoms, ...) finds pockets, handles periodic boundaries, and detects windows. It returns one dictionary (seg).

From seg you get a pore graph, pocket types, windows, and textural properties (LCD, PLD, surface area, void volume). This page runs all of it on IRMOF-1. Parameter safe ranges live on Tuning and safe ranges.

title: Quick start
text:
Imports and structure


Show code
import numpy as np
import mofography as mgr
from mofography.cif_io import read_cif_to_ase  # fast Rust CIF reader, returns ase.Atoms (see the Fast Rust CIF reader page)

atoms = read_cif_to_ase("IRMOF-1.cif")   # or examples/TestCIFs/P1-IRMOF-1.cif from the repo root; ase.io.read works too
print(f"{atoms.get_chemical_formula()}: {len(atoms)} atoms")
print("Cell (Å):", atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2))


C192H96O104Zn32: 424 atoms
Cell (Å): [25.83 25.83 25.83]

title: Quick start
text:
1. Distance grid


Show code
spacing = 0.5  # Å. Halving it gives 8x more voxels.
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing).astype(np.float32)
print(f"Grid {dgrid.shape}, largest void radius {dgrid.max():.2f} Å")


Grid (52, 52, 52), largest void radius 7.54 Å


radii=None uses Bondi van der Waals radii. For other grid backends see Distance grid and Distance grid methods.

title: Quick start
text:
2. Periodic segmentation


Show code
seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid, atoms,
    spacing=spacing,             # always pass it; otherwise it is inferred
    mask_thickness=0.05,         # Å, voxels closer than this to the framework are background
    h=0.2,                       # Å, maxima persistence
    min_distance=1.5,            # Å, minimum separation between maxima
    threshold_abs=1.5,           # Å, minimum height of a maximum
    watershed_backend="rust_det",
    compute_connections=True,    # windows + connections
    return_dgrid=True,           # keep dgrid inside seg for later steps
    disable_tqdm=True,
)
print(f"Pockets (PBC-merged): {len(seg['maxima_pbc'])}")
print(f"Unique regions:       {len(seg['unique_regions'])}")
print(f"Window connections:   {len(seg['connections'])}")
print(f"PBC groups:           {len(seg['pbc_groups'])}")


Pockets (PBC-merged): 8
Unique regions:       27
Window connections:   300
PBC groups:           8


Those are the defaults (written out for clarity). seg also holds regions_pbc (labelled grid), maxima_info, all_maxima and input_params. See Region segmentation and PBC considerations.






Note



Messages starting with [pocket_maxima_check] mean a pocket’s recorded maximum is a bit lower than the true peak of its region (a few tenths of an Å). They are informational. See the tuning page if you want to remove them.

3. Pore graph
Pockets become nodes. Windows between pockets become edges.


Show code
rag = mgr.rag_from_connections(seg["connections"], seg["all_maxima"])
print(rag)

It is a networkx graph. See Pore graph.

Show code

typed = mgr.assign_pocket_types(seg, atoms, method="env_cluster")
print(f"{typed.n_types} types across {typed.n_pockets} pockets")

5. Windows
Each entry of seg["connections"] is [region_pair, flag, "internal"|"periodic", centre, radius]. Keep those that touch a unique region to avoid counting windows from the padding.


Show code
unique = seg["unique_regions"]
windows = [c for c in seg["connections"] if np.any(np.isin(c[0], unique))]
radii = np.array([float(np.ravel(c[4])[0]) for c in windows])
print(f"{len(windows)} windows in the cell; radii {radii.min():.2f}-{radii.max():.2f} Å")

6. Textural properties
LCD and PLD come from the winding method, which tests percolation across periodic images. Surface area and void volume are computed on the same seg.

probe = 1.2  # Å, helium; use a probe radius below PLD/2 or nothing percolates

vv = mgr.compute_void_volume_from_results_winding(seg, atoms, probe_radius=probe)

      f"(total {sa['total_surface_area']:.0f})")
print(f"Void volume:  {vv['accessible_void_volume']:.3f} cm³/g "
      f"(total {vv['total_void_volume']:.3f})")

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
This tutorial demonstrates how to compute pore-structure properties of a hyper-crosslinked polymer (HCP) with mofography. Using the 75X_0DVB_4 structure as an example, it builds a periodic pore graph and computes the largest cavity diameter, pore limiting diameter, N₂ accessible surface area, percolating pore volume, average pore and window sizes, pore connectivity, percolating backbone fraction, and fractional free volume.
The structure is taken from https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jctc.2c00798
For detailed definitions of these properties, see our paper about methane diffusion: Zheng, C.; Gopalan, A.; Shi, K. Revisiting Percolation and Molecular Diffusion in Disordered Pore Networks (https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv.15011012/v1). Requirements
The workflow has six steps:

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
Imports
Limit Rust to eight threads (change this to match your machine), then import the libraries.


Show code
import os
os.environ["RAYON_NUM_THREADS"] = "8"

import pandas as pd
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
1. Atom radii and parameters
This polymer is modelled with united-atom sites, so the default Bondi radii do not apply. Instead each atom type gets half its TraPPE Lennard-Jones sigma as its radius.


Show code
# TraPPE sigma (Å) of the united-atom sites in 75X_0DVB_4.cif
trappe_dia = pd.Series(
        {'C1': 4.65,
         'C2': 3.95,
         'C3': 3.88,
         'C4': 3.695,
         'C6': 4.65,
         'C7': 3.95}
        )


Next, the distance grid and segmentation parameters. The spacing is the voxel size of the distance grid. h, threshold_abs, min_distance and min_region_size control which local maxima become pockets. preserve_threshold, smooth_threshold and max_smooth_radius control selective smoothing. extra_padding sets the padding around the cell for periodic segmentation, and minimum_window_separation the minimum distance between windows. See Tuning and safe ranges for what each one does.
The two probe radii are the methane probe (half the TraPPE sigma of CH₄), used for percolation, and the N₂ probe, used for the accessible surface area.


Show code
spacing = 0.5
mask_thickness = 0.0
h = 0.1
threshold_abs = 0.3
min_region_size = 0.00005
preserve_threshold = 103.0
smooth_threshold = 106.0
max_smooth_radius = 2.0
extra_padding = 2
min_distance = 1.0
minimum_window_separation = 1.5

# probe radii (Å)
probe_radius = 1.865      # CH4 (TraPPE sigma / 2), for percolation analysis
n2_probe_radius = 1.82    # N2, for accessible surface area

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
2. Helper functions
The pore graph does not carry volumes or per-pore connectivity by default, so three helpers add them as node attributes.
add_volume_to_graph stores the cell volume (in litres) on every node. add_pixel_ratio_to_graph counts the voxels of each pocket and stores the fraction of the whole grid that pocket occupies. That fraction is later summed to get pore volumes.


Show code
def add_volume_to_graph(graph, mat_atoms):

    vol = mat_atoms.get_volume()
    vol_L=vol/(1E27)
    for i in graph.nodes():
        graph.nodes[i]['cell_volume']=vol_L
    return graph

def add_pixel_ratio_to_graph(graph, regions_pbc):

    n=regions_pbc.size
    for i in graph.nodes():
        pixel_counts = np.count_nonzero(regions_pbc == i)
        graph.nodes[i]['pixel_counts']=pixel_counts
        graph.nodes[i]['total_pixel_amounts']=n
        graph.nodes[i]['pixel_ratio']=pixel_counts/n
    return graph


add_connectivities_to_nodes looks at all windows (edges) touching each pore. For each pore it records the number of windows (the connectivity), the average and minimum window radius, the average window-to-pore radius ratio, and the clearance of the windows relative to the probe (window radius minus probe radius). It also stores each of these multiplied by the connectivity, which the weighted averages below use.


Show code
def add_connectivities_to_nodes(
    graph,
    probe_radius,
    pore_radius_attr="pocket_radius",
    pixel_count_attr="pixel_counts",
    edge_radius_attr="window_radius",
):

    for node in graph.nodes():

        edges = {
            (u, v, key): data
            for u, v, key, data in (
                list(graph.in_edges(node, keys=True, data=True))
                + list(graph.out_edges(node, keys=True, data=True))
            )
        }

        connectivity = len(edges)

        if connectivity == 0:
            continue

        radii = np.array([
            float(data[edge_radius_attr])
            for data in edges.values()
        ])

        pore_radius = float(graph.nodes[node][pore_radius_attr])
        pixel_count = float(graph.nodes[node][pixel_count_attr])

        avg_radius = float(np.mean(radii))
        min_radius = float(np.min(radii))

        clearances = radii - probe_radius
        avg_clearance = float(np.mean(clearances))

        graph.nodes[node]["connectivity"] = connectivity
        graph.nodes[node]["pixel_count_times_connectivity"] = pixel_count * connectivity
        graph.nodes[node]["avg_window_radius"] = avg_radius
        graph.nodes[node]["avg_window_pore_ratio"] = avg_radius / pore_radius
        graph.nodes[node]["avg_radius_times_connectivity"] = connectivity * avg_radius
        graph.nodes[node]["min_window_radius"] = min_radius
        graph.nodes[node]["min_radius_times_connectivity"] = connectivity * min_radius
        graph.nodes[node]["avg_window_clearance"] = avg_clearance
        graph.nodes[node]["clearance_times_connectivity"] = connectivity * avg_clearance

    return graph

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
3. Structure and distance grid
Read the CIF with store_tags=True so the atom site labels (C1, C2, …) are kept. Look up each atom’s radius from its label and compute the distance grid with these radii. The grid stores, for every voxel, the distance to the nearest framework surface.


Show code
mat_atoms = read('../mofography/examples/TestCIFs/75X_0DVB_4.cif',store_tags=True)
site_labels = mat_atoms.info['_atom_site_label']
radii = trappe_dia[site_labels].values/ 2.0
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing, radii=radii)

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
4. Periodic segmentation
Run the watershed segmentation with periodic boundary conditions. It splits the pore space into pockets, merges the pieces that touch across cell boundaries, and finds the windows between neighbouring pockets (compute_connections=True). The result is one dictionary.


Show code
results = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
                dgrid,
                mat_atoms,
                mask_thickness=mask_thickness,
                h=h,
                spacing=spacing,
                return_dgrid=False,
                threshold_abs=threshold_abs,
                min_distance=min_distance,
                return_padded_regions=True,
                preserve_threshold=preserve_threshold,
                smooth_threshold=smooth_threshold,
                max_smooth_radius=max_smooth_radius,
                extra_padding=extra_padding,
                compute_connections=True,
                min_region_size=min_region_size,
                minimum_window_separation=minimum_window_separation,
                watershed_backend="rust_det",
            )


Pull out the pieces used below: the label grid for the unit cell (regions), the periodic label grid (regions_pbc), the list of windows (connections), and the maxima. Voxels labelled 0 are framework atoms, which is used later for the free volume.


Show code
regions = results["regions"]
maxima_info = results["maxima_info"]
connections = results["connections"]
regions_pbc = results["regions_pbc"]
regions_1d = regions.flatten()

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
5. Pore graph
Each node is a pore in the unit cell, and each edge is one window between two pores. Only windows between pores that own part of the original unit cell are kept, so every window is counted once. Windows that cross the cell boundary are kept as edges with a non-zero relative_offset.


Show code
#construct pore graph
graph=(mgr.make_window_resolved_graph_from_results(results))

graph = add_volume_to_graph(graph,mat_atoms)

graph = add_pixel_ratio_to_graph(graph,regions_pbc)

base_labels = (mgr.build_base_region_labels_from_results(results))

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
6. Properties

Largest cavity diameter
The largest cavity diameter is twice the largest value in the distance grid, whether or not that cavity is reachable from outside.


Show code
# Largest cavity diameter (Å): diameter of the largest sphere that fits in the pore space, regardless of percolation
lcd = dgrid.max() * 2




Pore limiting diameter
The pore limiting radius is the largest probe radius that can still travel through the periodic network (winding-number percolation). The diameter is twice that.


Show code
# Pore limiting diameter (Å): diameter of the largest spherical probe that can pass through the periodic percolating pore network
plr = mgr.find_pore_limiting_radius_winding(results,graph=graph,base_region_labels=base_labels,include_dangling=True)
pld = plr * 2




N₂-accessible surface area
Surface area is estimated by Monte Carlo sampling on a shell around the framework (50,000 samples). Only sample points that the N₂ probe can reach through the percolating network count as accessible. The seed makes the number reproducible.


Show code
# N2-accessible surface area (m²/g): surface area accessible to an N2-sized probe in the percolating pore network
np.random.seed(0)
n2_asa = (mgr.compute_surface_area_mc_winding(
                    results,
                    mat_atoms,
                    probe_radius=n2_probe_radius,
                    n_samples=50000,
                    shell_thickness=1,
                    return_details=False,
                    window_fp=False,
                    winding_kwargs=None,
                )["accessible_surface_area"]
            )




Methane-accessible percolating network
Keep only the pores and windows that a methane-sized probe can use to cross the cell. Two versions are extracted:

Before pruning, the whole percolating network, including self-loops and dangling branches.
After pruning, only the shortest percolating pathways (the backbone).

Connectivity data is added to each version.


Show code
# Methane-accessible percolating pore network
# before pruning: the whole percolating network, including self-loops and dangling branches
# after pruning: only the shortest percolating backbone pathways
percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning = (mgr.extract_percolating_pore_graph(graph,threshold=probe_radius,expand_components=True,include_dangling=True))
percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning = (add_connectivities_to_nodes(percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning,probe_radius=probe_radius))

percolation_pore_graph_after_pruning = (mgr.extract_percolating_pore_graph(graph,threshold=probe_radius,expand_components=False,include_dangling=False))
percolation_pore_graph_after_pruning = (add_connectivities_to_nodes(percolation_pore_graph_after_pruning,probe_radius=probe_radius))




Percolating pore volume
The pore volume fraction is the sum of the voxel fractions of the pores in the percolating network. Dividing by the framework bulk density turns it into a gravimetric pore volume in cm³/g.


Show code
# Percolating pore volume fraction: fraction of the cell volume occupied by the methane-accessible percolating pore network
percolating_pore_volume_fraction=sum(percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[node]["pixel_ratio"]for node in percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes())




Show code
# Percolating gravimetric pore volume (cm³/g): percolating pore volume divided by the framework mass
rho=0.82 # bulk density (g/cm³): framework mass / cell volume, from 10.1021/acs.jctc.2c00798
percolating_gravimetric_pore_volume=percolating_pore_volume_fraction/rho




Pore and window sizes
Average the pore radius, the mean window radius per pore, and the window-to-pore radius ratio over the pores in the percolating network.


Show code
# Average percolating pore radius (Å): mean radius of the pores in the percolating network
average_pore_radius = np.mean([percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[n]["pocket_radius"] for n in percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes()])

# Average accessible window radius (Å): for each pore, the mean radius of the accessible windows connected to it,
# averaged over all pores in the percolating network
average_accessible_window_radius = np.mean([percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[n]["avg_window_radius"] for n in percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes()])

# Average window-to-pore radius ratio: mean of (average radius of the windows connected to a pore / radius of that pore)
w_to_p = np.mean([percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[n]["avg_window_radius"] / percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[n]["pocket_radius"] for n in percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes()])




Connectivity
The plain average connectivity counts windows per pore. The window-size-weighted version gives more weight to pores with wide windows.


Show code
# Average pore connectivity: average number of accessible windows connected to each pore
average_connectivity = np.mean([percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[n]["connectivity"]for n in percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes()])

# Average-window-radius-weighted connectivity = sum_i(c_i * r_w,i) / sum_i(r_w,i),
# where c_i is the connectivity of pore i and r_w,i is the mean radius of its accessible windows
average_window_size_weighted_connectivity = (sum(percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[n]["avg_radius_times_connectivity"]for n in percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes())/sum(percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes[n]["avg_window_radius"]for n in percolation_pore_graph_before_pruning.nodes()))




Backbone fraction
The backbone fraction compares the pore volume of the shortest percolating pathways to that of the whole percolating network. A low value means most of the percolating volume sits in side branches and dead ends.


Show code
# Percolating backbone fraction = n_b / n_p: grid points in the shortest percolating backbone
# divided by grid points in the whole percolating network
percolating_pore_volume_fraction_backbone=sum(percolation_pore_graph_after_pruning.nodes[node]["pixel_ratio"]for node in percolation_pore_graph_after_pruning.nodes())
fB=percolating_pore_volume_fraction_backbone/percolating_pore_volume_fraction




Fractional free volume
Voxels labelled 0 belong to the framework. The fractional free volume uses their share of the grid together with the 1.3 factor from the cited definition.


Show code
# Fractional free volume = 1 - 1.3 * V_vdW / V_sp: fraction of the material volume not occupied by the framework
Vvdw=np.sum(regions_1d==0)
Vsp=len(regions_1d)
ffv=1-1.3*(Vvdw/Vsp)

title: Advanced geometric and topological pore network properties
text:
Summary
All properties in one table.


Show code
summary = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ["Largest cavity diameter (LCD)", lcd, "Å"],
        ["Pore limiting diameter (PLD)", pld, "Å"],
        ["N₂-accessible surface area", n2_asa, "m²/g"],
        ["Percolating pore volume fraction", percolating_pore_volume_fraction, "–"],
        ["Percolating gravimetric pore volume", percolating_gravimetric_pore_volume, "cm³/g"],
        ["Average percolating pore radius", average_pore_radius, "Å"],
        ["Average accessible window radius", average_accessible_window_radius, "Å"],
        ["Average window-to-pore radius ratio", w_to_p, "–"],
        ["Average pore connectivity", average_connectivity, "–"],

        ["Percolating backbone fraction (fB)", fB, "–"],

title: Pocket Type Detection
text: Pocket type detection for Cu-BTC (HKUST-1): (a) unit cell with 1.0 Å distance isosurface coloured by pocket type, (b) overlaid pocket probe-occupiable PSDs for the three types, (c) framework and connectivity spherical-harmonics power spectra, (d) pairwise fingerprint cosine similarity matrix (paper Figure 4)

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
Overview
Once you have a periodic segmentation, the next question is which pockets are the same kind of pocket? — i.e. how many pocket types does the MOF contain?
This is more than a clustering exercise. Chemically distinct adsorption sites (e.g. small tetrahedral cages vs large octahedral cages in UiO-66, or window families of slightly different aperture in ZIF-20) need to be:

Stable under reasonable numerical choices (grid spacing, VDW table).
Physically interpretable — a “type” should correspond to a real cavity family.
Robust to over-segmentation — watershed often splits one cage into multiple fragments; these must collapse into one type.

env_cluster is the default (and recommended) pocket-typing method. It uses multi-modal fingerprinting: it seeds bands from the peak probe radius \(r_{max}\) and then merges adjacent bands whose rotation-invariant fingerprints agree. The fingerprint has three channels: size (pocket PSD), a SOAP-like framework environment, and pore connectivity.





flowchart LR
    A[CIF] --> B[dgrid]
    B --> C[periodic segmentation]
    C --> D[pocket PSDs]
    D --> E[env_cluster typing]
    E --> F["typed.n_types, typed.type_summary"]

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
Prerequisites

A working mofography install (uv pip install -e .).
The Quick Start tutorial — read it first for the segmentation basics.

Step 1: Load a Structure
IRMOF-1 is a clean test case: two cage-size families in one cubic cell.


Show code

print(f"Cell: {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)} Å")


Atoms: 424

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
Step 2: Compute the Distance Grid
The dgrid is the foundation: a per-voxel radius of the largest probe sphere that fits. Every downstream feature is derived from it.


Show code
spacing = 0.5  # Å — the canonical default for pocket typing

dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
print(f"Grid shape: {dgrid.shape}  ({dgrid.size:,} voxels)")
print(f"Void max:   {dgrid.max():.2f} Å")

Don’t use dgrid_from_atoms_gpu or dgrid_from_atoms_cpu here. They are deprecated and known to mis-handle non-orthorhombic cells. The *_rust backends are correct for all cell types.

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
Step 3: Periodic Segmentation (Single Call)
do_periodic_segmentation_rust gives you the maxima, regions, PBC grouping, and connections in one call.


Show code
dgrid_f32 = dgrid.astype(np.float32)

seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid_f32, atoms,
    mask_thickness=0.05,
    h=0.2,
    min_distance=1.5,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    spacing=spacing,
    compute_connections=True,
    watershed_backend="rust_det",
    disable_tqdm=True,
)

print(f"Unique regions:        {len(seg['unique_regions'])}")

title: Pocket Type Detection
section: Step 5: Assign Pocket Types with env_cluster
text:
Step 5: Assign Pocket Types with env_cluster
This is the heart of the tutorial. The default method='env_cluster' runs:

Initial bands — sort pockets by peak probe radius (max_r); start a new band whenever the gap to the previous pocket exceeds 0.15 Å (one third of a grid spacing — a sensible grid-noise floor).
Merge adjacent bands repeatedly when their mean max_r differ by at most 0.50 Å (one grid spacing) and the mean fingerprint cosine over all cross-band pocket pairs is ≥ 0.90. Bands farther apart in max_r are never merged. (Internally a tighter/looser cosine tier exists for gaps ≤/> 0.20 Å; both default to 0.90.)
Singleton merge (on by default) — 1-pocket bands whose max_r is within 0.40 Å of a neighbour are folded in (e.g. ZIF-8 corner vs centre cages, grid-offset artefacts).

Each surviving band is one pocket type.


Show code
typed = mgr.assign_pocket_types(seg, atoms, method="env_cluster")
print(typed.ok, "—", typed.method)


True — env_cluster

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
How env_cluster Sees a Pocket
For each pocket, assign_pocket_types builds a PocketFingerprint that combines three orthogonal channels (paper Section 3.3):








Channel
What it measures
Why it helps




Pocket PSD
Normalized pocket-wise probe-occupiable PSD
Local size of the void


Framework environment
SOAP-like spherical-harmonic power spectrum (\(\ell = 0..6\)) of wall atoms: void voxels within 1.5 Å of the vdW surface define a shell, atoms within 3.5 Å of those voxels are included. Computed for all wall atoms (shape), per element (chemistry), plus per-element radial histograms
Wall shape and chemistry, independent of crystal orientation


Connectivity
Same power spectrum on minimum-image unit vectors to pore-graph neighbours
Pocket’s network role (how many windows, where they point)



The SOAP-like power spectrum. Void voxels within 1.5 Å of the framework van der Waals surface form a wall-proximity shell around the pocket, and the framework atoms within 3.5 Å of those voxels are the atoms that shape it. Unit vectors \(\hat{u}_k\) from the pore centre (the distance-grid maximum) to each wall atom \(k\) are expanded in spherical harmonics \(Y_{\ell m}\). The rotation-invariant power spectrum is
\[
P_\ell = \sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell} \left| \sum_k Y_{\ell m}(\hat{u}_k) \right|^2 , \qquad \ell = 0,\ldots,6 ,
\]
where the sum over \(k\) runs over the wall atoms with equal weight. It is computed for all wall atoms together (wall shape) and for each element separately (chemistry), and per-element radial histograms add distance information. Because \(P_\ell\) does not change when the structure is rotated, equivalent pockets match regardless of crystal orientation.
The connectivity channel. For each neighbour of the pocket in the pore graph, take the unit vector to the neighbour centre with the minimum-image convention. The same \(P_\ell\) construction on those directions encodes how many windows the pocket has and where they point.
Comparing pockets. Fingerprints are compared by cosine similarity. The fingerprint cosine is the mean over active channels. The connectivity channel is weighted fivefold when both pockets have at least 3 windows, and is omitted for pockets with fewer than 3 connections, so topologically distinct cages with similar walls stay separable (e.g. UiO-66). Pockets of the same type have cosines near 1, and distinct types in the benchmark set fall below the merge threshold of 0.90.
Assigning types takes two steps:

Sort pockets by \(r_\mathrm{max}\), the peak distance-field value in the pocket (peak probe radius), and start a new band wherever consecutive values differ by more than 0.15 Å (three times the 0.5 Å grid step, a noise floor).
Repeatedly merge adjacent bands when their mean \(r_\mathrm{max}\) differ by at most 0.5 Å and the mean fingerprint cosine over all pocket pairs across the two bands is at least 0.90. Bands further apart in \(r_\mathrm{max}\) are never merged.

So pockets with similar \(r_\mathrm{max}\) but different framework chemistry or connectivity stay separate types, and pockets with the same environment at slightly different sizes are merged.
For the full algorithm + parameter list, see mofography/pocket_typing.py::assign_pocket_types_env_cluster.






CautionCaution: radii and grid spacing



Pocket types are calibrated with Bondi radii on a 0.5 Å grid. By default the peak probe radius used for typing comes from a separate Bondi-radii grid, so changing the VDW table for the analysis does not change type counts. Passing your own radii as typing_radii can split or merge types in some structures (for example the micropores of NU-1000). Check the type count and typed.rep_to_type after changing radii or spacing.

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
Parameter Reference
mgr.assign_pocket_types(seg, atoms, method='env_cluster', **kwargs) forwards kwargs to assign_pocket_types_from_segmentation. For env_cluster the tunable ones are:








Parameter
Default
Effect




method
'env_cluster'
Recommended. Legacy alternatives ('shape_refined', 'max_probe_radius') are kept for reproducing old results only.


env_cluster_initial_band_gap_a
0.15 Å
Initial max_r band split (grid-noise floor; 3× the 0.5 Å grid step).


merge_singleton_bands
True
Fold 1-pocket bands into a neighbour.


singleton_band_gap_a
0.40 Å
Singleton fold tolerance.


typing_radii
'bondi_crc_fallback'
VDW table for max_r typing; 'segmentation' reuses the analysis dgrid; or a per-atom radii array.


probe_radius_psd
1.2 Å
Probe-centre radius for the pocket PSD (set it in enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds).



The merge thresholds (0.50 Å max_r gap, 0.90 cosine) are module constants in mofography.pocket_typing (ENV_CLUSTER_*), not call arguments. band_gap_a, subsplit_gap_a, adjacent_merge_max_r_gap_a and merge_cosine only affect the legacy shape_refined method.

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
Tips

Trust the defaults. The defaults are calibrated for the canonical workflow (spacing=0.5 Å, Bondi/CRC VDW, 0.15 Å band gap) and validated against NU-1000, ZIF-20, UiO-66, IRMOF-1, and Cu-BTC.
Always run enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds first. The pocket PSD is sampled in Rust and reused by both the typing and any downstream RAG feature code — running it once keeps the pipeline fast.
Inspect typed.rep_to_type first if results look wrong. If a known single cage has been split into two type_ids, the bands are too aggressive; if two chemically different cages are merged, the fingerprint merge is too lenient.
After changing radii, re-check the type count and typed.rep_to_type: type counts are calibrated to the Bondi, 0.5 Å regime (see the caution above).

title: Pocket Type Detection
text:
Next Steps

Quick Start tutorial — the segmentation basics this builds on.
Distance Grid tutorial — alternative dgrid backends for very large systems.
Pore Graph — what to do with the typed pockets (build a typed RAG).

title: Tuning and safe ranges
text: Defaults work for most MOFs. Change one parameter at a time and look at the pocket count (len(seg["maxima_pbc"])) and a picture. All distances are in Å, and “height” means distance to the framework surface. Ranges follow the paper’s SI; defaults are checked against the function signatures in mofography/rust_fun.py.

title: Tuning and safe ranges
text:
Distance grid: dgrid_from_atoms_rust(ase_atoms, spacing, radii=None)



Parameter
Default
Safe range
Notes




spacing
none (required)
0.25 to 0.75
Voxel size. Halving it costs 8x memory and time. 0.5 is the usual choice; 0.25 works for fine detail.


radii
None (Bondi, Mendeleev fill)
per-atom array
Pass the same radii you want in every downstream number. See vdW radii.




Too coarse (above about 0.7): narrow windows are blurred, PLD is underestimated, small pockets vanish.
Too fine (below about 0.3): slow, large, and no real gain. Noise can create extra maxima.
Pass the same spacing to do_periodic_segmentation_rust. If you omit it, it is inferred from the grid and is less accurate, which hurts padding, maxima and window positions.
Cast to float32 before segmentation: dgrid.astype(np.float32).
Large or amorphous systems: see Distance grid methods.

title: Tuning and safe ranges
text:
Segmentation: do_periodic_segmentation_rust(dgrid, mat_atoms, ...)

Maxima detection (tune these first)









Parameter
Default
Safe range
What it does




mask_thickness
0.05
0.05 to 1.5
Voxels closer than this to the framework are background and not segmented. 0.05 is the default and recommended; values up to 1.5 have worked without issues, but larger values erode more pore volume and can disconnect narrow windows. When plotting isosurfaces, keep the isovalue (about 1.0 to 1.5) well above it.


h
0.2
0.1 to 0.5
Minimum height drop between a maximum and its highest saddle (window) for it to count as its own pocket.


min_distance
1.5
1.0 to 2.0
Maxima closer than this are merged.


threshold_abs
1.5
1.0 to 2.0
Minimum height of a maximum. Lower it for ultramicroporous pockets.





Selective smoothing
Smoothing suppresses noise maxima in wide pores. Details in Selective smoothing.









Parameter
Default
Safe range
What it does




preserve_threshold
3.0
about 3 to 4
Maxima below this height are left alone.


smooth_threshold
6.0
about 5 to 7
Maxima above this height are always smoothed. Between the two, smoothing scales up.


max_smooth_radius
2.0
about 1 to 3
Cap on the smoothing radius.





Padding, walls, windows









Parameter
Default
Safe range
What it does




extra_padding
5
0 to 10
Periodic padding added beyond the internal dgrid.max() + 5 Å. Raise it for very large pores or windows that look clipped.


wall_thickness
0.05
0.05 to 0.10
Near-boundary band (fraction of the longest perpendicular cell length) used when filtering maxima.


minimum_window_separation
None (3 x spacing)
1 to 3
Min separation between windows of the same pocket pair. Lower splits one window into several. Higher merges neighbours.


min_region_size
0.001
0.0001 to 0.01
Regions smaller than this fraction of the padded grid are dropped and re-segmented.


compactness
0
0
Watershed compactness. Leave at 0 unless you know you need it.


skip_endchannel_pairs
True

Leave True. False only for cosmetic clean-up of end-channel slivers.



The paper’s SI lists extra_padding 2 and wall_thickness 0.08 as typical values; the shipped signature defaults are 5 and 0.05, which are what the tutorials use.


Watershed backend








watershed_backend
Deterministic
Use when




"rust_det" (default)
yes
Default. Single-thread heap.


"rust_det_parallel"
yes
Large grids, memory-limited. Same result, often faster.


"rust_bucket"
no
Max throughput. Boundaries can differ slightly, mostly in tortuous amorphous pores.


"skimage"
yes
Reference check. Uses watershed_connectivity (2 = 18 neighbours, 3 = 26).



See Watershed backends.


Switches
compute_connections (default True) turns window detection on or off. return_padded_regions (False) returns the padded labels for debugging, and the winding tutorials need it. return_dgrid (False) puts dgrid into seg, which is handy when later steps need it.

title: Tuning and safe ranges
text:
Symptoms and fixes








You see
Likely cause
Try




Many tiny pockets inside one obvious cage or channel (over-segmentation)
h too low, min_distance too small, noisy grid
Raise h (0.2 to 0.3 to 0.4), raise min_distance, finer spacing, or lower smooth_threshold


Two real cages merged into one pocket (under-segmentation)
h too high, min_distance too large
Lower h (to 0.1), lower min_distance


Small pockets missing
threshold_abs too high, smoothing too strong
Lower threshold_abs to 1.0, raise preserve_threshold


Wall fragments or thin slivers labelled as pockets
mask_thickness too low
Raise mask_thickness, raise min_region_size


One window reported many times
minimum_window_separation too small
Raise it


Windows missing or clipped at cell faces
Padding too small, spacing too coarse
Raise extra_padding, pass spacing, refine the grid


Pocket count changes between runs
rust_bucket backend
Use rust_det or rust_det_parallel


[pocket_maxima_check] messages
A pocket’s maximum sits a few tenths of Å below the region peak
Informational. Lower h or min_distance slightly if you need exact maxima


Out of memory
Grid too large
Coarser spacing, another dgrid backend, rust_det_parallel

title: Tuning and safe ranges
text:
Sanity checks

Pocket count should match the topology you expect (IRMOF-1 with defaults gives 8 PBC-merged pockets).
Stability: change h by +/-0.1. A good setting gives the same pockets.
Change spacing by about 20%. LCD and PLD should barely move.
Per-pocket checks: Pocket type detection and Connections and windows.

Back to Quick start.

title: Install
text:
This repository is the full Python package. There is no PyPI wheel yet: you install dependencies, compile mgr_rust with maturin in release mode (important for speed on your CPU), then pip install -e ..
Requirements: Python 3.10–3.12 (3.11 recommended) · Rust via rustup · Linux, macOS, or Windows. NumPy 1.20 and the 2.x series are both supported; if you hit a deprecation or type-promotion warning, open an issue with your numpy version.

Face Merging vs Winding: Periodic Percolation Algorithms
text:
Face-Merging: Detailed Line-by-Line Explanation (with UnionFind)

class UnionFind:
Implements the disjoint-set (union-find) data structure for efficient merging of region labels.
def __init__(self, n):
Initializes the parent array so each element is its own parent.
self.parent = np.arange(n)
Each label starts as its own cluster.
def find(self, x):
Finds the root of label x with path compression.
root = x
Start with the input label.
while self.parent[root] != root:
Traverse up the parent chain until the root is found.
root = self.parent[root]
Move to the parent.
while self.parent[x] != x:
Path compression: update parent pointers to point directly to the root.
x, self.parent[x] = self.parent[x], root
Set parent of x to root and move up the chain.
return root
Return the root label.
def union(self, x, y):
Merges the sets containing x and y.
xr, yr = self.find(x), self.find(y)
Find roots of both labels.
if xr != yr:
If they are in different sets, merge them.
self.parent[yr] = xr
Set the parent of yr to xr, merging the sets.
def union_pairs(self, a, b):
Merges all pairs of labels from arrays a and b.
for x, y in zip(a, b):
Iterate over pairs.
self.union(int(x), int(y))
Merge each pair using union.
def _merge_periodic_faces(labeled, axis, uf):
Merges region labels that touch across periodic faces of the specified axis.
if labeled.shape[axis] < 2:
If the grid is too thin along this axis, nothing to merge; return early.
slicer_lo = [slice(None)] * 3
Create a slicer for the lower face (all elements except along the axis).
slicer_hi = [slice(None)] * 3
Create a slicer for the upper face.
slicer_lo[axis] = 0
Set the lower face index for the axis.
slicer_hi[axis] = labeled.shape[axis] - 1
Set the upper face index for the axis.
face_lo = labeled[tuple(slicer_lo)]
Extract the lower face labels.
face_hi = labeled[tuple(slicer_hi)]
Extract the upper face labels.
mask = (face_lo != 0) & (face_hi != 0)
Find positions where both faces have nonzero (valid) labels.
if not np.any(mask):
If no overlap, nothing to merge; return.
idx_lo = face_lo[mask]
Get the lower face labels at overlap positions.
idx_hi = face_hi[mask]
Get the upper face labels at overlap positions.
if idx_lo.size == 0:
If no valid pairs, return.
pairs = np.stack((idx_lo, idx_hi), axis=1)
Stack the pairs of touching labels.
unique_pairs = np.unique(pairs, axis=0)
Remove duplicate pairs.
uf.union_pairs(unique_pairs[:, 0], unique_pairs[:, 1])
Merge the touching labels using union-find.
def percolation_all_axes_periodic(binary):
Main function to check percolation along all axes with periodic boundaries.
struct = generate_binary_structure(3, 1)
Create a 3D connectivity structure for labeling.
labeled, nlab = label(binary, structure=struct)
Label connected regions in the binary grid.
if nlab == 0:
If no regions, return empty results.
axes = {"x": 0, "y": 1, "z": 2}
Map axis names to indices.
results = {} and unioned_labels_dict = {}
Prepare output containers.
for name, axis in axes.items():
Loop over each axis.
uf = UnionFind(nlab + 1)
Create a union-find structure for label merging.
for other_axis in range(3):
Loop over transverse axes.
if other_axis == axis: continue
Skip the axis being checked.
_merge_periodic_faces(labeled, other_axis, uf)
Merge labels across periodic faces for transverse axes.
remap = np.arange(nlab + 1)
Prepare a remapping array.
for lbl in range(1, nlab + 1): remap[lbl] = uf.find(lbl)
Remap each label to its union-find parent.
unioned_labels = remap[labeled]
Apply remapping to the labeled grid.
unioned_labels_dict[name] = unioned_labels
Store the remapped labels for this axis.
faceA = set(np.unique(np.take(unioned_labels, 0, axis=axis))) - {0}
Get unique labels on the lower face.
faceB = set(np.unique(np.take(unioned_labels, -1, axis=axis))) - {0}
Get unique labels on the upper face.
results[name] = faceA.intersection(faceB)
Percolating clusters are those present on both faces.
return results, unioned_labels_dict
Return percolation results and remapped labels.

text:
Winding-Number: Line-by-Line Explanation

def percolation_winding_multidigraph(G):
Defines the function to detect percolation using winding numbers on a graph.
percolates = {"x": False, "y": False, "z": False}
Initialize percolation flags for each axis.
loops = []
List to store detected loops.
acc_offsets = {}
Accumulated periodic offsets for each node.
parent = {}
Parent pointers for BFS tree.
visited = set()
Track visited nodes.
undirected = nx.Graph(G.to_undirected(as_view=True))
Convert the directed graph to undirected for component analysis.
for comp_nodes in nx.connected_components(undirected):
Loop over connected components.
root = next(iter(comp_nodes))
Pick a root node for BFS.
if root in visited: continue
Skip already visited components.
visited.add(root)
Mark root as visited.
parent[root] = None
Root has no parent.
acc_offsets[root] = (0, 0, 0)
Start offset at zero.
queue = deque([root])
Initialize BFS queue.
while queue:
BFS loop.
u = queue.popleft()
Pop node from queue.
u_acc = np.array(acc_offsets[u], dtype=int)
Get current offset for node.
for nbr, key, canonical_offset, delta, forward in _iter_neighbor_edges(G, u):
Iterate over neighbors and edge data.
ced = CanonicalEdgeID.from_nodes(u, nbr, key)
Get canonical edge ID.
if nbr not in comp_nodes: continue
Stay within current component.
implied = tuple((u_acc + np.array(delta, dtype=int)).tolist())
Compute implied offset for neighbor.
if nbr not in visited:
If neighbor not visited, add to BFS tree.
visited.add(nbr)
Mark neighbor as visited.
parent[nbr] = u
Set parent pointer.
acc_offsets[nbr] = implied
Store offset.
queue.append(nbr)
Add neighbor to queue.
continue
Continue BFS.
current = acc_offsets[nbr]
Get current offset for neighbor.
if implied == current: continue
If offset unchanged, skip.
winding_array = np.array(implied, dtype=int) - np.array(current, dtype=int)
Compute winding difference.
winding = tuple(int(x) for x in winding_array)
Convert to tuple.
if winding == (0, 0, 0): continue
Only nonzero windings matter.
cycle_nodes = _tree_path(u, nbr, parent)
Get nodes forming the loop.
loop_info = {...}
Store loop details.
loops.append(loop_info)
Add to loop list.
if winding[0] != 0: percolates["x"] = True
Mark percolation in x if winding detected.
if winding[1] != 0: percolates["y"] = True
Mark percolation in y if winding detected.
if winding[2] != 0: percolates["z"] = True
Mark percolation in z if winding detected.
unique_loops = []
Prepare to filter unique loops.
seen = set()
Track seen loops.
for loop in loops:
Loop over detected loops.
key = (loop["winding"], tuple(loop["nodes"]), loop["edge"])
Unique key for each loop.
if key in seen: continue
Skip duplicates.
seen.add(key)
Mark as seen.
unique_loops.append(loop)
Add to unique list.
return percolates, unique_loops, acc_offsets
Return percolation flags, loops, and offsets.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
The distance grid is the foundation of every mofography pore analysis — segmentation, RAG, PSD, PLD, and surface area all consume the same dgrid array. Which function you call to build that array matters because each backend trades off accuracy, memory, and runtime differently, and two of the legacy backends are unsafe on non-orthogonal cells.
This tutorial covers:

The four active distance grid backends and their exact signatures
A decision tree mapping system size to the right method
The auto-AABB policy the interactive app uses
⚠️ The two broken methods to never use and why

If you have not done so, please complete the Distance Grid tutorial first — the rest of this page assumes you understand what a dgrid is and what spacing controls.

The four distance grid backends

Function
Strategy
Best for
Status

dgrid_from_atoms_rust

✅ Active

Warning⚠️ Do NOT use these two methods



dgrid_from_atoms_gpu and dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb are BROKEN on non-orthogonal (skewed) cells. They compute the minimum-image convention with per-axis NINT, which is only correct for orthogonal cells. Most MOFs (and all triclinic/monoclinic cells) violate this assumption, so these functions produce systematically wrong distance grids on real materials. They are kept in the codebase for legacy code paths but must not be used in new work. The Rust backend uses the same correct MIC path for every cell type. See the Broken methods section for details.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Signatures

1. dgrid_from_atoms_rust — exact, brute-force
dgrid_from_atoms_rust(ase_atoms, spacing, radii=None)









Parameter
Type
Default
Meaning




ase_atoms
ase.Atoms
—
Framework structure


spacing
float
—
Grid spacing in Å


radii
np.ndarray or None
None
Per-atom VDW radii (Å). None → Bondi (1964) with Mendeleev fill



Returns: np.ndarray of shape (nx, ny, nz), signed distance to the nearest atom surface.
Strategy: Thread-parallel (Rayon) brute-force — every grid point is checked against every atom using an exact minimum-image convention. Orthogonal cells use a SIMD-optimized SoA path; skewed cells fall back to a 7-image Wassenaar construction. O(N_atoms × N_grid) work, O(N_grid) memory.
Use when: you want the most accurate distance grid and you have enough RAM for one float32 per voxel.


2. dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust — R-tree, memory-efficient
dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(ase_atoms, spacing, radii=None, n_neighbors=10)









Parameter
Type
Default
Meaning




ase_atoms
ase.Atoms
—
Framework structure


spacing
float
—
Grid spacing in Å


radii
np.ndarray or None
None
Per-atom VDW radii (Å)


n_neighbors
int
10
Number of nearest atoms to query per grid point



Strategy: Builds a Rust AABB (axis-aligned bounding box) tree on the atoms, then queries n_neighbors nearest atoms for every grid point under PBC. The minimum of dist - radii[nbr] becomes the surface distance. Memory is dominated by the R-tree, not by the grid → much smaller RAM footprint than brute force on large cells.
Use when: cells > 50 Å or atoms > 1000 and the brute-force Rust path runs out of memory. Accuracy depends on n_neighbors: 10 is safe for typical MOFs; reduce to 4–6 if the structure has very large open channels where the nearest atoms may be far apart, and consider whether you need 20+ for tiny-pore systems.


3. dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust — coarse + trilinear
dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(
    ase_atoms, spacing, coarse_factor=2, radii=None, n_neighbors=10,
)









Parameter
Type
Default
Meaning




ase_atoms
ase.Atoms
—
Framework structure


spacing
float
—
Fine grid spacing in Å


coarse_factor
int
2
Coarsening factor for the AABB sampling grid (must be > 1)


radii
np.ndarray or None
None
Per-atom VDW radii (Å)


n_neighbors
int
10
AABB neighbor count



Returns: np.ndarray (float32) of shape (nx, ny, nz) matching the fine spacing.
Strategy: Computes the AABB distance grid on a coarse grid (spacing × coarse_factor), then trilinearly interpolates back to the fine grid. Reduces compute by coarse_factor³ (default 8×) and also acts as a mild low-pass filter. The grid shape is identical to the brute-force result, so downstream code is unchanged.
Use when: systems so large that even the AABB Rust path is too slow, and you can tolerate a slightly smoother distance field (mild trilinear averaging of nearby values). Good for HT screens where you want a ballpark PSD, less ideal for resolving sub-Å features like pore-limiting windows. Increase coarse_factor to 3 or 4 for very large cells; decrease toward 1 (in practice, use the plain AABB method) when you need sharper windows.


4. dgrid_from_atoms_cpu — freud + Dask, Python
dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(
    ase_atoms, radii=None, spacing=0.25, block_size=50000,
    n_neighbors=10, probe_radius=0, precompute=True,
)









Parameter
Type
Default
Meaning




ase_atoms
ase.Atoms
—
Framework structure


radii
np.ndarray or None
None
Per-atom VDW radii (Å). None → uses a hand-rolled Bondi table


spacing
float
0.25
Grid spacing in Å


block_size
int
50000
Dask chunk size (grid points per block)


n_neighbors
int
10
AABB neighbor count for freud query


probe_radius
float
0
Probe radius added on top of atom radii (Å)


precompute
bool
True
If True, call .compute() and return a NumPy array; if False, return a lazy Dask array



Strategy: Builds a freud AABBQuery on the framework, lays out the grid as a Dask array of block_size chunks, and maps gpd_aabb (a NumPy reduction over the freud neighbor list) over every block. Uses complete_cell().T for the box, so the MIC is correct on skewed cells — this is not one of the broken methods.
Use when: you need Python-level introspection of intermediate values, are running on a machine without the Rust extension, or want lazy Dask composition with other grid ops. Performance is generally 5–20× slower than the Rust path on the same machine.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Decision tree
flowchart TD
    A[System: ASE Atoms + spacing] --> B{Atoms × grid voxels<br/>fits in RAM<br/>and runtime OK?}
    B -- Yes --> C[rust_exact<br/>dgrid_from_atoms_rust]
    B -- No, OOM or too slow --> D{Is mild smoothing<br/>of the dgrid OK?}
    D -- Yes --> E[rust_aabb_interp<br/>dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust]
    D -- No, need exact --> F[rust_aabb<br/>dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust]
    A --> G[Need Python-level<br/>introspection?]
    G -- Yes --> H[cpu / Dask<br/>dgrid_from_atoms_cpu]
    G -- No --> C
    A -.->|NEVER| X[gpu or cpu_no_aabb<br/>broken on skewed cells]
    X -.->|redirect| C

Rule of thumb








System size (atoms × grid voxels)
Recommended method
Why




< 5 × 10⁷ (small-to-medium)
dgrid_from_atoms_rust
Brute-force is fast enough and the most accurate


5 × 10⁷ to 5 × 10⁸ (large)
dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust
AABB tree cuts memory; same accuracy as brute force


> 5 × 10⁸ (very large, HT screens)
dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust with coarse_factor=2 or 3
8–27× compute savings; smooths fine features


Need Python / Dask composition
dgrid_from_atoms_cpu
Slowest but flexible; uses correct freud MIC



These are rough numbers — the actual crossover depends on cell shape, number of periodic images the AABB has to handle, and how much RAM you have. The auto-AABB policy in the interactive app uses a similar memory budget to switch.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Auto-AABB policy (interactive app)
The Streamlit app (mofography_dash / hosted demo) does not expose the distance-grid method as a user knob by default. Instead it runs a two-step policy:

Estimate the float32 memory cost of the brute-force grid: 4 × nx × ny × nz bytes.
If that estimate exceeds the configured RAM budget (default: ~512 MB), it auto-switches to dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust with n_neighbors=10 (or to dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust with coarse_factor=2 for very large systems). A short status line in the UI tells you which backend was used.

This means the app “just works” for both IRMOF-1 and a 100-atom × 200-Å supercell, but it also means you should check the UI output before running a 1000-frame batch — silently hitting the AABB path on a system that needs brute-force precision can change window diameters by a few percent. The notebook and CLI surfaces do not auto-switch; you choose the backend explicitly.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Setup


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np
import time

# Load a MOF structure
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")  # 424 atoms, ~26 Å cubic cell
print(f"Loaded {len(atoms)} atoms, cell: {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)}")


Loaded 424 atoms, cell: [25.83 25.83 25.83]

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Method 1: dgrid_from_atoms_rust (default)


Show code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
dgrid_exact = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5)
t_exact = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"rust_exact:    shape={dgrid_exact.shape}, "
      f"min={dgrid_exact.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_exact.max():.2f}, "
      f"time={t_exact*1000:.0f} ms")


rust_exact:    shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.70, max=7.54, time=48 ms


Pros: exact MIC for all cell types, thread-parallel, no accuracy trade-off. Cons: O(N_atoms × N_grid) — memory scales with grid size.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Method 2: dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust (memory-efficient)


Show code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
dgrid_aabb = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10)
t_aabb = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"rust_aabb:     shape={dgrid_aabb.shape}, "
      f"min={dgrid_aabb.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_aabb.max():.2f}, "
      f"time={t_aabb*1000:.0f} ms")

# Agreement with exact method
print(f"max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_aabb| = {np.abs(dgrid_exact - dgrid_aabb).max():.3e}")


rust_aabb:     shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.70, max=7.54, time=36 ms
max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_aabb| = 0.000e+00


Uses a Rust AABB tree to find nearby atoms for each grid point. n_neighbors controls the search radius — higher = more accurate but slower. For typical MOFs, n_neighbors=10 agrees with the exact method to ~1e-3 Å. If you see a few-voxel disagreement near a wall, raise n_neighbors to 16 or 20.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Method 3: dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust (very large systems)


Show code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
dgrid_interp = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(
    atoms, spacing=0.5, coarse_factor=2, n_neighbors=10,
)
t_interp = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"rust_aabb+int: shape={dgrid_interp.shape}, "
      f"min={dgrid_interp.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_interp.max():.2f}, "
      f"time={t_interp*1000:.0f} ms")

print(f"max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_interp| = {np.abs(dgrid_exact - dgrid_interp).max():.3e}")


rust_aabb+int: shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.26, max=7.54, time=8 ms
max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_interp| = 8.061e-01


The coarse grid is at 1.0 Å spacing (spacing × coarse_factor), and the result is trilinearly interpolated back to 0.5 Å. The interpolation step is what introduces the mild smoothing — you can see it as a slight rounding of the surface near tight windows. Do not crank coarse_factor above ~3 if you care about sub-Å window diameters; beyond that the interpolation swamps the true signal.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Method 4: dgrid_from_atoms_cpu (legacy / Python)


Show code
t0 = time.perf_counter()
dgrid_cpu = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000)
t_cpu = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"cpu/dask:      shape={dgrid_cpu.shape}, "
      f"min={dgrid_cpu.min():.2f}, max={dgrid_cpu.max():.2f}, "
      f"time={t_cpu*1000:.0f} ms")

# Note: dgrid_from_atoms_cpu is correct on skewed cells (uses freud AABB)
print(f"max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_cpu| = {np.abs(dgrid_exact - dgrid_cpu).max():.3e}")


cpu/dask:      shape=(52, 52, 52), min=-1.98, max=7.54, time=1033 ms
max |dgrid_exact - dgrid_cpu| = 2.800e-01


5–20× slower than the Rust path on a single thread, but the Dask graph is composable: pass precompute=False to get a lazy array and chain downstream reductions. This is the right entry point if you need to plug dgrid into an existing Dask pipeline.

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Side-by-side timing


Show code
methods = {
    "rust_exact":     mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5),
    "rust_aabb":      mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10),
    "rust_aabb+int":  mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, coarse_factor=2),
    "cpu/dask":       mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000),
}
ref = methods["rust_exact"]
print(f"{'method':<18}  {'shape':<14}  {'min':>7}  {'max':>7}  max|diff|")
for name, g in methods.items():
    diff = float(np.abs(g - ref).max()) if name != "rust_exact" else 0.0
    print(f"{name:<18}  {str(g.shape):<14}  {g.min():>7.2f}  {g.max():>7.2f}  {diff:.3e}")

rust_aabb           (52, 52, 52)      -1.70     7.54  0.000e+00
rust_aabb+int       (52, 52, 52)      -1.26     7.54  8.061e-01

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text: Broken methods

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
section: Two functions you must NOT use: dgrid_from_atoms_gpu and dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb
text:
Two functions you must NOT use: dgrid_from_atoms_gpu and dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb
Both compute the minimum-image convention with per-axis NINT rounding:
# WRONG on a skewed cell
dx = dx - cell[0, 0] * NINT(dx / cell[0, 0])
dy = dy - cell[1, 1] * NINT(dy / cell[1, 1])
dz = dz - cell[2, 2] * NINT(dz / cell[2, 2])
This is only correct for orthogonal cells (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic). On a monoclinic or triclinic cell — which includes most real MOFs — the per-axis NINT picks the wrong image for some atom–grid pairs, and the distance grid develops systematic stripes near the cell walls. The bug is silent: the function returns without warning and the dgrid looks plausible until you compare it to the exact result.
Use the Rust backend (dgrid_from_atoms_rust) instead. Its MIC path uses a 7-image Wassenaar construction on skewed cells, which is correct for all cell types. The CPU/Dask method (dgrid_from_atoms_cpu, without the _no_aabb suffix) is also correct because it routes through freud’s AABB query, which uses the proper box geometry.
If you see dgrid_from_atoms_gpu or dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb in legacy code, replace the call with:
# Replace dgrid_from_atoms_gpu(...)
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5)

# Replace dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb(...)
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000)

title: Distance Grid Methods — Choosing the Right Backend
text:
Quick decision recap

Default → dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5) — exact MIC, correct for all cell types.
OOM on big cell → dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10) — R-tree, same accuracy, less RAM.
HT screen / very large system → dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, coarse_factor=2) — 8× faster, mild smoothing.
Python/Dask composition → dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000) — slowest, but lazy-friendly.
NEVER → dgrid_from_atoms_gpu, dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb — broken on skewed cells.

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
mgrcli is the command-line companion to the MOFography Python API. It wraps the same Rust-accelerated pipeline (dgrid_from_atoms_rust → do_periodic_segmentation_rust → downstream analysis) so you can analyze one or many CIFs without writing any Python.
The main entry is mgrcli process:
mgrcli process <cifs...> [flags]
A single invocation can produce:

Per-CIF *_results.npz — the same segmentation dict you’d get from the Python API (dgrid, maxima, regions, connections, RAG-as-arrays).
Pore-diameter CSV with LCD, PLD, DFSD, and percolation history (with --pore-dia).
PSD CSVs — uniform, pocketwise, and accessible variants (with --psd, --psd-accessible).
Surface-area and void-volume CSVs + Plotly bar charts (with --sa / --vol).
RAG pickle — a NetworkX graph of the pore network (with --rag).
Pocket types — env_cluster multi-modal fingerprints (with --types).
HTML visualizations — Plotly or Three.js (with --plot-html).

This tutorial walks through installation, the canonical command, every key flag, the output layout, and how to drop down to the Python API when the CLI is not enough.

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Prerequisites

A working MOFography environment (see the Installation guide).
A CIF file. The tutorials use docs/IRMOF-1.cif from this repo.
About 5–10 seconds per CIF on a modern laptop for the canonical flags (--pore-dia --psd --rag --types on IRMOF-1 takes ~4 s end-to-end on M-series).

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Installation

From PyPI (recommended)
pip install mgrcli
This pulls in mgrcli plus its pinned runtime dependencies (ase, pymatgen, plotly, scikit-image, networkx, …) and the prebuilt Rust extension for your platform.


From source (editable)
If you want to hack on the CLI or pin a development branch:
git clone https://github.com/arung-northwestern/mgr_cli_py.git
cd mgr_cli_py/python_cli
pip install -e .
pip install -e . picks up your local edits to mgrcli/cli.py without a reinstall.


Sanity check
mgrcli --version     # prints the package version
mgrcli --help        # top-level subcommand list
In a Python notebook, you can also confirm the binary is on PATH and report its version:


Show code
import shutil, subprocess
print("mgrcli on PATH:", shutil.which("mgrcli"))
print(subprocess.run(["mgrcli", "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())


mgrcli on PATH: /Users/arungopalan/miniforge3/envs/mgr_env/bin/mgrcli
mgrcli 2026.05.16.0

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
The canonical command
For most MOFs — IRMOF-1, UiO-66, ZIF-8, HKUST-1 — this one command is all you need to get the full pore-network picture:
mgrcli process IRMOF-1.cif \
  --dgrid-method rust_exact \
  --vdw-radii-set bondi \
  --b rust_det \
  --pore-dia \
  --psd \
  --rag
It:

Computes the distance grid with the thread-parallel rust_exact backend (default-correct for all cell types).
Runs periodic segmentation with the deterministic rust_det watershed.
Adds pore-diameter analysis (LCD, PLD, DFSD + percolation history).
Adds the PSD (uniform + pocketwise probe sampling).
Saves the RAG as a pickle for downstream graph work.

Add --types to also detect pocket-type families via env_cluster:
mgrcli process IRMOF-1.cif \
  --dgrid-method rust_exact --vdw-radii-set bondi --b rust_det \
  --pore-dia --psd --rag --types
This is the command to copy-paste for a “one-shot full analysis”.

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
End-to-end smoke test
Run the canonical command from inside this docs folder. The output lands in hts_output/IRMOF-1/ (the convention used by the Streamlit HTS tab — any directory you pass to -o works, but hts_output/<stem>/ is the standard layout for batch HTS runs).

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Reading the .npz back in Python
The CLI saves a compressed NumPy archive so you can mix batch CLI runs with custom Python post-processing without re-running segmentation.


Show code
import numpy as np

# The CLI's results .npz contains object arrays (connections, pocket_type_summary,
# mat_atoms, ...), so allow_pickle=True is required.
with np.load(out_dir / "IRMOF-1_results.npz", allow_pickle=True) as z:
    print("keys:", sorted(z.files))
    print(f"  dgrid shape:           {z['dgrid'].shape}")
    print(f"  regions_pbc shape:     {z['regions_pbc'].shape}")
    print(f"  n maxima (pbc):        {len(z['maxima_pbc'])}")
    conns = z['connections']
    # Stored as a 0-d object array — .item() unpacks the inner Python list
    conn_list = conns.item() if conns.dtype == object and conns.shape == () else conns
    print(f"  n connections:         {len(conn_list)}")
    if 'pocket_type_summary' in z.files:
        summary = z['pocket_type_summary']
        # Stored as a 0-d object array containing a Python list[dict]
        if summary.dtype == object and summary.shape == ():
            summary = summary.item()
        print(f"  n pocket types:        {len(summary)}")
        for t in summary:
            print(f"    type {t['type_id']}: n={t['n_pockets']}, "

                  f"vol ∈ [{t['volume_min_a3']:.0f}, {t['volume_max_a3']:.0f}] Å³")
