title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Key flags reference
The process subcommand has ~30 flags. They split into five groups: input/output, analysis parameters, boolean flags, analysis options, and visualization. The defaults mirror the Streamlit web app so a CLI run produces the same numbers as a click-through on the site.

Distance-grid method (--dgrid-method)



Value
Backend
When to use




rust_exact
Thread-parallel Rust, voxel-exact
Default. Correct for all cell types, including non-orthorhombic.


rust_aabb
R-tree accelerated
Large unit cells; trades a small approximation for ~2-5× less RAM. See Distance Grid tutorial.


rust_aabb_interp
Coarse R-tree + trilinear interp
Very large cells where even rust_aabb is heavy.


python_aabb
Pure-Python AABB
Slowest; use only for parity checks against the Python API.




Do not use the deprecated dgrid_from_atoms_gpu or dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb paths — they mis-handle non-orthorhombic cells. The *_rust backends are the only correct path on skewed cells.

Tuning knobs for the AABB backends:








Flag
Default
Effect




--dgrid-block-size
50000
Voxels per block for python_aabb. Lower = less RAM, more Python overhead.


--dgrid-n-neighbors
10
R-tree neighbor count for rust_aabb / rust_aabb_interp. Higher = more accurate, slower.


--dgrid-coarse-factor
2
Coarsening factor for rust_aabb_interp only. Higher = much faster, coarser approximation.



For most MOFs the auto policy is fine: by default mgrcli will auto-switch from rust_exact to rust_aabb for very large cells. Pass --no-auto-dgrid to disable that policy and stay on rust_exact.


Watershed backend (-b / --backend / --watershed-backend)








Value
Backend
When to use




rust_det
Deterministic Rust watershed
Default. Deterministic, fast, matches the web app.


rust_det_parallel
Same algorithm, parallelized
Larger cells where serial rust_det is the bottleneck.


rust_bucket
Rust 0-arg bucket queue
Legacy. Faster on some inputs but the basin order can differ — keep rust_det for reproducibility.


skimage
scikit-image watershed
Pure-Python; only useful as a cross-check. Requires scikit-image.





VDW radii set (--vdw-radii-set)








Value
Source
Notes




bondi
Bondi (1964)
Default. Matches the web app and the validated canonical workflow.


crc
CRC Handbook
Slightly smaller radii on metals; can change pocket-typing band counts.


alvarez
Alvarez (2018)
Heavier on metals; recommended when probing open-metal sites.



See VDW Radii Comparison for the full sensitivity study.


Surface area integration (--sa-method)







Value
Algorithm




mc (default)
Monte Carlo shell sampling. Fast, accurate; same as web app.


mesh
Marching-cubes surface area. Slower; closer to pymatgen-style estimates.





Accessibility method (--accessibility-method, --lattice-variant)
Drives the percolation test that decides which pockets are reachable from outside the unit cell:







Value
What it does




winding (default)
Winding-number percolation. Fast, robust, matches web app.


lattice
Lattice-based percolation. --lattice-variant chooses v1 (older) or v2 (newer, default).



Accessibility applies to --pore-dia, --sa, and --vol. Combine with --no-window-fp to disable the window-fingerprint rescue for accessible SA / vol (only meaningful with winding).


Segmentation parameters
These map 1:1 to the Python API parameters of do_periodic_segmentation_rust:








Flag
Default
Effect




-s, --spacing
0.5 Å
Grid resolution. Halve → 8× more voxels; the single most expensive knob.


-H, --h
0.2 Å
H-maxima persistence. Higher = fewer, larger pockets.


-mt, --mask-thickness
0.05 Å
Void-space threshold. Increase to merge nearby pockets.


-ta, --threshold-abs
1.5 Å
Maxima must be at least this far from the framework.


-md, --min-distance
1.5 Å
Minimum separation between distinct maxima.


-ms, --minimum-window-separation
1.0 Å
Minimum separation between detected windows.


-wt, --wall-thickness
0.05
Wall-thickness fraction for window detection.


-ep, --extra-padding
5.0 Å
Extra PBC padding beyond the +5 Å default.


-mrs, --min-region-size
0.001
Filter regions smaller than this fraction of the padded grid.




Heads up: the legacy “batch” profile used mask_thickness=0.5 and rust_bucket (see mgrcli generate-config --profile legacy). The web / default profile is the validated one for pocket typing — keep it unless you have a specific reason to regress.



Probe radius








Flag
Default
Effect




--probe-radius
1.2 Å (He)
Probe for surface area, void volume, and accessible PSD.


--probe-radius-psd
1.2 Å
Probe for the pocket PSD used in env_cluster typing.





Pocket typing (--types / --pocket-typing)







Value
Algorithm




env_cluster (default with --types)
Multi-modal fingerprinting: pocket PSD + framework SH + connectivity SH. The validated, recommended method.


legacy_js
Older RAG + Jensen-Shannon divergence clustering. Kept for regression; less stable.


none (default without --types)
Skip typing — just save the RAG.



--types is a shorthand for --pocket-typing env_cluster. It always saves the RAG pickle (<stem>_rag_clustered.pkl) in addition to running the typing pass.


Boolean flags







Flag
Effect




--no-connections
Skip window + connection detection. Faster, but you lose the pore graph.


--no-auto-dgrid
Disable auto-switch from rust_exact → rust_aabb for large cells.


--no-window-fp
Disable window-fingerprint rescue for accessible SA / vol (winding).


--return-padded-regions
Include the padded region array in the .npz (default off).


--return-dgrid
Keep dgrid in the .npz (default on).


--disable-tqdm
Suppress progress bars (good for log files).


--plot-html
Save a standalone 3D HTML viewer after processing.


--no-stylize
Disable stylized framework rendering in plots.


--pore-dia
Compute LCD/PLD/DFSD + percolation history.


--percolation-plot
Save <stem>_percolation.html (cluster growth).


--sa-plot-html
Save <stem>_surface_area_plot.html.


--vol-plot-html
Save <stem>_void_volume_plot.html.


--psd
Compute pore size distribution.


--psd-accessible
Compute accessible (percolation-filtered) PSD at --probe-radius.


--sa
Compute surface area.


--vol
Compute void volume.


--auto-params
Auto-estimate optimal parameters from the cell geometry.


--types
Detect pocket types via env_cluster.


--rag
Save the RAG pickle (no typing).


--theme {dark,white}
Plot theme (default dark).





Visualization backends








Flag
Default
Effect




--plot-html
off
Save <stem>.html viewer.


--plot-backend {plotly,threejs}
plotly
Viewer engine. Three.js exports smaller, more portable HTML.


--percolation-plot-backend {plotly,threejs}
threejs
Percolation plot engine.


--html-dir
same as -o
Separate folder for HTML outputs.

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Re-running from a saved config
If you’ve been clicking around the web app and want to capture the exact parameter set as a JSON config:
mgrcli generate-config -o my_run.json
# edit my_run.json …
mgrcli process IRMOF-1.cif -c my_run.json
generate-config writes a config matching the current defaults (web profile by default; --profile legacy for the older batch defaults). The process subcommand accepts it via -c/--config.

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Processing many CIFs
The positional argument is variadic — pass as many CIFs as you like:
mgrcli process mofs/*.cif -o ./results/ --pore-dia --psd --rag --disable-tqdm
Each CIF is processed in turn; outputs are prefixed with the CIF stem (<stem>_results.npz, <stem>_pore_dia.csv, …). Failed CIFs are logged and skipped — a single bad file does not abort the run.

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Plotting an existing .npz
If you already saved a *_results.npz (via the CLI or the Python API) and want to (re)render its HTML viewer:
mgrcli plot IRMOF-1_results.npz -o ./plots/ --plot-backend threejs --theme dark
plot reads the .npz, attaches a .html viewer with the same name stem into the output directory, and respects the same --plot-backend / --theme / --no-stylize / --surface-taubin-intensity knobs as --plot-html on process.

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Launching the web app
If you’d rather click through, mgrcli interactive boots the same Streamlit app you can use locally:
mgrcli interactive             # default port
mgrcli interactive --port 8501 # specific port
mgrcli interactive --clean     # kill stale Streamlit processes first
interactive is the same backend as the deployed Hugging Face Space; the CLI just removes the need to clone + install the Streamlit code by hand.

title: CLI Quick Start
section: When to drop down to the Python API
text:
When to drop down to the Python API
The CLI is the right tool for:

One-shot analysis of a handful of MOFs.
Batch HTS-style runs on hundreds to thousands of CIFs.
Capturing reproducible parameter sets in a JSON config.
Producing standardized artifacts (.npz + CSVs) for downstream pipelines.

But the Python API is strictly more flexible. Drop down to Python when you need:

Custom post-processing on the segmentation dict (dgrid, regions_pbc, connections, pbc_groups).
Typed PocketTypingResult with .n_types, .n_pockets, .type_summary, .rep_to_type, .regions_cluster (see Pocket Type Detection).
Custom visualizations (e.g. show_mof_plotly(seg, atoms, typed_result=...)).
Tighter integration with Dask, MOFDB, or PoroNet pipelines (see HTS Dask and the PoroNet tutorial).
Access to close_or_inside_maxima (voxel coords of pockets’ interior maxima) or other low-level arrays the CLI does not surface.

The handoff is clean: every artifact the CLI writes is also a valid input to the Python API. You can read the .npz with numpy.load, or just re-load the CIF and re-run a single step from the CLI’s compute_* functions (they are importable from mgrcli.cli).

title: CLI Quick Start
text:
Tips

Start with the canonical command, then add flags. Defaults mirror the web app and are validated against IRMOF-1, UiO-66, ZIF-8, HKUST-1, NU-1000, and ZIF-20.
Use -o hts_output/<stem>/ so the per-CIF artifacts live in a predictable folder layout — that’s what the Streamlit HTS tab expects.
Reproducibility: pair -c my_run.json with --disable-tqdm for clean logs you can diff between runs.
For very large cells, the default auto-AABB policy already switches to rust_aabb — you only need to override --dgrid-method if you want to force one specific backend.
VDW sensitivity: if pocket-type counts look wrong, re-run with --vdw-radii-set bondi and compare against crc / alvarez. See the pocket type detection page for the caution on radii.
The CLI hides nothing the API exposes — every artifact on disk is also reachable from Python. The *_results.npz is the canonical handoff.

title: Aromatic ring detection
text:
MOFography detects small aromatic rings (typically 5–9 members: imidazole, benzene, pyridine, fused linker cores) to draw white ring outlines and semi-transparent fills on framework plots.
Entry points:



Layer
Function




Detection
compute_aromatic_cycles()


Plotly
plot_aromatic_rings(), show_mof_plotly()


Three.js
make_aromatic_rings_trace(), show_mof_threejs()



Both backends call the same compute_aromatic_cycles detector. Results are cached on atoms.info["aromatic_cycles"] so Plotly mesh + ring traces do not detect twice. show_mof_plotly / show_mof_threejs enable rings by default (plot_framework_show_rings=True).
Always call update_with_covalent_bonds() first (or let compute_aromatic_cycles do it).


import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read

atoms = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(read("framework.cif"))
cycles = mgr.compute_aromatic_cycles(atoms)  # cached in atoms.info["aromatic_cycles"]

# Plotly
fig = mgr.show_mof_plotly(seg, atoms=atoms, plot_aromatic_rings=True)

# Three.js HTML
mgr.show_mof_threejs(seg, atoms=atoms, plot_aromatic_rings=True)



Bond orders come from pymatgen CovalentBond.get_bond_order (tolerance tol=0.2 in update_with_covalent_bonds). Orders are binned:



Bond order
Label




(0, 1]
single


(1, 2]
double


(2, 3]
triple



Crystallographic aromatic and fused-ring contacts often sit on bin edges. Examples from real MOF linkers:









Structure
Symptom
MIC distance
Fix




NU-1000 TBAPy
Fused benzene C–C classified single
~1.56 Å
C–C distance fallback


ZIF-20 imidazole + benzene
Short C–N classified triple
~1.30 Å
C–N triple demotion



Pure bond-order filtering then drops valid rings even though the geometry is clearly aromatic.



Typical contact lengths (Å) for organic / MOF linkers (room temperature):








Contact
Range (Å)
Notes




Aromatic C–C
1.38 – 1.42
Benzene mean ~1.397 (Allen et al., Acta Cryst. B 2002, CSD)


Kekulé C–C in ring
1.44 – 1.47
“Single” bond in benzene Kekulé form


Fused aromatic C–C
1.47 – 1.58
Naphthalene fusion; porphyrin/benzene ~1.55–1.56


Aromatic C–N
1.30 – 1.37
Pyridine ~1.34; imidazole ~1.33–1.37


C≡N nitrile
1.15 – 1.16
True triple — not aromatic






Defined in mofography/analyze.py (search for _AROMATIC_*_MAX_DIST). MIC distances use periodic boundary conditions when the cell is set.








Constant
Value (Å)
Role




_AROMATIC_CC_MAX_DIST
1.62
Promote borderline single C–C to aromatic double; validate 6-rings with long fusion bonds


_AROMATIC_CN_MAX_DIST
1.50
Same for C–N pairs


_AROMATIC_CN_TRIPLE_MAX_DIST
1.42
Demote misclassified triple C–N to aromatic double when distance is still in the aromatic range (above nitrile, below saturated C–N)



Additional rules:

Chordless C/N cycles of requested sizes (default 5–9).
At most one optional MIC closure edge (≤ 1.5 Å) per ring for duplicate-site bond gaps.
Ring must be compact after PBC unwrapping (span < 4.5 Å).




from mofography.analyze import (
    find_aromatic_cycles_in_unit_cell,
    get_bond_types,
    sgraph_from_atoms,
)

atoms = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(atoms)
cycles = find_aromatic_cycles_in_unit_cell(atoms, default_ring_sizes=[5, 6])
print(len(cycles), {len(c) for c in cycles})

g = sgraph_from_atoms(atoms)
import networkx as nx
bt = nx.get_edge_attributes(g, "bond_type")
# Inspect bond_type for atom pair (i, j): bt.get(tuple(sorted((i, j))))
If a ring is still missing, check MIC distance and bond_type for each edge in the cycle. Adjust thresholds only when you have a concrete false negative; the defaults were validated on ZIF-8, NU-1000, and ZIF-20.




Flexible framework movies (Three.js) — ring traces in HTML export
get_bond_types — bond-order binning + aromatic promotion

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
text:
A porous crystal does not just have pores — it has accessible pores. “Accessible” means a spherical probe of radius \(r\) can travel from one face of the unit cell to the opposite face, weaving through windows that are at least as wide as the probe. The largest probe that can do this is the Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD), and the act of testing whether such a path exists at a given \(r\) is the percolation test.
This tutorial covers the winding accessibility method — mofography’s default — and contrasts it with the lattice method, which is closer in spirit to the Zeo++ voxel-sweep approach. On a simple cubic MOF like IRMOF-1 both methods give the same answer (modulo the voxel resolution); the differences emerge on contorted, low-symmetry frameworks where the winding algorithm’s graph topology is more robust.
You will:

Run do_periodic_segmentation_rust to get a pore graph.
Compute PLD / LCD / DFSD with get_pore_dia_mgr_winding.
Step the probe radius and watch the percolating cluster grow / shrink with compute_percolation_history_winding.
Run the equivalent lattice v2 sweep and compare.
Render an interactive Three.js scene with show_percolation_threejs for any chosen probe radius.

Prerequisites: the Distance Grid tutorial, Region Segmentation, and Connections and Windows. The conceptual background for the two algorithms is in the face_merging_vs_winding.qmd slides and in pore_limiting_diameter_pld_and_percolation.md.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
text:
Why two algorithms?
Both methods answer the same question — is the void connected across the periodic cell at probe radius \(r\)? — but on different representations:








Method
Representation
What it checks




Winding (graph)
The deduplicated pore graph (nodes = cage centres, edges = windows). Each edge carries a window_radius and a periodic relative offset \((di, dj, dk) \in \{-1, 0, 1\}^3\).
A BFS from a source node that tracks accumulated periodic offsets. If the BFS visits a node with offset \(\Delta \ne 0\) along axis \(a\), the cluster wraps across axis \(a\) — percolation along \(a\).


Lattice v2 (voxel)
The PBC-merged labeled regions array. Each face pair \((x_0, x_{N-1})\), \((y_0, y_{N-1})\), \((z_0, z_{N-1})\) is unioned via a UnionFind.
After the union, the percolating labels are those present on both faces of an axis.



The winding method is the better default because it:

Avoids the label-merging ambiguity that voxel methods suffer when two cages nearly touch across a periodic face.
Captures topology (which cages connect through which windows), not just voxel contiguity.
Is much faster on large cells — percolation is decided by walking the graph, not by re-labelling the grid at every probe radius.

The lattice method is preserved mainly for direct comparability with Zeo++ papers, which report pld from a voxel-sweep algorithm. The variant='v2' lattice path is the recommended lattice sweep; v1 is the older UnionFind-only path retained for legacy comparisons.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
text:
Imports and setup


Show code
import logging
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
logging.getLogger("mofography").setLevel(logging.ERROR)

import numpy as np
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 1: Load IRMOF-1 and build the distance grid
text:
Step 1: Load IRMOF-1 and build the distance grid
IRMOF-1 is a cubic MOF (\(a = b = c \approx 25.83\) Å) with two families of cages — small and large — connected through a 3D pore network. The cubic symmetry is convenient: any method that works correctly on a cubic cell will produce the same PLD up to a half-voxel.


Show code
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
print(f"IRMOF-1: {len(atoms)} atoms, cell = {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)} Å")

spacing = 0.5                                  # Å — see distance_grid.qmd
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)               # Rust kernel requires float32
print(f"dgrid: {dgrid.shape}, void max = {dgrid.max():.2f} Å")


IRMOF-1: 424 atoms, cell = [25.83 25.83 25.83] Å
dgrid: (52, 52, 52), void max = 7.54 Å

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
text:
Step 2: Run periodic segmentation
do_periodic_segmentation_rust builds the pore graph. We pass back the dgrid so downstream functions do not have to recompute it. The return_padded_regions=True flag is required for the percolation routines — they need the periodic copies of the regions array to evaluate window connections across cell boundaries.


Show code
results = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid, atoms,
    mask_thickness=1.5, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
    spacing=spacing, return_dgrid=True,
    return_padded_regions=True, extra_padding=2,
)
regions = results["regions"]
print(f"regions: shape={regions.shape}, {int(regions.max())} unique labels")
print(f"maxima_info: {results['maxima_info'].shape} (label, i, j, k, di, dj, dk)")
print(f"connections: {len(results['connections'])} inter-region windows")


regions: shape=(52, 52, 52), 27 unique labels
maxima_info: (125, 7) (label, i, j, k, di, dj, dk)
connections: 300 inter-region windows


The result is a richly populated dictionary. The two keys the percolation routines need are regions (the labeled volume) and maxima_info (one row per local maximum, including the PBC image it belongs to). The connections list carries (region_a, region_b, di, dj, dk, window_radius) tuples — these become the edges of the pore graph.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 3: Compute PLD, LCD, DFSD via the winding algorithm
text:
Step 3: Compute PLD, LCD, DFSD via the winding algorithm
get_pore_dia_mgr_winding is the one-shot entry point. Pass the segmentation results and the framework atoms; it builds the directed pore graph and returns the three classical textural properties:

LCD (Largest Cavity Diameter): \(2 \times \max(\texttt{dgrid})\). The diameter of the single largest sphere that fits anywhere in the void — no connectivity requirement.
PLD (Pore Limiting Diameter): \(2 \times r_{\max}\) where \(r_{\max}\) is the largest probe radius at which the void percolates. The diameter of the largest sphere that can traverse the material end-to-end.
DFSD (Directional Free Sphere Diameter): \(2 \times \max(\texttt{dgrid}[\text{percolating labels}])\). The largest sphere that fits inside a percolating region. Always \(\text{DFSD} \le \text{LCD}\) by construction.



Show code
lcd, pld, dfsd, _ = mgr.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding(atoms, dgrid=dgrid, results=results)
print(f"LCD = {lcd:.3f} Å    (largest cavity anywhere)")
print(f"PLD = {pld:.3f} Å    (largest traversing probe)")
print(f"DFSD = {dfsd:.3f} Å   (largest cavity in a percolating region)")


LCD = 15.076 Å    (largest cavity anywhere)
PLD = 7.914 Å    (largest traversing probe)
DFSD = 15.076 Å   (largest cavity in a percolating region)


The inequality \(\text{PLD} \le \text{DFSD} \le \text{LCD}\) should hold — the PLD is bounded by the smallest window along the percolating route, the DFSD by the largest cavity along that same route, and the LCD by the largest cavity anywhere (which may be a dead-end pocket that the probe can never reach).

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 4: Percolation history — probe by probe
text:
Step 4: Percolation history — probe by probe
The single triple (lcd, pld, dfsd) is the answer to one question. The full percolation history answers a richer one: as the probe grows, when does each axis stop percolating, and which regions drop out of the percolating cluster at each step?


Show code
hist_w, pld_locs_w, clusters_w = mgr.compute_percolation_history_winding(
    results=results, step=0.1, min_threshold=0.0,
)
print(f"winding history: {len(hist_w)} entries from "
      f"{hist_w[0][0]:.2f} Å to {hist_w[-1][0]:.2f} Å probe radius")
print(f"  PLD locations: {pld_locs_w.shape}  (grid coords of the bottleneck)")
print(f"  final clusters: {len(clusters_w)}  (one per percolating axis)")


winding history: 40 entries from 0.00 Å to 3.90 Å probe radius
  PLD locations: (0, 3)  (grid coords of the bottleneck)
  final clusters: 3  (one per percolating axis)


The history is a list of (probe_radius, axis_clusters) tuples. axis_clusters is a dict {"x": [...], "y": [...], "z": [...]} where each value is a list of percolating groups; each group is a list of region labels in that group.
Let me see how IRMOF-1 percolates as a function of probe radius:


Show code
print(f"\n{'probe r (Å)':>12s}  {'x':>3s}  {'y':>3s}  {'z':>3s}  "
      f"{'x cluster sizes':>20s}")
print("-" * 50)
for t, axes in hist_w[::4]:           # every 4th entry to keep output small
    sizes_x = [len(g) for g in axes['x']]
    print(f"{t:>12.2f}  "
          f"{'Y' if axes['x'] else '.':>3s}  "
          f"{'Y' if axes['y'] else '.':>3s}  "
          f"{'Y' if axes['z'] else '.':>3s}  "
          f"{str(sizes_x):>20s}")



 probe r (Å)    x    y    z       x cluster sizes
--------------------------------------------------
        0.00    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        0.40    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        0.80    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        1.20    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        1.60    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        2.00    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        2.40    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        2.80    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        3.20    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]
        3.60    Y    Y    Y  [27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27, 27]


IRMOF-1 is fully 3D-percolating at every probe radius up to ~3.9 Å: the x, y, and z channels are all open through the entire range. Above the PLD threshold (3.955 Å in the binary search that backs get_pore_dia_mgr_winding), no axis percolates. The step=0.1 here is the history display step — the underlying PLD search uses a finer binary search.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 5: Final percolating cluster — what is connected at PLD?
text:
Step 5: Final percolating cluster — what is connected at PLD?
The third return value of compute_percolation_history_winding is final_clusters: a dict keyed by cluster id, with metadata for each percolating cluster at the last probe radius where percolation still exists.


Show code
for cid, cdata in clusters_w.items():
    print(f"\ncluster {cid}:")
    print(f"  regions ({len(cdata['regions'])}): {cdata['regions'][:8]}"
          f"{' …' if len(cdata['regions']) > 8 else ''}")
    print(f"  nodes  ({len(cdata['nodes'])}):  {cdata['nodes']}")
    print(f"  edges  ({len(cdata['edges'])}):  {cdata['edges'][:4]}"
          f"{' …' if len(cdata['edges']) > 4 else ''}")
    print(f"  axes percolating: {cdata['axes']}")



cluster 1:
  regions (20): [1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13] …
  nodes  (4):  [1, 3, 5, 8]
  edges  (6):  [(1, 8, 0), (1, 8, 1), (3, 8, 0), (3, 8, 1)] …
  axes percolating: ['x']

cluster 2:
  regions (20): [1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13] …
  nodes  (4):  [1, 3, 5, 8]
  edges  (6):  [(1, 8, 0), (1, 8, 1), (3, 8, 0), (3, 8, 1)] …
  axes percolating: ['y']

cluster 3:
  regions (20): [1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13] …
  nodes  (4):  [1, 3, 5, 8]
  edges  (6):  [(1, 8, 0), (1, 8, 1), (3, 8, 0), (3, 8, 1)] …
  axes percolating: ['z']


A few things to notice:

edges are triples (u, v, axis_index) recording which window (which periodic direction) carries the percolation. On a cubic MOF the windows along the three axes are geometrically equivalent; the algorithm still distinguishes them by relative offset.
dangling_nodes is empty here. On a more contorted MOF it would list pockets that touch the percolating cluster through only one window — a topological “leaf” that the probe can enter but not exit. See pore_limiting_diameter_pld_and_percolation.md for the dangling-node discussion.
The percolating cluster is the same along x, y, and z because IRMOF-1 is cubic. The winding algorithm returns one cluster per axis, not one cluster per direction — on a chiral MOF with a 1D channel you would see one entry here, for the axis the channel runs along.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 6: Compare with the lattice (Zeo++-style) algorithm
text:
Step 6: Compare with the lattice (Zeo++-style) algorithm
compute_percolation_history_from_results2 runs the lattice v2 sweep on the same segmentation and stores the history under percolation_history_lattice. This is the same data the CLI reports with --accessibility-method lattice --lattice-variant v2.


Show code
mgr.compute_percolation_history_from_results2(results)

hist_l = results["percolation_history_lattice"]
pld_locs_l = results.get("pld_locations_lattice", np.empty((0, 3)))
print(f"lattice v2 history: {len(hist_l)} entries from "
      f"{hist_l[0][0]:.2f} Å to {hist_l[-1][0]:.2f} Å probe radius")
print(f"  PLD locations: {pld_locs_l.shape}  (one per voxel of the limiting window)")


lattice v2 history: 80 entries from 0.00 Å to 3.95 Å probe radius
  PLD locations: (24, 3)  (one per voxel of the limiting window)


Side-by-side comparison of the two methods on IRMOF-1:


Show code
def last_percolating_radius(history):
    """Return the largest probe radius in `history` that still has any axis percolating."""
    last = 0.0
    for t, axes in history:
        if any(axes[a] for a in axes):
            last = t
    return last

pld_radius_winding   = last_percolating_radius(hist_w)
pld_radius_lattice   = last_percolating_radius(hist_l)
pld_diam_winding     = 2.0 * pld_radius_winding
pld_diam_lattice     = 2.0 * pld_radius_lattice

print(f"\n{'method':<14s}  {'r_max (Å)':>10s}  {'PLD (Å)':>10s}")
print("-" * 38)
print(f"{'winding':<14s}  {pld_radius_winding:>10.3f}  {pld_diam_winding:>10.3f}")
print(f"{'lattice v2':<14s}  {pld_radius_lattice:>10.3f}  {pld_diam_lattice:>10.3f}")
print(f"{'winding 1-shot':<14s}  {pld/2:>10.3f}  {pld:>10.3f}    "
      f"(from get_pore_dia_mgr_winding — binary search, finer step)")
print(f"\ndifference (lattice - winding, diameter): "
      f"{(pld_diam_lattice - pld_diam_winding):+.3f} Å")



method           r_max (Å)     PLD (Å)
--------------------------------------
winding              3.900       7.800
lattice v2           3.950       7.900
winding 1-shot       3.957       7.914    (from get_pore_dia_mgr_winding — binary search, finer step)

difference (lattice - winding, diameter): +0.100 Å


Both methods agree to within the grid resolution. With spacing=0.5 Å, a half-voxel is 0.25 Å, so the expected agreement is \(\pm 0.25\) Å. The get_pore_dia_mgr_winding one-shot value (3.955 Å × 2 = 7.91 Å) sits between the two histories because it uses a finer binary search than the 0.1 Å step we asked for above. This is the expected behaviour on a cubic, well-behaved MOF.
Where the two methods differ is on non-cubic, contorted pore networks — for example NU-1000 (see face_merging_vs_winding.qmd). There, the lattice method can miss wind-around paths that require the probe to leave the cell, wrap around, and re-enter, because its UnionFind only tracks face-touching labels, not the offset between them. The winding method tracks offsets explicitly and recovers the path.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 7: Visualise the percolating cluster interactively
text:
Step 7: Visualise the percolating cluster interactively
show_percolation_threejs returns a self-contained HTML string with an interactive Three.js scene: the framework as ball-and-stick, the pore maxima, the connections, and — at the chosen probe radius — the percolating regions as isosurface meshes and the PLD-critical windows highlighted. You can orbit, zoom, and toggle the layer visibility from the scene’s UI.
The function needs an analysis dict with the percolation history attached; we already have one inside results. We save the HTML to a file (it is too large to embed inline) and link to it from the tutorial.


Show code
analysis = {
    "dgrid": results["dgrid"],
    "regions": results["regions"],
    "maxima": results.get("all_maxima"),
    "connections": results.get("connections", []),
    "pld_locations": results.get("pld_locations"),
    "percolation_history": results.get("percolation_history_winding", []),
    "isovalue": 1.6,
}

# Pick a probe radius just below the PLD so we still see the percolating cluster
# fully intact (3.5 Å gives the full cluster with a comfortable margin to the limit).
probe_radius = 3.5
html = mgr.show_percolation_threejs(analysis, atoms, probe_radius=probe_radius)

out_path = Path("accessibility_percolation_irmof1.html")
out_path.write_text(html, encoding="utf-8")
print(f"wrote {out_path}  ({len(html) / 1024:.1f} KB)")


wrote accessibility_percolation_irmof1.html  (797.4 KB)


Open accessibility_percolation_irmof1.html in a browser. You should see:

The IRMOF-1 framework as a ball-and-stick model.
The percolating cluster at the chosen probe radius as a coloured isosurface (one trace per percolating axis).
The connections between regions as lines.
The PLD-critical windows — windows within 0.25 Å of the percolation cutoff — highlighted separately.

Try changing probe_radius to smaller values (2.0, 2.5, 3.0) and re-rendering: the percolating cluster stays the same on IRMOF-1 because the pore network is fully 3D-connected across the entire range. The interesting case is when you reach the PLD — above 3.955 Å the cluster is empty.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 8: Probe-by-probe visualisation with the lattice method
text:
Step 8: Probe-by-probe visualisation with the lattice method
For direct visual comparison, build the same scene from the lattice history. The analysis dict is method-agnostic — only the percolation_history key changes.


Show code
analysis_lattice = {
    "dgrid": results["dgrid"],
    "regions": results["regions"],
    "maxima": results.get("all_maxima"),
    "connections": results.get("connections", []),
    "pld_locations": results.get("pld_locations_lattice"),
    "percolation_history": results.get("percolation_history_lattice", []),
    "isovalue": 1.6,
}
probe_radius = 3.5
html_lat = mgr.show_percolation_threejs(analysis_lattice, atoms, probe_radius=probe_radius)

out_path_lat = Path("accessibility_percolation_irmof1_lattice.html")
out_path_lat.write_text(html_lat, encoding="utf-8")
print(f"wrote {out_path_lat}  ({len(html_lat) / 1024:.1f} KB)")


wrote accessibility_percolation_irmof1_lattice.html  (797.4 KB)


The two HTML files are visually similar on IRMOF-1, as expected. The differences would show up on a framework with a long, winding channel that touches the periodic boundary obliquely.

title: Accessibility: Winding vs Lattice Percolation
section: Step 9: Sanity checks on the result
text:
Step 9: Sanity checks on the result
A few invariants that should always hold on the result of compute_percolation_history_winding + get_pore_dia_mgr_winding:


Show code
# 1. PLD ≤ DFSD ≤ LCD
assert pld <= dfsd <= lcd, f"PLD≤DFSD≤LCD violated: {pld=} {dfsd=} {lcd=}"
print(f"  PLD ≤ DFSD ≤ LCD  ✓  ({pld:.3f} ≤ {dfsd:.3f} ≤ {lcd:.3f})")

# 2. At the reported PLD, the winding history still shows at least one percolating axis
last_t, last_axes = hist_w[-1]
assert any(last_axes[a] for a in last_axes), "last history entry has no percolation"
print(f"  history[-1] at r={last_t:.2f} Å percolates on "
      f"{[a for a in last_axes if last_axes[a]]}")

# 3. The one-shot PLD is within one grid step of the history's last percolating radius
assert abs(pld / 2 - pld_radius_winding) < spacing, "one-shot PLD disagrees with history"
print(f"  one-shot PLD/2 = {pld/2:.3f}, history last = {pld_radius_winding:.3f}  "
      f"(Δ = {abs(pld/2 - pld_radius_winding):.3f} Å)")

# 4. Winding and lattice agree to within one grid step
assert abs(pld_diam_winding - pld_diam_lattice) < spacing, \
    f"winding vs lattice disagree by {abs(pld_diam_winding - pld_diam_lattice):.3f} Å"
print(f"  winding vs lattice PLD agree within {spacing} Å  ✓")


  PLD ≤ DFSD ≤ LCD  ✓  (7.914 ≤ 15.076 ≤ 15.076)
  history[-1] at r=3.90 Å percolates on ['x', 'y', 'z']
  one-shot PLD/2 = 3.957, history last = 3.900  (Δ = 0.057 Å)
  winding vs lattice PLD agree within 0.5 Å  ✓

title: PoroNet: H2 adsorption on pore graphs
text:
PoroNet is a graph neural network built on mofography pore graphs. This example predicts H₂ adsorption at 160 K and 5 bar. Because the prediction is a sum over pores, it also gives the contribution of each individual pore, which makes the model interpretable.
For details, see PoroNet: An Intrinsically Interpretable Pore Graph Neural Network (J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2026, 22, 5716). The pore graphs come from the pore graph tutorial workflow.

Load the pore graphs
Download (once) and load the precomputed pore graphs, one region adjacency graph per MOF, with pockets as nodes and windows as edges.


Show code
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

# Data files are cached in DATA_DIR (set PORONET_DATA to change it) and downloaded once.
RELEASE = "https://github.com/mofography/mofography/releases/download/poronet-data-v1"

def fetch(name):

Show code
#Divide the pore graphs into training, validation, and testing dataset
RAG_Training=RAG_2D[0:900]
RAG_Validation=RAG_2D[900:990]

RAG_Training[0].nodes[1]

title: PoroNet: H2 adsorption on pore graphs
text:
Features
Convert each pore graph into a DGL graph whose node features are the local pocket properties, then batch all graphs into one large graph for training.


Show code
# Convert graphs to DGL graphs and set node features
def Process_Graphs_Labels(RAGs):
  DGL_Graphs = []
  for g in RAGs:
    if g is not None:
        # dgl.from_networkx relabels nodes in sorted order, so read node data in sorted order too
        nodes = sorted(g.nodes)
        DGL_g = dgl.from_networkx(g)
        DGL_g = dgl.add_self_loop(DGL_g)  # Add self-loops
        DGL_g.ndata['feat'] = torch.tensor(np.array([g.nodes[n]['eh_y'] for n in nodes]))
        DGL_g.ndata['maxima_radii'] = torch.tensor([g.nodes[n]['pocket_radius'] for n in nodes])
        DGL_g.ndata['cell_volume'] = torch.tensor([g.nodes[n]['cell_volume'] for n in nodes])
        DGL_g.ndata['pixel_ratio'] = torch.tensor([g.nodes[n]['pixel_ratio'] for n in nodes])
        DGL_Graphs.append(DGL_g)
  return DGL_Graphs

# Get DGL graphs and Labels
DGL_Graphs_Training=Process_Graphs_Labels(RAG_Training)
DGL_Graphs_Validation=Process_Graphs_Labels(RAG_Validation)
DGL_Graphs_Testing=Process_Graphs_Labels(RAG_Testing)

# Convert list of DGL graphs into a single batched graph
Batched_Graph_Training = dgl.batch(DGL_Graphs_Training)
Batched_Graph_Validation=dgl.batch(DGL_Graphs_Validation)
Batched_Graph_Testing = dgl.batch(DGL_Graphs_Testing)

# Extract node features for all graphs
Features_Training = Batched_Graph_Training.ndata['feat'].float()
Features_Validation = Batched_Graph_Validation.ndata['feat'].float()
Features_Testing = Batched_Graph_Testing.ndata['feat'].float()

title: PoroNet: H2 adsorption on pore graphs
section: Cell volume, pore volume, and pore pixel ratio
text:
Cell volume, pore volume, and pore pixel ratio
Collect per-MOF cell and pore volumes, which are needed to convert per-pore predictions into MOF-level quantities.


Show code
def Grab_Cell_Volume(RAGs):
    Cell_Volume=[]
    for i,g in enumerate(RAGs):
        vol=g.nodes[1]['cell_volume']
        Cell_Volume.append(vol)
    return torch.tensor(Cell_Volume).unsqueeze(1)

Cell_Volume_Training=Grab_Cell_Volume(RAG_Training)
Cell_Volume_Validation=Grab_Cell_Volume(RAG_Validation) 
Cell_Volume_Testing=Grab_Cell_Volume(RAG_Testing)




Show code
def Grab_Pore_Volume(RAGs):
    Pore_Volume=[]
    for i,g in enumerate(RAGs):
        for x in sorted(g.nodes):  # same node order as DGL and Extract_Pixel_Ratio
            cell_vol=g.nodes[x]['cell_volume']
            pore_ratio=g.nodes[x]['pixel_ratio']
            pore_vol=cell_vol*pore_ratio
            Pore_Volume.append(pore_vol)
    return torch.tensor(Pore_Volume).unsqueeze(1)

Pore_Volume_Training=Grab_Pore_Volume(RAG_Training)
Pore_Volume_Validation=Grab_Pore_Volume(RAG_Validation)
Pore_Volume_Testing=Grab_Pore_Volume(RAG_Testing)

 pixel_ratio_list=[]

title: PoroNet: H2 adsorption on pore graphs
text:
The PoroNet model
PoroNet predicts a value for every pore from its features and sums the contributions, so the MOF-level prediction can be interpreted pore by pore.


Show code
class PoroNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self,input_size,hidden_sizes,hidden_activations,dropout):
        super(PoroNet,self).__init__()
        layers=[]
        in_feat=input_size
         
        for i,hidden_size in enumerate(hidden_sizes):
            layers.append(nn.Linear(in_feat,hidden_size))
            hidden_activation=hidden_activations[i]
            if hidden_activation=='relu':
                layers.append(nn.ReLU())
            in_feat=hidden_size

        layers.append(nn.Dropout(p=dropout))
        layers.append(nn.Linear(in_feat,1))
        self.model = nn.Sequential(*layers)
         
         
    def forward(self,g,input_feature):

        x=self.model(input_feature)

        return x

title: PoroNet: H2 adsorption on pore graphs
text:
Hyperparameters
Set the cross-validation folds, the learning schedule and the network size used for training.


Show code
#5 fold
cv=5

#maximum of training epoch
num_epoch=5000




Show code
def objective(trial):
    # Suggest values for the hyperparameters
    num_patience=trial.suggest_int('num_patience', 10, 2000)
    num_layers=trial.suggest_int('num_layers', 1, 3)
    hidden_sizes = [trial.suggest_int(f'hidden_size{i}', 16, 128) for i in range(num_layers)]
    hidden_activations=[trial.suggest_categorical(f'hidden_activation{i}',['relu','none'])for i in range(num_layers)]
    dropout = trial.suggest_float('dropout', 0.2, 0.4)
    initial_lr = trial.suggest_float('lr', 1e-5, 1e-1, log=True)
    weight_decay = trial.suggest_float('weight_decay', 1e-9, 1e-3, log=True)
    factor=trial.suggest_float('factor', 0.1, 0.9)
    

    # K-Fold CV
    kf = KFold(n_splits=cv, shuffle=False)
    mae_list = []
    for fold, (train_index, test_index) in enumerate(kf.split(range(len(RAG_Training)))):
     
     # Extract pore graphs and labels according to index
     RAG_training = [RAG_Training[i] for i in train_index]
     Labels_training = [Labels_Training_mof[i] for i in train_index]
     RAG_validation = [RAG_Training[i] for i in test_index]
     Labels_validation = [Labels_Training_mof[i] for i in test_index]
     
     Labels_training = np.array([float(x[0]) for x in Labels_training])
     Labels_validation = np.array([float(x[0]) for x in Labels_validation])
    
     # Get DGL graphs and Labels
     DGL_Graphs_training=Process_Graphs_Labels(RAG_training)
     DGL_Graphs_validation=Process_Graphs_Labels(RAG_validation)
     # Convert labels to tensor
     Labels_training=torch.tensor(Labels_training).view(-1,1)
     Labels_validation=torch.tensor(Labels_validation).view(-1,1)
     
     # Convert list of DGL graphs into a single batched graph
     Batched_Graph_training = dgl.batch(DGL_Graphs_training)
     Batched_Graph_validation=dgl.batch(DGL_Graphs_validation)
     # Extract node features for all graphs
     Features_training = Batched_Graph_training.ndata['feat'].float()
     Features_validation = Batched_Graph_validation.ndata['feat'].float()
        
     Pixel_Ratio_List_training=torch.tensor(Extract_Pixel_Ratio(RAG_training)).float().view(-1,1)
     Pixel_Ratio_List_validation=torch.tensor(Extract_Pixel_Ratio(RAG_validation)).float().view(-1,1)
        
     # Initialize the model and optimizer
     model = PoroNet(Features_training.size(1),hidden_sizes,hidden_activations,dropout)
     optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=initial_lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)
     scheduler = ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, mode='min', factor=factor, patience=int(0.9 * num_patience))
        
     # Initialize early stopping parameters
     best_val_loss = float('inf') 
     stop_patience = num_patience 
     counter = 0   
     early_stopped = False  
     best_epoch_loss = None     
     
     # Training loop
     for epoch in range(num_epoch):
         model.train()
         Embeddings_training_1 = model(Batched_Graph_training,Features_training)  # Forward propagation, get embeddings
         Embeddings_training_2 = Embeddings_training_1 * Pixel_Ratio_List_training  #Times the density of pores
         Batched_Graph_training.ndata['h'] = Embeddings_training_2  # Assign embeddings to 'h' field
         Logits_training = dgl.sum_nodes(Batched_Graph_training, 'h')  # Sum the embeddings across nodes
         Loss_training = F.l1_loss(Logits_training, Labels_training)  # Compute loss
         optimizer.zero_grad()
         Loss_training.backward()
         optimizer.step()
        
    
         model.eval()  # Set model to evaluation mode
         with torch.no_grad():
          Embeddings_validation_1 = model(Batched_Graph_validation,Features_validation) 
          Embeddings_validation_2 = Embeddings_validation_1 * Pixel_Ratio_List_validation  
          Batched_Graph_validation.ndata['h'] = Embeddings_validation_2  
          Logits_validation = dgl.sum_nodes(Batched_Graph_validation, 'h')  
          Loss_validation = F.l1_loss(Logits_validation, Labels_validation)  
          scheduler.step(Loss_validation)
         
             
         # Early stopping
         if Loss_validation < best_val_loss:
          best_val_loss = Loss_validation
          best_epoch_loss = Loss_validation.item()
          counter = 0
         else:
            counter += 1
            
         if counter >= stop_patience:
            print(f'Early stopping at epoch {epoch+1}')
            early_stopped = True
            mae_list.append(best_epoch_loss)
            break
        
     if not early_stopped:  # If not early stopped, record the loss of the last epoch
            mae_list.append(Loss_validation.item())

    mae_average = np.mean(mae_list) 
    
    if trial.should_prune():
     raise optuna.exceptions.TrialPruned()
    mae_average=np.mean(mae_list)
    trial.set_user_attr('mae_list', mae_list)

    return mae_average




Show code
sampler = optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=1)
study = optuna.create_study(sampler=sampler,direction='minimize', pruner=optuna.pruners.HyperbandPruner())
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=100)

print('Best trial:')
trial = study.best_trial
print('  Trial Number: ', trial.number)
print('  Value: ', trial.value)
print('  Params: ')
for key, value in trial.params.items():
    print('    {}: {}'.format(key, value)) 
print('  Fold MAEs: ', trial.user_attrs['mae_list'])

Train the model with early stopping on the validation loss and keep the best weights.

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.0019286667936327432, weight_decay=1.6685073137586203e-09)
scheduler = ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, mode='min', factor= 0.10056880106742247, patience=int(0.9 * num_patience))




Show code
# Initialize early stopping parameters
best_val_loss = float('inf') 
stop_patience =num_patience # Number of epochs to wait for improvement
counter = 0  # Counter for patience  
# Initialize the loss of training and validation set
Loss_Training_List=[]
Loss_Validation_List=[]

# Training loop
for epoch in range(num_epoch):
        model.train()
        Embeddings_Training_1 = model(Batched_Graph_Training,Features_Training) 
        Embeddings_Training_2 = Embeddings_Training_1 * Pixel_Ratio_List_Training  
        Batched_Graph_Training.ndata['h'] = Embeddings_Training_2  
        Logits_Training = dgl.sum_nodes(Batched_Graph_Training, 'h') 
        Loss_Training = F.l1_loss(Logits_Training, Labels_Training_mof) 
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        Loss_Training_List.append(Loss_Training.item())
        Loss_Training.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        
        # Set model to evaluation mode
        model.eval() 
        with torch.no_grad():
         Embeddings_Validation_1 = model(Batched_Graph_Validation,Features_Validation) 
         Embeddings_Validation_2 = Embeddings_Validation_1 * Pixel_Ratio_List_Validation 
         Batched_Graph_Validation.ndata['h'] = Embeddings_Validation_2  
         Logits_Validation = dgl.sum_nodes(Batched_Graph_Validation, 'h')  
         Loss_Validation = F.l1_loss(Logits_Validation, Labels_Validation_mof)  
         Loss_Validation_List.append(Loss_Validation.item())
         scheduler.step(Loss_Validation)
        # Early stopping
        if Loss_Validation < best_val_loss:
         best_val_loss = Loss_Validation
         counter = 0
        else:
         counter += 1
        if counter >= stop_patience:
            print(f'Early stopping at epoch {epoch+1}')
            break

title: Adding to the gallery
text: How to add a new interactive scene (or a new picture of an existing one) to the gallery. Commands run from the repository root with the mgr_env Python (/Users/arungopalan/miniforge3/envs/mgr_env/bin/python, called $PY below).

title: Adding to the gallery
text:
Where files live








What
Where
In the main git repo?




Interactive scenes (standalone HTML)
docs/interactive/
No, docs/interactive/*.html is git-ignored


Gallery pictures (PNG or WebP)
docs/tutorial_images/gallery/<material>_<variant>.png
Yes


Backup / source of truth for the HTML
private repo mofography/mofography-gallery-assets (one folder per material), which mirrors both of the above
Separate repo



So the HTML files travel through the assets repo: generate or export, copy into docs/interactive/ for the site build, and push the same files to the assets repo (see the checklist).

title: Adding to the gallery
text:
Size rules

Keep each HTML under about 15 MB (the current scenes are 1.5 to 8.5 MB). Hard limit 50 MB. GitHub rejects files over 100 MB.
Use a coarse distance-grid spacing: mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5).
Save with fig.to_html(path, pack_binary=True): arrays become base64 blobs, about 3 to 4 times smaller.
Turn per-vertex hover text off on surfaces: fig.plot_surface(..., hover_label="").
Raise step_size on surfaces (marching cubes stride, step_size=2 or 3) if a mesh is still too big. The generator exposes it as --step-size.
Use instanced atoms (plot_framework_instanced_3js) instead of per-atom meshes.
Check the result: ls -lh docs/interactive/*.html.

title: Adding to the gallery
section: Making a scene with the generator
text:
Making a scene with the generator
scripts/dev/gen_gallery_assets.py builds every curated scene. It writes to /tmp/mofography-gallery-assets/<material>/ by default (override with --out).
$PY scripts/dev/gen_gallery_assets.py --material cubtc            # one of cubtc nu1000 lta zif8 irmof1
$PY scripts/dev/gen_gallery_assets.py --material nu1000 --out /tmp/x --step-size 2
$PY scripts/dev/gen_gallery_assets.py --material --perc            # only the NU-1000 percolation-history scene
$PY scripts/dev/gen_gallery_assets.py --material --sa-vv           # only the Cu-BTC Plotly charts
To add a material:

Put the CIF in examples/TestCIFs/ and add "key": ("Display name", CIFS / "file.cif") to MATERIALS.
Add a background to BACKGROUNDS (see below).
build_simple(key, out) already builds pockets, windows, extra region colourings and the pore graph for any material, so --material key just works. Copy build_cubtc if you want a custom layer set.

Backgrounds: BACKGROUNDS[key] is passed to to_html(background=...): a hex string ("#ffffff"), ("linear", c1, c2) (left to right), or ("radial", centre, edge). The viewer’s Bg picker and gradient buttons still override it, and PNG export captures it.
Name the layers clearly: set name= on every trace, and use legend_label (see set_legend_label in the script) when the generic legend text would be misleading. For example the Cu-BTC blue translucent layer is a distance-grid isosurface, so it is labelled “Pore surface (distance grid, isovalue 1.0 A)”, not a segmentation; region-labelled surfaces are “Regions (no PBC)” and “Regions (PBC-merged)”.

title: Adding to the gallery
text:
Exporting from the web app
The Streamlit app in the mgr_cli_py repo (mgrcli interactive) can also produce a scene:

Run mgrcli interactive, load your CIF and run the analysis.
Set the visualisation backend to Three.js (the Plotly backend gives a different HTML without the gallery viewer).
Click Download interactive HTML.
Copy the file to docs/interactive/<material>_<what>_threejs.html and check its size against the rules above. Check the size: if the export is over about 15 MB, regenerate the scene with the generator instead.

title: Adding to the gallery
text:
Screenshots
scripts/dev/gallery_screenshot.py drives the scene through its own DOM (hides the sidebar, sets layers, framework style, Ortho, Exploded slider, view direction, background) and saves only the WebGL canvas, 1600 x 1000 by default. It needs Playwright with Chromium and internet (the HTML loads Three.js from a CDN).
export PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=$HOME/Library/Caches/ms-playwright

# 1. list the legend entries to use with --only / --on / --off
$PY scripts/dev/gallery_screenshot.py docs/interactive/nu1000_pockets_windows_threejs.html --list

# 2. take a picture
$PY scripts/dev/gallery_screenshot.py docs/interactive/nu1000_pockets_windows_threejs.html \
    docs/tutorial_images/gallery/nu1000_exploded_ortho.png \
    --ortho --explode 0.6 --only Framework "Pocket types" --view 0 0 1 --zoom 0.95
Options (all optional; legend names match as case-insensitive substrings):







Option
Meaning




--only A B
show only legend entries matching A, B, and hide the rest


--on A / --off A
additionally turn matching entries on / off


--repr
ball_and_stick, stick or space_filling (Representation dropdown)


--ortho
switch to orthographic projection


--explode 0.6
Exploded slider value


--view X Y Z
view direction (same as the view-dir boxes)


--zoom 1.2
camera distance multiplier; the default framing is cropped at 16:10, so use 1.1 to 1.4 to zoom out, below 1 to zoom in


--bg
"#ffffff", radial:#centre:#edge, linear:#c1:#c2, or transparent


--width/--height
window size, default 1600 x 1000


--jpeg Q
write a JPEG at quality Q (opaque backgrounds only)


--eval JS
extra JavaScript to run before the shot



Tips:

Keep each picture under about 700 KB. Raw PNGs of these scenes are 0.5 to 1.7 MB; convert large ones to WebP, which is 5 to 10 times smaller and keeps transparency: $PY -c "from PIL import Image; Image.open('a.png').save('a.webp', 'WEBP', quality=88, method=6)"
Look at every picture before keeping it: discard clipped, cluttered, tiny or dark-on-dark ones.
Clicking Ortho in the viewer switches the lighting and lightens the default background, so the orthographic captures of dark-background scenes look lighter than their perspective twins. (This is a viewer quirk: an explicit --bg did not change it either.)
Transparent images should still read on both the light and dark site themes.

title: Adding to the gallery
text:
Checklist

No private data in the scene (no unpublished structures or file paths in names or metadata).
HTML under about 15 MB and well under 50 MB. The page needs internet to load Three.js from the CDN; say so if you describe it.
Pictures look right on both the light and dark site themes (toggle the theme switch) and on a phone width.
Layer and legend names are accurate (see the naming note above).
Render the page from docs/: cd docs && quarto render gallery.qmd, then open _site/gallery.html. Render one page at a time.
Copy the HTML into your clone of the assets repo and push:

cd /tmp/mofography-gallery-assets      # or: git clone https://github.com/mofography/mofography-gallery-assets.git
git pull
cp /path/to/docs/interactive/<file>.html <material>/
cp /path/to/docs/tutorial_images/gallery/<material>_*.{png,webp} <material>/   # optional mirror of the pictures
git add <material>
git commit -m "Add <material> scene"
git push
Add a row for new files to MANIFEST.md in that repo (layers on by default, size, regenerate command).

title: Adding to the gallery
text:
What not to commit

Scratch or full-detail HTML over 50 MB, in either repo (GitHub rejects files over 100 MB, and they bloat history forever). If one slipped into a commit that has not been pushed, git reset --soft HEAD~1 and recommit without it.
Anything in examples/viz_outputs/ and other generated HTML in the main repo.

title: Guide to choosing functions
text:
Mofography exposes hundreds of functions, but only a subset is thoroughly tested and recommended for everyday use. This page is a quick-reference handbook: for each task it lists the functions to reach for, and which alternatives are legacy, deprecated, or experimental. Every function name links to its page in the API reference.
The Status column uses the same tags as the reference:
go-to the recommended default, used throughout the tutorials · alternate valid, but not the default choice · other helper or building block · experimental · legacy kept for comparison or old results · deprecated avoid in new code.

title: Guide to choosing functions
text:
Notes on function stability

go-to functions are the recommended defaults and are the ones the tutorials use. They are validated against Zeo++ and PoreBlazer on CoRE MOFs (see the paper).
alternate and other functions are stable but have narrower use cases.
Functions that appear only in the API reference and not on this page should be treated as experimental: they may have incomplete documentation, untested edge cases, or performance limits.
legacy and deprecated functions stay for backward compatibility with existing scripts and saved results dictionaries. New analyses should use the go-to alternatives.
For when to prefer winding over lattice accessibility, see Accessibility methods and Face merging vs winding.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text: Window detection algorithm: the window is the voxel with the largest non-overlapping sphere in the shared boundary of two adjacent regions; works for on-axis and off-axis windows and handles non-convex cavities (paper Figure 6)

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Overview
Pore windows (also called connections or neck regions) are the narrow passages that connect neighboring pores in a crystalline material. In mofography, every connection in the segmentation result is a 5-tuple describing two touching regions, the type of contact, the window centroid, and the window radius.
In this tutorial we will:

Run a single-call periodic segmentation with compute_connections=True so that windows are detected automatically.
Inspect seg['connections'] — the list of 5-tuples describing every window.
Trim to unit-cell connections and split them into internal vs periodic.
Compute window-size statistics, including the Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD).
Visualize everything interactively with show_mof_plotly(seg, atoms, ...), which already includes window markers.

If you have not done so, please complete the Quick Start: Full MOF Pore Analysis tutorial first — the rest of the page assumes you have run a segmentation and have a seg dict in hand.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Why windows matter

Transport control — windows gate molecular diffusion through the material. Their size distribution dictates selectivity in gas-separation MOFs.
Pore Limiting Diameter (PLD) — the smallest window in a continuous path determines which molecules can pass.
Energy barriers — narrow windows create higher diffusion barriers and influence kinetic selectivity.
Connectivity of the pore graph — each window is an edge in the region-adjacency graph (RAG).


How windows are defined
A window is the centroid of points in the shared boundary of two adjacent pore regions. The detection algorithm distinguishes two contact types:








Type
Description
In pore graph




Internal
Both regions lie fully inside the unit cell
Edge between nodes


Periodic
One region sits across a unit-cell boundary
Edge with an offset



When two regions touch at multiple distinct points, mofography reports each window separately. The minimum spatial gap between two distinct windows is controlled by the minimum_window_separation parameter (Å). Internally this is an agglomerative-clustering distance threshold on the boundary points.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Imports and structure


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 1: Compute the distance grid
dgrid_from_atoms_rust is the thread-parallel Rust backend — the correct choice for every cell type.


Show code
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
spacing = 0.5  # Å — see Quick Start for trade-offs
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
print(f"Grid shape: {dgrid.shape} ({dgrid.size:,} voxels)")
print(f"Void max:   {dgrid.max():.1f} Å")


Grid shape: (52, 52, 52) (140,608 voxels)
Void max:   7.5 Å

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 2: Periodic segmentation with windows
Set compute_connections=True (default) so that the same call returns both the segmentation grid and the window list. The relevant tuning knobs for window detection are:

minimum_window_separation (Å) — distance threshold that splits boundary points into distinct windows. Default is None, which the function resolves internally; pass an explicit value to control window multiplicity.
wall_thickness — near-boundary band, as a fraction of the longest perpendicular cell length (not Å), used to filter maxima.
extra_padding (Å) — extra padding around the unit cell so that periodic windows are not clipped.



Show code
dgrid_f32 = dgrid.astype(np.float32)

seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid_f32, atoms,
    spacing=spacing,
    mask_thickness=0.05,        # void-space threshold (Å)
    h=0.2,                      # H-maxima persistence
    min_distance=1.5,           # min separation between distinct maxima (Å)
    threshold_abs=1.5,          # absolute threshold for maxima (Å)
    minimum_window_separation=1.5,  # Å — see "Tuning" section below
    wall_thickness=0.05,        # Å
    extra_padding=5,            # Å — PBC padding for window detection
    compute_connections=True,   # detect windows + build pore graph
    watershed_backend="rust_det",
    disable_tqdm=True,
)

print(f"Pockets (PBC-grouped): {len(seg['maxima_pbc'])}")
print(f"Unique regions:        {len(seg['unique_regions'])}")
print(f"Window connections:    {len(seg['connections'])}")


Pockets (PBC-grouped): 8
Unique regions:        27
Window connections:    300

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 3: Inspect seg['connections']
The connections entry is a list of numpy arrays, one per window. Each array has five elements:







Index
Meaning




c[0]
Two region labels that the window connects


c[1]
Confirmation flag (currently always True for a detected window)


c[2]
'internal' or 'periodic'


c[3]
Window centroid coordinates (shape (1, 3))


c[4]
Window radius in Å (shape (1,))





Show code
connections = seg["connections"]
c = connections[0]
print("Type:    ", type(c).__name__)
print("Length:  ", len(c))
print("c[0] regions:", c[0])
print("c[1] flag:   ", c[1])
print("c[2] type:   ", c[2])
print("c[3] centre: ", c[3])
print("c[4] radius: ", c[4], "Å  →  diameter =", float(c[4][0]) * 2, "Å")


Type:     ndarray
Length:   5
c[0] regions: [49 83]
c[1] flag:    True
c[2] type:    periodic
c[3] centre:  [[ 33.53192308 -12.916       38.748     ]]
c[4] radius:  [3.67783356] Å  →  diameter = 7.3556671142578125 Å

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 4: Trim to unit-cell connections
do_periodic_segmentation_rust reports every window it finds in the padded analysis domain, including windows between regions that only exist in the padding. To get a single, non-over-counted set of connections inside the unit cell, keep the windows that touch at least one region in unique_regions.


Show code
unique_regions = seg["unique_regions"]
connections_trimmed = np.array([
    c for c in connections
    if np.any(np.isin(c[0], unique_regions))
])
print(f"All detected windows:  {len(connections)}")
print(f"Unit-cell windows:     {len(connections_trimmed)}")


All detected windows:  300
Unit-cell windows:     108

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 5: Internal vs periodic windows


Show code
internal = [c for c in connections_trimmed if c[2] == "internal"]
periodic = [c for c in connections_trimmed if c[2] == "periodic"]
print(f"Internal:  {len(internal)}")
print(f"Periodic:  {len(periodic)}")

# Window positions and radii
all_radii    = np.array([float(c[4][0]) for c in connections_trimmed])
all_centres  = np.array([c[3].flatten()  for c in connections_trimmed])
all_diameters = 2.0 * all_radii


Internal:  54
Periodic:  54

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 6: Window-size statistics


Show code
print("=" * 50)
print("WINDOW SIZE STATISTICS")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Total windows:        {len(all_diameters)}")
print(f"Pore Limiting Diam.:  {all_diameters.min():.3f} Å")
print(f"Largest diameter:     {all_diameters.max():.3f} Å")
print(f"Mean diameter:        {all_diameters.mean():.3f} Å")
print(f"Median diameter:      {np.median(all_diameters):.3f} Å")
print("=" * 50)


==================================================
WINDOW SIZE STATISTICS
==================================================
Total windows:        108
Pore Limiting Diam.:  7.356 Å
Largest diameter:     7.914 Å
Mean diameter:        7.632 Å
Median diameter:      7.420 Å
==================================================


The PLD (min diameter) is the smallest window in the unit cell — it is a hard upper bound on the diameter of a sphere that can diffuse through a single repeating cell of this MOF.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 7: Visualize windows with show_mof_plotly
show_mof_plotly consumes the full seg dict, so window markers come along for the ride. There is no need to call plot_connections_as_it_is separately — pass stylize=True for a clean dark theme and fig.show() to render the interactive Plotly figure inline.


Show code
fig = mgr.show_mof_plotly(
    seg, atoms,
    framework_atoms=atoms,
    stylize=True,
)
fig.update_layout(title=dict(text="IRMOF-1: Pore Windows", x=0.5))
fig.write_image("tutorial_images/connections_and_windows_windows.png", width=1100, height=800)  # static preview for the docs


No node props provided, using default set: [position, scaled_position, element and atomic_number]
No edge properties provided. Use the default set: [bond_order, bond_type]
[TIMING batched_mesh_for_atoms] 472 atoms, 1024 bonds | spheres: 0.00s, cylinders: 0.00s, concat: 0.00s | total faces: 212480


No node props provided, using default set: [position, scaled_position, element and atomic_number]
No edge properties provided. Use the default set: [bond_order, bond_type]





IRMOF-1 pore windows








NoteInteractive version





fig = mgr.show_mof_plotly(seg, atoms, framework_atoms=atoms, stylize=True)
fig.show()   # rotate, zoom, hover over windows



Open the interactive version
You should see:

coloured surfaces for the pore regions,
spheres at pore centres (maxima),
markers at the windows between regions, and
a translucent framework mesh.

Because the figure is a Plotly Figure (in the interactive version), you can rotate, zoom, and hover over each window to read its region labels, contact type, and diameter directly from the metadata baked into the trace.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Step 8: Histogram of window diameters
A quick sanity check on the size distribution:


Show code
fig3 = px.histogram(
    x=all_diameters,
    nbins=25,
    labels={"x": "Window diameter (Å)"},
    title="IRMOF-1: Distribution of window diameters",
    color_discrete_sequence=["steelblue"],
)
fig3.add_vline(
    x=all_diameters.min(),
    line_dash="dash",
    line_color="red",
    annotation_text=f"PLD = {all_diameters.min():.2f} Å",
)
fig3.update_layout(showlegend=False)
fig3.show()


                            
                                            


For IRMOF-1 you should see a narrow, roughly symmetric peak centred near the mean diameter, with the red dashed line marking the PLD at the left tail.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Tuning minimum_window_separation
This parameter is the distance threshold that the internal agglomerative clustering uses to split boundary points into distinct windows. Concretely:

Larger value → boundary points further apart than minimum_window_separation Å are not merged → fewer, more distinct windows per region-pair.
Smaller value → closer points are allowed to cluster together → fewer windows per region-pair, but each centroid is more stable.
Set to None (default) → the function chooses a sensible internal default. Set it explicitly whenever you have a domain-specific expectation (e.g. you know two apertures must be resolved).

If the windows appear in the wrong positions, or two clearly distinct windows are being merged into one, start by adjusting minimum_window_separation before re-tuning h or threshold_abs.

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Troubleshooting








Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




No connections found
compute_connections=False, or segmentation produced a single region
Re-run with compute_connections=True; relax h / threshold_abs


Windows appear in the wrong positions
Boundary points being merged across distinct apertures
Lower minimum_window_separation


Too few windows overall
Over-aggressive merging
Raise minimum_window_separation and/or relax h


Periodic windows clipped
Padding too small
Increase extra_padding


Window radii are noisy
Boundary points straddling multiple regions
Lower wall_thickness and rerun

title: Connections and Pore Windows
text:
Where to go next

Quick Start: Full MOF Pore Analysis — the canonical 3-function workflow this tutorial builds on.
Pore Graph (RAG) — once you have windows, you can build the Region Adjacency Graph.
Pockets detection — classify each pore as a cage, channel, or dead-end pocket.


Advanced window analysis
These notes document experimental refinements on top of the basic connections list:

Window fingerprinting — direction-invariant element-weighted fingerprints of the framework shell around each window. Used for accessible surface-area and void-volume curation, the Mechanism A / Mechanism B PLD distinction, optional DFSD signals, and prototype window-type detection.

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
The distance grid is a 3D array where each voxel stores the signed distance from that point to the nearest framework-atom surface (atom center minus van der Waals radius). Positive values = void space; negative values = inside framework atoms. It is the sole input to do_periodic_segmentation_rust and all downstream pore analysis.



Every downstream step (maxima detection, watershed segmentation, pore graph, PSD, PLD, surface area) starts from the distance grid
Grid resolution (spacing) is the single most impactful parameter: halving spacing → 8× more voxels
The correctness of your distance grid determines the correctness of everything else

❌ Broken on skewed cells




Quick Recommendation

Default choice → dgrid_from_atoms_rust(spacing=0.5) — thread-parallel Rust, correct MIC on all cell types
Memory constrained → dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10) — R-tree based, uses less RAM
Very large systems (>5000 atoms, coarse acceptable) → dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(spacing=1.0, coarse_factor=2) — trilinear interpolation from coarse grid



⚠️ Deprecated / Broken Methods
dgrid_from_atoms_gpu and dgrid_from_atoms_cpu_no_aabb are broken on non-orthogonal (skewed) cells. They use per-axis NINT (nearest-integer) for minimum-image convention, which is incorrect on skewed cells — common in MOFs with non-cubic unit cells. The project CHANGELOG documents this as “Bug B” and recommends delegating to dgrid_from_atoms_rust. Do not use these functions. The Rust backend uses the same correct MIC path for all cell types.

text:
Setup


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np

# Load a MOF structure
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")  # or any CIF/PDB file

text:
Understanding Grid Spacing
The spacing parameter (Å) controls resolution. It is the single most impactful choice:



Spacing
Voxels (IRMOF-1, ~26Å cell)
Memory
Use Case




0.5 Å
~52³ = 140K
~1 MB
Default — good balance


0.25 Å
~104³ = 1.1M
~9 MB
Fine detail, small windows


0.2 Å
~130³ = 2.2M
~18 MB
High precision needed


0.1 Å
~260³ = 17.6M
~140 MB
Research only





Show code
# Compute with default spacing
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5)

print(f"Grid shape: {dgrid.shape}")
print(f"Void max: {dgrid.max():.1f} Å (largest included sphere radius)")
print(f"Framework min: {dgrid.min():.1f} Å")


Grid shape: (52, 52, 52)
Void max: 7.5 Å (largest included sphere radius)
Framework min: -1.7 Å

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
Method 1: Rust Backend (Recommended)


Show code
# Thread-parallel brute-force distance computation
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5)

# With explicit VDW radii (optional — defaults to Bondi/CRC radii with Mendeleev fill)
from mofography.vdw_radii import default_vdw_radii_angstrom
radii = default_vdw_radii_angstrom(atoms)
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, radii=radii)


Pros: Exact MIC for all cell types, thread-parallel (Rayon), no accuracy trade-offs. Cons: O(N_atoms × N_grid) — memory scales with grid size.

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
Method 2: Rust AABB (Memory-Efficient)


Show code
# R-tree based — only computes distances for atoms near each grid point
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5, n_neighbors=10)


Uses an AABB (axis-aligned bounding box) cell list via freud to find nearby atoms for each grid point. n_neighbors controls the neighbor search radius — higher = more accurate but slower.
When to use: Large unit cells (>50 Å) or many atoms (>1000) where brute-force Rust would use too much RAM.


Show code
# For very large systems: coarse grid + trilinear interpolation
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_aabb_interp_rust(
    atoms, spacing=1.0, coarse_factor=2, n_neighbors=10
)
# Equivalent to computing at spacing=1.0 then interpolating to 0.5

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
Method 3: CPU/Dask (Legacy)


Show code
# freud AABB celllist in Python, parallelized with Dask
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(atoms, spacing=0.5, block_size=50000)


Uses freud’s AABBQuery for neighbor searches and Dask for parallelism. Correct MIC (uses complete_cell().T) unlike the deprecated _no_aabb variant.
When to use: When you need Python-level control over the computation, or for systems where the Rust backend is unavailable.

trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(

    isovalue=1.0,        # Show surface at 1.0 Å from framework
    ase_atoms=atoms,

    specs=[[{"type": "scene"}, {"type": "scene"}]],

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
Next Steps: Segmentation
Once you have a distance grid, run do_periodic_segmentation_rust to detect pore regions, compute connections, and build the pore graph:


Show code
import numpy as np
# Cast to float32 (required by Rust backend)
dgrid_f32 = dgrid.astype(np.float32)

# Single call replaces 5-7 old manual steps
seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid_f32, atoms,
    mask_thickness=0.05,     # void-space threshold
    h=0.2,                   # H-maxima persistence
    min_distance=1.5,        # min separation between maxima
    threshold_abs=1.5,       # absolute threshold for maxima
    spacing=0.5,
    compute_connections=True,
    watershed_backend="rust_det",
    disable_tqdm=True,
)

print(f"Found {len(seg['maxima_pbc'])} pore pockets (PBC-grouped)")
print(f"Found {len(seg['connections'])} window connections")
print(f"Regions array shape: {seg['regions_pbc'].shape}")


Found 8 pore pockets (PBC-grouped)
Found 300 window connections
Regions array shape: (52, 52, 52)



See Region Segmentation for the segmentation parameters and output keys, and Tuning and safe ranges for how to adjust them.

title: Computing the Distance Grid
text:
Performance Notes

IRMOF-1 (424 atoms, 26 Å cubic cell, 0.5 Å spacing): ~52³ grid, ~1 second on M4 Pro
NU-1000 (558 atoms, 40 Å hexagonal cell, 0.5 Å spacing): ~80×81×34 grid, ~2 seconds
Scaling: O(N_atoms × N_grid) for brute-force; ~O(N_atoms × log N_atoms × N_grid) for AABB
Memory: ~4 bytes per voxel (float32); a 200³ grid ≈ 32 MB

title: Fast Rust CIF reader
text:
mofography ships a Rust CIF parser (mgr_rust.read_cif) with a thin Python wrapper, read_cif_to_ase. It returns a normal ase.Atoms, so everything else in mofography (dgrid_from_atoms_rust, do_periodic_segmentation_rust, …) works unchanged. It is the reader behind the mofography web app.
You do not have to use it. ase.io.read works everywhere in mofography and stays the reference reader. The Rust reader is an option that is in many ways better:
For typical single MOFs (a few hundred atoms) on a laptop, both readers take a fraction of a second, so the choice makes little practical difference. It is not yet the default in the library functions because it has been tested less than ASE on unusual CIFs. If it fails on a file, read_cif_to_ase logs a warning and falls back to ase.io.read.

title: Fast Rust CIF reader
text:
Usage


Show code
import time
from ase.io import read
from mofography.cif_io import read_cif_to_ase

path = "P1-Cu-BTC.cif"   # or examples/TestCIFs/P1-Cu-BTC.cif from the repo root

t = time.perf_counter(); atoms = read_cif_to_ase(path); t_rust = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); ref = read(path);              t_ase = time.perf_counter() - t

print(f"{atoms.get_chemical_formula()}: {len(atoms)} atoms")
print(f"Rust {t_rust*1e3:.1f} ms | ASE {t_ase*1e3:.1f} ms")


C288H96Cu48O192: 624 atoms
Rust 63.7 ms | ASE 1002.5 ms
