High-throughput use
Use it whenever you read many CIFs in a loop, for example before do_periodic_segmentation_rust over a database:
from pathlib import Path
from mofography.cif_io import read_cif_to_ase

all_atoms = {p.stem: read_cif_to_ase(p) for p in Path("cifs").glob("*.cif")}
The high-throughput tutorial reads its structures this way.

title: Fast Rust CIF reader
text:
Options and caveats

Set the environment variable MGR_FAST_CIF=0 to make read_cif_to_ase use ase.io.read only.
A few unusual CIFs (for example disordered sites or odd numeric formats) can parse differently or fail in the Rust reader. Check len(atoms) against a one-off ASE read when you start working with a new source of structures. For example, in COD_2100028.cif the two readers return different atom counts (49 vs 98).
For CIFs in P1 symmetry (as most computation-ready MOF databases provide) the two readers should agree.

title: mofography
text:
Mofography segments the void space of periodic nanoporous materials (any structure with a valid unit cell, periodic in all three directions) into pockets and builds pore graphs from them. One segmentation gives you global and pocket-level textural properties, pore types, windows, and percolation, plus interactive 3D views and graph descriptors for screening and machine learning (see Features).
Core numerics run in a Rust backend (mgr_rust) behind a Python API.
The path from a CIF file to that graph is the Quick start. To install, see the install page; all tutorials are in Learn and every function is in Functions.

title: mofography
text:
Features
Everything below is available from the Python module. Global properties and pocket-level properties come from the same segmentation, so you can go from a material-level number down to the individual pore that produced it.



Capability
What you get
Learn more




Pore diameters
Largest cavity diameter (LCD), pore limiting diameter (PLD), and largest included sphere (LIS) along percolating pathways
Compute pore diameters, PLD and percolation


Surface area and void volume
Total (probe-center occupiable) and accessible (probe-center accessible) values, globally and per pocket
Surface area, Property calculation


Pore size distributions
Global distributions, and pocket-wise distributions that do not undersample small pockets
Pore size distributions


Pocket segmentation
The void space split into convex pockets with periodic boundary conditions handled
Region segmentation, PBC considerations


Pocket types
Fingerprinting of pockets by their local environment, to group chemically and geometrically similar pores
Pocket type detection


Pore windows
Detection of the windows that connect pockets, including across periodic boundaries
Connections and windows, Window fingerprinting


Pore graphs
Pockets as nodes and windows as edges, annotated with local properties, as input for analysis and graph learning
Region adjacency graph, PoroNet


Percolation
Percolation thresholds for a given probe, and 3D plots of the accessible, percolating clusters of pockets
PLD and percolation


Visualization
Interactive 3D views of the framework, pore surfaces, pockets, and pore graphs
Visualization


High throughput
Parallel characterization of whole databases with a Rust core
High-throughput characterization



Not a Python user? The same core is available as a CLI (mgr_cli_py) for terminal users and AI agents, and as a web app for anyone who prefers a GUI and does not code or use a terminal. Both expose a subset of the features above; see Who should use what.
Using an AI coding agent? Copy skills/mofography/SKILL.md into your agent’s skills folder (for Claude Code, .claude/skills/mofography/) so it knows the Python API, the textural-property and percolation functions, and common pitfalls.

title: PBC considerations
text:
Periodic boundary conditions (PBC) are what turn a one-unit-cell snapshot of a MOF into a truly infinite material. mofography’s job is to recognize that several distinct maxima/regions you see inside the unit cell are in fact one cavity wrapping through the periodic boundary.
do_periodic_segmentation_rust() handles periodicity as part of the core workflow: there is nothing to apply afterwards (the old legacy workflow did this as a separate post-processing step, now apply_pbc). The PBC information is exposed through these output keys:







Key
What it is




seg['pbc_groups']
list of sets — pbc_groups[i] is the set of region labels wrapped into cavity i


seg['maxima_pbc']
\((N, 3)\) array of merged maxima (one per group, not per fragment)


seg['regions_pbc']
3D label array of the central cell — regions already merged through PBC


seg['close_or_inside_maxima']
\((N, 3)\) array — voxel coords of boundary maxima in the padded grid


seg['close_or_inside_regions']
1-based region labels of boundary-touching regions



This tutorial is the PBC deep dive. For the canonical 3-call workflow, see the Quick Start tutorial.

Imports


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np

title: PBC considerations
text:
Step 1: Load a MOF
IRMOF-1 is the canonical PBC teaching example: the central pore sits at the cell center, and identical fragments appear at every face, edge, and corner — 8 fragments per cavity in total, by Euler’s formula for a cube.


Show code
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")

print(f"Atoms:        {len(atoms)}")
print(f"Cell (Å):     {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)}")
print(f"Formula:      {atoms.get_chemical_formula()}")


Atoms:        424
Cell (Å):     [25.83 25.83 25.83]
Formula:      C192H96O104Zn32

title: PBC considerations
text:
Step 2: Compute the Distance Grid
We use the thread-parallel Rust backend. spacing=0.5 Å is the sweet spot for most MOFs — fast and accurate enough for PBC detection.


Show code
spacing = 0.5  # Å
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
print(f"Grid shape: {dgrid.shape} ({dgrid.size:,} voxels)")
print(f"Void max:   {dgrid.max():.1f} Å")


Grid shape: (52, 52, 52) (140,608 voxels)
Void max:   7.5 Å

title: PBC considerations
section: Step 3: One Call, Full PBC-Aware Segmentation
text:
Step 3: One Call, Full PBC-Aware Segmentation
do_periodic_segmentation_rust does maxima detection, watershed, PBC merging, and (optionally) window detection — all in one go. The merged maxima/regions are returned in the same dict.


Show code
dgrid_f32 = dgrid.astype(np.float32)

seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid_f32, atoms,
    mask_thickness=0.05,
    h=0.2,
    min_distance=1.5,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    spacing=spacing,
    compute_connections=True,    # also build the pore graph
    extra_padding=5.0,           # default — extra PBC halo (Å)
    watershed_backend="rust_det",
    disable_tqdm=True,
)




Show code
print("=== All output keys ===")
for k in seg:
    v = seg[k]
    if hasattr(v, "shape"):
        print(f"  {k:35s} ndarray  shape={v.shape}  dtype={v.dtype}")
    elif isinstance(v, dict):
        print(f"  {k:35s} dict    ({len(v)} entries)")
    elif isinstance(v, (list, tuple, set)):
        print(f"  {k:35s} {type(v).__name__:6s}  ({len(v)} items)")
    else:
        print(f"  {k:35s} {type(v).__name__}")


=== All output keys ===
  dgrid                               ndarray  shape=(52, 52, 52)  dtype=float32
  mat_atoms                           Atoms

title: PBC considerations
section: Step 4: The Three PBC Output Keys
text:
Step 4: The Three PBC Output Keys

4a. pbc_groups — the equivalence map
pbc_groups is a list whose i-th entry is the set of region labels in the central cell that have been merged into a single cavity. Index i corresponds to row i of maxima_pbc — the two are aligned by position.


Show code
print(f"Number of PBC groups: {len(seg['pbc_groups'])}")
print()
for grp_idx, region_set in enumerate(seg['pbc_groups']):
    print(f"  group {grp_idx:>2}  →  {len(region_set)} region(s):  {sorted(region_set)}")


Number of PBC groups: 8

  group  0  →  4 region(s):  [1, 9, 10, 11]
  group  1  →  2 region(s):  [2, 12]
  group  2  →  4 region(s):  [3, 13, 14, 15]
  group  3  →  1 region(s):  [4]
  group  4  →  4 region(s):  [5, 16, 17, 18]
  group  5  →  2 region(s):  [6, 19]
  group  6  →  2 region(s):  [7, 20]
  group  7  →  8 region(s):  [8, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27]


For IRMOF-1 there are 8 groups — one central cavity, plus identical fragments at every face (×6), edge (×12), and corner (×8). The group sizes follow Euler’s cube formula:
\[
\text{fragments per cavity} = 1 + 6\cdot\tfrac{1}{2} + 12\cdot\tfrac{1}{4} + 8\cdot\tfrac{1}{8} = 8
\]


4b. maxima_pbc — group representatives
maxima_pbc is an \((N_\text{groups}, 3)\) array of one representative maximum per group — usually the highest-valued maximum within that group (use all_maxima for the full set of unmerged fragments). Row i of maxima_pbc corresponds to pbc_groups[i].


Show code
maxima_pbc = seg['maxima_pbc']
print(f"Shape: {maxima_pbc.shape}")
print(f"\nGroup sizes (from pbc_groups):")
for grp_idx, region_set in enumerate(seg['pbc_groups']):
    n_frag = len(region_set)
    px, py, pz = maxima_pbc[grp_idx]
    print(f"  group {grp_idx:>2}: {n_frag} fragment(s)  representative at "
          f"({px:5.1f}, {py:5.1f}, {pz:5.1f})")


Shape: (8, 3)

Group sizes (from pbc_groups):
  group  0: 4 fragment(s)  representative at (  0.0,  25.0,  50.0)
  group  1: 2 fragment(s)  representative at (  0.0,  26.0,  25.0)
  group  2: 4 fragment(s)  representative at (  0.0,  50.0,  26.0)
  group  3: 1 fragment(s)  representative at ( 24.0,  26.0,  25.0)
  group  4: 4 fragment(s)  representative at ( 25.0,   0.0,   1.0)
  group  5: 2 fragment(s)  representative at ( 26.0,  26.0,   0.0)
  group  6: 2 fragment(s)  representative at ( 26.0,  51.0,  25.0)
  group  7: 8 fragment(s)  representative at ( 51.0,  51.0,   0.0)




4c. regions_pbc — central cell with PBC-merged labels
regions_pbc is a 3D label array the same shape as dgrid, but with labels renumbered so that fragments on opposite walls of the same cavity share a single label.


Show code
print(f"regions_pbc shape:  {seg['regions_pbc'].shape}")
print(f"unique labels (excl. 0 background): "
      f"{int(seg['regions_pbc'].max())}")

# Each label corresponds to one row in maxima_pbc
import collections
counts = collections.Counter(seg['regions_pbc'].ravel())
counts.pop(0, None)
print(f"voxel count per PBC label:")
for lbl, n in sorted(counts.items()):
    print(f"  label {lbl:>2}:  {n:>6,} voxels  "
          f"({100*n/seg['regions_pbc'].size:.2f}%)")

This is the array you want to use for pore-size-distribution calculations: one label = one physical cavity.

title: PBC considerations
text:
Step 5: Visualize PBC Groups
Each PBC group should appear in the same color in the isosurface plot.


Show code
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
import mofography as mgr

# Map region label → group id (so all members of a group share a color)
label_to_group = {}
for grp_idx, region_set in enumerate(seg['pbc_groups']):
    for lbl in region_set:
        label_to_group[int(lbl)] = int(grp_idx)

# Re-color regions_pbc by PBC group for visualization
regions_pbc_colored = np.zeros_like(seg['regions_pbc'])
for lbl, grp in label_to_group.items():
    regions_pbc_colored[seg['regions_pbc'] == lbl] = grp + 1

cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel
iso = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
    dgrid, ase_atoms=atoms,
    isovalue=1.75, cscale=cscale, opacity=1,
    stylize=True, region_labels=regions_pbc_colored,
)
cell = mgr.plot_cell(atoms)
fig = go.Figure(data=[iso, cell])
fig.update_layout(mgr.dark_layout, title="IRMOF-1: each color = one PBC group")
fig.show()


                            
                                            


You should see 8 distinct colors, each appearing in 1 (center), 6 (face), 12 (edge), or 8 (corner) places — exactly the topology of a single cavity wrapped through the unit cell.

title: PBC considerations
text:
Step 6: The extra_padding Parameter
PBC merging works by padding the grid with ghost copies of the void, then asking the watershed to flood across the wall. If the padding is too thin, the flood misses the back-side maxima entirely and no group is formed.
The total padding thickness is: \[
\text{padding} = \underbrace{\text{ceil}\!\left(\frac{\text{extra\_padding}}{\text{spacing}}\right)}_{\text{extra halo}} + \underbrace{\text{standard padding from pore radius}}_{\text{baseline}}
\]
extra_padding is the user-tunable knob on top of the standard +5 Å cushion. Default is 5 Å — sufficient for most MOFs.

Effect of increasing extra_padding


Show code
def n_groups(seg_dict):
    return len(seg_dict['pbc_groups'])

results = {}
for pad in (0.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0):
    s = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
        dgrid_f32, atoms,
        mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5,
        threshold_abs=1.5, spacing=spacing,
        compute_connections=False,
        extra_padding=pad,
        disable_tqdm=True,
    )
    results[pad] = n_groups(s)
    print(f"  extra_padding={pad:5.1f} Å  →  {results[pad]} PBC group(s)")


  extra_padding=  0.0 Å  →  8 PBC group(s)


  extra_padding=  2.0 Å  →  8 PBC group(s)


  extra_padding=  5.0 Å  →  8 PBC group(s)


  extra_padding= 10.0 Å  →  8 PBC group(s)








Tip



How to spot a too-small extra_padding. If you find more PBC groups than you expect (e.g. IRMOF-1 returning > 8), the PBC flood is not reaching across the wall. Increase in 1–2 Å steps. The cost is mostly memory — runtime grows with the padded grid volume. Note: IRMOF-1 returns 8 groups even at extra_padding=0 because the standard halo (computed from dgrid.max() + a +5 Å cushion) is already generous — this rule applies to materials with large mesopores that exceed the standard halo.




Trade-off
The standard PBC halo is already computed from dgrid.max() and a +5 Å cushion, so the baseline padding is generous for most MOFs. extra_padding is the user-tunable knob on top of that.

title: PBC considerations
text:
Step 7: Boundary Maxima — close_or_inside_maxima
Some maxima sit on the cell wall (e.g. the centers of the face-fragments in IRMOF-1). These are the maxima most likely to need PBC merging. close_or_inside_maxima returns their 3D voxel coordinates in the padded grid (i.e. coordinates that extend past the unit cell — entries can be negative or larger than the grid shape when the maximum is in a ghost copy).


Show code
pad = seg['input_params']['padding_thickness']
boundary_coords = seg['close_or_inside_maxima']   # (N, 3) padded-grid coords
print(f"Boundary maxima count: {len(boundary_coords)}")
print(f"Boundary maxima (padded-grid coords, first 5 rows):")
print(boundary_coords[:5])
print()
print("Their (x, y, z) positions in the unit cell (Å):")
for ix, iy, iz in boundary_coords[:8]:
    # padded coords → central-cell coords → Å
    x = (ix - pad) * spacing
    y = (iy - pad) * spacing
    z = (iz - pad) * spacing
    on_wall = sum(coord < 0.5 or coord > atoms.cell.cellpar()[ax] - 0.5
                  for ax, coord in enumerate((x, y, z)))
    print(f"  ({ix:>3},{iy:>3},{iz:>3})  →  ({x:5.1f}, {y:5.1f}, {z:5.1f}) Å  on {on_wall} wall(s)")
print(f"  ... ({len(boundary_coords) - 8} more)")

Boundary maxima (padded-grid coords, first 5 rows):
[[ 0 25 -2]

close_or_inside_regions
A list of unmerged region labels — i.e. labels in seg['regions'] (the 3D grid before PBC merging), not in regions_pbc. These are the regions that sit near a unit-cell wall and might be PBC-mirrors of something on the other side — useful when validating your own segmentation outside the merged pipeline.

title: Pore size distributions
text:
Global textural properties such as largest cavity diameter, pore limiting diameter, and pore size distributions (PSDs) are easy to compute but can hide distinct pockets and network topology behind one curve. Mofography segments void space into pockets and can report the same Gelb–Gubbins histogram per pocket, so local cage sizes are visible instead of being washed out by volume-weighted sampling.
A PSD starts from largest-including-sphere diameters (Gelb & Gubbins): at each sample site in the void, mofography finds the largest sphere that contains the site without overlapping framework atoms. The sphere radius at the center equals the distance-grid value there; the reported size is the diameter (2× radius).
Two sampling strategies matter:

Global (uniform) PSD — compute_psd_uniform_rust draws a fixed total number of points uniformly in the unit cell. Large cages dominate by volume, so small pocket families are undersampled and may not appear as peaks.
Pocket-wise PSD — compute_psds_pocketwise_rust draws a fixed number of samples per segmented pocket (regions_pbc). Each pocket gets equal statistical weight. This is the PSD that feeds pocket typing via enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds (see Pocket detection).

Accessibility at a probe radius uses the same winding percolation as accessible surface area: only void that percolates through the pore network at that probe size counts as accessible. Total PSDs use all void; accessible PSDs drop pockets (or void fragments) that do not percolate.
This page uses Cu-BTC (P1-Cu-BTC.cif), which has three cage families (~5.6, ~11, and ~12.6 Å peaks in the paper). IRMOF-1 is a poor teaching example here: its two cage peaks are close in size and global vs accessible curves barely differ at helium probe size.
You need a seg dict from do_periodic_segmentation_rust with return_dgrid=True. See Quick start first.



num_samples_total (global) and num_samples_per_region (pocket-wise) control Monte Carlo noise, not physics. More samples → smoother curves; 800–8000 is usually enough for tutorials.
max_diameter should exceed the largest void radius in the structure (check dgrid.max() × 2). Cu-BTC cages stay below ~15 Å; we use 20 Å (PoreBlazer’s default).
binsize sets the PSD resolution. We use 0.25 Å, PoreBlazer’s default, so curves compare directly with PoreBlazer; finer bins sharpen peaks but make the (-V/D) derivative noisier and need more samples.

title: Pore size distributions
text:
How the curve is calculated
The sampling gives a list of pore diameters (D_s) (one per sample point). The plotted curve is the Gelb–Gubbins PSD, computed exactly like PoreBlazer so results compare one-to-one:

Cumulative pore volume. With bins of width () (0.25 Å), the fraction of the void whose largest-including sphere has diameter at least (D_k = k) is [ V(D_k) = , V()=1 . ]
Derivative. The PSD is the negative derivative of this cumulative curve, by a central difference, [ (D_i) = -|_{D_i} -, ] reported at the bin centre (D_i = i- /2) (PoreBlazer’s convention).
Peak normalisation. Each curve is divided by its own maximum, (/), so the y axis is in arbitrary units and curves from different samplers or materials share a scale.

mgr.psd_gelb_gubbins(counts, binsize) implements steps 1 and 2 and is unit-tested against a direct port of PoreBlazer’s pore_distribution. The pocket-wise PSD applies the same transformation to the diameters sampled inside each pocket.

title: Pore size distributions
text:
Imports and settings


Show code
import logging
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import mofography as mgr
from mofography.cif_io import read_cif_to_ase

logging.getLogger("mofography").setLevel(logging.WARNING)

num_samples_total = 50000       # global sampler (paper-style)
num_samples_per_region = 5000   # per pocket
max_diameter = 20.0
binsize = 0.25                  # PoreBlazer default bin width (Å)
bins = np.arange(0, max_diameter + binsize / 2, binsize)


def gelb_gubbins(counts):
    """Diameter histogram -> -dV/dD (the Gelb-Gubbins curve), peak-normalized (a.u.)."""
    _, y = mgr.psd_gelb_gubbins(counts, binsize)
    m = y.max()
    return y / m if m > 0 else y

# diameters (Å) that the -dV/dD values belong to (interior bins)
x_gg, _ = mgr.psd_gelb_gubbins(np.ones(len(bins) - 1), binsize)


def peak_diameter(y, x=x_gg):
    return float(x[int(np.argmax(y))])


The sampling helpers return histograms of diameters. The curve in the paper (and in PoreBlazer’s Total_psd.txt) is not that histogram but the Gelb–Gubbins PSD, (-V/D): build the cumulative pore volume (V(D)) from the samples, normalise it to 1 at (D=0), and take its central difference with the same 0.25 Å bins as PoreBlazer. mgr.psd_gelb_gubbins(counts, binsize) does this conversion. We then divide each curve by its own maximum (arbitrary units), exactly as in the paper figure, so curves from different samplers are comparable and the results can be compared one-to-one with PoreBlazer.

Step 1: Structure, distance grid, segmentation

atoms = read_cif_to_ase("P1-Cu-BTC.cif")
print(f"{atoms.get_chemical_formula()}: {len(atoms)} atoms")
print("Cell (Å):", atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2))

spacing = 0.5
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing).astype(np.float32)
print(f"dgrid {dgrid.shape}, max void radius {dgrid.max():.2f} Å")

seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid, atoms,
    spacing=spacing,
    mask_thickness=0.05,
    h=0.2,
    min_distance=1.5,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    watershed_backend="rust_det",
    compute_connections=True,
    return_dgrid=True,
    disable_tqdm=True,
)
regions_pbc = seg["regions_pbc"]
n_pbc_groups = len(seg["pbc_groups"])
print(f"PBC pockets: {len(seg['maxima_pbc'])} | PBC groups: {n_pbc_groups}")


C288H96Cu48O192: 624 atoms
Cell (Å): [26.34 26.34 26.34]
dgrid (53, 53, 53), max void radius 6.30 Å


PBC pockets: 16 | PBC groups: 16


return_dgrid=True keeps dgrid inside seg; accessible PSD helpers also need window connections for percolation.

title: Pore size distributions
section: Step 2: Pick a probe radius for accessibility
text:
Step 2: Pick a probe radius for accessibility
We sweep probe radii and count PBC-complete pocket groups that still percolate (via compute_accessible_psd_from_results, same winding logic as compute_psd_global_accessible).
Probe radii are taken from the Bondi van der Waals table (the same CRC/Bondi table mofography uses for atoms, mofography.vdw_radii.CRC_VDW_RADII_PM), by element name: H 1.20, He 1.40, N 1.55, Ar 1.88 Å. Any of these can be the probe (nitrogen is the usual choice for textural properties, helium and hydrogen are common too), as long as the radius matches the name you report and you use it consistently across properties. For this tutorial the choice only matters for contrast: in Cu-BTC, H, He and N all reach every pocket, while Ar is large enough to be blocked from the small cages.


Show code
regions = seg["regions"]
void_voxels = int((regions != 0).sum())
from mofography.vdw_radii import CRC_VDW_RADII_PM
probe_names = ["H", "He", "N", "Ar"]
probe_candidates = [float(CRC_VDW_RADII_PM[n]) / 100.0 for n in probe_names]  # Å, Bondi table

print(f"{'probe':>6} {'r (Å)':>6}  {'PBC groups acc':>16}  {'void frac acc':>14}")
accessible_rows = []
for name, pr in zip(probe_names, probe_candidates):
    out = mgr.compute_accessible_psd_from_results(
        seg, atoms, pr, bin_edges=bins,
        samples_per_region=num_samples_per_region, accessible_only=True,
    )
    acc_fragments = set(out["accessible_region_ids"])
    acc_groups = sum(
        1 for g in seg["pbc_groups"]
        if acc_fragments.intersection(int(x) for x in g)
    )
    acc_vox = int(np.isin(regions, list(acc_fragments)).sum())
    void_frac = acc_vox / void_voxels
    accessible_rows.append((pr, acc_groups, void_frac))
    print(f"{name:>6} {pr:6.2f}  {acc_groups:5d} / {n_pbc_groups:5d}      {void_frac:14.4f}")

# Ar (Bondi 1.88 Å): small tetrahedral pockets drop out; large/medium cages remain.
probe_name = "Ar"
probe_radius = float(CRC_VDW_RADII_PM[probe_name]) / 100.0
acc_groups, void_frac = next(r[1:] for r in accessible_rows if r[0] == probe_radius)
print(
    f"\nUsing {probe_name} probe, radius = {probe_radius:.2f} Å: "
    f"{acc_groups}/{n_pbc_groups} PBC pocket groups accessible, "
    f"accessible void fraction {void_frac:.4f} (vs 1.0000 for a small probe)."
)


 probe  r (Å)    PBC groups acc   void frac acc
     H   1.20     16 /    16              1.0000
    He   1.40     16 /    16              1.0000
     N   1.55     16 /    16              1.0000
    Ar   1.88      8 /    16              0.9246

Using Ar probe, radius = 1.88 Å: 8/16 PBC pocket groups accessible, accessible void fraction 0.9246 (vs 1.0000 for a small probe).


H, He and N reach every pocket (void fraction 1). Ar (1.88 Å) removes the eight small-cage PBC groups while keeping the medium and large cages—clear contrast for accessible PSDs.

title: Pore size distributions
section: Step 3: Global PSD — all void vs accessible (peak-normalized)
text:
Step 3: Global PSD — all void vs accessible (peak-normalized)


Show code
hist_global = mgr.compute_psd_uniform_rust(
    dgrid, atoms,
    num_samples_total=num_samples_total,
    bins=bins,
    density=False,   # raw counts; psd_gelb_gubbins builds -dV/dD from them
    material="Cu-BTC (all void)",
)

hist_global_acc = mgr.compute_psd_global_accessible(
    seg, atoms,
    probe_radius=probe_radius,
    bins=bins,
    samples_per_region=num_samples_per_region,
    density=False,
)

y_all = gelb_gubbins(hist_global)
y_acc = gelb_gubbins(hist_global_acc)
pk_all = peak_diameter(y_all)
pk_acc = peak_diameter(y_acc)

fig_global = go.Figure()
fig_global.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x_gg, y=y_all, mode="lines", name="Global — all void",
    line=dict(width=2.5),
))
fig_global.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x_gg, y=y_acc, mode="lines",
    name=f"Global — accessible ({probe_name}, {probe_radius:.2f} Å)",
    line=dict(width=2.5, dash="dash"),
))
for xpk, label in [(pk_all, f"{pk_all:.1f} Å"), (pk_acc, f"{pk_acc:.1f} Å")]:
    fig_global.add_annotation(
        x=xpk, y=1.02, text=label, showarrow=False, yref="paper", font=dict(size=11),
    )
fig_global.update_layout(
    title="Cu-BTC: global pore size distribution (peak-normalized, a.u.)",
    xaxis_title="Pore diameter (Å)",
    yaxis_title="-dV/dD, peak-normalized (a.u.)",
    template="plotly_white",
    legend=dict(yanchor="top", y=0.99, xanchor="right", x=0.99),
    width=900,
    height=480,
)
fig_global.write_image("tutorial_images/psd_global_cubtc.png", width=900, height=480)
print(f"Global peak (all void): {pk_all:.2f} Å — dominated by large cages")
print(f"Global peak (accessible @ {probe_name} {probe_radius:.2f} Å): {pk_acc:.2f} Å")



Creating region-wise PSD plots...
Global peak (all void): 12.38 Å — dominated by large cages
Global peak (accessible @ Ar 1.88 Å): 12.38 Å





Cu-BTC global PSD: all void vs probe-accessible


The global all-void curve peaks near 12.6 Å; the ~5.6 Å small-cage mode is absent because those pockets contribute little volume. Accessible global PSD with the Ar probe peaks among the remaining large cages (small pockets already non-percolating).

title: Pore size distributions
section: Step 4: Pocket-wise PSD — three cage families
text:
Step 4: Pocket-wise PSD — three cage families
Pocket labels are grouped into small / medium / large cages from the inscribed diameter at each PBC representative label. Each family trace is the mean of peak-normalized pocket histograms in that family.


Show code
pocket_psds = mgr.compute_psds_pocketwise_rust(
    dgrid, regions_pbc, atoms,
    num_samples_per_region=num_samples_per_region,
    bins=bins,
    material="Cu-BTC — all pockets",
)

def cage_family(diameter):
    if diameter < 7.0:
        return "small cage (~5.6 Å)"
    if diameter < 12.0:
        return "medium cage (~11 Å)"
    return "large cage (~12.6 Å)"

family_hist = {}
family_members = {}
for g in seg["pbc_groups"]:
    rep = int(min(g))
    d_pocket = 2.0 * float(dgrid[regions_pbc == rep].max())
    fam = cage_family(d_pocket)
    h = gelb_gubbins(pocket_psds[rep]["hist"])
    family_hist.setdefault(fam, []).append(h)
    family_members.setdefault(fam, []).append(rep)

# Volume-weighted global curve for overlay (same density + peak norm)
y_global_overlay = y_all

colors = {
    "small cage (~5.6 Å)": "#d62728",
    "medium cage (~11 Å)": "#1f77b4",
    "large cage (~12.6 Å)": "#2ca02c",
}

fig_pock = go.Figure()
fig_pock.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x_gg, y=y_global_overlay, mode="lines",
    name="Global uniform (peak-norm.)",
    line=dict(width=2, color="black", dash="dot"),
))
for fam in sorted(family_hist.keys()):
    mean_h = np.mean(family_hist[fam], axis=0)
    pk = peak_diameter(mean_h)
    fig_pock.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x_gg, y=mean_h, mode="lines", name=fam,
        line=dict(width=2.5, color=colors.get(fam, "gray")),
    ))
    fig_pock.add_annotation(
        x=pk, y=float(mean_h.max()) + 0.06,
        text=f"{pk:.1f} Å", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=11, color=colors.get(fam, "gray")),
    )

fig_pock.update_layout(
    title="Cu-BTC: pocket-wise vs global PSD (peak-normalized, a.u.)",
    xaxis_title="Pore diameter (Å)",
    yaxis_title="-dV/dD, peak-normalized (a.u.)",
    template="plotly_white",
    legend=dict(yanchor="top", y=0.99, xanchor="left", x=0.01),
    width=900,
    height=480,
)
fig_pock.write_image("tutorial_images/psd_pocketwise_cubtc.png", width=900, height=480)
print("Pocket families:", {k: len(v) for k, v in family_members.items()})

title: Pore size distributions
section: Step 5: Pocket-wise accessible PSD at the chosen probe
text:
Step 5: Pocket-wise accessible PSD at the chosen probe


Show code
pocket_psds_acc = mgr.compute_psds_pocketwise_accessible(
    seg, atoms,
    probe_radius=probe_radius,
    num_samples_per_region=num_samples_per_region,
    bins=bins,
    material=f"Cu-BTC — accessible @ {probe_name} {probe_radius:.2f} Å",
)
# Keys are fragment region ids in seg["regions"], not regions_pbc labels.
print(f"Accessible fragment regions with PSDs: {len(pocket_psds_acc)}")

acc_family_hist = {}
for rid, psd in pocket_psds_acc.items():
    mask = regions == int(rid)
    if not mask.any():
        continue
    d_pocket = 2.0 * float(dgrid[mask].max())
    fam = cage_family(d_pocket)
    acc_family_hist.setdefault(fam, []).append(gelb_gubbins(psd["hist"]))

fig_acc = go.Figure()
for fam in sorted(acc_family_hist.keys()):
    mean_h = np.mean(acc_family_hist[fam], axis=0)
    pk = peak_diameter(mean_h)
    fig_acc.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x_gg, y=mean_h, mode="lines", name=fam,
        line=dict(width=2.5, color=colors.get(fam, "gray")),
    ))
    fig_acc.add_annotation(
        x=pk, y=float(mean_h.max()) + 0.06,
        text=f"{pk:.1f} Å", showarrow=False, font=dict(size=11, color=colors.get(fam, "gray")),
    )

fig_acc.update_layout(
    title=f"Cu-BTC: accessible pocket-wise PSD ({probe_name} probe {probe_radius:.2f} Å, peak-normalized)",
    xaxis_title="Pore diameter (Å)",
    yaxis_title="-dV/dD, peak-normalized (a.u.)",
    template="plotly_white",
    width=900,
    height=480,
)
fig_acc.write_image("tutorial_images/psd_pocketwise_accessible_cubtc.png", width=900, height=480)


Accessible fragment regions with PSDs: 27





Cu-BTC accessible pocket-wise PSD


All small-cage pockets are gone with the Ar probe; only medium and large percolating groups remain (compute_psds_pocketwise_accessible drops non-percolating regions before sampling).
For pocket typing, run enrich_segmentation_with_pocket_psds(seg, atoms) to cache these pocket-wise histograms on seg before assign_pocket_types (Pocket detection).

go-to Plotly-style chained builder for Three.js scenes; use .show() or .save_html().
threejs_viz.Figure3js(layout='dark', stylize=True)
Plotly-like granular builder for Three.js MOF visualisations.
Mirror of the plotly trace API from mgr.visualize (plot_surface_dgrid, plot_cell, plot_maxima, plot_connections_as_it_is, plot_windows, draw_framework) but targeting the Three.js backend (MovieFigure).
All plot_* / draw_* methods return self so they can be chained::
fig = (
    Figure3js()
    .plot_framework(atoms)
    .plot_cell(atoms, color="orange")
    .plot_surface(dgrid, regions, atoms, name="Regions", opacity=1.0)
    .plot_surface(dgrid, regions_pbc, atoms, name="Regions PBC",
                  trace_id="surface_pbc", opacity=0.35)
    .plot_maxima(dgrid, all_maxima, atoms, name="Maxima", cscale=cscale)
    .plot_connections(connections, all_maxima, dgrid.shape, atoms)
    .plot_windows(connections, atoms=atoms, name="Windows",
                  marker_color="yellow")
    .to_html("output.html")
)
The underlying MovieFigure is always accessible via .figure.

Pocket typing: max_r initial bands, fingerprint-driven merge only.



Sort pockets by max_probe_radius.
Start a new band whenever the gap to the next pocket exceeds initial_band_gap_a (grid-noise floor, < grid spacing).
Iteratively merge adjacent bands (by mean max_r) when:

|mean_max_r_A − mean_max_r_B| ≤ merge_max_r_gap_a (physical proximity)
mean cosine over all cross-pairs ≥ merge_cosine (same environment)

Optionally merge 1-pocket max_r bands into the nearest neighbor when peak radii are within singleton_band_gap_a (e.g. ZIF-8 corner vs center cages, grid-offset max_r only).
Each remaining band → one pocket type.




initial_band_gap_a : 0.15 Å Gap above which two consecutive pockets form separate initial bands. Should be less than the grid spacing (0.5 Å) to catch only grid-noise. merge_max_r_gap_a : 0.50 Å Hard upper bound on the mean max_r gap between two bands for them to be merge candidates (= one grid spacing). merge_gap_threshold_a : 0.20 Å Gap boundary between tight and loose cosine thresholds. merge_cosine : 0.90 Tight cosine threshold for gaps ≤ merge_gap_threshold_a (prevents spurious merges of similar-but-different window types, e.g. ZIF-20 2.56 vs 2.74 Å). merge_cosine_large_gap : 0.90 Loose cosine threshold for gaps > merge_gap_threshold_a. Set equal to merge_cosine so adjacent bands merge only when fingerprints are truly near-unity (e.g. keeps ZIF-20 large cages 7.26 vs 7.61 Å separate).

title: blocking_spheres_greedy
text:
alternate Greedy cover without PBC distances; examples compare to largest_including.
raspa_helper.blocking_spheres_greedy(
    results,
    ase_atoms,
    threshold,
    spacing=None,
    block_accessible=False,
    radius_scale=1.0,
)
Greedy blocking spheres (org-note style): place spheres at pocket maxima for each target region, then repeatedly add the sphere with the largest remaining dgrid value until all masked voxels are covered.
Coverage uses Euclidean distances in Å (no minimum-image / PBC). Use :func:blocking_spheres_largest_including if you need PBC-consistent including spheres on the same mask.

Inferred from results / cell if omitted. block_accessible : bool, default False * False — Mask all voxels in non-percolating regions at threshold. For standard RASPA BlockPockets (block side pockets). * True — Mask voxels in percolating regions with dgrid >= threshold. For InvertBlockPockets. radius_scale : float, default 1.0 Multiply every sphere radius by this factor; each radius is at least 0.5 Å (same floor as :func:blocking_spheres_largest_including).

Same intent as :func:blocking_spheres_overlap_into_accessible_regions, but sample accessible void on a coarser grid (e.g. 0.5 Å) for speed.
Each coarse cell center maps to the nearest fine segmentation voxel (same fractional mapping as :func:mofography.compute.dask_grid_over_atoms). A sample point counts as accessible if that fine voxel lies in a label that percolates at probe_radius (and optionally dgrid >= probe).
Returns label sets, fine-grid counts for context, and a per-label breakdown of how many coarse samples per percolating region fell inside the blocking-sphere union (MIC and raw).
Implemented via :func:blocking_spheres_overlap_leakage (resolution="coarse", per_label=True).


sample_spacing : float Coarse probe grid in Å (e.g. 0.5). fine_spacing : float, optional Spacing of results['regions']; inferred if omitted.

title: blocking_spheres_overlap_into_accessible_regions
text:
raspa_helper.blocking_spheres_overlap_into_accessible_regions(
    results,
    ase_atoms,
    spheres,
    probe_radius,
    spacing=None,
    accessible_dgrid_ge_probe=False,
    atol=0.0001,
    chunk_size=65536,
)
Estimate how much blocking-sphere volume intrudes into accessible void.
Accessible voxels = segmentation labels that percolate at probe_radius (same definition as :func:percolated_region_labels_winding). Optionally restrict to voxels with dgrid >= probe_radius (accessible_dgrid_ge_probe).
For each grid point in that accessible set, test whether its Cartesian position lies inside the union of blocking spheres (fractional center + radius in Å). Uses minimum-image distance (PBC) for the primary metric, and also reports raw Cartesian distance (no PBC) for comparison.
The grid is the same ordering as dask_grid_over_atoms / dgrid.ravel().


results : dict Must contain regions, dgrid. ase_atoms : ase.Atoms spheres : sequence of [sx, sy, sz, r] Fractional centers, radii in Å (RASPA convention). probe_radius : float Percolation threshold defining accessible labels. spacing : float, optional Grid spacing; inferred from results / cell if omitted. accessible_dgrid_ge_probe : bool If True, count only accessible-label voxels with dgrid >= probe_radius. atol : float Tolerance on distance <= r + atol. chunk_size : int Chunk size over accessible points for memory.



dict Keys include n_spheres, n_accessible_voxels (denominator), n_overlapped_mic, frac_overlapped_mic, n_overlapped_raw, frac_overlapped_raw, approx_voxel_volume_ang3, approx_overlap_volume_mic_ang3, frac_unit_cell_overlapped_mic.
Implemented via :func:blocking_spheres_overlap_leakage (resolution="fine").

Pair of :func:blocking_spheres_overlap_leakage runs for BlockPockets QA.
When spheres are built to cover inaccessible void, you usually want both:

Leakage — denominator_domain="accessible": among accessible sample points, what fraction fall inside the sphere union (spill into transport void)?
Coverage gap — denominator_domain="inaccessible": among inaccessible sample points, what fraction fall outside the union (missed cages)? Reported as frac_covered_inaccessible_mic and frac_missed_inaccessible_mic.

resolution is passed to the accessible leg. The inaccessible leg uses the same resolution except when resolution="interface" (interface is only defined for accessible); then inaccessible defaults to "fine" unless you set inaccessible_resolution.

title: check_percolation_periodic
text:
check_percolation_periodic
legacy Pad-and-label percolation test; superseded by axis-wise and winding solvers. Use check_percolation_periodic2 instead.
compute.check_percolation_periodic(distance_grid, threshold)
Return True if void voxels above threshold form a periodically infinite (winding) network.
Components are labelled inside the cell (no halo), then stitched across opposite faces while tracking the cell-image offset of each component. A component that returns to itself at a different image offset winds around the torus. This is independent of where the cell origin sits, unlike matching one label on opposite faces of a halo-padded grid (the halo copies are not tied to the real boundary voxels, so a channel cut by the cell origin was missed).

title: compute_accessible_psd_from_results
text:
go-to Full accessible global PSD dict with winding percolation and pocket weighting.
rust_fun.compute_accessible_psd_from_results(
    results,
    mat_atoms,
    probe_radius,
    bin_edges,
    samples_per_region=10000,
    accessible_only=True,
    pb_normalization=False,
    probe_center_min_radius=None,
    enforce_probe_center_occupiable=False,
)
Compute a volume-weighted accessible PSD from segmentation at a given probe radius.
Computes a PoreBlazer-style accessible PSD by: 1) identifying percolating pockets at the given probe_radius via winding-number percolation, 2) sampling pore sizes pocketwise (fixed samples per region), 3) weighting each pocket’s PDF by its voxel fraction to recover a volume-weighted global PSD.


results : dict Segmentation results from do_periodic_segmentation_rust (needs regions_pbc, maxima_info, regions, connections, etc.). If results does not contain ‘dgrid’, you must have passed return_dgrid=True when generating it, or supply dgrid separately. mat_atoms : ase.Atoms ASE Atoms with the simulation cell (used only to build the cell matrix for sampling). probe_radius : float Probe radius (Å) used as the percolation threshold. bin_edges : array-like Bin edges for diameters (Å). Use PB-style bins for direct comparison. samples_per_region : int Fixed number of samples per pocket for the pocketwise sampler. accessible_only : bool If True, restrict to percolating (accessible) regions; if False, include all regions.



dict with keys: - pdf: global volume-weighted PDF over bin centers - cum: cumulative (descending) of pdf - psd: finite-difference derivative of cum - bin_centers: centers from bin_edges - per_region: dict of per-pocket PDFs (unweighted), voxel counts, and weights - accessible_region_ids: list of region ids used

title: compute_surface_area_mc
text:
experimental Monte Carlo shell surface estimator; kept for method comparison, not main tutorials.
compute.compute_surface_area_mc(
    results_dict,
    mat_atoms,
    probe_radius=None,
    n_samples=20000,
    shell_thickness=0.5,
    return_details=False,
    window_fp_for_accessible=True,
    winding_kwargs=None,
    accessibility_method='winding',
    lattice_variant='v2',
)
Experimental Monte Carlo shell-based surface area estimator.
This function reuses the existing distance grid, region labels, and percolation history to estimate total and accessible surface area at a given probe radius by sampling points in a thin shell around the isosurface f(x) = probe_radius.


results_dict : dict Results dictionary containing at minimum: - ‘dgrid’ or ‘distance_grid’: Distance grid array - ‘pbc_groups’: PBC groups dictionary - ‘regions_pbc’: Periodic regions array - Optional: ‘percolation_history’ from compute_percolation_history mat_atoms : ase.Atoms Atomic structure for mass calculation and coordinate transformations. probe_radius : float, optional Probe radius for surface area calculation. If None, uses helium radius. n_samples : int, optional Number of Monte Carlo samples per structure. shell_thickness : float, optional Thickness of the shell around probe_radius used for the estimator. return_details : bool, optional If True, returns additional diagnostic information. window_fp_for_accessible : bool, optional Winding only: window-fingerprint bridging when True; strict winding when False. winding_kwargs : dict, optional Extra keyword arguments for winding fingerprint bridging (merged over results_dict['winding_kwargs'] when present). accessibility_method : str, optional "winding" (default) or "lattice". lattice_variant : str, optional "v2" or "v1" for lattice accessibility.



dict Dictionary with at least: - ‘total_surface_area’: Total SA (m²/g), MC estimate - ‘accessible_surface_area’: Accessible SA (percolated regions) (m²/g) - ‘accessible_fraction’: Accessible / total - ‘probe_radius’: Probe radius used - ‘sa_mc_diagnostics’: Dict with sampling diagnostics
For now, per-region/pocket/cluster breakdowns are populated only for
accessible (percolating) regions, mirroring the semantics of
compute_surface_area_mesh (by_region = accessible SA).

The spacing parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms function represents the distance between grid points in the mesh grid that is created over the atoms. probe_radius

The probe_radius parameter in the dgrid_from_atoms function represents the radius of the probe used in the calculation. This parameter is used in the computation of the distance grid over atoms. The probe radius is typically used in molecular modeling and simulations to mimic the size of a solvent molecule or, defaults to 0 (optional)
0

go-to Default Rust distance grid; first step of the main segmentation workflow.
rust_fun.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(ase_atoms, spacing, radii=None)
Compute a distance grid from atomic positions using the Rust backend.
Uses optimized exact MIC (SoA, SIMD on orthogonal cells, Wassenaar 7-image fallback on skewed cells).
This function calculates the distance field (dgrid) for a given atomic structure, where each grid point represents the minimum distance to the nearest atom surface, accounting for van der Waals radii.

title: egrid_from_atoms2
text:
legacy Dask vdW energy grid for clustering; Rust tricubic grid is more accurate for screening. Use egrid_tricubic_from_atoms_rust instead.
compute.egrid_from_atoms2(
    ase_atoms,
    spacing=0.5,
    blocksize=20000,
    forcefield_mixed=None,
    cutoff=12.5,
    probe_symbol='He',
    return_ncells=False,
    precompute_aabb=True,
)
Sample vdW interaction energies on a grid (Dask); prefer Rust tricubic for production accuracy.
The function is a bit long, but it’s not too complicated.
The first part of the function is just to get the grid points.
The second part is to get the forcefield parameters for the atoms.
The third part is to get the positions of the atoms in the unit cell, and to get the unit cell vectors.
The fourth part is to repeat the unit cell to get the positions of the atoms in the repeated unit cell.
The fifth part is to map the grid point energy function onto the grid points.
The sixth part is to reshape the grid points into a 3D array.
The seventh part is to return the grid points.
The eighth part is to return the number of repetitions of the unit cell if that return_ncells parameter is turned on.











Name
Type
Description
Default




ase_atoms

an ase atoms object
required


spacing

the spacing of the grid points
0.5


blocksize

the size of the chunks that the grid is split into. This is important for memory management, defaults to 20000 (optional)
20000


forcefield_mixed

This is a list of the forcefield parameters for each atom in the unit cell
None


cutoff

the cutoff distance for the Lennard-Jones potential
12.5


probe_symbol

the symbol of the probe atom used to calculate the van der Waals radii, defaults to He (optional)
'He'


return_ncells

if True, returns the number of cells needed to meet the cutoff, defaults to False (optional)
False


precompute

if True, then the AABB is precomputed and passed to the function. If False, then the positions and cell are passed to the function, defaults to True (optional)
required














Name
Type
Description






The grid2 is a dask array, which is a lazy array. It is not computed until you call compute() on it.

Keep only percolated paths whose limiting window meets a size threshold.
The function filters paths based on whether their corresponding path windows meet a certain size threshold.

analyze.find_aromatic_cycles_in_sgraph(
    sgraph,
    default_ring_sizes=[5, 6, 7, 8, 9],
)
Find all aromatic cycles in the graph.
Returns a list of lists, where each inner list contains the indices of atoms in an aromatic cycle (all edges are double bonds).
For large graphs (> _MAX_NODES_FOR_EXPANSION), the isomorphism expansion step is skipped because GraphMatcher.subgraph_isomorphisms_iter() is O(|V|^k) on a k-node template and hangs on MOF-scale structures. The unique aromatic cycles (deduplicated by atom membership) are returned directly — they already contain every distinct ring embedding.

title: fingerprint_cosine_similarity
text:
fingerprint_cosine_similarity
pocket_framework_env.fingerprint_cosine_similarity(
    a,
    b,
    *,
    angular_only=False,
    use_psd=True,
    use_connectivity=True,
)
Mean cosine over environment + PSD + connectivity channels (rotation-invariant).
Channels: * global_radial, global_sh_power — atom environment shell * per-element radial, sh_power — element-resolved atom environment * psd_vec — pocket PSD histogram (size fingerprint) * conn_sh_power — SH power of directions to trusted neighbours
angular_only suppresses radial channels (better for small pockets). use_psd includes the pocket PSD channel when available (default True). use_connectivity includes the connectivity-direction channel when both pockets have ≥1 trusted connection (default True).

title: get_pbc_groups
text:
get_pbc_groups
compute.get_pbc_groups(unmerged_regions, maxima_info)
Group unmerged regions based on periodic boundary conditions (PBC).
This function organizes unmerged regions into groups based on their maxima indices. Each group is identified by a unique tuple of maxima indices (columns 2-4 of maxima_info), and contains the corresponding region indices (column 1 of maxima_info).
Args: unmerged_regions (iterable): A collection of region indices that are not yet merged. maxima_info (array-like): A 2D array where each row contains: - Column 0: Region index - Columns 1-3: Maxima indices (used as grouping keys) - Column 4: Offsets in each direction You get this as output when you call the ‘do_periodic_segmentation’ on the distance grid (dgrid)
Returns: dict: A dictionary where keys are tuples of maxima indices (columns 2-4), and values are sets of region indices (column 1) belonging to each group.

title: get_pore_dia_mgr_winding2
text:
alternate Same as winding but re-segments with thick mask when watershed spill is detected. Use get_pore_dia_mgr_winding instead.
winding_percolation.get_pore_dia_mgr_winding2(
    mat_atoms=None,
    dgrid=None,
    kwargs=None,
    results=None,
    include_dangling=True,
    expand_components=True,
    auto_rerun=True,
)
Compute pore diameters using winding percolation with spill guardrail.
Identical to get_pore_dia_mgr_winding but adds automatic re-segmentation when deterministic watershed spill is detected. Spill is flagged when any node’s self-loop radii spread exceeds 30% of its pocket radius.
When auto_rerun is True and spill is detected: - Re-segments with mask_thickness=1.5 using the same backend and dgrid. - Recomputes PLD from the guarded segmentation. - Stores _spill_corrected, _original_pld, _corrected_pld in results (if mutable) for diagnostics.


mat_atoms : ase.Atoms, optional ASE Atoms object. Required if results is None. dgrid : ndarray, optional Pre-computed distance grid. kwargs : dict, optional Keyword arguments for do_periodic_segmentation_rust. results : dict, optional Pre-computed segmentation results. include_dangling : bool Whether to include dangling edges. expand_components : bool Whether to expand components. auto_rerun : bool If True, silently re-segment with guard mask when spill is detected. Requires results['dgrid'] and results.get('mat_atoms') (or mat_atoms passed separately). Raises ValueError if neither is available.



tuple[float, float, float, ndarray] (lcd, pld, dfsd, dgrid)

Build sparse-index movie with separate guest traces per component.



If framework_movie_path is set, framework mesh, unit cell, surface, maxima, windows, and connection traces are stored per animation frame so the viewer can show a flexible framework and recomputed segmentation for each sparse snapshot.
If framework_movie_path is omitted, the framework comes from cif_path and stays static (segmentation once); only guest traces animate.
Segmentation dictionaries are computed for every selected frame and returned in the second tuple element for downstream analysis.

title: regions_from_dgrid
text:
go-to Watershed region labeling from a distance grid; core segmentation step.
compute.regions_from_dgrid(
    dgrid,
    mask_thickness=1,
    h=0.2,
    compactness=0,
    threshold_abs=0.5,
)
Label pore regions and maxima from a distance grid using watershed segmentation.











Name
Type
Description
Default




dgrid

The dgrid parameter is a 2D array representing the input data grid. It is used in the function to perform calculations and identify regions based on the data values in the grid
required


mask_thickness

The mask_thickness parameter in the regions_from_dgrid function determines the thickness of the mask used in the watershed segmentation algorithm. It is used to create a mask where regions with values greater than the mask_thickness are considered as markers for segmentation. Increasing the mask_thickness value, defaults to 1 (optional)
1


h

The h parameter in the regions_from_dgrid function is used to specify the height threshold for detecting local maxima in the input dgrid array. It is used in the extrema.h_maxima function to find the local maxima points based on the specified height
0.2


min_distance

The min_distance parameter in the regions_from_dgrid function specifies the minimum distance between peaks in the peak_local_max function. It is used to find peaks in the input data that are separated by at least this distance. Peaks that are closer than min_distance to each other are, defaults to 2 (optional)
required


compactness

The compactness parameter in the regions_from_dgrid function controls how uniform the region sizes are in the output. A higher value for compactness will result in more equally sized regions, while a lower value will allow for more size variation among the regions. Adjusting the , defaults to 0 (optional)                                  |0`

Type
Description






The function regions_from_dgrid returns two values: reg_labels and new_max_indices.T.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
do_periodic_segmentation_rust runs h-maxima detection on a spatially-varying smoothed version of the distance grid, not on the raw grid. The idea is simple: small pores are real and should be kept; the surfaces of large channels are noisy and should be smoothed away. Between those regimes, smoothing is interpolated linearly.
This tutorial explains the three knobs that control this behavior and shows how to tune them in practice. The companion Region Segmentation tutorial gives the broader picture; Quick Start walks the full pipeline. Read those first if you have not.
The three parameters — all passed directly to do_periodic_segmentation_rust — are:








Parameter
Default
Role




preserve_threshold
3.0 Å
Below this distance, smoothing is off (real pockets preserved as-is)


smooth_threshold
6.0 Å
Above this distance, smoothing is at max (surface roughness removed)


max_smooth_radius
2.0
Cap on the per-voxel Gaussian σ in grid units (voxel factors)

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
do_periodic_segmentation_rust runs h-maxima detection on a spatially-varying smoothed version of the distance grid, not on the raw grid. The idea is simple: small pores are real and should be kept; the surfaces of large channels are noisy and should be smoothed away. Between those regimes, smoothing is interpolated linearly.
This tutorial explains the three knobs that control this behavior and shows how to tune them in practice. The companion Region Segmentation tutorial gives the broader picture; Quick Start walks the full pipeline. Read those first if you have not.
The three parameters — all passed directly to do_periodic_segmentation_rust — are:








Parameter
Default
Role

3.0 Å
Below this distance, smoothing is off (real pockets preserved as-is)

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
What Selective Smoothing Does
Inside mgr_rust.detect_maxima_selective_smoothing_parallel the algorithm first builds a per-voxel “smooth radius” field from the local dgrid value v:
\[
\sigma(v) = \begin{cases}
0 & v \le \text{preserve\_threshold} \\
\text{max\_smooth\_radius} \cdot \dfrac{v - \text{preserve\_threshold}}{\text{smooth\_threshold} - \text{preserve\_threshold}} & \text{preserve\_threshold} < v < \text{smooth\_threshold} \\
\text{max\_smooth\_radius} & v \ge \text{smooth\_threshold}
\end{cases}
\]
The grid is then convolved with a Gaussian of that σ, but only at voxels where the assigned σ is non-trivial. Finally, h-maxima runs on the smoothed grid.
In words:

Small features (dgrid < preserve_threshold) are real pockets. The distance value is small because a framework atom is close; smoothing would merge them with neighbors. Leave them alone.
Large features (dgrid > smooth_threshold) are wide channels or open cages. Their walls have small ripples from the underlying framework; smoothing removes those ripples so h-maxima does not see spurious “peaks” inside the channel.
In between, smooth just enough to suppress noise without erasing the pore.

The three parameters partition the dgrid range into three regimes — no smoothing, full smoothing, and a linear ramp in between. The shape of the ramp is always a straight line; only the endpoints move.
sigma
  ↑
  │                    ●──────────────────  max_smooth_radius
  │                  ╱
  │                ╱
  │              ╱         linear ramp
  │            ╱
  │          ╱
  │        ╱
  │      ╱
  │    ●                              preserve_threshold
  │  (0, no smoothing)                smooth_threshold
  └─────────────────────────────────────→  dgrid value (Å)
max_smooth_radius is a cap on the Gaussian σ, not a separate parameter for a different algorithm. With the default max_smooth_radius=2.0 and spacing=0.5 Å, the strongest smoothing uses a kernel of width ~4 voxels — enough to suppress grid noise but not so much that it eats real pores.

Note on units. max_smooth_radius is the Gaussian σ in grid units (multiples of spacing). With spacing=0.5 and max_smooth_radius=2.0, σ ≈ 1.0 Å in physical distance. The Rust kernel is anisotropic per axis when voxel_lengths is passed (always, in the current Python wrapper), so non-cubic cells are handled correctly.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
Prerequisites

A working mofography install (see Install).
Familiarity with do_periodic_segmentation_rust — see Quick Start and Region Segmentation.
A MOF CIF; we use IRMOF-1.cif here.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
Imports


Show code
import mofography as mgr
import mgr_rust                      # for direct comparison with the underlying Rust function
from ase.io import read
from ase.geometry import cellpar_to_cell
import numpy as np
import logging

# Quiet the noise — segmentation is chatty by default
logging.getLogger("mofography").setLevel(logging.WARNING)

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
section: Step 1: Load IRMOF-1 and Compute the Distance Grid
text:
Step 1: Load IRMOF-1 and Compute the Distance Grid
IRMOF-1 has two families of cages (small and large) and is a clean test case. The defaults produce 8 PBC-grouped pockets, which is what you should see in the cells that follow.


Show code
atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
print(f"IRMOF-1: {len(atoms)} atoms, cell = {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)} Å")

spacing = 0.5                                # Å — see distance_grid.qmd
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)             # Rust kernel requires float32
print(f"dgrid: {dgrid.shape}, void max = {dgrid.max():.1f} Å")


IRMOF-1: 424 atoms, cell = [25.83 25.83 25.83] Å
dgrid: (52, 52, 52), void max = 7.5 Å

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
section: Step 2: Run Segmentation with Four Smoothing Configs
text:
Step 2: Run Segmentation with Four Smoothing Configs
The full pipeline includes PBC merging, wall-maximum removal, and small-region cleanup. The smoothing parameters affect the raw maxima detected by the Rust function; the downstream post-processing then collapses most of the noise. For a well-behaved structure like IRMOF-1, the final PBC-merged pore count is therefore stable across reasonable settings, even when the raw count varies by 10×. That is the desired behavior — the algorithm should not be brittle to small parameter changes. We sweep both numbers to show the contrast.


Show code
configs = {
    "no_smoothing":   dict(preserve_threshold=0.0, smooth_threshold=0.0, max_smooth_radius=0.0),
    "defaults":       dict(preserve_threshold=3.0, smooth_threshold=6.0, max_smooth_radius=2.0),
    "aggressive":     dict(preserve_threshold=3.0, smooth_threshold=4.0, max_smooth_radius=4.0),
    "very_aggressive":dict(preserve_threshold=3.0, smooth_threshold=3.0, max_smooth_radius=8.0),
}

results = {}
for name, params in configs.items():
    seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
        dgrid, atoms,
        mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
        spacing=spacing, compute_connections=False,
        watershed_backend="rust_det", disable_tqdm=True,
        **params,
    )
    results[name] = seg
    print(f"  {name:18s}  raw_maxima={len(seg['all_maxima']):>3d}  "
          f"pbc_grouped={len(seg['maxima_pbc']):>2d}  "
          f"regions_pbc.max={int(seg['regions_pbc'].max()):>2d}")


  no_smoothing        raw_maxima=125  pbc_grouped= 8  regions_pbc.max= 8


  defaults            raw_maxima=125  pbc_grouped= 8  regions_pbc.max= 8


  aggressive          raw_maxima=125  pbc_grouped= 8  regions_pbc.max= 8


  very_aggressive     raw_maxima= 62  pbc_grouped= 4  regions_pbc.max= 4


What you should see on IRMOF-1:

The final PBC-grouped count stays at 8 for the first three configs (well-behaved structure). The fourth config (very aggressive — smooth_threshold=3.0 so essentially everything is smoothed at σ=8) collapses adjacent cage families down to 4 pores because extreme smoothing merges pockets that should be separate.
The raw count (the size of all_maxima, which is the number of voxels flagged as maxima before PBC grouping) is much more sensitive to the parameters. It does not always go down with more smoothing — the smoothed field develops new local maxima, so a very large kernel can create more “hills” than it removes. This is why the defaults matter.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
section: Step 3: Look Directly at the Underlying Rust Detector
text:
Step 3: Look Directly at the Underlying Rust Detector
To isolate the effect of the smoothing parameters from the downstream PBC merge, call the Rust function directly. This is what do_periodic_segmentation_rust does internally before adding the PBC and post-processing steps.


Show code
cell = cellpar_to_cell(atoms.cell.cellpar()).T
voxel_lengths = (spacing, spacing, spacing)   # cubic cell → isotropic

print(f"{'config':18s}  {'raw':>4s}  {'merged':>7s}  {'unmerged':>9s}")
print("-" * 44)
for name, params in configs.items():
    merged, unmerged, raw = mgr_rust.detect_maxima_selective_smoothing_parallel(
        dgrid,
        h=0.2, threshold_abs=1.5, min_distance=1.5,
        cell=cell, voxel_lengths=voxel_lengths,
        **params,
    )
    print(f"{name:18s}  {len(raw):>4d}  {len(merged):>7d}  {len(unmerged):>9d}")


config               raw   merged   unmerged
--------------------------------------------
no_smoothing          64        8         27
defaults             184        8         27
aggressive           304       27         64
very_aggressive      824      178        236



Why the raw count is not monotonic in the smoothing strength. Smoothing a noisy field does not always reduce the number of maxima. A large kernel flattens small bumps but can create broad plateaus that, after h-maxima subtraction, become new maxima. The “right” smoothing is the smallest kernel that suppresses the surface noise — not the largest one. That is why the defaults are conservative: max_smooth_radius=2.0 is calibrated to grid spacing 0.5 Å, the canonical analysis resolution.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
section: Step 4: When to Tune — The Recipes
text:
Step 4: When to Tune — The Recipes
The defaults are calibrated for spacing=0.5 Å with Bondi/CRC VDW radii on typical MOFs (IRMOF-1, UiO-66, ZIF-8, NU-1000, Cu-BTC). Depart from them only when you have a specific complaint about the output.








Symptom
First parameter to change
Why




Over-segmentation — too many tiny pockets, pockets inside large channels, pockets you can see are spurious on the dgrid isosurface
Lower smooth_threshold (e.g. 6.0 → 4.0) and/or raise max_smooth_radius (2.0 → 3.0)
Aggressive smoothing removes the wall roughness that produces spurious maxima.


Missing small pockets — you expect a small cage (e.g. a tetrahedral pocket of radius ~2 Å) but it is gone
Lower preserve_threshold (3.0 → 2.0) or raise smooth_threshold (6.0 → 8.0)
Smoothing is encroaching on the small-feature regime. The “no smoothing” band needs to extend down to the radius of the missing pocket.


Pockets detected in wall / framework
Raise preserve_threshold (3.0 → 4.0)
A higher preserve_threshold extends the “no smoothing” band upward and prevents smoothing from creating peaks inside thick walls.


Default count looks right but you want to verify robustness
Sweep max_smooth_radius from 0 to 4 in steps of 1
A robust result has a plateau of pore count vs max_smooth_radius. If the count drops as soon as you increase it, the original was on a knife-edge.


Slow run on a huge structure
Lower max_smooth_radius to 1.0
Larger kernels cost more per voxel. (This is the only reason to ever reduce max_smooth_radius.)



The four-config sweep above is a useful starting diagnostic. If your real run uses different h and threshold_abs than the canonical 0.2 and 1.5, the count plateau may shift — re-run the sweep at your operating point.

Heads up. All four parameters (h, min_distance, threshold_abs, plus the smoothing trio) interact. If you change one, you usually need to re-tune the others. Start with h and min_distance (they control what counts as a peak); only then consider the smoothing trio (which controls which peaks are real).

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
Step 5: Visualize One Comparison
A picture is worth a thousand len(seg['maxima_pbc']). Compare the defaults and the very aggressive configs to see what over-smoothing actually does.


Show code
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

# Pull out the unit-cell maxima (the first N, where N = regions_pbc.max())
def unit_cell_maxima(seg):
    n = int(seg["regions_pbc"].max())
    return seg["all_maxima"][:n]

fig = go.Figure()
cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel

for name, seg in results.items():
    if name not in ("defaults", "very_aggressive"):
        continue
    maxima = unit_cell_maxima(seg)
    result = mgr.plot_maxima(
        dgrid, maxima, atoms,
        show_spheres=True,
        sphere_opacity=0.6,
        name=f"{name} ({len(maxima)} pores)",
    )
    # plot_maxima returns (scatter_trace, mesh_trace) when show_spheres=True
    if isinstance(result, tuple):
        for tr in result:
            fig.add_trace(tr)
    else:
        fig.add_trace(result)

# Light framework so we can see the cages
mat = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(atoms)
framework_traces = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(
    mat, stylize=True,
    kwargs_frame_mesh={"opacity": 0.25},
)
for tr in framework_traces:
    fig.add_trace(tr)

fig.update_layout(
    scene_aspectmode="data",
    title=dict(
        text="IRMOF-1: defaults vs very-aggressive smoothing",
        x=0.5, xanchor="center", font=dict(color="white", size=16),
    ),
    paper_bgcolor="black",
)
fig.write_image("tutorial_images/selective_smoothing_compare.png", width=1100, height=800)  # static preview for the docs


[TIMING batched_mesh_for_atoms] 472 atoms, 1024 bonds | spheres: 0.00s, cylinders: 0.00s, concat: 0.00s | total faces: 212480


No node props provided, using default set: [position, scaled_position, element and atomic_number]
No edge properties provided. Use the default set: [bond_order, bond_type]





IRMOF-1: defaults vs very-aggressive smoothing








NoteInteractive version





# build `fig` as above, then:
fig.show()   # rotatable Plotly figure
fig.write_html("smoothing_compare.html")



Open the interactive version
You should see two sets of sphere markers — one at the 8 PBC-grouped pockets produced by the defaults, and a smaller set at the 5 collapsed pockets produced by the very-aggressive config.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
section: A Worked Example: Finding the Right smooth_threshold
text:
A Worked Example: Finding the Right smooth_threshold
Here is a practical scan to find the right setting. We vary smooth_threshold (the parameter that controls where the smoothing kicks in) at fixed preserve_threshold=3.0 and max_smooth_radius=2.0:


Show code
print(f"{'smooth_threshold':>16s}  {'raw_maxima':>11s}  {'pbc_grouped':>11s}  {'regions_max':>11s}")
print("-" * 56)
for st in [3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0]:
    seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
        dgrid, atoms,
        mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
        preserve_threshold=3.0, smooth_threshold=st, max_smooth_radius=2.0,
        spacing=spacing, compute_connections=False,
        watershed_backend="rust_det", disable_tqdm=True,
    )
    print(f"{st:>16.1f}  {len(seg['all_maxima']):>11d}  "
          f"{len(seg['maxima_pbc']):>11d}  "
          f"{int(seg['regions_pbc'].max()):>11d}")


smooth_threshold   raw_maxima  pbc_grouped  regions_max
--------------------------------------------------------


             3.0          125            8            8


             4.0          125            8            8


             5.0          125            8            8


             6.0          125            8            8
             7.0          125            8            8


             8.0          125            8            8


For IRMOF-1, the final pore count plateaus at 8 from smooth_threshold=3.0 to 8.0 — IRMOF-1 is robust to this parameter. On a noisier structure (a defective MOF, a structure with adsorbed guest molecules, or a large unit cell with many small cages), you would see the count drop as smooth_threshold falls below the radius of the smallest real pocket.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
Common Pitfalls







Pitfall
Fix




Treating max_smooth_radius as Å
It is a grid-unit factor. With spacing=0.5 and max_smooth_radius=2.0, σ ≈ 1.0 Å. If you switch to spacing=1.0, divide max_smooth_radius by 2 to keep the same physical smoothing.


Smoothing so hard that real pores merge
If regions_pbc.max() drops when you raise max_smooth_radius, you are erasing real features — back off.


Tuning smoothing when h is the actual problem
If over-segmentation is severe, raising h (e.g. 0.2 → 0.4) almost always helps more than tuning smoothing. Smoothing removes spurious maxima; h removes weak maxima. They overlap but are not the same.


Expecting the raw maxima count to monotonically decrease with more smoothing
It does not. A large kernel can create new local maxima in the smoothed field. Trust regions_pbc.max() (the PBC-merged count) as the metric, not the raw size.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
Summary







Concept
What it does




preserve_threshold
Below this dgrid value, smoothing is off — real small pockets are kept.


smooth_threshold
Above this dgrid value, smoothing is at max — large-channel surface noise is removed.


max_smooth_radius
Cap on the Gaussian σ in grid units. Larger = more aggressive smoothing everywhere it is applied.


The three together
Define a piecewise-linear σ(dgrid) ramp from 0 to max_smooth_radius between preserve_threshold and smooth_threshold.



Key takeaways:

The defaults (preserve_threshold=3.0, smooth_threshold=6.0, max_smooth_radius=2.0) are calibrated for spacing=0.5 Å with Bondi/CRC VDW. They work for most MOFs.
The parameters operate on the raw maxima before PBC merging and post-processing. The final PBC-merged count is robust for well-behaved structures even when the raw count varies.
Over-segmentation → lower smooth_threshold or raise max_smooth_radius. Missing small pockets → lower preserve_threshold or raise smooth_threshold.
max_smooth_radius is a grid-unit factor, not Å. Rescale it when you change spacing.

title: Selective Smoothing in MOFography
text:
Next Steps

Quick Start — the canonical three-call pipeline; this tutorial assumes you have read it.
Region Segmentation — the conceptual overview of h-maxima, watershed, and PBC; explains why selective smoothing exists in the first place.
Distance Grid — how the dgrid itself is built; smoothing operates on the dgrid, so the quality of the dgrid bounds the quality of the segmentation.
Connections and Windows — the next step in the pipeline once you have well-segmented regions.

title: Three.js plotting
text:
Mofography has a Three.js backend that mirrors the Plotly plotting API. The scenes are fully interactive (rotate, zoom, layer toggles, lighting, view buttons, measure tool, PNG export) and show up directly inside a notebook, like plotly’s fig.show().
This page uses eval: false blocks, because the documentation site cannot run Python. The screenshots are real renders of the code shown, with the control panel visible. Each scene links to a standalone HTML file you can open and rotate.

title: Three.js plotting
text:
Use in a notebook
Build a Figure3js (alias Figure3JS), chain plot_* calls, and either call .show() or leave the figure as the last expression of a cell:


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from mofography import Figure3js
from ase.io import read

atoms = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(read("examples/TestCIFs/P1-IRMOF-1.cif"))

fig = Figure3js(layout="white").plot_framework_as_mesh_3js(atoms).plot_cell_3js(atoms, color="orange")
fig.show(height=600)          # or just: fig
fig.save_html("irmof1.html")  # standalone file, same controls


How it works:

The scene is embedded as an <iframe srcdoc="..."> with the HTML escaped, so it needs no server and works in Jupyter classic, JupyterLab, VS Code, and static nbconvert or Quarto output. Each figure gets a unique iframe id.
show(height=600, width="100%") sets the size. Outside a Jupyter kernel show() serves the scene on 127.0.0.1 and opens your browser. Force either with show(renderer="notebook") or show(renderer="browser").
show_percolation_threejs(...) returns an HTML string that also renders inline and has .show() and .save_html(path).

Limits:

The scene HTML loads three.js from the jsdelivr CDN, so the viewer needs internet access. Offline or JupyterLite pages without outbound access will show an empty frame.
The whole scene is inside the page. Isosurface scenes are several MB, and a notebook with many figures grows quickly. Use save_html and link to the file for large scenes.
Remote kernels work, because rendering happens in your browser from the notebook output.

title: Three.js plotting
text:
Setup used on this page


Show code
import numpy as np
from mofography.threejs_viz import qualitative_colorscale

sp = 0.5
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=sp).astype(np.float32)
seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid, atoms, spacing=sp, mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5,
    threshold_abs=1.5, compute_connections=True, return_dgrid=True,
)
regions, conns, maxima = seg["regions"], seg["connections"], seg["all_maxima"]
cs = qualitative_colorscale("Pastel")


The plot_*_3js methods on Figure3js mirror the Plotly functions, and each returns the figure, so they chain. plot_framework_as_mesh_3js and plot_cell_3js correspond to plot_framework_as_mesh and plot_cell.

title: Three.js plotting
text:
Everything on one page
The Cu-BTC all-in-one scene puts every layer above into one file, each toggleable from the side panel: unit cell, framework with aromatic rings, surface, regions (no-PBC and PBC merged), pocket types, maxima, windows, pore graph, and a percolated cluster. It is about 8 MB, so it is served as a separate page rather than embedded.
Build a scene like it by adding one call per layer to a single Figure3js and saving once:
import numpy as np
import mofography as mgr
from mofography import Figure3js
from mofography.movies import make_aromatic_rings_trace, make_percolation_clusters_trace
from ase.io import read

atoms = read("P1-Cu-BTC.cif")
fw = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(atoms)
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5).astype(np.float32)
seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(dgrid, atoms, spacing=0.5, mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2,
        min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5, extra_padding=5.0, compute_connections=True,
        return_dgrid=True, disable_tqdm=True)
typed = mgr.assign_pocket_types(seg, atoms, method="env_cluster")

fig = Figure3js(layout="white")
fig.plot_framework_instanced_3js(fw, atom_scale=0.45, name="Framework")
fig.add_traces(make_aromatic_rings_trace(fw))
fig.plot_cell(atoms, color="orange", name="Unit cell")
fig.plot_maxima(seg, atoms, name="Local maxima (PBC)", trace_id="maxima")
fig.plot_surface(seg["dgrid"], seg["regions_pbc"], atoms, isovalue=1.0, name="Regions (PBC merged)",
                 trace_id="surface_regions_pbc", stylize=True)
fig.plot_surface(seg["dgrid"], typed.regions_cluster, atoms, isovalue=1.0, name="Pocket types",
                 trace_id="surface_regions_cluster", stylize=True)
fig.to_html("cubtc_all_in_one.html", pack_binary=True)
The full recipe (pore graph, windows, percolated cluster, Taubin smoothing, which layers start hidden) is scripts/dev/gen_gallery_assets.py::build_cubtc.






NoteAbout the example scenes



The hosted example HTML files (the gallery scenes and the scenes on this page) are slimmed to keep the docs light, a few MB each:

Meshes use full detail at 0.5 Å grid spacing (marching-cubes step_size=1).
Atoms and bonds are instanced spheres and cylinders drawn by the viewer, not per-atom meshes.
Per-vertex hover text on surfaces is off (hover_label="" in plot_surface).
Binary packing is on: to_html(..., pack_binary=True) stores arrays as base64 float32/uint16 blobs, typically 3 to 4 times smaller than JSON lists.

Framework display styles are included through the Representation dropdown (Ball-and-stick, Stick, Space-filling). Each style is its own instanced trace, added with plot_framework_instanced_3js(..., representation="stick") or representation="space_filling", and the dropdown shows only the selected one. In the Cu-BTC scene the region-labelled surfaces (Regions (no PBC), Regions (PBC-merged)) and the pocket types are off by default but can be toggled in the legend.
To turn omitted features back on, see scripts/dev/gen_gallery_assets.py: call add_framework(..., extra_styles=True) for the extra framework styles, lower step_size or keep it at 1 for finer meshes (raise it to shrink files), drop hover_label="" to get per-vertex hover text, and pass visible=True to add_surface (or remove the id from the hide list) for layers that should start visible. Expect larger files.



Background and legend labels
to_html(path, background=...) sets the initial viewer background (default None keeps the standard look). It accepts a hex colour, ("linear", c1, c2, ...) (left to right), ("radial", centre, edge), or a dict {"type": ..., "colors": [...]}. The Bg picker and gradient buttons in the viewer override it, and Export PNG captures it.
fig.to_html("scene.html", pack_binary=True, background="#ffffff")                   # solid
fig.to_html("scene.html", pack_binary=True, background=("linear", "#0d4f55", "#25282d"))
fig.to_html("scene.html", pack_binary=True, background=("radial", "#1d3b73", "#040a1c"))
Give a layer a custom legend text with legend_label on its trace; it replaces the generic label:
for t in fig.data:
    if t.get("id") == "surface":
        t["legend_label"] = "Pore surface (distance grid, isovalue 1.0 A)"
