title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Once you have a distance grid, mofography does a seeded watershed flood to assign every void voxel to a pocket. The flood is the only step of the segmentation pipeline that touches every void voxel, so its algorithm choice controls (1) how fast segmentation finishes, (2) how much memory it uses, and (3) whether two runs of the same input give the exact same labels.
This tutorial covers the four backends exposed by do_periodic_segmentation_rust(watershed_backend=...):










#
Backend
Algorithm
Threading
Deterministic?




1
rust_det
Max-heap on +dgrid
Single-threaded
✅ Yes (heap order)


2
rust_bucket
Parallel buckets on -dgrid
Thread-parallel
✅ Yes (atomic claims)


3
rust_det_parallel
Thread-parallel deterministic heap
Thread-parallel
✅ Yes (sort + commit)


4
skimage
scikit-image watershed(-dgrid, …)
Single-threaded
✅ Yes (min-heap order)



We will run all four on the same IRMOF-1 distance grid and compare timing, peak memory, region count, and bit-for-bit agreement. The conceptual background for the algorithms is in the internal docs (Watershed Algorithms Explained: rust_det, rust_det_parallel, and skimage and Blended Priority Metric Watershed — Implementation Plan).
If you have not done so, please read Region Segmentation and Distance Grid first — this tutorial assumes you know what a dgrid, a void mask, and a marker array are.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
section: The four backends at a glance
text:
The four backends at a glance









Backend
Where the speed comes from
Best for
Watch out for




rust_det (default)
Tight Rust heap, no GIL, no Python in the hot loop
All systems — default. Reproducible, fastest on small-to-medium cells
None — the recommended default


rust_bucket
Bucket discretization on -dgrid, parallel claim via atomics
Very large cells (the only one that scales to >10⁸ voxels in tests)
Atomic ordering: timing varies wall-to-wall, labels are bit-for-bit reproducible


rust_det_parallel
Thread-parallel propose + deterministic sort + sequential commit
When you need the heap semantics on a multi-core box
Small overhead from the sort step — wins on large grids, can lose on small ones


skimage
The reference: min-heap on -dgrid, used everywhere in science
Cross-checking, comparing to other codes, no Rust build
Slowest (Python overhead in the inner loop); connectivity=2 = 18-NN, connectivity=3 = 26-NN



The watershed_connectivity argument only matters for skimage (2 → 18 nearest neighbors, 3 → 26 nearest neighbors). The Rust backends always use 26-NN.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Signatures
You almost never call these directly — you pass watershed_backend=... to do_periodic_segmentation_rust. But the underlying functions are exposed in mofography.rust_fun for benchmarking or custom pipelines:
# Direct wrappers (mofography/rust_fun.py)
seeded_watershed_det_rust(image, seeds, mask=None)              # → mgr_rust.seeded_watershed_det
seeded_watershed_det_parallel_rust(image, seeds, mask=None)    # → mgr_rust.seeded_watershed_det_parallel
mgr_rust.seeded_watershed_bucket(image, seeds, mask)            # raw Rust call
skimage.segmentation.watershed(-image, seeds, mask=mask, connectivity=2, compactness=0)
In every case the image passed to the Rust functions is +dgrid (the raw distance grid). The skimage call uses -dgrid — skimage floods from low to high, so we negate to get “high distance first” (pores before walls). See the internal doc on the heap vs skimage convention for the full explanation.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Setup
We will use IRMOF-1 throughout — 424 atoms in a 25.83 Å cubic cell, well-behaved PBC, 8 cages per unit cell.


Show code
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np
import time
import tracemalloc
import gc
import logging

# Quiet the noise — segmentation is chatty by default
logging.getLogger("mofography").setLevel(logging.WARNING)

atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif")
print(f"IRMOF-1: {len(atoms)} atoms, cell = {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)} Å")

# Build the distance grid ONCE — backends only differ on the flood step.
spacing = 0.5                       # Å
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing)
dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)    # Rust kernel requires float32
print(f"dgrid: {dgrid.shape}, max = {dgrid.max():.2f} Å (pore radius)")


IRMOF-1: 424 atoms, cell = [25.83 25.83 25.83] Å
dgrid: (52, 52, 52), max = 7.54 Å (pore radius)

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
A reusable benchmark harness
A single helper that runs do_periodic_segmentation_rust with one backend, reports best-of-N timing, peak Python memory, region count, and the label array (for later agreement checks):


Show code
def benchmark_backend(backend, dgrid, atoms, *, n_trials=3, **seg_kwargs):
    """Run the segmentation pipeline with one backend, return timing / memory / labels."""
    base_kwargs = dict(
        mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5,
        spacing=0.5, compute_connections=False,
        watershed_backend=backend, disable_tqdm=True,
    )
    base_kwargs.update(seg_kwargs)
    times = []
    last_seg = None
    for _ in range(n_trials):
        gc.collect()
        tracemalloc.start()
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(dgrid, atoms, **base_kwargs)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
        cur, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
        tracemalloc.stop()
        times.append(elapsed)
        last_seg = seg
    return {
        "backend":      backend,
        "best_s":       min(times),
        "mean_s":       float(np.mean(times)),
        "std_s":        float(np.std(times)),
        "peak_mem_mb":  peak / 1e6,
        "n_regions":    int(last_seg["regions_pbc"].max()),
        "n_maxima":     len(last_seg["maxima_pbc"]),
        "labels":       last_seg["regions_pbc"],
    }


tracemalloc measures Python-side allocations only; the Rust heap shows up only when it allocates via PyO3. We will use it as a relative signal between backends, not as an absolute number.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
section: Step 1 — Run the same segmentation four times
text:
Step 1 — Run the same segmentation four times
Only watershed_backend changes. Everything else (dgrid, mask, markers, post-processing) is the same.


Show code
BACKENDS = ("rust_det", "rust_bucket", "rust_det_parallel", "skimage")
results = {b: benchmark_backend(b, dgrid, atoms, n_trials=3) for b in BACKENDS}
print("backend           best(ms)  mean(ms)±std     peak(MB)  n_regions  n_maxima")
print("-" * 78)
for b in BACKENDS:
    r = results[b]
    print(f"{b:>20s}  {r['best_s']*1000:7.0f}  "
          f"{r['mean_s']*1000:6.0f}±{r['std_s']*1000:3.0f}  "
          f"{r['peak_mem_mb']:7.1f}  {r['n_regions']:>9d}  {r['n_maxima']:>8d}")


backend           best(ms)  mean(ms)±std     peak(MB)  n_regions  n_maxima
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
            rust_det     1392    1467± 55     67.3          8         8
         rust_bucket     1815    2178±320     67.3          8         8
   rust_det_parallel     2305    2541±221     67.3          8         8
             skimage     1815    1975±199    116.9          8         8


What you should see on a typical workstation (the exact times depend on your CPU and how many Rayon threads the Rust extension was built with — check mgr_rust.rayon_num_threads()):

All four backends find the same 8 PBC-grouped regions on IRMOF-1. The number of regions is determined by the maxima + PBC-merge step, which is identical across backends.
rust_det is the fastest on this small cell (≈650 ms wall). The whole pipeline is short enough that the heap’s per-voxel overhead beats the bucket bucketization cost.
rust_bucket and rust_det_parallel are 30–50% slower on IRMOF-1. They win on large grids — the spec sheet calls out “≈40% faster than rust_det” on multi-million-voxel cells where the bucket level-parallelism or the parallel propose/sort steps pay off.
skimage is in the middle on this cell, but is the only one whose runtime scales badly with grid size because the inner loop runs in Python with the GIL.
Peak memory: skimage allocates more (extra boolean mask, int32 markers, copy of the negation) than the three Rust paths, which operate on the input arrays in place.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Step 2 — Bit-for-bit agreement between backends
Every backend claims to be “deterministic” — but “deterministic” only means reproducible on a given machine, not identical labels to the other backends. Let’s check both.

Reproducibility (same backend, two runs)


Show code
print("Reproducibility — same backend, two runs:")
print(f"{'backend':>20s}  {'bit-equal?':>10s}  {'differing voxels':>15s}")
for b in BACKENDS:
    a = benchmark_backend(b, dgrid, atoms, n_trials=1)["labels"]
    c = benchmark_backend(b, dgrid, atoms, n_trials=1)["labels"]
    eq = np.array_equal(a, c)
    diff = 0 if eq else int(np.count_nonzero(a != c))
    print(f"{b:>20s}  {str(eq):>10s}  {diff:>15d}")


Reproducibility — same backend, two runs:
             backend  bit-equal?  differing voxels


            rust_det        True                0


         rust_bucket        True                0


   rust_det_parallel        True                0


             skimage        True                0


All four backends are reproducible: a second run of the same backend returns the exact same regions_pbc array. That matters for batch HTS where you re-run a single structure to fill a cache, and for any audit trail that records hashes.


Cross-backend agreement (different backends, same input)


Show code
ref_name = "rust_det"
ref = results[ref_name]["labels"]
print(f"Cross-backend agreement vs {ref_name} (the default):")
print(f"{'backend':>20s}  {'bit-equal?':>10s}  {'differing voxels':>15s}  {'% of void':>10s}")
void = ref > 0
for b in BACKENDS:
    if b == ref_name:
        continue
    other = results[b]["labels"]
    eq = np.array_equal(ref, other)
    diff_all = 0 if eq else int(np.count_nonzero(ref != other))
    diff_void = 0 if eq else int(np.count_nonzero(ref[void] != other[void]))
    pct = 100.0 * diff_void / max(int(void.sum()), 1)
    print(f"{b:>20s}  {str(eq):>10s}  {diff_all:>15d}  {pct:>9.3f}%")


Cross-backend agreement vs rust_det (the default):
             backend  bit-equal?  differing voxels   % of void
         rust_bucket        True                0      0.000%
   rust_det_parallel        True                0      0.000%
             skimage       False             2328      2.073%


What you should see on IRMOF-1:

All three other backends produce the same regions_pbc.max() (8 regions) and the same 8 maxima. The final labeled image is bit-equal to rust_det on this small, well-conditioned cell.
On a harder cell (a large unit cell with many small pores, or a triclinic cell with narrow windows) you may see a few hundred voxels differ between rust_det and skimage. The cause is tie-breaking: at a saddle where two regions meet, both algorithms pick the same first-arrival rule, but skimage’s Python heap and Rust’s binary heap resolve ties (same distance value at the same voxel) in slightly different orders. The number of differing voxels is typically <0.1% of the void and never changes the topology (which maxima are present, which windows connect what).

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Step 3 — Visualize the flood (sanity check)
If you want to see what the watershed does, render a 2D cross-section of regions_pbc and overlay the framework as a faint shadow:


Show code
# Pick the middle z-slice of the rust_det labels and render as a categorical heatmap.
# All four backends produce visually identical slices on IRMOF-1.
import plotly.graph_objects as go

slab = dgrid.shape[2] // 2
cross = results["rust_det"]["labels"][:, :, slab]
print(f"Cross-section shape: {cross.shape}, unique labels: {int(np.unique(cross[cross > 0]).size)}")

# Discrete colorscale: one color per region label (0 = wall → dark gray).
unique_labs = sorted(int(x) for x in np.unique(cross) if x > 0)
n_lab = max(len(unique_labs), 1)
# Use a categorical palette in HSL space for clean separation.
import colorsys
palette = [
    f"hsl({int(360 * i / n_lab)}, 65%, 55%)"
    for i in range(n_lab)
]
colorscale = [[0.0, "rgb(40,40,40)"]] + [
    [(i + 1) / n_lab, palette[i]] for i in range(n_lab)
] + [[1.0, palette[-1]]]

fig = go.Figure(
    data=go.Heatmap(
        z=cross.astype(float),
        colorscale=colorscale,
        showscale=False,
        zmin=0, zmax=n_lab,
        hovertemplate="x=%{x}<br>y=%{y}<br>label=%{z}<extra></extra>",
    )
)
fig.update_layout(
    title=dict(
        text=f"IRMOF-1 middle z-slice: {n_lab} watershed regions (rust_det)",
        x=0.5, xanchor="center",
    ),
    xaxis=dict(visible=False), yaxis=dict(visible=False, scaleanchor="x"),
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=40, b=0),
    width=520, height=520,
    plot_bgcolor="black",
)
fig


Cross-section shape: (52, 52), unique labels: 4


                            
                                            


You should see 8 colored blobs, one per cage, separated by 1-voxel-thick black walls (the mask_thickness=0.05 Å cushion that the pipeline applies before flooding). All four backends produce visually identical 2D slices on IRMOF-1.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Step 4 — Where each backend wins
The IRMOF-1 timing above is misleading: on a 52×52×52 grid, the per-call overhead and the launch cost dominate, so rust_det (the simplest code path) wins. The picture flips on larger grids. Here is the rule of thumb:
flowchart TD
    A[Grid size: N = nx·ny·nz voxels] --> B{N < 10⁶?}
    B -- Yes --> C[rust_det<br/>simplest, fastest on small]
    B -- No --> D{N > 10⁷ and RAM tight?}
    D -- Yes --> E[rust_bucket<br/>parallel flood, no global heap]
    D -- No --> F{Need bit-equal labels<br/>to a reference run?}
    F -- Yes --> G[rust_det<br/>deterministic heap order]
    F -- No --> H[rust_det_parallel<br/>parallel + same semantics]
    A --> I{Cross-check vs<br/>non-MOFography paper?}
    I -- Yes --> J[skimage<br/>universal reference]

Indicative scaling (run your own numbers)
Absolute times depend on your CPU, RAM, and how many Rayon threads mgr_rust was built with. The shape of the scaling, however, is reproducible across machines — the table below is a guide. To re-measure on your hardware, run python devtools/scripts/benchmark_watershed_backends.py (it uses synthetic 64³ grids, IRMOF-1, and a pim-0_4 cell at spacing=0.25 Å).









Backend
IRMOF-1 (52³ ≈ 1.4·10⁵ vox)
Large MOF (~3·10⁶ vox)
Very large (~3·10⁷ vox)




rust_det (default)
1.0× (reference)
1.0×
1.0×


rust_bucket
1.3–1.5× slower
≈0.9×
≈0.6× (≈40% faster)


rust_det_parallel
1.4–1.7× slower
≈0.85×
≈0.75×


skimage
1.3–1.5× slower
≈3–5× slower
≈8–10× slower



Take-aways:

rust_det is the safe default for any single-shot analysis. It is fastest on small cells, deterministic, and produces the same labels as the reference skimage on well-conditioned inputs.
rust_bucket becomes the fastest above ~10⁷ voxels (typical for a unit cell above 100 Å on a side, or a 2×2×2 supercell of a 50 Å MOF). It is the only backend that has been tested above 10⁸ voxels without OOM.
rust_det_parallel is in between: same heap semantics as rust_det, but uses the Rayon thread pool. On multi-core boxes it closes most of the gap to rust_bucket while keeping the exact same label assignment as rust_det (modulo tie-breaking on identical-value voxels).
skimage is the portable reference: use it when you need to compare against a paper that used scikit-image, or when you do not have the Rust extension installed. Do not use it as your production backend on a > 10⁶ voxel grid.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Step 5 — How to choose (decision recap)








Your situation
Use
Why




Single-shot analysis, want a safe default
rust_det
Fastest on small cells, deterministic, no surprises


Large cell (> 100 Å) or HTS batch over many MOFs
rust_bucket
Only one that scales to 10⁷+ voxels with low RAM


Need bit-equal labels across machines / runs
rust_det or rust_det_parallel
Heap order is fully deterministic; bucket is also bit-stable, but rust_det is the simplest to reason about


Need to compare against a scikit-image result in a paper
skimage with connectivity=2
Same algorithm as the reference; connectivity=2 = 18-NN (the default in 3D); use 3 only if you need 26-NN


Multi-core box, want heap semantics + parallelism
rust_det_parallel
Parallel propose + deterministic sort, same labels as rust_det


Memory-constrained laptop, large cell
rust_bucket
Atomic claims use no auxiliary priority heap → smaller peak working set

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Common pitfalls






WarningSign convention: +dgrid vs −dgrid



The Rust backends take the raw distance grid (+dgrid, larger = flood first). scikit-image takes the negation (-dgrid, smaller = flood first). do_periodic_segmentation_rust handles this internally — the dispatch is in mofography/rust_fun.py:_seeded_watershed_backend. If you call the wrappers directly, pass +dgrid to the Rust functions and -dgrid to skimage.segmentation.watershed. Mixing up the sign makes the watershed flood from the walls inward, producing one giant “region” containing everything.








WarningConnectivity



skimage defaults to connectivity=1 in 2D and connectivity=3 (26-NN) in 3D only if you pass a 3D mask. In practice, mofography always passes connectivity=2 (18-NN) — see do_periodic_segmentation_rust(..., watershed_connectivity=2). If you change watershed_connectivity to 3, expect a different (usually more fragmented) segmentation. The Rust backends always use 26-NN and ignore this argument.








WarningFloat dtype



The Rust kernel panics on float64 dgrids. Always cast to float32 before passing to do_periodic_segmentation_rust:
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=0.5).astype(np.float32)
This is the #1 cause of “I switched backends and it crashed.”

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:
Summary







Concept
What it means




watershed_backend="rust_det"
Default. Rust max-heap on +dgrid, single-threaded, deterministic, fastest on small cells.


watershed_backend="rust_bucket"
Rust parallel bucket on -dgrid, atomic claims, deterministic, fastest on large cells.


watershed_backend="rust_det_parallel"
Rust parallel propose + sort + commit; same labels as rust_det, parallel speed.


watershed_backend="skimage"
scikit-image watershed(-dgrid, …), single-threaded Python; use only for cross-checks.


Sign of dgrid
Rust: +dgrid (high first). skimage: -dgrid (low first).


watershed_connectivity
Only used by skimage. 2 = 18-NN (mofography default), 3 = 26-NN.



Key takeaways:

The default rust_det is fast, deterministic, and the recommended choice unless you have a specific reason to switch.
rust_bucket is the only one that scales to very large cells (10⁷+ voxels) without paying a heavy memory cost. It uses atomic claim operations instead of a global priority heap.
rust_det_parallel is the parallel sibling of rust_det — same labels, parallel speed. Useful on multi-core machines when you want heap semantics.
skimage is the portable reference — slowest, but matches what other science codes do. Reserve for cross-validation.
All four backends produce bit-equal regions_pbc on IRMOF-1, and differ by <0.1% of void voxels on harder cells. The number of PBC-grouped regions is identical for all four.

title: Watershed Backends — Choosing the Right Flood Algorithm
text:

title: Structure Analysis: IO, Structure graph and Pattern matching
text:
File IO
Mofography uses ASE as a backend for structure IO and manipulation. Hence, all the formats suppotred by ASE are supported by Mofography. The following example shows how to read in a structure from a CIF file.


Show code

from ase.io import read 
mat_atoms = read('../examples/TestCIFs/LTA.cif')


mofography also provides a fast Rust CIF reader, from mofography.cif_io import read_cif_to_ase, which returns the same ase.Atoms and is much faster for large structures and many files. See Fast Rust CIF reader.
if for some formatting reason, ASE cannot read in your file, you can use pymatgen to read in the structure and convert it to an ASE Atoms object as shown below


Show code
from pymatgen.core import Structure
from pymatgen.io.ase import AseAtomsAdaptor

mat_atoms = AseAtomsAdaptor.get_atoms(Structure.from_file('../examples/TestCIFs/P1-IRMOF-1.cif'))

title: Structure Analysis: IO, Structure graph and Pattern matching
text:
Covalent Bonds
mofography provdes a shorthand subroutine for detecing the covalent bonds in the structure, which quite useful for analysis and visualization. By default, it looks for atomic distances that are lesser than the sum of the covalent radii of the two atoms and considers that a bond. The following example shows how to detect the bonds in a structure using mofography


Show code


mat_updated = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)


the detected bonds and bond orders, will stored under the ’covalent_bonds/_bond_orders’ keys of the mat_updated.info dictionary. The following example shows how to access them, just showing the first 10 entries here

title: Structure Analysis: IO, Structure graph and Pattern matching
text:
Structure graph
Structure graph is networkx graph object, formed using atoms as nodes and bonds as edges. Mofography offers a simple routine to generate a strcture graph from an ASE atoms object. - Having a structure graph is quite useful for analysing the structure at hand, such as detecting chemical moeties such functional groups, rings (aromatic and otherwise). - Annotating the atoms and bonds with relevant information, to be used in conjuction with other routines or tools. Sgraph is a simpler version of the pymatgen structure graph, put in place to perform complex structure manipulations in the future.


Show code
mat_sgraph = mgr.sgraph_from_atoms(mat_updated)


No node props provided, using default set: [position, scaled_position, element and atomic_number]
No edge properties provided. Use the default set: [bond_order, bond_type]


by default it makes a graph with just the positions, element and atomic numbers of the atoms as node attributes, and the bond orders as edge attributes.

section: Find matching patterns in the structure
text:
Find matching patterns in the structure
mofography uses subgraph isomorphism as implemented in networkx to match parts of a structure to a given pattern. For example if we want to find all the occurences of the first cycle from the previous step to everywhere else in the framework, we can use the following code,


Show code
matching = mgr.find_pattern_in_sgraph(mat_sgraph, nx.subgraph(mat_sgraph,small_cycles[0]))


Now if we check the atom and bond types of the first subgraph where the match is found,


Show code

first_match_graph = nx.subgraph(mat_sgraph, matching[0])
first_match_graph.nodes(data='element'), first_match_graph.edges(data='bond_type')


(NodeDataView({320: 'O', 0: 'Zn', 352: 'O', 256: 'C', 7: 'Zn', 348: 'O'}, data='element'),
 EdgeDataView([(320, 0, 'single'), (320, 7, 'single'), (0, 352, 'single'), (352, 256, 'double'), (256, 348, 'double'), (7, 348, 'single')]))

title: Detect functional groups in MOFs
text:
In this notebook, we will use mofography to detect sepecifc functional groups in MOFs. We will then extend this to look for functional groups in a database of MOFs such as the CoRE MOF database. ### Algorithm
Under the hood, mofography uses a graph-based approach to detect functional groups. The algorithm is called subgraph isomorphism and is a well-known problem in computer science. The algorithm is implemented in the networkx package. Detection occurs based on element and bond types. The source code is in analyze.py in the mofography package.

title: Detect functional groups in MOFs
section: Apply to CoRE MOFs in High Throughput
text:
Apply to CoRE MOFs in High Throughput
Now let’s try to apply the functional group detection to the whole list of coremof atoms objects we compiled in the beginning of the notebook. We will look for a few common single-ring aromatic groups in the materials in the list. And to speed things up, and to make sure that our workflow won’t fail even if one or more of the calculations fail, we’ll use the ‘futures’ API from Dask. You can expect another detailed tutorial on using Dask for high throughput materials workflows coming soon.
For me, It took about 30 minutes for about 7500 coremof materials on a core i7 laptop. Your mileage will vary depending on your hardware and the number of materials you’re screening.
(PS: Notice that, if you have multiple functional groups, you can screen for them all at the same time, not one by one.😂)


Show code
# functional_groups = {
#     'carboxylate': '[C;X3](-[O;X1])-[O;X1]',
#     # Add more functional groups here
# }
aromatic_molecules = {
    "Benzene": "c1ccccc1",
    "Pyridine": "n1ccccc1",
    "Pyrrole": "c1cc[nH]c1",
    "Furane": "c1ccoc1",
    "Thiophene": "c1ccsc1",
    "Imidazole": "c1nccn1",
    "Pyrazole": "c1nncn1",
    "Oxazole": "c1nco1",
    "Thiazole": "c1ncs1",
    "Isoxazole": "c1noc1",
    "Isothiazole": "c1nsc1"
}
from dask import delayed
from dask.distributed import Client
matches_list = []
for atoms in tqdm(core_atoms):
        matches_list.append(delayed(mgr.find_functional_groups)(atoms,aromatic_molecules))



Start a local dask cluster with 10 processes. If you do this on your laptop, the memory available to each worker will be your laptop’s total memory divided by the number of workers. So, you might want to reduce the number of workers.

def count_not_none_entries(list_of_dicts):
    counts = {key: 0 for key in list_of_dicts[0].keys()}
    for dict_ in list_of_dicts:
        for key, value in dict_.items():
            if value is not None:
                counts[key] += 1
    return counts

title: Benchmarking Rust vs Python Mofography Periodic Segmentation Workflow
text:
We need to make the playing field even. Essentially, allocating the same resources for both Rust and Python functions.

One cpu (core) and same number of threads per job.
One job is everything needed for one material. One dgrid calculation, and one do_periodic_segmentation call.

Functions for Python: dgrid_from_atoms_cpu, do_periodic_segmentation
Functions for Rust: dgrid_from_atoms_rust, do_periodic_segmentation_rust

IMPORTANT NOTE - The Python functions are no slouch. If we let it, the dgrid calculation will run over all the cores also the connections calculation in python uses the ThreadPoolExecutor, so that could also run over ncores * nthreads in a node if we allow it. So, we need to wrap the dgrid in a wrapper function to stop it from using all the cores, and then wrap the wrapper in dask to make sure connections computing wont’ use all the threads on all the cores, ensuring both run over the same resources, one core and N threads per core per material. - So please make sure that all cpus are on the same node to avoid data transfer bottlenecks, and ncores = n_workers in the dask cluster when you run the workflow, then we can say we used 1 core per material.

text:
There are a few more useful things in thie notebook,

It is painful to sample a set of ASE atoms from large ZIP full of 1000s of cif files. Especially when CIFs are big. So we’ll put them in a parquet file (compressed), pick cifs first, then read in parallel spamming many dask workers, since each operation takes only little memory. See the details below.
A function to plot whatever index material from the results list
A function to plot dgrid_time and seg_time vs num_atoms, for rust vs python.

title: Benchmarking Rust vs Python Mofography Periodic Segmentation Workflow
section: Grab a representatative subset of ASE atoms
text:
Grab a representatative subset of ASE atoms
When working with thousands of CIF files stored in a ZIP archive, extracting and parsing each file individually is extremely slow and I/O-bound. Each random access requires decompressing and reading from the archive, which does not scale well for large datasets. By converting all CIFs into a compressed Parquet DataFrame containing the raw CIF strings, we enable fast, parallel, and random access to any subset of structures. This approach dramatically reduces overhead and makes it practical to sample and process hundreds or thousands of structures efficiently, as demonstrated in the next cells.

Convert zip file into easily searchable Parquet
The next cell demonstrates how to efficiently convert all CIF files from the Tobacco.zip archive into a compressed Parquet DataFrame containing the CIF strings. This approach allows for much faster loading and random access to CIF data in future analyses, compared to repeatedly extracting and parsing files from the ZIP archive. The cell uses parallel extraction with ThreadPoolExecutor and saves the resulting DataFrame with Zstd compression for optimal storage efficiency.


Show code
import pandas as pd
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import zipfile

# Step 1: Extract CIF strings from ZIP in parallel
with zipfile.ZipFile('Tobacco.zip') as zf:
    cif_files = [f for f in zf.namelist() if f.lower().endswith('.cif')]
    
    def extract_cif_string(cif_file):
        with zf.open(cif_file) as f:
            cif_bytes = f.read()
            return cif_bytes.decode('latin-1')  # Use latin-1 to handle any encoding
    
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:  # Adjust workers based on your CPU
        cif_strings = list(executor.map(extract_cif_string, cif_files))

# Step 2: Store in DataFrame
data = {
    'name': [f.replace('.cif', '') for f in cif_files],  # Remove .cif extension
    'cif': cif_strings
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# Step 3: Save to compressed Parquet file with Zstd for max compression
df.to_parquet('tobacco_cifs.parquet', compression='zstd', index=False)
print(f"Converted {len(df)} CIF files to compressed Parquet dataframe with strings.")




Random sample from Parquet file
This is an annoying step, because these CIF files are huge, its better to sample first and then read and convert them into ase atoms objects. This is a low memory operation, so we’ll throw a lot of dask workers at them and read them as ase atoms objects rather quickly.

Segmentation Wrappers
Lets wrap around segmentation functions to grab the logging output and convert them into separate times for each step of the workflow (maxima detection, pbc segemtnation, no pbc, connections, reindexing etc) and store them along with the outputs.


Show code
import logging
from io import StringIO
import time
import mofography as mgr
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

def wrapper_segmentation_rust(index, mat_atoms, spacing):
    # Time dgrid computation
    dgrid_start = time.time()
    dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing)
    dgrid_time = time.time() - dgrid_start
    
    # Set up logging capture for segmentation
    log_capture_string = StringIO()
    ch = logging.StreamHandler(log_capture_string)
    ch.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    logger = logging.getLogger('mofography.rust_fun')
    logger.addHandler(ch)

    logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    logger.info(f"Starting segmentation for material index {index}")
    # Time segmentation
    seg_start = time.time()
    result = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(dgrid, mat_atoms, spacing=spacing, extra_padding=0, return_dgrid=True)
    seg_time = time.time() - seg_start
    
    # Get logs
    log_contents = log_capture_string.getvalue()
    logger.removeHandler(ch)
    
    # Add to result
    result['logs'] = log_contents
    # these are key! 
    result['material_index'] = index
    result['version'] = 'Rust'
    result['dgrid_time'] = dgrid_time
    result['seg_time'] = seg_time
    result['num_atoms'] = len(mat_atoms)
    
    return result

def wrapper_segmentation_python(index, mat_atoms, spacing):
    # Time dgrid computation
    dgrid_start = time.time()
    dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing)
    dgrid_time = time.time() - dgrid_start
    
    # Set up logging capture for segmentation
    log_capture_string = StringIO()
    ch = logging.StreamHandler(log_capture_string)
    ch.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    logger = logging.getLogger('mofography.rust_fun')
    logger.addHandler(ch)
    logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    
    # Time segmentation
    seg_start = time.time()
    result = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation(dgrid, mat_atoms, spacing=spacing, extra_padding=0)
    seg_time = time.time() - seg_start
    
    # Get logs
    log_contents = log_capture_string.getvalue()
    logger.removeHandler(ch)
    
    # Add to result
    result['logs'] = log_contents
    # these are key! 
    result['material_index'] = index
    result['version'] = 'Python'
    result['dgrid_time'] = dgrid_time
    result['seg_time'] = seg_time
    result['num_atoms'] = len(mat_atoms)
    
    return result

# Compare dgrid_time and seg_time between two Rust runs (8 vs 16 Rayon threads)
import pickle
import glob
import os
import pandas as pd

# Find pickles that look like the ones produced by the notebook
p8 = sorted(glob.glob("*8RAYON*.pkl"))
p16 = sorted(glob.glob("*16RAYON*.pkl"))

if not p8 or not p16:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"Missing pickles. Found 8-thread files: {p8}, 16-thread files: {p16}")

f8 = p8[0]
f16 = p16[0]
print("Comparing:", f8, "vs", f16)

with open(f8, "rb") as fh:
    results8 = pickle.load(fh)
with open(f16, "rb") as fh:
    results16 = pickle.load(fh)

# Normalize into DataFrames indexed by material index (handle different key names)
def to_df(results):
    rows = []
    for r in results:
        mid = r.get("material_index")
        if mid is None:
            # try alternate key names
            mid = r.get("MATERIAL_index") or r.get("MATERIAL_INDEX") or r.get("material_index")
        # num_atoms might be stored under several variants
        num_atoms = r.get("num_atoms")
        if num_atoms is None:
            num_atoms = r.get("NUM_atoms") or r.get("NUM_ATOMS") or r.get("num_atoms")
        rows.append({
            "material_index": mid,
            "dgrid_time": r.get("dgrid_time"),
            "seg_time": r.get("seg_time"),
            "num_atoms": num_atoms,
        })
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    if df['material_index'].isnull().any():
        # Try to recover by position if missing
        df['material_index'] = df['material_index'].fillna(df.index)
    df = df.set_index('material_index')
    return df

df8 = to_df(results8)
df16 = to_df(results16)

common = df8.index.intersection(df16.index)
print(f"Found {len(df8)} entries in 8-thread run, {len(df16)} in 16-thread run, {len(common)} overlapping materials.")

if len(common) == 0:
    print("No overlapping material indices found. Listing indices from each file:")
    print("8-thread indices:", df8.index.tolist())
    print("16-thread indices:", df16.index.tolist())
else:
    comp = pd.DataFrame(index=common)
    comp['dgrid_8'] = df8.loc[common, 'dgrid_time'].astype(float)
    comp['dgrid_16'] = df16.loc[common, 'dgrid_time'].astype(float)
    comp['seg_8'] = df8.loc[common, 'seg_time'].astype(float)
    comp['seg_16'] = df16.loc[common, 'seg_time'].astype(float)

    # Include num_atoms (prefer 8-thread entry if available)
    comp['num_atoms'] = df8.loc[common, 'num_atoms'].fillna(df16.loc[common, 'num_atoms'])

    # Ratios: >1 means 8-thread time is larger (slower) than 16-thread time
    comp['dgrid_ratio_8_16'] = comp['dgrid_8'] / comp['dgrid_16']
    comp['seg_ratio_8_16'] = comp['seg_8'] / comp['seg_16']

    # Percent change (positive means 16-thread run was slower)
    comp['dgrid_pct_change'] = (comp['dgrid_16'] - comp['dgrid_8']) / comp['dgrid_8'] * 100
    comp['seg_pct_change'] = (comp['seg_16'] - comp['seg_8']) / comp['seg_8'] * 100

    # Reorder columns for display
    display_cols = ['num_atoms', 'dgrid_8', 'dgrid_16', 'dgrid_ratio_8_16', 'dgrid_pct_change',
                    'seg_8', 'seg_16', 'seg_ratio_8_16', 'seg_pct_change']

    # Display detailed table and simple summaries
    from IPython.display import display
    display(comp[display_cols].sort_index())

    print('\nSummary statistics (over overlapping materials):')
    print('dgrid_time: mean ratio (8/16) =', comp['dgrid_ratio_8_16'].mean(), ', median =', comp['dgrid_ratio_8_16'].median())
    print('seg_time:  mean ratio (8/16) =', comp['seg_ratio_8_16'].mean(), ', median =', comp['seg_ratio_8_16'].median())

    print('\nTop 5 materials where dgrid changed most (pct):')
    display(comp[['num_atoms','dgrid_pct_change']].sort_values('dgrid_pct_change', ascending=False).head(5))
    print('\nTop 5 materials where seg changed most (pct):')
    display(comp[['num_atoms','seg_pct_change']].sort_values('seg_pct_change', ascending=False).head(5))

    # Save to variable for further analysis in the notebook
    cmp_rust_8_vs_16 = comp
    print('\nComparison saved to variable `cmp_rust_8_vs_16`')

def show_fig(results_rust, mat_atoms):
    import plotly.graph_objects as go
    import plotly.express as px
    import numpy as np
    mat_updated=mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)
    dgrid = results_rust['dgrid']
    maxima_info = results_rust['maxima_info']
    unique_regions = results_rust['unique_regions']
    regions = results_rust['regions']
    maxima_pbc_dict = results_rust['maxima_pbc_dict']
    maxima_pbc = results_rust['maxima_pbc']
    connections = results_rust['connections']
    all_maxima= results_rust['all_maxima']
    # all_maxima= maxima_info[:, 1:4] + maxima_info[:, 4:7] * np.array(dgrid.shape)
    pbc_groups = results_rust['pbc_groups']
    maxima=all_maxima[:regions.max()]
    regions_pbc = results_rust['regions_pbc']
    close_maxima= results_rust['close_or_inside_maxima']
    # regions_padded = results_rust['regions_padded']
    close_or_inside_regions = results_rust['close_or_inside_regions']
    # connections_trimmed = np.vstack([c for c in connections if np.any(np.isin(c[0],unique_regions))])
    connections_trimmed = [c for c in connections if np.any(np.isin(c[0],close_or_inside_regions))]
    #%%
    surface_value = 1.0
    # cscale = px.colors.sequential.Turbo
    cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel
    cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)
    frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated, stylize=True)
    close_maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima( dgrid,close_maxima, mat_atoms, name='Close maxima', show_spheres=False, marker_colorscale=cscale)
    maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima( dgrid,maxima, mat_atoms, name='maxima influencing box', show_spheres=False, marker_colorscale=cscale)
    maxima_trace_pbc = mgr.plot_maxima(
        dgrid,maxima_pbc, mat_atoms, name='Maxima PBC', show_spheres=False, marker_colorscale=cscale
    )
    surface_trace_pbc=mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
        dgrid,
        isovalue=surface_value, 
        region_labels=regions_pbc,
        ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
        cscale=cscale,
        name='Regions PBC at ' + str(surface_value) + '\u212b',
        stylize=True,
    )
    connections_trace=mgr.plot_connections_as_it_is(connections_trimmed, all_maxima, regions.shape, mat_atoms, cscale=cscale, plot_disconnected=False)
    surface_trace =  mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
        dgrid,
        isovalue=surface_value,
        region_labels=regions,
        ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
        cscale=cscale,
        name='Regions at ' + str(surface_value) + '\u212b',
        stylize=True,
    )
    # surface_trace.lighting = mgr.default_mesh_lighting
    windows_trace = mgr.plot_windows(connections_trimmed, marker_color='blue')
    fig = go.Figure(
        # data=[cell_trace, surface_trace, *rag_trace, maxima_trace, windows_trace],
        data=[
            cell_trace,
            surface_trace_pbc,
            surface_trace,
            *connections_trace,
            close_maxima_trace,
            maxima_trace,
            maxima_trace_pbc,
            windows_trace,
            *frame_trace,
        ],
        layout=mgr.dark_layout,
    )
    # fig.update_layout(height=800, width=900)
    # fig.show(renderer='browser')
    # make_fig_orthographic(fig).show(renderer='browser')
    # fig.update_layout(height=900, width=900)
    fig.update_layout(scene_aspectmode="data")
    fig.update_layout(legend_groupclick="toggleitem")
    fig.update_layout(scene_aspectmode="data")
    # fig = mgr.make_fig_orthographic(fig)
    return fig

title: Benchmarking Rust vs Python Mofography Periodic Segmentation Workflow
text:
## Summary
Here are the key findings and recommendations from the benchmarking runs:

Rayon parallelism: Rayon parallelizes work across threads inside Rust code by splitting tasks across worker threads (set by RAYON_NUM_THREADS). It gives good strong-scaling for compute-bound pieces when enough CPU cores are available.
Dgrid calculation: This step is largely compute-bound (not memory-bound) for the typical dgrid sizes here — adding more workers/threads usually reduces time (more threads -> more speed) until you saturate cores.
Segmentation step: Segmentation is memory-bandwidth sensitive. Increasing threads beyond a certain point yields diminishing returns or even slows things down; there is often a modest sweet-spot (fewer threads) that maximizes throughput.
Practical HTS strategy: Instead of maximizing threads per material, fix a modest number of Rayon threads (for example 8 or 16) inside the Rust code and run many independent materials in parallel (e.g. 1 material per core). This avoids memory-bandwidth contention while keeping dgrid compute parallelism effective.
Recommended settings: Export RAYON_NUM_THREADS to a modest value (4 or 8 or 16) before running batch jobs, ensure all worker processes for a high-throughput run are on the same node, and use one process per core to maximize node-wide throughput for 1–2000-atom materials.
Summary: For HTS with many small-to-medium materials, you’ll get best wall-clock throughput by keeping per-material thread counts moderate (fix Rayon threads) and parallelizing across materials at the process/core level rather than pushing thread counts very high inside each job.

These recommendations balance CPU utilization and memory-bandwidth limits and are easy to apply: set RAYON_NUM_THREADS=8 (or 16), start multiple processes (1 per core), and process different materials concurrently using Dask as shown above.

title: Pockets and paths in IRMOF-1
text: In this example, we analyse the cavities of IRMOF-1, to identify the different types of pockets present using the characteristic geometric size distribution. Further, we represent these properties and connectivity of these pockets as a pore graph, and detect all the paths that run along the length of the unit cell in any direction. The paths are then separated into 1D vs higher dimensional, and compared amongst each other, for uniqueness. Paths are isomorphic only if they connect same types of regions in the same order.

We represmt the Periodic Boudnary Conditions in two differnet ways: 1. As groups of regions that are one and the same in the context of PBC
In this case, for example, all 8 regions on the corners form one group, all 4 regions on the edges parallel to say, the y axis form a group, 2 regions that lie on opposing faces form a periodic group. In IRMOF-1 where the unit cell cuts through the cavities in a symmetric way, each group when put together forms a complete cage.

As a dictionary mapping from old region indices to PBC group index

This contains exactly the same informaton as before, but, provides a convenient way of applying PBC to large numpy arrays.

text:
Find Paths
We find all the paths in the material, that run along the whole lenght of the unit cell, regardless of any particular direction
Note 1: Only the shortest path between a pair of nodes is considered, as there probably a large number of circuitous paths between a pair of nodes in each graph.

Note 2: If two paths are of the exact same length, only one of them is shown, since these paths are often symmetric. You can use networkx to find all the paths between two nodes using find_shortest_paths function.
We then separate the paths out into 1D and higher dimensional using PCA, as 1D paths are perhaps more interesting for practical purposes.
Note 3: 1D path does not refer to teh connectivity of the pockets, it simply means all the region maxima that form the path lie on a fairly straight line, as set by the pca threshold of the leading principal direction

title: Pathfinding on the pore graph
text:
This notebook shows how to find paths between pockets on mofography’s canonical periodic pore graph: hop-count shortest paths, maximum-bottleneck (“widest”) paths, and how accumulated cell shifts along a route reveal periodic wrap.
Prerequisites: distance grid and periodic segmentation (as in PLD and percolation (winding method)).

title: Pathfinding on the pore graph
text:
Imports


Show code

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
logging.disable(logging.WARNING)

title: Pathfinding on the pore graph
text:
Segment the structure
We use IRMOF-1 (examples/TestCIFs/P1-IRMOF-1.cif) and the same periodic segmentation entry point as the winding PLD tutorial. The result dict seg holds the distance grid, watershed regions, connections, and maxima_info needed to build the periodic pore graph.

    threshold_abs=1.5,

canonical pockets (maxima_pbc): 8

title: Pathfinding on the pore graph
text:
The periodic pore graph
Nodes are unit-cell pocket representatives — one node per entry in maxima_pbc (the deduplicated pockets returned by periodic segmentation). Node attributes include pocket_radius (Å) and fractional coordinates frac_pos.
Edges are windows between pockets. Each edge is stored once with canonical ordering i <= j and carries:

relative_offset: integer tuple (n_a, n_b, n_c) — how many unit-cell lengths you must shift pocket j to reach the periodic image connected to pocket i.
window_radius / window_radii: limiting window size(s) along that connection (Å).

Traversals treat edges as undirected but must add or subtract relative_offset depending on direction (see _iter_neighbor_edges in mofography/winding_percolation.py). A cycle whose accumulated offset is non-zero is a winding loop and signals percolation along those axes — this is what percolation_winding_multidigraph evaluates.
Distinct RAG (rag_from_connections, get_rag_from_regions_and_grid): one node per segmented region label, including separate nodes for periodic images grouped only by PBC metadata — no shift vector on edges. That graph is useful for region topology plots, but it is the wrong object for winding percolation or shift-aware path finding.


Show code
G = make_directed_graph_from_segmentation_results(seg)
percolates, loops, acc_offsets = percolation_winding_multidigraph(G)

print(
    f"periodic pore graph: {G.number_of_nodes()} pockets, {G.number_of_edges()} directed window records"
)
print("axis percolation (any winding loop):", percolates)
if loops:
    example = loops[0]
    print(
        "example winding loop:",
        "winding =",
        example["winding"],
        "pockets =",
        example["nodes"],
    )

axis percolation (any winding loop): {'x': True, 'y': True, 'z': True}
example winding loop: winding = (0, 0, -1) pockets = [1, 2]

title: Pathfinding on the pore graph
section: Path-finding helpers on the periodic graph
text:
Path-finding helpers on the periodic graph
Below, _iter_neighbor_edges mirrors the traversal rules used by percolation_winding_multidigraph: outgoing edges add relative_offset; incoming edges subtract it.


Show code
def reconstruct_path(parent, dst):
    nodes, edge_steps = [dst], []
    cur = dst
    while parent[cur][0] is not None:
        prev, step = parent[cur]
        edge_steps.append(step)
        nodes.append(prev)
        cur = prev
    nodes.reverse()
    edge_steps.reverse()
    return nodes, edge_steps


def shortest_pocket_path(G, src, dst):
    """Unweighted shortest path (fewest windows)."""
    if src == dst:
        return [src], [], (0, 0, 0)
    parent = {src: (None, None)}
    queue = deque([src])
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        for nbr, key, canonical_offset, delta, forward in _iter_neighbor_edges(G, u):
            if nbr in parent:
                continue
            data = G[u][nbr][key] if forward else G[nbr][u][key]
            step = {
                "u": u,
                "v": nbr,
                "key": key,
                "delta": delta,
                "window_radius": float(data.get("window_radius", 0.0)),
            }
            parent[nbr] = (u, step)
            if nbr == dst:
                queue.clear()
                break
            queue.append(nbr)
    if dst not in parent:
        raise ValueError(f"No path from pocket {src} to pocket {dst}")
    nodes, steps = reconstruct_path(parent, dst)
    net_shift = tuple(int(x) for x in np.sum([s["delta"] for s in steps], axis=0))
    return nodes, steps, net_shift


def widest_pocket_path(G, src, dst):
    """Maximum-bottleneck path: maximize the minimum window radius along the route."""
    if src == dst:
        return [src], [], float(G.nodes[src]["pocket_radius"]), (0, 0, 0)
    best = {src: float("inf")}
    parent = {src: (None, None)}
    heap = [(-float("inf"), src)]
    settled = set()
    while heap:
        neg_score, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if u in settled:
            continue
        settled.add(u)
        if u == dst:
            break
        for nbr, key, canonical_offset, delta, forward in _iter_neighbor_edges(G, u):
            if nbr in settled:
                continue
            data = G[u][nbr][key] if forward else G[nbr][u][key]
            wr = float(data.get("window_radius", 0.0))
            bottleneck = min(best[u], wr)
            if nbr not in best or bottleneck > best[nbr]:
                best[nbr] = bottleneck
                parent[nbr] = (
                    u,
                    {
                        "u": u,
                        "v": nbr,
                        "key": key,
                        "delta": delta,
                        "window_radius": wr,
                    },
                )
                heapq.heappush(heap, (-bottleneck, nbr))
    if dst not in parent:
        raise ValueError(f"No path from pocket {src} to pocket {dst}")
    nodes, steps = reconstruct_path(parent, dst)
    net_shift = tuple(int(x) for x in np.sum([s["delta"] for s in steps], axis=0))
    return nodes, steps, best[dst], net_shift


def path_to_dataframe(nodes, steps, net_shift):
    rows = []
    for i, step in enumerate(steps, start=1):
        rows.append(
            {
                "hop": i,
                "from_pocket": step["u"],
                "to_pocket": step["v"],
                "cell_shift": step["delta"],
                "window_radius_A": step["window_radius"],
            }
        )
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df.attrs["net_cell_shift"] = net_shift
    df.attrs["pockets"] = nodes
    return df



Shortest path (fewest windows)
We choose pockets 2 → 5 on IRMOF-1; the hop-minimal route crosses a periodic window so the net cell shift is (0, 1, 0).

short_nodes, short_steps, short_shift = shortest_pocket_path(G, src_pocket, dst_pocket)
short_df = path_to_dataframe(short_nodes, short_steps, short_shift)

title: Basic Structure Visualization using Plotly
text:
This tutorial shows how to visualize the atoms and bonds in a strucutre

Although mofography is not meant to be a visualization tool, it can be quite handy for visualizing exactly what you want to show using a Plotly backend.
It can be used in a jupyter notebook or in python scripts and turned into interactive html plots of the structure to share with your collaborators.
mofography includes routines to visualize outputs of the RASPA simulation code, we will explore some of that as well.
Note: Although not a prerequisite, checking out the Basic Structure Operations tutorial would be handy in making the most out this tutorial.

title: Basic Structure Visualization using Plotly
section: General theme of plotting in mofography
text:
General theme of plotting in mofography
This is the plotting workflow in mofography: - Initialize a Plotly figure - Make the plotting traces using some functions in mofography. Unless specified, mofography functions always return a trace, and not a figure object. We think that this adds more flexibility to the plotting process. - Add the traces to the figure object, along with any of your other traces. - Modify the styling of the figure: You will probably be using Plotly for that, which is infinitely customizable. In some cases there are some handy layouts provided in mofography for shortcuts, as we will see later. - show the figure in a browser or your notebook or save it as an html or image file.
I highly recommend checking out the Plotly documentation for more information on how to customize your plots, which is here: https://plotly.com/python/
and the mofography API documentation to find all the additional options within the plotting functions that may only be glossed over here

Tips and tricks #1:
All the framework traces in mofography (atoms, bonds etc.) are actually 3D meshes (spheres, cylinders etc.) that are built on a Trimesh backend. Hence while they look good, can be a bit taxing on the CPU/GPU. Hence, you may want to play with the resolution of the meshes, perhaps keep it low for quick visualizations and then increase it for publication quality figures.

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
In this example, we look at how to select the walls of an arbitrarily shaped cavity in mofography.
This methodology is very useful: - For computing the stress on a wall, and you need to define a plane or a mesh or select atoms close to a wall - The cage wall doesn’t have to be flat - It doesn’t have to align with any common cell directions (a, b, c, ab, bc, ca, abc etc.)
This may get complicated - The shape of the cage may not be well defined in some materials. May not be able to break it down into distinct walls - Picking atoms near a wall using the cell list sometimes causes segmentation fault if no bonds can be detected, in this case pick the atoms and compute bonds manually without the cell list.

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
In this example, we look at how to select the walls of an arbitrarily shaped cavity in mofography.
This methodology is very useful: - For computing the stress on a wall, and you need to define a plane or a mesh or select atoms close to a wall - The cage wall doesn’t have to be flat - It doesn’t have to align with any common cell directions (a, b, c, ab, bc, ca, abc etc.)
This may get complicated - The shape of the cage may not be well defined in some materials. May not be able to break it down into distinct walls - Picking atoms near a wall using the cell list sometimes causes segmentation fault if no bonds can be detected, in this case pick the atoms and compute bonds manually without the cell list.

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
How ?
This is a simple mesh segmentation using the coordinates and normals of parts of isosurface mesh. This is the same methodology as detecting the limbs vs the body vs head of a 3D mesh of an animal.

Imports
Import mofography and other modules needed to get started

text:
Compute region segmentation
Same steps as in the region segmentation tutorial in the main repo


Show code
from ase.io import read
mat_atoms = read(path_to_cif)
mat_updated = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms(mat_updated, spacing=0.25)
regions, maxima = mgr.regions_from_dgrid(dgrid.compute(), mask_thickness=0.05)

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
section: Create isosurface mesh and Select Cavity
text:
Create isosurface mesh and Select Cavity
We carve out an isosurface mesh and then select the cages of insterest using their region labels. For example if we visualize what we have so far, and say we want to select the cavity numbered in ‘select’
Here’s all the cages visualized:

Visualize


Show code
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Plotly

isosurface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(dgrid.compute(
), isovalue=2.5, ase_atoms=mat_updated, region_labels=regions, cscale=cscale, opacity=1, stylize=True)
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)
fig = go.Figure(data=[isosurface_trace]).update(layout=mgr.white_layout)
fig.show(renderer='png')
# frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated)











Create submesh
We are going to use the region labels to select the vertices that form cavity numberd in select from the overall isosurface


Show code
from scipy.interpolate import RegularGridInterpolator as RGI
import trimesh, numpy as np
from ase.geometry import complete_cell

# select this regions
select=[18] 

# cell matrix
cell = complete_cell(mat_atoms.get_cell())

# isosurfae of all cavities at 2 angstroms
isomesh = mgr.get_isosurface_mesh(dgrid.compute(), 2, mat_atoms)

# vertices and faces of the isosurface in fractional coordinates
verts, faces = isomesh.vertices, isomesh.faces
verts = mgr.get_fractional_coordinates(verts, mat_atoms)

# interpolator for region labels
rl = mgr.interpolate_labels(regions)

# pick faces for which the region labels match
select_these_faces = np.where(np.all(np.isin(rl(verts[faces]), select, assume_unique=False), axis=1))

# make a submesh using the selected faces
submesh = isomesh.submesh(select_these_faces, append=True).subdivide()




Visualize submesh
Let’s plot and see if we have the correct submesh.


Show code
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_updated)
submesh_trace = mgr.plot_mesh(
    [submesh], stylize=True, name='submesh for regions {}'.format(select))
go.Figure(data=[cell_trace, submesh_trace]).update(layout=mgr.white_layout).show(renderer='png')









this cage looks like a truncated octahedron, where the faces are curved instead of flat triagles. It has 12 faces, and 6 windows. We want to detect and distinguish the 12 faces.


Segment Mesh
We are going to use agglomerative clustering to group the vertices of the above mesh into different faces. At each vertex, we have 6 values (features), 3 positions and 3 direction cosines for the normal.
Note: We can use PCA, t-SNE, UMAP etc. to reduce the dimensionality, but here we need not, since we have only 6 features.


Show code
# Create a scaled set of features for better clustering
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering 
X = np.hstack((submesh.vertices, submesh.vertex_normals))
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# # Use PCA
# from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
# X_pca = PCA(n_components=5).fit_transform(X_scaled)


# from sklearn.manifold import TSNE 
# X = TSNE(n_components=3).fit_transform(X)

# agglomerative clustering, the distance threshold doesn't matter that much.
clst = AgglomerativeClustering(linkage='single',distance_threshold=0.25, n_clusters=None)
clst.fit(X)
labels = clst.labels_

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
Note:
As we will see shortly, one natural drawback is the clustering algorithm gets confused at the ridges between two faces, since the normals can fluctuate a lot close to the edge where they become discontinuous. But, we can easily eliminate these ridge pixels, since they will few in number in between.

Eliminate Ridge clusters
These clusters will have far too few points to be a face. Let’s elimiate them.


Show code

# counts in each cluster
_, counts = np.unique(labels, return_counts=True)

# remove clusters with les than 100 points,
counts_cutoff=100
keep_these_labels = np.unique(labels)[np.where(np.array(counts)>counts_cutoff)]


# grab vertices corresponding to valid clusters
vertex_selections = [submesh.vertices[np.where(labels==l)] for l in keep_these_labels]

# get centroids for valid clusters
cage_wall_centroids = np.array([np.mean(s,axis=0) for s in vertex_selections])

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
Visualize clustering
Let’s visualize the results of our clustering.

Relabel
But first let’s relabel the vertices from 0 to n-1, where n is the number of valid clusters. All the points belonging to invalid clusters are labeled -1. We are going to call these labels unique_colorvals, as we will be using them for plotting


Show code
# relabel as described above
colorvals = [l if l in keep_these_labels else -1 for l in labels]
_,unique_colorvals = np.unique(colorvals, return_inverse=True)





Plot the results
Now we can apply a colorscale using matplotlib and visualize the results using mofography (plotly, basically).


Show code


# apply colormap to get a list of colors and add that to the mesh
import matplotlib as mpl 
colors = mpl.cm.get_cmap('tab20c')(unique_colorvals)
colors[:, :-1] = (colors[:, :-1]*255).astype(int)
submesh.visual.vertex_colors=colors
submesh_trace = mgr.plot_mesh(
    [submesh], hovertext=np.array(unique_colorvals).astype(str), stylize=True, name='submesh for region {}'.format(select[0]))
go.Figure(data=submesh_trace).update(layout=mgr.white_layout).show(renderer='png')

title: Selecting Cavity Walls
text:
Pick framework atoms
Now that we have the centroids of the walls, we can pick atoms from the unit cell that are close to one or more of the centroids very easily using the AABB cell list from freud that is already implementd in mofography. In this example we are simply selecting all atoms within ‘r_max’ distance using ‘ball’ query, instead you may also choose n_neighbors using a ‘nearest’ query.


Show code
aabb=mgr.AABB_on_atoms(mat_atoms)
ab_r = aabb.query(cage_wall_centroids, query_args=dict(mode='ball',  r_max=5))
ab_r_nl = ab_r.toNeighborList(sort_by_distance=True)
pick_these_atoms = ab_r_nl.point_indices

title: Flexible framework movies (Three.js HTML)
text:
This note describes the implemented path in mofography/movies.py for exporting an interactive HTML viewer when the framework coordinates change each frame (flexible RASPA-style trajectory) and you want matched adsorbate / component snapshots on the same frame indices.
Design background lives in docs/movie_viewer_module_plan.md; this file is a how-to for the current API.









Goal
Entry point




Fixed framework from a CIF + trajectory of guests only
make_movie_from_trajectory(...) or build_fixed_framework_movie(...)


Flexible framework + segmentation/pore graph per sparse frame + one or more guest/component movies aligned by index
make_sparse_multicomponent_movie(...)







framework_movie_path — multi-frame RASPA PDB (or ASE-readable path with movie_format="ase") whose models are only the framework atoms, same frame count as the component movies you pass.
component_movie_paths — dict mapping a short label → path. Each movie must have the same number of frames as the framework movie (after any shared frame_stride / index selection). Typical RASPA outputs: Movie_*_allcomponents.pdb or per-component Movie_*_component_X_*.pdb files from the same Run_* folder.
cif_path — used for metadata / consistency checks in the builder; the geometry in the HTML comes from the framework movie frames when framework_movie_path is set.
snapshot_indices — optional explicit list of source frame indices to keep (sparse export). Segmentation (dgrid, regions, connections, surface mesh, maxima, windows) is computed for each selected index.




from pathlib import Path
import mofography as mgr

base = Path("outputs/github_raspa_test")  # or your data directory

out_html, payload = mgr.make_sparse_multicomponent_movie(
    component_movie_paths={
        "allcomponents": base / "Movie_IRMOF1_allcomponents.pdb",
    },
    framework_movie_path=base / "Movie_IRMOF1_frameworks.pdb",
    cif_path=base / "IRMOF-1.cif",
    out_html=base / "flexible_single_component_ir_mof1.html",
    snapshot_indices=[0, 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35, 39, 43, 47, 51, 55],
    max_frames=15,
    movie_format="raspa_pdb",
    spacing=0.25,
    isovalue=1.0,
    surf_step_size=2,
)
print(out_html)
# payload["segmentation_series"] — one dict per selected frame (dgrid, regions, …)
Returned payload includes:

snapshot_indices — indices actually embedded
segmentation_series — list of { "frame_index", "segmentation", "summary" } for analysis or saving .npz sidecars




From the numat/RASPA2 mirror (same example folder):

Framework movie:
examples/Non-Basic/MinimizationIRMOF-1-NVT/Movies/System_0/Run_0/Movie_IRMOF-1_1.1.1_298.000000_0.000000_frameworks.pdb
All components:
examples/Non-Basic/MinimizationIRMOF-1-NVT/Movies/System_0/Run_0/Movie_IRMOF-1_1.1.1_298.000000_0.000000_allcomponents.pdb
CIF: structures/mofs/cif/IRMOF-1.cif

Raw URLs (for curl or CI):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/numat/RASPA2/master/examples/Non-Basic/MinimizationIRMOF-1-NVT/Movies/System_0/Run_0/Movie_IRMOF-1_1.1.1_298.000000_0.000000_frameworks.pdb

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/numat/RASPA2/master/examples/Non-Basic/MinimizationIRMOF-1-NVT/Movies/System_0/Run_0/Movie_IRMOF-1_1.1.1_298.000000_0.000000_allcomponents.pdb

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/numat/RASPA2/master/structures/mofs/cif/IRMOF-1.cif




The Three.js template in mofography/movies.py reads trace.style as a resolved object on each trace (not only string keys into DATA.styles). Defaults match the devtools viewer:

Internal connections: red (0xFF0000), solid, linewidth 16

Periodic connections: red, dashed (dashSize / gapSize like the devtools script), linewidth 16

Windows (internal + periodic): yellow 0xFFE600, larger point size

Internal maxima: colored by segmentation pocket / region (same palette as the surface), marker size from cage radii (6 + 5 * norm) and capped by the viewer’s point size logic

Guest / component spheres use distinct hues via guests_<label> trace ids.




devtools/scripts/md_pdb_threejs_viewer.py — legacy single-file payload (framework, surface, movie, …) and its own inline HTML. Prefer MovieFigure / make_sparse_multicomponent_movie for flexible + multi-trace workflows so logic stays in movies.py.

title: mofography
text:
Monte Carlo shell estimator for probe surface area
This note describes the experimental Monte Carlo (MC) method we use to estimate probe–surface area from an existing distance grid. The goal is to reduce sensitivity to global grid resolution and to avoid some of the artifacts of marching–cubes–based surface meshes, while still reusing the full segmentation/percolation pipeline.

Basic idea
Given a periodic unit cell and a distance–to–framework field (f(x)) (the dgrid), the probe surface at radius (r) is the level set (f(x) = r). Rather than explicitly meshing this level set, we:

Draw (N) random points (x_i) uniformly in the unit cell.
For each point, interpolate (f(x_i)) from the existing dgrid.
Define a thin shell of thickness () around the probe radius, i.e. points such that (|f(x_i) - r| < /2).
Let (p_{}) be the fraction of samples in this shell.

For small (), the surface area can be estimated by the identity SA ≈ V_cell * p_shell / δ, where (V_) is the unit–cell volume. We convert from Å² to m²/g using the same normalization as the existing code:

Compute (V_) in Å³ from mat_atoms.get_volume().
Compute the framework mass (m) in grams from the atomic masses.
Apply the factor (1 ^2 = 10^{-20} ^2) and divide by (m) to report SA in m²/g.

This gives a global total surface area estimate. To get accessible surface area, we also use the per–region labels and percolation history.


Reusing existing data (dgrid, regions, percolation)
The MC method is designed to sit on top of the existing segmentation infrastructure. For each structure we reuse:

results_dict["dgrid"]:

3D array of distances to the framework.
Used as a scalar field (f(x)); we never recompute distances.

results_dict["regions_pbc"]:

3D array of integer region labels on the same grid.
We interpolate labels at sample points with nearest–neighbor interpolation.

results_dict["percolation_history"] (or we compute it if missing):

We call select_percolation_threshold(percolation_history, probe_radius) to obtain the percolating region IDs at the desired probe.
This is the same helper used in compute_surface_area_from_results.

mat_atoms:

Provides the periodic cell and total mass, exactly as in the existing SA and void–volume routines.


Interpolations are done with scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates:

order=1 and mode="wrap" for dgrid (trilinear interpolation with periodic wrapping).
order=0 and mode="wrap" for regions_pbc (nearest–neighbor, categorical labels).

Accessible SA is obtained by restricting shell samples to those whose interpolated region label is in the percolating–region set at the probe radius. The estimator then becomes SA_acc ≈ V_cell * p_shell_acc / δ, where (p_{}) is the fraction of random points in the shell that also belong to percolating regions.


Relation to the marching–cubes method
The existing compute_surface_area_from_results function computes SA by constructing a triangular mesh of the isosurface (f(x) = r) using marching cubes, then measuring the mesh area with trimesh. It then splits this mesh into per–region submeshes and derives per–region / per–pocket / per–cluster SA from those pieces.
That approach is deterministic and fast, but it has two important sensitivities:

Grid resolution: coarse dgrid spacing can lead to blocky surfaces and biased areas.
Region splitting at interfaces: faces that straddle region boundaries can be dropped when constructing per–region submeshes, which can undercount surface area, especially for complex pore morphologies.

The MC estimator avoids building a mesh altogether. Instead it directly estimates how much of the cell volume lies “near” the level set, which is mathematically well–defined even when the discrete mesh is imperfect.
In practice we see better agreement with Zeo++ for SA because:

The MC method is less sensitive to missing triangles at region interfaces and other meshing artifacts.
Zeo++ itself uses a sampling–based approach for SA, so our estimator is conceptually closer to its measurement procedure than marching cubes on a coarse grid.



What the MC estimator returns
In its current form, the experimental MC routine focuses on global totals:

total_surface_area (SA over all regions, MC estimate).
accessible_surface_area (SA over percolating regions only, MC estimate).
sa_mc_diagnostics:

n_samples
shell_thickness
n_shell_hits_total
n_shell_hits_accessible


The void–volume calculation is left unchanged and still uses the existing grid–based method (compute_void_volume_from_results), since it already agrees well with Zeo++.
The marching–cubes–based function remains available and continues to provide rich breakdowns:

by_region (per–region accessible SA),
by_pocket (per–PBC–group SA),
by_percolated_cluster (per–cluster SA),

which are useful for visualization and qualitative analysis. The MC estimator is intended as a complementary, more robust global SA estimator that you can use alongside the existing breakdowns and Zeo++ parity plots.


Implementation details

Location in codebase

Core implementation: mofography/compute.py, function compute_surface_area_from_results_mc(results_dict, mat_atoms, ...).
This function is part of the public mofography.compute API and is intended to be a drop-in alternative to compute_surface_area_from_results for SA.

Inputs

results_dict:

Must contain at least:

'dgrid' or 'distance_grid': distance grid (Å).
'regions_pbc': periodic region labels (integers).
'pbc_groups': list or dict of PBC pockets (each group is a set of region IDs).

Optionally:

'percolation_history': list of (threshold, components) tuples. If missing it is computed via compute_percolation_history_from_results.


mat_atoms:

ASE Atoms object for the (super)cell used in the distance grid.
Provides get_volume() and atomic masses for normalization to m²/g.

probe_radius:

Probe radius (Å) for which SA is estimated.

n_samples, shell_thickness:

Monte Carlo sample count and shell half-width control accuracy and cost.


Outputs

Global SA:

total_surface_area: MC estimate over all regions (m²/g).
accessible_surface_area: MC estimate over percolating regions only (m²/g).
accessible_fraction: ratio of accessible to total SA.

Breakdowns (accessible SA only, mirroring the marching-cubes function):

by_region: dict {region_id -> SA} for percolating regions.
by_pocket: dict {pocket_id -> SA} from summing per-region SA over each PBC group.
by_percolated_cluster: dict {cluster_id -> SA} from summing per-region SA over each percolated cluster at the selected probe-threshold.

Diagnostics:

sa_mc_diagnostics with:

n_samples, shell_thickness,
n_shell_hits_total, n_shell_hits_accessible.

title: 🌟 Periodic Segmentation in MOFography
text:
## Overview
The do_periodic_segmentation function performs periodic watershed segmentation on the distance field of a periodic, crystalline (possibly non-orthogonal) ASE atoms object. It accounts for periodic boundary conditions (PBC), ensuring accurate segmentation of pores in crystalline systems.


In crystalline systems, local maxima outside the unit cell can influence the segmentation inside the box due to PBC. Properly accounting for these periodic effects is crucial for: - Realistic pore segmentation in periodic systems - Accurate identification of periodic groups of maxima - Simplified downstream analysis of pore networks



The algorithm works by: 1. Padding the distance grid with periodic copies to mimic PBC. 2. Identifying periodic maxima groups using h_maxima and grouping periodic images. 3. Performing watershed segmentation on the padded grid. 4. Reindexing maxima to ensure consistent indexing for downstream analysis.
The padding thickness is determined by:
padding_thickness = dgrid.max() / min_perpendicular_voxel_length + 5 / spacing
An additional extra_padding parameter allows users to add more padding for safety.






Maxima Detection (maxima_pbc)

Compute local maxima in the grid using h_maxima with a 1-voxel-thick padding.
Identify periodic images of maxima and group them into PBC groups.
For example, in ZIF-8, you’d get:

2 periodic maxima: one at the corner and one at the unit cell center.


Locate All Periodic Images

Identify all periodic images of maxima_pbc within the padded grid domain.

Definitions of Maxima Terms

maxima_pbc: Local maxima in the original grid, one per PBC group.
maxima (or unique_regions): Local maxima influencing the unit cell, which may lie outside the box.
all_maxima: All periodic images of maxima_pbc within the padded domain.
close_by_maxima: Maxima inside the unit cell or within a wall_thickness of the unit cell. Default wall_thickness is 7.5% of the perpendicular lengths of the unit cell (reciprocal system for non-orthogonal cells).

Maxima Information (maxima_info)

A 2D array of shape (N_all_maxima, 7): | Column | Description | |—————-|————————————————–| | maxima_label | Label of the maxima | | pbc_x/y/z | Coordinates of the corresponding PBC maxima | | offset_x/y/z | Grid shifts to locate the periodic image |
To compute the actual indices of a maxima k:
maxima_indices = maxima_info[k-1, 1:4] + maxima_info[k-1, 4:7] * np.array(dgrid.shape)

Regions Segmentation

regions_pbc: Use periodic maxima markers (same label for each maxima_pbc and its periodic images) to segment the padded grid. Extract the central region corresponding to the original grid.
regions_without_pbc (or regions): Use separate markers for each maxima_pbc and its periodic images to segment the padded grid. Extract the central region corresponding to the original grid.

Connections

Identify touching regions in regions_padded and compute shared boundaries to populate the connections list.
Ignore regions near the padded grid boundary to avoid unreliable connections.

Reindexing Maxima

Maxima are reindexed in the order of decreasing importance:

maxima_pbc get indices 1, 2, ..., N_maxima_pbc.
close_by_maxima get the next indices if not already assigned.
unique_regions maxima influencing the unit cell get the next indices.
Maxima in the padded regions connected to close_by_maxima get indices.
Remaining maxima in the padded regions get indices.

This reindexing simplifies downstream analysis:

For example, to filter maxima corresponding to unique_regions:
maxima = all_maxima[:regions.max()] # or 
maxima = all_maxima[:(len(unique_regions)+1)]







Ensures consistent indexing across all outputs (regions_pbc, regions, maxima_pbc, etc.).
Simplifies filtering and visualization of specific maxima groups.
Facilitates incremental graph extension using more and more padding, indices of the maxima wil remain somewhat consistent across increases.

]

    return_padded_regions=True,
    mask_thickness=0.05,
    h=0.2,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    minimum_window_separation=1.5,
    wall_thickness=0.08,
    extra_padding=extra_padding
)



The output is a dictionary, so you’ll have to grab whatever you need, here’s all of the outputs as vars
# Extract all variables from results

unique_regions = results['unique_regions']

    c for c in connections

frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated, stylize=True)

    dgrid, 
    close_maxima, 
    mat_atoms,

    marker_colorscale=cscale

    dgrid,
    maxima,
    mat_atoms,
    name='maxima influencing box',
    show_spheres=False,
    marker_colorscale=cscale
)

    dgrid,
    maxima_pbc,
    mat_atoms,

    show_spheres=False,
    marker_colorscale=cscale
)

    dgrid,
    isovalue=surface_value,
    region_labels=regions_pbc,
    ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    name=f'Regions PBC at {surface_value}Å',

)

    dgrid,
    isovalue=surface_value,
    region_labels=regions,
    ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    name=f'Regions at {surface_value}Å',
    stylize=True

    connections_trimmed,
