title: 🌟 Building Pore Graphs (Region Adjacency Graphs)
text:
A beginner-friendly guide to constructing and analyzing pore networks in crystalline materials




This is part of the MOFography tutorial series. For the main quick start guide, see: - Periodic Segmentation Quick Start - Complete workflow - Region Segmentation - Segmentation fundamentals - Connections and Windows - Window detection




A Pore Graph (also called a Region Adjacency Graph or RAG) represents the pore network of a material as a mathematical graph:

Nodes = Individual pores (regions from segmentation)
Edges = Physical connections between pores (windows)
Node positions = Located at pore centers (local maxima)




Compact Representation 📦

Instead of working with large 3D grids, work with a graph
Easy to analyze, visualize, and compare

Network Analysis 🕸️

Calculate coordination numbers (how many neighbors each pore has)
Find shortest paths between pores
Identify bottlenecks and well-connected regions

Machine Learning Ready 🤖

Natural input for graph neural networks (GNNs)
Extract node, edge, and graph-level features
Compare structures mathematically

Property Mapping 📊

Annotate nodes with pore volumes, surface areas, etc.
Annotate edges with window sizes, pore-limiting diameters
Correlate graph properties with material performance





Pore Graph = Segmented regions + Their connections
Physical Space (Unit Cell)           Graph Representation
┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌───┐     ┌───┐
│    ●───────────────●    │         │ 1 │─────│ 2 │
│   ╱│    ↑        ╱ │    │    →    │   │     │   │
│  ● │   │        ●  │    │         │   │     │   │
│  ╲ │   ↓        ╲ │    │         │   │     │   │
│    ●───────────────●    │         │ 3 │─────│ 4 │
└─────────────────────────┘         └───┘     └───┘
   Segmented regions                   Pore graph
Each node in the graph represents a physical pore region. Edges represent windows connecting pores.





When working with crystalline materials, periodic boundary conditions (PBC) are essential. A pore that spans across unit cell boundaries will have periodic images in neighboring cells.





Physical pore space vs pore graph concept


The left panel shows the physical pore space with numbered pore compartments. The right panel shows the corresponding pore graph with nodes (circles) and edges (lines). Periodic images are shown as dashed outlines.
Key observations: - Physical space: Pores are numbered 1-4 within the unit cell. Each has periodic images in neighboring cells. - Pore graph: Each unique pore type becomes one node. Edges connect neighboring pores. - Numbering convention: A node is labeled as pore_id (offset_x, offset_y, offset_z) where (0,0,0) means it’s the original in the unit cell.
Example: - 1 (0,0,0) = Pore 1 at its original position in the unit cell - 1 (1,0,0) = Periodic image of pore 1 shifted by one unit cell in the x-direction - 1 (0,1,0) = Periodic image of pore 1 shifted by one unit cell in the y-direction - 1 (1,1,0) = Periodic image at the diagonal (x+1, y+1)





This is a FOUNDATIONAL tutorial on pore graph construction.
✅ What this tutorial covers: - What a pore graph is and why it matters - How periodic boundary conditions affect the graph - How to build a pore graph from periodic segmentation - Understanding internal vs. periodic connections - Visualizing the pore graph in 3D - Basic graph analysis with NetworkX
❌ What this tutorial does NOT cover: - Pocket type classification - see Pockets Detection - Percolation analysis - see PLD & Percolation - Path finding - see Percolated Paths Tutorial - Graph neural networks




By the end of this tutorial, you’ll be able to:

✅ Understand what a pore graph represents
✅ Explain the difference between internal and periodic connections
✅ Build a pore graph from periodic segmentation results
✅ Visualize the pore network using plot_connections_as_it_is()
✅ Use NetworkX to analyze graph properties
✅ Interpret node and edge attributes






Python 3.8+
MOFography installed (uv pip install -e .)
Periodic Segmentation Quick Start completed
Region Segmentation completed
NetworkX installed
(Optional) ASE for structure handling







import os
import sys
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import networkx as nx

# Set up paths
repo_root = Path('/path/to/mofography')
path_to_cif = repo_root / 'examples' / 'TestCIFs' / 'P1-IRMOF-1.cif'




mat_atoms = read(path_to_cif)
mat_updated = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)

print(f"Loaded: {mat_atoms.get_chemical_formula()}")
print(f"  Atoms: {len(mat_atoms)}")
print(f"  Cell: {mat_atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3]} Å")




The key advantage of the new workflow is that connections are computed automatically:
# Parameters
spacing = 0.5
mask_thickness = 0.05
h = 0.2
threshold_abs = 1.5
minimum_window_separation = 1.5
wall_thickness = 0.08
extra_padding = 10

# Compute distance grid
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_cpu(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing, block_size=50000)
dgrid = mgr.zoom_grid(dgrid, zoom_factor=1).compute()
dgrid = mgr.periodic_gaussian_filter(dgrid, sigma=spacing*2)
dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)

# Run periodic segmentation (computes connections automatically!)
results = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid,
    mat_atoms,
    spacing=spacing,
    mask_thickness=mask_thickness,
    h=h,
    threshold_abs=threshold_abs,
    minimum_window_separation=minimum_window_separation,
    wall_thickness=wall_thickness,
    extra_padding=extra_padding,
    return_padded_regions=True,
    compute_connections=True
)

print(f"✅ Segmentation complete!")
print(f"  Found {len(results['maxima_pbc'])} unique pores")
print(f"  Found {len(results['connections'])} connections")




# Extract key results
maxima_pbc = results['maxima_pbc']           # One per unique pore
regions_pbc = results['regions_pbc']         # Merged regions

    mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms),

title: 🌟 Building Pore Graphs (Region Adjacency Graphs)
text:
A Pore Graph (also called a Region Adjacency Graph or RAG) represents the pore network of a material as a mathematical graph:

Nodes = Individual pores (regions from segmentation)
Edges = Physical connections between pores (windows)
Node positions = Located at pore centers (local maxima)




Compact Representation 📦

Instead of working with large 3D grids, work with a graph
Easy to analyze, visualize, and compare

Network Analysis 🕸️

Calculate coordination numbers (how many neighbors each pore has)
Find shortest paths between pores
Identify bottlenecks and well-connected regions

Machine Learning Ready 🤖

Natural input for graph neural networks (GNNs)
Extract node, edge, and graph-level features
Compare structures mathematically

Property Mapping 📊

Annotate nodes with pore volumes, surface areas, etc.
Annotate edges with window sizes, pore-limiting diameters
Correlate graph properties with material performance





Pore Graph = Segmented regions + Their connections
Physical Space (Unit Cell)           Graph Representation
┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌───┐     ┌───┐
│    ●───────────────●    │         │ 1 │─────│ 2 │
│   ╱│    ↑        ╱ │    │    →    │   │     │   │
│  ● │   │        ●  │    │         │   │     │   │
│  ╲ │   ↓        ╲ │    │         │   │     │   │
│    ●───────────────●    │         │ 3 │─────│ 4 │
└─────────────────────────┘         └───┘     └───┘
   Segmented regions                   Pore graph
Each node in the graph represents a physical pore region. Edges represent windows connecting pores.

title: 🌟 Building Pore Graphs (Region Adjacency Graphs)
text:
When working with crystalline materials, periodic boundary conditions (PBC) are essential. A pore that spans across unit cell boundaries will have periodic images in neighboring cells.





Physical pore space vs pore graph concept


The left panel shows the physical pore space with numbered pore compartments. The right panel shows the corresponding pore graph with nodes (circles) and edges (lines). Periodic images are shown as dashed outlines.
Key observations: - Physical space: Pores are numbered 1-4 within the unit cell. Each has periodic images in neighboring cells. - Pore graph: Each unique pore type becomes one node. Edges connect neighboring pores. - Numbering convention: A node is labeled as pore_id (offset_x, offset_y, offset_z) where (0,0,0) means it’s the original in the unit cell.
Example: - 1 (0,0,0) = Pore 1 at its original position in the unit cell - 1 (1,0,0) = Periodic image of pore 1 shifted by one unit cell in the x-direction - 1 (0,1,0) = Periodic image of pore 1 shifted by one unit cell in the y-direction - 1 (1,1,0) = Periodic image at the diagonal (x+1, y+1)

Using accurate pore size analysis to characterize nanoporous materials at both global and pocket levels




Gelb & Gubbins Method: The Pore Size Distribution method described by: - Gelb, L.D., & Gubbins, K.E. (1998). “Characterization of Porous Solids and Pore-Size Distributions Using a Mean-Field Method.” Langmuir, 14(8), 1887-1902.
@article{gelb1998,
  title={Characterization of porous solids and pore-size distributions using a mean-field method},
  author={Gelb, L. D. and Gubbins, K. E.},
  journal={Langmuir},
  volume={14},
  number={8},
  pages={1887--1902},
  year={1998}
}




Pore Size Distribution (PSD) is a histogram of the largest inscribed sphere sizes for points sampled throughout the void space of a nanoporous material.


For any point in the void space: 1. Find the largest sphere that includes this point 2. This sphere must NOT overlap with any framework atom 3. Record the diameter of this sphere 4. Repeat for many sample points 5. Create histogram of all diameters
This is fundamentally different from simple distance grid analysis: - Distance Grid: Gives distance to nearest atom surface from the grid - Gelb-Gubbins PSD: Finds the LARGEST inscribed sphere at each sample point




Accurate for Non-Spherical Pores 🎯

Cubic or irregular pores have sharp corners
Largest inscribed spheres vary significantly throughout the pore
Distance grid alone misses these variations

Captures Pore Geometry 📐

Different parts of the same pore have different sphere sizes
Provides detailed geometric characterization
Essential for understanding molecular transport

Two Levels of Analysis 📊

Global PSD: Material-wide average across unit cell
Pocket-wise PSD: Individual distributions per pore region
Enables comparing heterogeneity within structure

Benchmarking Standard 📏

Well-established method in literature (since 1998)
Widely used for nanoporous materials characterization
Comparable across different studies







This is an INTERMEDIATE tutorial, not a beginner guide!
✅ What this tutorial covers: - Computing global PSD using uniform sampling across unit cell - Computing pocket-wise PSDs for individual pore regions - Understanding the difference between the two approaches - Visualizing and comparing both methods - Using PSDs for pocket type detection
❌ What this tutorial does NOT cover: - Basic periodic segmentation - see Periodic Segmentation Quick Start - Surface area and void volume calculations - coming soon - Accessibility criteria and percolation - coming soon - Energy-based pore size calculations
🔗 Prerequisites: 1. Complete Periodic Segmentation Quick Start 2. Have Rust backend installed (for speed) 3. Understand segmentation outputs (regions_pbc, maxima_pbc) 4. Basic knowledge of histograms and statistical analysis





Python 3.8+
MOFography installed (uv pip install -e .)
Rust backend compiled and installed (mgr_rust module available)
Periodic Segmentation Quick Start completed
NumPy, Matplotlib, Plotly installed

import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import logging

# Enable progress output
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

# Setup paths
repo_root = Path('/path/to/mofography')
path_to_cif = repo_root / 'examples' / 'TestCIFs' / 'NU-1000_S1.cif'
What is this? - Importing all necessary libraries - Setting up logging to see progress - Configuring paths for reproducibility




# Load structure
mat_atoms = read(str(path_to_cif))
print(f"✅ Loaded structure: {mat_atoms.info.get('chemical_formula')}")

# Compute distance grid with Rust backend
spacing = 0.25  # Fine spacing for accurate PSD
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing)

print(f"✅ Distance grid shape: {dgrid.shape}")
print(f"   Spacing: {spacing} Å")
print(f"   Voxel size: {dgrid.nbytes / 1e6:.1f} MB")
What is this? - Computing distance from framework atoms to every grid point - Fine spacing (0.25 Å) is recommended for accurate PSD - Rust backend provides 10-15x speedup
Parameter Guide:








Parameter
What it does
Typical range




spacing
Grid spacing (Å)
0.25 - 0.5 (finer = more accurate but slower)


Grid shape
(nx, ny, nz)
Depends on cell size and spacing







# Run periodic segmentation to get pore regions
results = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid=dgrid,
    mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
    spacing=spacing,
    mask_thickness=0.05,
    h=0.2,
    threshold_abs=1.5,
    minimum_window_separation=1.5,
    wall_thickness=0.08,
    extra_padding=5.0,
    compute_connections=True,
    return_padded_regions=False
)

# Extract key outputs
regions_pbc = results['regions_pbc']
maxima_pbc = results['maxima_pbc']
connections = results['connections']
all_maxima = results['all_maxima']
unique_regions = results['unique_regions']

print(f"\n✅ Segmentation complete!")
print(f"   Found {len(np.unique(regions_pbc))} unique pore regions")
print(f"   Found {len(maxima_pbc)} periodic maxima groups")
What is this? - Identifying individual pore regions - Merging regions connected across periodic boundaries - Getting regions_pbc for pocket-wise PSD
Key Outputs:








Output
What is it?
Why care?




regions_pbc
Pore regions with PBC merged
Labels for pocket-wise sampling


maxima_pbc
Representative maxima per pore
One per unique pore


connections
Windows between pores
Pore network analysis




Note: For detailed explanation of these outputs, see Outputs from Periodic Segmentation.







Global PSD samples points uniformly across the entire unit cell: - Every part of the unit cell has equal probability of being sampled - Provides material-wide average pore size - Good for comparing different materials - Standard approach in literature
# Compute pore sizes with uniform sampling
num_samples_total = 10000  # Total samples across unit cell

sample_points_uniform, pore_sizes_uniform = mgr.compute_pore_sizes_uniform_rust(
    dgrid,
    mat_atoms,
    num_samples_total=num_samples_total
)

print(f"\n✅ Global PSD computed!")
print(f"   Number of samples: {len(pore_sizes_uniform)}")
print(f"   Mean pore diameter: {np.mean(pore_sizes_uniform * 2):.2f} Å")
print(f"   Std dev: {np.std(pore_sizes_uniform * 2):.2f} Å")
What just happened? 1. Generated 10,000 random points uniformly in unit cell 2. For each point, found largest inscribed sphere 3. Recorded sphere diameter (pore size) 4. Returned all pore sizes as array (in Angstroms, radius)
Visualizing Global PSD:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Create histogram
bins = np.linspace(0, 50, 200)  # 0 to 50 Å
hist, bin_edges = np.histogram(pore_sizes_uniform * 2, bins=bins, density=False)
bin_centers = (bin_edges[1:] + bin_edges[:-1]) / 2

# Create figure
fig_global = go.Figure()
fig_global.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=bin_centers,
    y=hist,
    name='Global PSD',
    marker_color='#66c2a5',
    marker_line_color='black',
    marker_line_width=1,
    opacity=0.8
))

# Add statistics
mean_pore = np.mean(pore_sizes_uniform * 2)
std_pore = np.std(pore_sizes_uniform * 2)

fig_global.update_layout(
    title=f'Global Pore Size Distribution (NU-1000)<br><sub>Uniform sampling, {num_samples_total} points</sub>',
    xaxis_title='Pore Diameter (Å)',
    yaxis_title='Counts',
    showlegend=True,
    width=1000,
    height=600
)

fig_global.show()
 Global PSD showing material-wide pore size distribution







Pocket-wise PSD samples points within each identified pore region: - Each region gets num_samples_per_region points - Different pores can have very different distributions - Reveals heterogeneity within the material - More compute-intensive but more detailed
# Compute pore sizes for each pocket
num_samples_per_region = 1000  # Samples per pore region

sample_points_pocketwise, pore_sizes_pocketwise, region_labels = mgr.compute_pore_sizes_pocketwise_rust(
    dgrid,
    regions_pbc,
    mat_atoms,
    samples_per_region=num_samples_per_region
)

print(f"\n✅ Pocket-wise PSD computed!")
print(f"   Number of pockets: {len(np.unique(region_labels))}")
print(f"   Total samples: {len(pore_sizes_pocketwise)}")
print(f"   Samples per pocket: {num_samples_per_region}")
What just happened? 1. Generated num_samples_per_region random points within each region 2. For each point, found largest inscribed sphere 3. Grouped results by region label 4. Returned sample points, pore sizes, and region labels
Visualizing Pocket-wise PSD:
# Compute PSDs for each pocket
from mofography.helper import compute_psds_from_points_pocketwise

# Convert pore sizes to diameters (pore_sizes are radii)
pore_diameters = pore_sizes_pocketwise * 2

# Compute histograms per pocket
pocket_psds = compute_psds_from_points_pocketwise(
    region_labels,
    pore_diameters,
    bins=bins
)

# Create comparison figure
fig_pocketwise = go.Figure()

# Add overall histogram (gray)
fig_pocketwise.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=bin_centers,
    y=hist,
    name='Overall (uniform)',
    marker_color='gray',
    marker_line_color='black',
    marker_line_width=1,
    opacity=0.3
))

# Add individual pocket PSDs
colors = ['#66c2a5', '#fc8d62', '#8da0cb', '#e78ac3']
for i, (label, psd_data) in enumerate(pocket_psds.items()):
    if i >= len(colors):
        break
    fig_pocketwise.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=psd_data['bin_centers'],
        y=psd_data['hist'],
        mode='lines',
        name=f'Pocket {label}',
        line=dict(width=2, color=colors[i]),
        hovertemplate=f'Pocket {label}<br>Diameter: %{{x:.1f}} Å<br>Count: %{{y}}'
    ))

fig_pocketwise.update_layout(
    title=f'Pocket-wise Pore Size Distributions (NU-1000)<br><sub>{len(pocket_psds)} pockets, {num_samples_per_region} samples each</sub>',
    xaxis_title='Pore Diameter (Å)',
    yaxis_title='Counts',
    showlegend=True,
    legend=dict(x=0.8, y=0.99),
    width=1000,
    height=600
)

fig_pocketwise.show()
 Individual pore size distributions for each identified pocket region
Key Insight: - Different pockets often have different average pore sizes - This heterogeneity is invisible in global PSD - Pocket-wise PSD reveals material complexity





Understanding the differences between the two approaches is crucial for material analysis.
# Create side-by-side comparison
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig_comparison = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=('Global PSD', 'Pocket-wise PSD'))

# Left: Global PSD
fig_comparison.add_trace(
    go.Bar(x=bin_centers, y=hist, marker_color='#66c2a5',
              marker_line_color='black', opacity=0.8),
    row=1, col=1
)

# Right: Pocket-wise PSD (overlay curves)
fig_comparison.add_trace(
    go.Bar(x=bin_centers, y=hist, marker_color='gray',
              marker_line_color='black', opacity=0.3),
    row=1, col=2
)

for i, (label, psd_data) in enumerate(pocket_psds.items()):
    if i >= len(colors):
        break
    fig_comparison.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=psd_data['bin_centers'], y=psd_data['hist'],
                   mode='lines', name=f'Pocket {label}',
                   line=dict(width=2, color=colors[i])),
        row=1, col=2
    )

fig_comparison.update_layout(height=500, width=1400, showlegend=True)
fig_comparison.show()
 Side-by-side comparison of global vs pocket-wise PSD methods

PSDs can be used as features for clustering pockets into types, similar to CSD but more accurate.











Method
Speed
Accuracy
Best Use Case




CSD
Very fast
Approximate
Quick screening, pocket detection


PSD
Slow
Accurate
Detailed characterization, publication



PSD Features for Clustering: - More sensitive to pore shape variations - Better for distinguishing similar-sized pockets with different geometries - Computationally expensive but worth it for publication quality
# Example: Extract PSDs as features
# Each pocket now has a histogram (bins, hist)
# Can use these histograms as features in clustering
# Similar to how CSD is used in pocket detection tutorial

# For publication-quality analysis:
# 1. Use smaller bin_width (e.g., 0.25 Å instead of 0.25 Å default)
# 2. Increase num_samples_per_region (e.g., 2000-5000)
# 3. Use PSD-based clustering instead of CSD

# Note: This is advanced usage - see Pocket Detection tutorial for implementation












Issue
Solution




ImportError: No module named ‘mgr_rust’
Compile Rust backend: cd mgr_rust && maturin build --release && pip install target/wheels/*.whl


MemoryError during PSD
Reduce num_samples_total or num_samples_per_region


Computation too slow
Increase grid spacing to 0.3-0.5 Å, or reduce samples


Wrong dtype error
Ensure dgrid is float32: dgrid = dgrid.astype(np.float32)


Few regions found
Check segmentation parameters (h, threshold_abs, extra_padding)


PSD looks noisy
Increase number of samples or smooth the histogram


Inconsistent results
Set random seed for reproducibility: np.random.seed(42)

Key Takeaway: Gelb & Gubbins PSD provides accurate pore size distributions at both global and pocket levels, enabling detailed geometric characterization of nanoporous materials!

For convenience, MOFography provides wrapper functions that combine all steps:


# Compute global PSD and get figure in one call
psd_hist, fig = mgr.compute_psd_uniform_rust(
    dgrid, mat_atoms,
    num_samples_total=10000,
    bins=np.linspace(0, 50, 200),
    density=False,
    material='NU-1000',
    return_fig=True
)

fig.show()



# Compute pocket-wise PSDs and get figure in one call
pocket_psds, fig = mgr.compute_psds_pocketwise_rust(
    dgrid, regions_pbc, mat_atoms,
    num_samples_per_region=1000,
    bins=np.linspace(0, 50, 200),
    material='NU-1000',
    return_fig=True
)

fig.show()
These functions are convenient for: - Quick analysis without manually implementing plotting - Standardized visualization across different materials - Publication-ready figures with proper formatting





Use Rust Backend - Provides 8-12x speedup for pore size calculations
Adjust Sampling - More samples = more accurate but slower
Balance Accuracy vs Speed - 0.25 Å spacing is a good default
Parallel Processing - Rust automatically uses multiple CPU cores
Memory Management - For large structures, use dask or reduce samples


Happy pore size analyzing! 🎊

MOFography includes a high-performance Rust backend that provides optimized implementations for computationally intensive tasks in porous material analysis. The Rust functions are exposed to Python through PyO3 bindings, offering significant performance improvements over pure Python implementations while maintaining the same API.

💡 Pro Tip: If you’re analyzing large MOF structures or need faster computations, the Rust backend can provide 5-20x speed improvements!






The Rust backend requires Rust and Cargo to be installed on your system. Follow the platform-specific instructions below:



Download the Rust installer from https://rustup.rs/
Run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions
Open a new Command Prompt or PowerShell window
Verify installation:
rustc --version
cargo --version

Install Rust:
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
Follow the on-screen instructions

This will be different from PSD computed using uniform sampling across the box, as the points are sampled differently (region-weighted vs. uniform spatial sampling).








import mofography as mgr
from ase.io import read
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) # this will print out progress statements

# Load structure
path_to_cif = '../examples/TestCIFs/NU-1000_S1.cif'
mat_atoms = read(path_to_cif)

# Set parameters
spacing = 0.5  # Angstroms
extra_padding = 5  # Angstroms

# Generate distance grid using Rust backend
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=spacing)

# Perform periodic segmentation using Rust workflow
results = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid=dgrid,
    mat_atoms=mat_atoms,
    spacing=spacing,
    extra_padding=extra_padding,
    return_padded_regions=True,
    return_dgrid=True
)

# Extract results
regions = results['regions']
maxima_pbc = results['maxima_pbc']
connections = results['connections']
all_maxima = results['all_maxima']
dgrid = results['dgrid']

print(f"Segmentation completed in {results.get('computation_time', 'N/A')} seconds")
print(f"Found {len(maxima_pbc)} periodic maxima groups")
print(f"Identified {len(np.unique(regions))} regions")



# Update structure with bonds for visualization
mat_updated = mgr.update_with_covalent_bonds(mat_atoms)

# Set visualization parameters
surface_value = 1.25
cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel

# Create visualization traces
cell_trace = mgr.plot_cell(mat_atoms)
frame_trace = mgr.plot_framework_as_mesh(mat_updated, stylize=True)

# Plot different types of maxima
close_maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima(
    dgrid, 
    results['close_or_inside_maxima'], 
    mat_atoms, 
    name='Close maxima', 
    show_spheres=False, 
    marker_colorscale=cscale
)

maxima_trace = mgr.plot_maxima(
    dgrid, 
    all_maxima[:regions.max()], 
    mat_atoms, 
    name='Maxima influencing box', 
    show_spheres=False, 
    marker_colorscale=cscale
)

maxima_trace_pbc = mgr.plot_maxima(
    dgrid, 
    maxima_pbc, 
    mat_atoms, 
    name='Maxima PBC', 
    show_spheres=False, 
    marker_colorscale=cscale
)

# Plot surfaces for different region types
surface_trace_pbc = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
    dgrid,
    isovalue=surface_value,
    region_labels=regions_pbc,
    ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    name=f'Regions PBC at {surface_value} Å',
    stylize=True
)

surface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
    dgrid,
    isovalue=surface_value,
    region_labels=regions,
    ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    name=f'Regions at {surface_value} Å',
    stylize=True
)

# Plot connections and windows
connections_trimmed = [c for c in connections if np.any(np.isin(c[0], results['unique_regions']))]
connections_trace = mgr.plot_connections_as_it_is(
    connections_trimmed, 
    all_maxima, 
    regions.shape, 
    mat_atoms, 
    cscale=cscale, 
    plot_disconnected=False
)

windows_trace = mgr.plot_windows(connections_trimmed, marker_color='blue')

# Create and display figure with all traces
fig = go.Figure(
    data=[
        cell_trace,                    # Unit cell boundaries
        surface_trace_pbc,            # PBC-aware regions surface
        surface_trace,                # Standard regions surface
        *connections_trace,           # Connections between regions
        close_maxima_trace,           # Maxima close to unit cell
        maxima_trace,                 # All maxima influencing the box
        maxima_trace_pbc,             # Periodic boundary condition maxima
        windows_trace,                # Window connections
        *frame_trace,                 # Framework atoms/bonds
    ],
    layout=mgr.dark_layout
)

# Configure layout for optimal viewing
fig.update_layout(scene_aspectmode="data")
fig.update_layout(legend_groupclick="toggleitem")

# Display the figure
fig.show(renderer="browser")

    region_labels=regions_pbc,
    ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    name=f'Regions PBC at {surface_value} Å',
    stylize=True
)

surface_trace = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid(
    dgrid,
    isovalue=surface_value,
    region_labels=regions,
    ase_atoms=mat_atoms,
    cscale=cscale,
    name=f'Regions at {surface_value} Å',
    stylize=True
)

# Plot connections and windows
connections_trimmed = [c for c in connections if np.any(np.isin(c[0], results['unique_regions']))]
connections_trace = mgr.plot_connections_as_it_is(
    connections_trimmed, 
    all_maxima, 
    regions.shape, 
    mat_atoms, 
    cscale=cscale, 
    plot_disconnected=False
)

windows_trace = mgr.plot_windows(connections_trimmed, marker_color='blue')

# Create and display figure with all traces
fig = go.Figure(
    data=[
        cell_trace,                    # Unit cell boundaries
        surface_trace_pbc,            # PBC-aware regions surface
        surface_trace,                # Standard regions surface
        *connections_trace,           # Connections between regions
        close_maxima_trace,           # Maxima close to unit cell
        maxima_trace,                 # All maxima influencing the box
        maxima_trace_pbc,             # Periodic boundary condition maxima
        windows_trace,                # Window connections
        *frame_trace,                 # Framework atoms/bonds
    ],
    layout=mgr.dark_layout
)

# Configure layout for optimal viewing
fig.update_layout(scene_aspectmode="data")
fig.update_layout(legend_groupclick="toggleitem")

# Display the figure
fig.show(renderer="browser")

# Load structure and compute distance grid
from ase.io import read
import mofography as mgr
import numpy as np

mat_atoms = read('../examples/TestCIFs/NU-1000_S1.cif')
dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(mat_atoms, spacing=0.25)

# Compute overall PSD with uniform sampling across the unit cell
psd, fig_psd = mgr.compute_psd_uniform_rust(
    dgrid, 
    mat_atoms, 
    num_samples_total=10000, 
    bins=np.linspace(0, 50, 200), 
    density=False, 
    material='NU-1000', 
    return_fig=True
)

# Display the figure
fig_psd.show(renderer='chrome')
 Example output: Uniform pore size distribution for NU-1000
# Bonus: Get raw sample points and pore sizes for custom analysis
sample_points, pore_sizes = mgr.compute_pore_sizes_uniform_rust(
    dgrid, 
    mat_atoms, 
    num_samples_total=10000
)

# Perform periodic segmentation for pocket-wise analysis
results = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust(
    dgrid=dgrid, 
    mat_atoms=mat_atoms, 
    return_dgrid=True, 
    spacing=0.25, 
    extra_padding=0.0, 
    return_padded_regions=False
)

# Compute pocket-wise PSDs
regions_pbc = results['regions_pbc']
pocket_psds, fig_pocket_psds = mgr.compute_psds_pocketwise_rust(
    dgrid, 
    regions_pbc, 
    mat_atoms, 
    num_samples_per_region=1000, 
    bins=np.linspace(0, 50, 200), 
    material='NU-1000', 
    return_fig=True
)

# Display pocket-wise PSDs
fig_pocket_psds.show()

sample_points, pore_sizes, sample_point_labels = mgr.compute_pore_sizes_pocketwise_rust(
